Nahum Sokolow

[Essay — personalities.] (On his stay in Poland)
Not a politician and leader of ordinary scale, but a statesman, a first-rank diplomat, endowed with the ability and deserving the honour to represent the reviving Jewish people in the arena of world politics, one[?] who can maintain relations with international rulers and diplomats.
Jewish national politics, which counts its years from Theodor Herzl on, is still too young to have already reared and supplied us with suitable representatives in sufficient number. And even the few whom we do have in our ranks came to us from outside. They are therefore European Jewish politicians who serve our cause; he, however, is the only one who grew up in the homely folk atmosphere and has[?] made his glorious path of development, deeply steeped in the folk spirit — and hence[?] the people's deepest and legendary reverence for him.
Theodor Herzl perhaps did not influence the psyche of the Jewish masses so much with his ideal of revival. What stirred the popular imagination more were his audiences with kings and world rulers, and their calling him the Jewish prince. That brought a smile[?] to the humbled[?] Jewish spirit. Since then we have gone through much. Our place in the world is far more respected. Our representatives have contact with the world's powers, but still close to the people's heart is the majestic figure whom one longs to call: Excellency... who is received at royal courts, in the palaces of state presidents, with honour and splendour, as representative of the Jewish people.
And now the journalistic giant, the veteran of the Hebrew press in Poland, the pioneer of modern Jewish publicism. A whole generation was brought up on his witty writing. No one will be able to boast of such an enthusiastic reading public, which literally swallows every word — and that so many years ago.. How much profundity and specifically Jewish shrewdness his articles and feuilletons contained! With how much humour and at the same time polished style they were written! Popular and arbiter elegantiarum at once. And above all his spirit bubbled[?]; in all fields of journalism his pen was active. And when his duty to the people called him away abroad, we see what became of the Hebrew press.
Already then, as spokesman and educator, legends were spun around his name in the Jewish shtetls of Poland. He himself once told of a watchmaker who came specially to Warsaw from the far provinces and stood a whole day in a house on Mariańska Street in order to have the privilege of seeing him himself, him himself...
And amid his ceaseless political activity, his constant travelling among all kinds of scattered Jewish settlements to awaken the people, his frequent visits to kings and ministers, he still finds time to immerse himself in Baruch Spinoza and his generation, to penetrate the mystically veiled life of the Marranos in Spain. Here he is a scholar of great[?] erudition, of broad scope, the Jewish genius of keen mind and vast learning.
And few now know — perhaps old Hebrew readers remember — that the poetic Shekhinah also rested upon him: in the "HaAsif" almanacs he made his debut with some poems, and here too his talent proved itself of no average measure. A poet by the grace of God. But the great mind conquered the great heart and he abandoned his poetic talent; yet the poetic spirit is poured out over his whole personality, over his writing and speaking, over his movements and manners.
What especially distinguishes his personality is also his traditional cult — the great Talmudic scholar, known in our old literature no less than certain famous rabbinic authorities, the author of "LiMranan veRabanan"...
———
Yes, if each of the talents mentioned were possessed separately by one person, he too would be a genius; but all this is concentrated in one man, all of it together. And that is: Nahum Sokolow.
Nahum Sokolow — the majestic diplomat, the journalistic eagle, the scholarly keen and learned mind, the talented poet and the great gaon and Talmudic scholar.
Proud is Polish Jewry of its great son.
Y. Y.

Over 200 zł. a bridegroom runs away from the chuppah.
On Sunday an unheard-of incident happened here.
Some time ago the local girl Hela Hakman became engaged (the tenoim were written) to Mr. Yitskhok Wielgus of Pilica, and because the bride's side was unable to deposit the whole dowry, it was agreed that the rest of the dowry would be paid before the wedding. The groom agreed to this, and on Sunday the wedding was celebrated, but when it was time to go to the chuppah the groom vanished[?]. After a long search the „gem“ was found at a neighbour's, and he declared categorically that if he were not given an extra 500 zł. he would not go to the chuppah... After the negotiations which the in-laws conducted with him, he gave „the last word“: for less than 200 zł. he would not go. The bride, learning of the „tactics“ of her intended, had spasms[?] and fainted; after being revived she falls asleep, and in the middle of her sleep she begins to scream in wild voices that her late father had come to her and promised to take revenge on the groom.
When the groom hears this he becomes „softer“, and only at 12 at night does he go to the chuppah. But the tragicomic story does not end here: the next day the wedding of the groom's sister to the bride's brother took place, and the latter, out of revenge, refused to go to the chuppah until he was given an additional 500 zł. of dowry..

The Jewish "Self-Governments"

(What do we do here, and what not? — How do we here overlook urgent help?)
Once upon a time a mentally ill person was a rarity, a "precious find". Every town had, as people used to say, its own madman; there was one in a town, and that was enough. That [?] has changed. Now the illness has spread and "become popular", so that in Zagłębie we already find dozens of madmen. At the same time one must not forget that we see only those who appear in the streets, those who run about; but there is also a fairly large number of hidden mentally ill people whom we do not notice at all.
While they were still few in number, the magistrates [municipalities] in Zagłębie dealt with them; they provided the sick with hospitals, and a large number were indeed cured of their illness.
But since the illness began to make progress, since "progress" began to become popular, the magistrates have lagged behind, and we come across a great many mentally ill people.
We do not know how it is: whether the magistrates cannot or will not help the unfortunates — but it is a fact that the question is not being solved, and one has no choice but to deal with it.
One must admit that the Jewish mentally ill form a large proportion; it would therefore be a matter of great justice to take up the question seriously. But what is to be done? How can the problem be solved? Who can deal with the matter? How can one be freed from this calamity? Well, if we had rich, firmly rooted hospital institutions, we would say that such a department must be set up in such an institution; unfortunately, however, we cannot even dream of [?] such things. We are so poor and broken; our institutions stand, after all, on chicken legs, so that to knock them over one needs no storm wind — the slightest rustle is enough to reduce them to a heap of ruins; so we cannot even dream of such help being provided in our institutions.
But what is to be done? How can one allow the illness to keep progressing like this while we put up no resistance to it? Surely we must see to healing the sick and not let things be brought to an ever worse state.
True, we have our kehilla administrations, which draw up quarter-million budgets and even have the right to collect them by compulsion. Well, had these been our local parliaments, as people once dreamed, one could rightly have placed such a duty on such an institution, which would have dared to regard it as a sacred duty that such a question could be solved through it.
Unfortunately these institutions have become caricatures in the true sense of the word. The Jewish kehillot have, regrettably, become institutions that give the population nothing; they know nothing more than to draw up the annual budget, and as soon as that is done there is time until, a year later, they draw up the next budget again. That is what the "activity" of our Jewish kehillot consists of.
An exception is Sosnowiec. There, to this very day, they know how to give free medical help to everyone who needs it, and, as we know, this item takes up quite an honourable place in the budget. Of course, in this state of ruin the old tradition is to be welcomed. The "Gemilut Chasadim" [interest-free loan] fund is also administered by the Jewish kehilla to this day. On the other hand, in towns such as Dąbrowa, Zawiercie and Będzin nothing at all is done.
Będzin, which draws up the largest annual budget of all the towns in Zagłębie, does not lift a finger [lit. does not put its hand into cold water]; it gives the town nothing, it maintains no institution whatsoever. Its only work consists in drawing up bigger budgets from year to year, so that the members are ever more heavily burdened, at a time when nobody gets anything from the institution.
True, it enters subventions for various institutions [in the budget], and that is all; but one must not forget that most of the subsidies, incidentally, are never paid out; so what is the use of handing out subsidies like Sabbath fruit — better to strike them all out and reduce the budget.
What is the point of turning such a big wheel when nobody gains anything by it and the town is being fleeced.
What does matter is that all the Jewish kehillot in Zagłębie should not forget to put larger sums into the current budget for rescuing the mentally ill. However broken our kehilla administrations may be, however indifferent and apathetic their attitude to Jewish troubles and suffering, they must not remain indifferent to this terrible disease, which strolls about freely in all the towns of Zagłębie while there is no one to take pity on them.
If our magistrates do not have the means to root out mental illnesses, our Jewish kehillot, renowned since olden times as "merciful sons of the merciful", must not for that reason stand aside.
Our kehilla administrations, which do nothing and stand aside with enormous apathy, must now no longer remain indifferent to this disease.
There is no one [?] to turn [?] to for help. It does not belong at all to some particular enterprise, which incidentally does not have the means to do as much as our Jewish kehilla administrations, which have the power to tax the citizens compulsorily. The Jewish kehilla is the only institution that has such power, and we therefore have the right to demand that it take such an undertaking under its authority.
Let our representatives in the Jewish kehillot of Zagłębie stop and consider this question; let them examine the matter seriously and with full attention — they will then surely come to the conviction that they are the only ones entitled to deal with this painful question, which keeps growing from year to year and to which we must not remain indifferent.
Our mentally ill — if they are not rescued by the municipal self-governments, they must be rescued by the Jewish self-governments, in which [people] take part as representatives of our Jewish kehillot.
Let our kehilla trustees not regard the matter as a trifle, for the help is necessary, the help is urgent.
Selekt.
I'm Looking for a Table. Troubles of a Modern Man.

[Feuilleton — New Year satire.] By Y. Oberżanek.
Geyn[?]!
It's unbearable!
It's bitter!
It's nasty[?]!
Why is it nasty? Why is it bitter? Because it's hard to become „postępowe“ [Polish: progressive] all at once.
What do you know of the peppered[?] troubles a Jew who is a „postępowiec“ [a progressive] has to endure! Go and do it in your old years, when you already stand with one foot on the other side of the rogatka [city toll-gate, i.e. at the grave's edge], when the cemetery flowers are already [sprouting?] out of your head, when your head is spun round with all kinds of troubles and blows, when half a dozen grown-up daughters, ripe for the wedding canopy, are turning about the house, when every day another child is sent home from school for not paying the tuition fee. In such a „situation“ I became a „postępowiec“ — a modern man, it's called. The long [?] beard shaved off into a „łopatka“ [spade shape], the hair cut into a „jeż“ [hedgehog crop], the [chopped?] „jupica“ [long Jewish coat] cut off by half, and out sprang a frock coat; round the neck a „chomąto“ [horse collar] tied with a necktie. Every morning I must wash with scented soap, the gaiters must be polished to a shine. Henekh Leyzer has been turned into Henryk Leopold; instead of going to the shtibl for melave-malke, one must go dancing at the „dancing“; instead of studying a page of Gemara, I must go to a „poranek“ [morning party]. And now the „ladies' honour“ — may no good Jew ever know it, sweet Father! Oh, listen, the „ladies' honour“ is quite a job: you see a woman going to put on her coat — you must stand there like a veritable[?] lackey and help her into it. Oh, what kind of relative am I to a strange woman? In which Shulchan Arukh is it written that I must help her put on her coat? That I must be her lackey? Why not the other way round? The excuse is — ladies' honours.
If, God forbid, you go out of the door before the lady, you have broken a prohibition. Is it possible? How can one go out before the lady, where is [the shame?] and the ladies' honour?..
You get on a tram or on the train, you're sitting and a woman comes in — you must, begging your pardon, get up and politely give up your seat to the woman, and you yourself are not too sick to stand on your weak, sick feet.
Oh, where does it come from that I have to yield my seat to the woman with healthy feet and get swollen feet myself? Why shouldn't it be the other way round? After all I am also some kind of a „Mannsperson“ [male person], to all the devils!
But talk this way, talk that way — that's how it is! Once you're a „postępowiec“, man[?], you must, willy-nilly, bite your lips and keep quiet. Whether you want to or not, you must make the gesture of politeness, for you are, after all, a „postępowiec“!
Well, all year one gets by somehow, as you say: one gets used to the troubles; but you see, when the carnival comes my skin trembles. A trifle: weeks and months going about in a frock coat with the stiff white shirt, and on top of it whole nights without shutting an eye. Today a masked ball, tomorrow a dancing, a five o'clock, or simply some charity dance, and such charity dances, thank God, are not lacking in Zagłębie. Once „Dobroczynność“ [the charity society], once „WIZO“[?], „Kasa Chorych“ [the sick fund], „Komitet Szpitalny“ [the hospital committee]. One must go everywhere, everywhere one must do one's duty. At every ball one must go for a little dance; the eyes stick shut and the feet tremble. Well, how can one endure such troubles?
As every year at this time, my wife already at Hanukkah began preparing for the carnival. She held „narady“ [consultations] on how to celebrate holy Sylvester; whole days she pondered how to outdo her „koleżanki“ [lady friends] with her toilette. Whole days she studied the newest Parisian fashion[?] magazines, and finally, at the sixth Hanukkah candle, she says to me:
Henekh Leyzer (Henryk Leopold she calls me only when people can hear..), do you at least know that the carnival is coming?
When I heard the word „carnival“, black wheels began to run before my eyes; I understood that this would come out of my pocket, my head and above all: my feet... Yes, I say, of course I know, the calendar tells me so; I know that a quarter's rent is approaching, that by the first one has to buy out a trade licence [patent], that on the first a whole gang of bills of exchange fall due — of course, I say, I know the first is approaching, oh, do I know!..
Again with his bills! my wife flares up, what do I care about your business, your rent, your „podatki“ [taxes], your licences. A „postępowa“ woman does not meddle in any business, you understand, Henekh Leyzer, I don't want to know anything, did you hear or not?
I don't understand, I say to her, today is only Hanukkah and you're already talking about the carnival?
Is that so? — only then did she come out with her „ober-tse“[?]. And when will I have my carnival costume „poprawić“ [altered]? Maybe on the eve of the carnival? And when will I order the „golkh-kalishaukes“[?]? And a white frock coat, when will I buy it? I hate, she stamps her feet, waiting till the last minute!..
Well, all right, I began to calm her down; but if you start today, will you at least be ready by the carnival?
Not to sin with words, she goes on, the others — Gutshe the baker's wife already has a brand-new „domino“ lying ready, Chava Gitl, the [?] shoemaker's wife, has an elegant Chinese costume, even Zelde the fishwife already has a „cudowna“ [wonderful] „rusałka“ [water-nymph costume] lying in the wardrobe. And he, the robber, the cold lung and liver, tells me: taxes, licence, rent and other [nonsense?], things a „modern mężatka“ [married woman] need not know about.
Who won? Probably she — who else, me? What she did — may I know as little of evil. A woman's carnival costume, she says, must be a „niespodzianka“ [surprise] for the husband — as long as she leaves my head in peace.
This Tuesday, 31 December that is, I ran around with a bleeding head. Where does one snatch an interest-free loan to buy out the licence? On the second of January, writes a Zaglembier Tsaytung, there will be inspections. With great trouble I bought out the licence and a stone fell from my heart.
I came home tired, [worn out?] from a whole day of running around; as soon as I opened the door my wife asks me:
Henrykl (so she calls me when she is in a good mood), have you settled it already?
Yes, I say, with great trouble.
Health into your bones! she falls upon me. I know you are a man with sense; what, should we make ourselves a laughing-stock — others yes and this one not!
But you know, I say, how hard it was for me — full of fears.
What's the difference, my wife answers, as long as you already have it, and may your enemies burst.
In the evening I come home. My wife stands decked out like a princess, with spangles and little stones of „gold“ and „silver“; she shines like a menorah.
What is this? I stand there bewildered. What celebration is there today?
What do you mean? she opens a pair of eyes at me; well, she says, for Sylvester!
Sylvester? The whole business had gone out of my head. Why, I say, didn't you remind me during the day?
Are you mad or out of your mind? she flares up like a candle; you said yourself today that it was hard for you, but that you already have a table.
A table? Did I say anything about a table?
Didn't you say that you already have it? Whom are you going to [fool?]?
True, I said I already have it, but not a table.
What then?
A licence, a licence for the new year 1930!
What happened afterwards — forgive me; that[?] one whole plate of the new dinner set remained was nothing short of a miracle; and after the scene she made me, I had, to our shame, to take out the frock coat with the patent-leather shoes, and we went off to [Katowice?] to look for a table.
We ran from one restaurant to another; everywhere it was crowded like flies, it buzzed like in beehives, everywhere occupied — not a single table to be had for love or money.
What was the end? The end was a sad one: after a three-hour „emigration“ we went home without a table..
Now my wife lies ill; that same night, poor thing, from great vexation she had a „napad“ [attack]; doctors come and go, one doctor says: gallstones, a second wise man says: kidneys[?], and I know the real secret: — a table!..
Hard, I say, very hard to be a „postępowiec“! Especially for a Jew who already stands with one foot on the other side of the rogatka.
Orientation, Consciousness. (The Chaos among the Jewish Town Councillors. — Where Are They Heading?)

[Będzin — town council.] Eight days ago we discussed the activity of the Będzin [Bendin] municipal self-government; we dwelt on the failures we have there in plenty, even though we Jews are so well represented there and our group ought to have been reckoned with, even if with its votes it cannot push through what it needs, what it must have for its day-to-day life, for its everyday needs.
Were the Christian councillors of the town administration tolerant enough towards their Jewish colleagues, they would surely have had to understand that one must reckon with half the members of a municipal self-government; one must reckon with their sorrows and joys, with their demands and needs, even if they cannot push anything through on their own. Their Jewish colleagues, for their part, do understand this: when it concerns a matter that really is rational, our representatives do vote for it, and then the Jews do not take into account that without their votes they [the Christians] would not carry the important measure.
And since the Jews never offer any resistance, the Christian colleagues think it must be so, and therefore they have to get the better of[?] their Jewish colleagues by doing everything contrary to what the Jews want, or to what local conditions and civic duties demand.
We have a saying: "Too good is half foolish." It can be applied perfectly to our self-government. In drawing up the budget, care is taken that the revenues come mainly from Jewish sources, whereas in expenditure the Jews at best get a little bone tossed to them..
The Christian councillors see this very well: our representatives agree to everything for the sake of peace; they, on the other hand, think it must be so, and therefore they get carried away more and more each time.
In this case the situation becomes serious, and it would be only right to look at everything with open eyes and with a clear mind: first of all it is necessary that unity and oneness should reign in the Jewish camp. But it is easy to say "unity and oneness" when our councillors would first have needed a kind of school where people could learn to find their bearings, to be conscious, to look at a question with a clear eye and with lucidity of understanding; only then can one begin to speak of unity and oneness. But as long as the sense of orientation of the moment is missing, there can be no talk of unity and oneness.
Why fool ourselves: how many times have proposals in favour of the Jewish population failed thanks to the fact that our councillors did not find their bearings, and many of them did not understand at all what was at stake and therefore did not know how to vote. This is not just talk — these are facts that happened. And how often is a quorum not provided when important questions are at issue, and then the result is failures that weigh heavily on the shoulders of the Jewish people.
So why should we demand[?] unity and oneness from these people when what is more needed is a school where they would first of all learn the elementary political ABC, and afterwards one could climb one step higher.
It goes without saying that for this purpose the concentration of the Jewish councillors is very, very useful. We have always sympathised with the same standpoint: that a Jewish club must be created, a kind of local "Koło" [caucus], where the councillors would be schooled to a certain extent and, above all, be prepared before every session, so that on arriving at the session they would already know what is at stake and be oriented as to what position to take on the question put forward.
Such a club, despite its first-class necessity, we did not manage to realise. Now such a club has indeed come into being, but unfortunately not all the councillors have joined it, which is truly a pity.
This concentration should have been heartily welcomed, because there are now many councillors who, as said, need first of all a school of political education where one would begin teaching them from the letter alef.
There are, after all, representatives in the present Będzin town council who are not only crossing the threshold of economic management for the first time, but who have in general stood far from any public life and do not know "how to go in and how to go out" — so what can one demand of such "nowobrańcy" (raw recruits)? They absolutely must go through some kind of political school, and only then will they begin to grasp that they understand so little and still know almost nothing.
We often blush with shame as we watch people sitting in the town council who have no idea at all what they were sent there for and what they should demand there.
That is about those who know nothing. Besides them, however, there are those who do know what they came into the town council for, but unfortunately either they keep their mouths shut [lit. take a mouthful of water] and are not heard at all, or they start quarrelling for all they are worth, so that we blush with shame.
And we now have yet another category of representatives, who take[?] the whole economic activity lightly and do not come to the sessions. It goes without saying that this is an unheard-of offence, which must not be tolerated. As soon as a representative has taken upon himself the mission of representing [us] in the municipal self-government, he is obliged to fulfil his mission completely; otherwise he harms Jewish civic interests, which depend on every single Jewish vote.
It must no longer be allowed that disharmony should reign among the Jewish councillors at the sessions; this causes us enormous shame and pain and harms our interests.
A sacred duty lies upon the Jewish councillors to concentrate into one mighty, strong and useful force, where they would learn to handle questions with full consciousness, and know how to react to injustices and fight to ease and improve the interests of the citizens who sent them there.
R. Let.
Nachmanides — Pioneer of the Jewish Settlement in the Land of Israel

By Leon[?] Szpajer.
IV.
Nachmanides in the Land of Israel.
Nachmanides' view that the Land of Israel cannot be made fruitful[?] by any people but the Jews. — Nachmanides sets to work. — He restores a synagogue and creates a centre; he founds a great yeshiva. — The large Jewish communities of Damascus and Aram Tzova [Aleppo] as a reservoir for aliyah to the Land of Israel. — Nachmanides' commentary on the Torah written in the Land of Israel. — Nachmanides collects curiosities of the Land of Israel. — A coin with an ancient Hebrew inscription. — Nachmanides' kabbalistic studies in the Land of Israel. — The death of Nachmanides in the year 1270. — Where is his grave?

At first Nachmanides is enraptured[?], and it pains him to see how desolate it is[?], while there is such wealth in the land, which the Christians and Mohammedans who inhabit it enjoy in such abundance. Nachmanides falls on his face and weeps. But he soon consoles himself: Jerusalem, Jerusalem! You are like a nursing woman who has an only, pampered child. If the child falls ill and cannot nurse "for the time being", the faithful mother fears that during the child's illness her breasts will dry up, and when the little child recovers it will have no milk from its mother — so she goes and takes a strange child to nurse temporarily, until her own child recovers and nurses again at its mother's breast...¹) As he writes: "My mother (Jerusalem) is likened to a nursing woman[?] whose child has died in her lap, and the milk in her breasts pains her; she goes and suckles young puppies"...²) But they, the strangers, are[?] not worthy of you, Jerusalem, and you too are not suited to them; and therefore, despite your natural wealth, your foreign inhabitants are poor, because God once said: "I will bring the land into desolation, and your enemies which dwell therein shall be astonished at it"³). This refusal of the land to yield to any other nation whatsoever Nachmanides regards as a prophecy that the land does not want to accept our enemies, and this is the most solemn declaration that the land is ours alone. "For you will not find in the whole inhabited world a land that is good and broad, that was always inhabited, and is now so desolate; and since the time we left it, it has not accepted any nation. All try to settle it and they do not succeed"⁴).
And this very argument of Nachmanides is used by Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev, who proclaims, holy and certain: the Land of Israel is ours and cannot be settled by strangers⁵).
But Nachmanides sees that there is no time for idle musings, and he sets to work at once with the fire and energy of a young man. He was already at the end of his life, standing at the edge of the grave.
On the third day after his arrival he travels straight to Hebron to choose himself a grave — and yet he is possessed by a young[sic: "yuggen"] enterprising spirit that works wonders. Among the many ruins abandoned to whoever would take them he finds a house built on marble pillars with a beautiful vaulted roof, and consecrates it as a synagogue, thereby creating a centre, a point of concentration, which the synagogue has always been for Jews. From the few Jewish inhabitants he takes money and has the synagogue repaired. To Shechem he sends for the Jerusalem Torah scrolls, which had been taken there at the time of the Tatar invasion. He also builds a house of study, which is called by his name: the Midrash of Nachmanides.⁶)
In Damascus there was then a respected and numerous Jewish community. The traveller R' Petachiah of Regensburg found there in the year 1175 some ten thousand Jewish souls. R' Benjamin of Tudela[?] also tells of three thousand Jewish families. The well-known poet Judah al-Harizi, who visited Syria at the beginning of the 13th century, found in Damascus many Jewish scholars and poets who played a great role — culturally as well as financially — in the country. They were co-builders of Arabic literature, like the great doctor of medicine Rav Moshe ibn Tzedakah, who frequented the imperial court a great deal. In Aram Tzova too, the capital of Syria, there was a fine Jewish community that produced many great men, such as the scholar R' Joseph ben Judah ibn Aknin, a devoted disciple of Maimonides, to whom he dedicated his grandiose work "The Guide for the Perplexed"⁷).
This Syria, the neighbouring country, was a reservoir for Jewish emigration to the Land of Israel. Nachmanides founds a yeshiva which in time became a spiritual centre of the whole East. And now masses of students begin to come from all the neighbouring countries, wishing to study Torah and secular studies with this brilliant great man of Israel, and so the Land of Israel is revived; soon communities are already being founded there, and the Land of Israel awakens.
Nachmanides feels overjoyed; he is refreshed as in his youth. In the Land of Israel he writes his commentary on the Torah⁸), which is his crowning work, his "crown jewel". In this work he sums up all the thoughts and views he arrived at in his long life, rich in spirit. We find there a fusion of Kabbalah, philosophy, knowledge of language and all sorts of sciences. And wherever the subject leads him merely to speak of the Land of Israel, he gives expression to his warm feelings for the fatherland, its high significance and holiness⁹).
With careful love Nachmanides also investigates all kinds of curiosities, of which there are plenty in the Land of Israel. He is beside himself with joy when he finds in Akko, among the old people, a silver[?] engraved coin, on one side of which an almond branch in the form of a staff is incised, and on the other side — a small jar; around it an illegible script is written. Nachmanides is greatly interested in the mysterious language, and after various investigations it turns out that this is the ancient Hebrew script which the Cutheans [Samaritans] could still read¹⁰). The Cutheans indeed explained the inscriptions to him, which meant "Shekel of Shekels" and "Jerusalem the Holy"; they also explained that the almond staff symbolises Aaron's rod¹¹) and the jar — the jar of manna¹²).
In the Land of Israel Nachmanides devoted himself much to Kabbalah, and his disciple-companion Rav Isaac of Akko was entirely engrossed in Kabbalah and devoted himself much to practical Kabbalah¹³). He also composed a commentary on Nachmanides' Torah commentary, with kabbalistic content¹⁴). How much Nachmanides' creative period in the Land of Israel was connected with Kabbalah can be seen from the legend that the Zohar, which was discovered so mysteriously in those years, was — some wish to claim — sent by Nachmanides from the Land of Israel¹⁵).
But it was not his lot to live long in his beloved fatherland, to further develop his creative building activity and to go on spinning the kabbalistic web[?]. Three years after his arrival in the country — in the year 1270 (5030) — he breathes out his holy soul and is buried — according to one legend — in Hebron, beside the Cave of Machpelah, in the very grave he had chosen for himself while still alive¹⁶). According to another claim his grave is in Akko at the foot of a hill¹⁷), and there is also a legend that he lies buried in Jerusalem below the hill near the village of Silwan¹⁸).

Adieu 1929, Vivat 1930!

(Political review).
Two days ago we escorted the old year to its eternal rest, and we took leave of it in these words: „Adieu, you old greybeard! Rest assured that you will at once be forgotten in our memory! But recorded[?] your name will remain in history, where you will be judged to your disgrace and very rarely to your praise. We wish ourselves — never to see you again!...“
Quite differently did we greet and receive the year 1930, which brings with it — so we believe — happiness and contentment. We welcomed the new year with timbrels and dances, with dancing, song and music. All the places of entertainment, theatres, cafés (kawiarnie) were stormed on the night of 31 December to 1 January by people who, in holiday clothes and trembling with joy, awaited the new, bright and innocent year. Although several days have already passed since New Year's Eve (Sylvester night), the mighty sounds still ring in my ears that burst spontaneously from thousands upon thousands of mouths: „Wiwat, Nowy Roku!“ [„Long live the New Year!“]
Not for nothing did we celebrate the New Year with such joy, ecstasy and enthusiasm; not for nothing did people kiss in the streets in its honour at midnight, and not in vain did they douse themselves with champagne and liqueur. What is the rejoicing about? Because we have at last freed ourselves from the old year, which was a hard year for tormented and exhausted mankind. Just consider what kind of a year we have behind us: government crises, political stagnation, bloodshed, revolutions, wars, dictatorship, the naked sword — in short, a year over which hovered the spectre of a new war. Was not our blessing justified: bon voyage to you, 1929?.. Is not the warm reception of 1930 understandable, since we hope that at long last the eternal war will cease, the eternal hatred between nations, that at last true peace will arise, for which we have longed and yearned so much since 1914?..
Peace, disarmament, arbitration, evacuation, armistice and other such fine words did not leave the lips of our statesmen throughout a full 12 months. Everywhere, far and near, east and west, one hears: bring peace! To tell the truth, people did try to „catch“ peace: they conferred, negotiated, deliberated[?], and enemies who yesterday could not sit at one table today stretched out their hands to one another in order to find mutual understanding. In The Hague, Washington, Geneva and other places politicians gathered who hold in their hands the fate of the world, planning to throw weapons onto the scrap heap, into the arsenal, dreaming of introducing, instead of fist and sword — an idyllic life, a life built on integrity, justice, peace and truth, just as in the future prophetic times of „And it shall come to pass in the end of days“...
In Europe people dreamed of creating, on the model of Columbus's land, „United States of Europe“, a Pan-Europe, where hitherto quarrelling nations, such as Russia and Italy, Germany and France, Poland and Lithuania, would sit at one green table, just as in the Rosh Hashanah prayers: „And they shall all form one band“...
MacDonald, the English Premier, who won a victory in the last parliamentary elections, took up his walking stick and set off across the ocean to America, where there was talk of reducing navies and warships. In Washington the gentleman from „Europe“ was received with great pomp, as in his time was Amanullah, the Afghan leader. In Western Europe and in the presidential „White House“ the conclusion was reached that this very month of January a „water conference“ [naval conference] should take place, at which the building of armoured ships would be limited...
In order to preserve peace, efforts were made to remove all obstacles and difficulties that hold back the world's redemption. Germany, which had grievances against the Treaty of Versailles, which set the occupation of the Rhineland at 15 years, was satisfied, and some months ago the clearing of English and Belgian troops from the Rhineland took place. The occupation fortifications[?] were taken down, Germany regained the independence of the Rhine[?] region, and once again there echoed: „Deutschland, Deutschland über alles“...
Seeing the great efforts that are being made to achieve peace, and believing innocently in their sincerity, I rejoiced greatly and thought at that moment: Praised be You, Almighty! The glorious era of „The wolf shall dwell with the lamb“ is coming; let us say Hallel, this is the day we have hoped for! At last mankind will be able to live in peace without fear of a future war...
But barely twenty-four hours passed, and my idyllic fantasy came to an end. In the newspaper, in which I expect to find dispatches and reports about the coexistence of nations, about the brotherhood of men — I am told in Kiddush-Levanah letters [i.e. in huge type] that Chang Hsi-liang [Zhang Xueliang], the ruler of Manchuria, has grievances against Russia's Foreign Minister, Litvinov, over the Chinese Eastern Railway, that Russia is waging a little war with the Chinese, that in the East human blood is being shed. True, wishing to avoid new world cataclysms, all disputes are being settled and liquidated peacefully, with appeal to the „Locarno agreement“ and the „Kellogg Pact“; and yet new means of warfare are being created in laboratories, tanks and warships are being dispatched to the English colonies, gas factories are being built in Germany, fortresses are being improved[?] in France, and new military camps are being mobilised in Italy. „Peace, peace and peace“!
A chapter of its own is the little political world here at home in Poland. Here it is homely, lively and it boils as in a cauldron. Although outwardly Poland has grown stronger, playing an important role in international politics, having freed itself from Lithuania's dethroned Voldemaras, who sharpened the sword and provoked us and who is — so we hear — soon going to serve a term of exile, the situation internally, within the camp, is anything but stable. Government crises, parliamentary battles, votes of no confidence, polemical press articles do not leave our agenda. The constant struggle between the governments and the Sejm, which has been waged since the May events [the May 1926 coup], may lead to quite undesirable results and may cause the decline of young Polish parliamentarism and the rule of the strong hand.
On the threshold of the new year we had in Poland a government crisis, caused by a vote of no confidence of the Sejm opposition in Mr. Świtalski's cabinet, and the new cabinet formed by the new Premier, Mr. Bartel, is still unknown to us by any deeds for the welfare of all Polish citizens without exception.
— We receive you worthily, 1930. And although we are disappointed in our hopes year after year — we are nonetheless full of faith and trust that you will at last bring mankind and us Jews redemption and deliverance.
M. Hampel.
Be Strong!

(Dedicated to the Maccabeans of today)
By M. Giler.
I see you —
you stand bent up to the loins,
sunk in life-threatening swamps,
where for generations no human foot has trod,
where for generations a wailing of wild jackals
tears the desert void to pieces
and strikes even terror, a trembling at the heart —
O dear, beloved Jewish children!
I see you!
You are like soldiers loaded
with steel, iron tools of labour,
sleeves rolled up, hearts aflame,
with hard and stiff sunburnt faces,
with eyes that speak of courage and stubbornness,
of the will and striving to be the redeemers,
liberators of ruined Zion!..
And hammers rise and spades rise
and there carries, there races ever higher and higher
a resounding echo of scythes and sickles
mixed with the voices of human breasts,
that ring through space like a holy song:
— We build, we create, we bring back to life
the distant, bygone Jewish past!...
And I tell you:
there rises from thousands of hearts,
from old, from young, from free-thinking, from pious,
a warm prayer, a heartfelt blessing,
and cuts its way into the glowing desert
and reaches you like a heavenly voice (bat kol) from the sky,
which cheers, which wakes and uplifts the soul:
— May your hands be strong, may your hands be strong!!!

A Little Letter from Zakopane

My dearest Szymsze Berele!
You did quite well, Szymszele Kron, not to come to Zakopane for New Year's Eve (Sylwester), because I partied a whole night, and the law is, after all, "one does not mix one joy with another"... (one doesn't mix one celebration with another celebration).
Szymszeleshku! Quite a thing went on here at the Sylwester holiday. And who do you think celebrated the holy Sylwester? Suffice it that I tell you a secret: at the whole holiday there was in total one gentile — the hall's usher (woźny). All the guests were "starozakonni" [old-law people, i.e. Jews], the whole cream (śmietanka) of the Sandoszewer[?] street, one and all. And who do you think was the chief in-law, the tone-setter of the Sylwester night? None other than your friend (przyjaciel) Getzel Hambergrik[?]: this very Hambergrik gave the ball a true Jewish character. When the clock showed 12 midnight he gave a command — "Turn down the lamps"! Not for one minute, as the gentiles are wont to do, but it was dark a whole hour, so that the joy should be complete..
Szymszele Kron! I can't write out for you everything — what a "zabawa" (party) it was in the darkness: the squealing and the shouting went up to the seventh heaven, people fell one on top of the other, and, needless to say, many shirt-fronts[?] (menushatkes) got crumpled[?].
The same to hear from you for ever and ever.
From me, your faithful wife
Yente Tsipe.

He waited in vain for his wife to come back to him.

(From the series "Stories that happen")
Heniek B. was such a dashing young fellow that all the Sosnowiec girls swooned over him, and when he invited a girl to a foxtrot at the "Lokarno", her girlfriends wished out of envy that the heel of her shoe would break while she danced.
Heniek lived the good life and spent merry nights, but his turn came too. At a "five o'clock" in Częstochowa he happened to meet a pretty young girl, and when he came home a few days later his "golden" pals simply did not recognise him: where had Heniek's humour vanished to? Heniek began to show up more rarely at the "Lokarno", and it soon came to the point that people stopped counting him among the "golden" ones.
But Heniek knew where the shoe pinched. He prevailed on his father to send him to Częstochowa on business for a longer time. Having spent a couple of months in Częstochowa, one fine day he came home from Częstochowa — but not alone: accompanied by a young lady whom he introduced to his parents as his wife. The parents were even a little offended that he had married without them and thus presented them with a fait accompli, but what won't one do for a beloved son — the parents forgave him and took the pretty young daughter-in-law to their hearts.
Heniek settled with his wife in Katowice, and there something happened to him that often happens to the golden youth. At some masked ball Heniek flirted with a mask so far that he came home when it was already broad daylight. The young wife did not reproach him at all, but that same evening she left, leaving no address.
At first Heniek reckoned she had gone to her parents, so he set off for Częstochowa to make it up with her there and bring her home. But to his surprise he did not find her in Częstochowa, and he understood that he had been caught out, and that his wife's departure was something more than a whim.
So he came back to Katowice, and day after day, week after week went by. Heniek became unrecognisable, when suddenly he learned that his wife was living in Warsaw — and not alone, at that, but with her lover, an acquaintance from her girlhood years. He went to Warsaw to look for his wife and win her back. Several days passed before he found her [and] was able to approach her in order to talk things over.
"My present husband," his wife explained to him, "loved me for years, but I did not accept his marriage proposal because I had met you. But since you have betrayed me, I do not want to know you any more." With these words she left him. No explanations, no pleas for forgiveness helped; her decision was firm.
But Heniek did not give up: in Warsaw he rented an elegant room for her on Przejazd, had a telephone installed, paid for the room in advance, and left the key of the room with the landlady, telling her to give the key to a lady if she should ask about him, about Heniek. Heniek wrote his wife a letter asking her to return to him and meanwhile to occupy the room on Przejazd.
Every day at 4 in the afternoon Heniek rang, hoping someone might answer. But in vain. The telephone bell rang lonely in the empty room, and nobody lifted the receiver, nobody answered. Heniek aged from his troubles, and grey hairs appeared on the temples of the young man of twenty-odd..
These days he learned that his former wife had given birth to a boy. Now he sees that he has nothing more to wait for.

[Będzin — Religious education.] For several weeks now order has begun to be introduced in the Talmud Torah. The new committee, headed by Mr. M. Dafner[?], found the institution in a state of chaos [tohu va-vohu] in the full sense of the word. Passengers want train tickets and the cashier is asleep...

[Będzin — Railway, incident.] On the night from Tuesday to Wednesday, when passengers came to the station to buy tickets for the Kielce train, they found the ticket window closed. Seeing that the time was approaching when the train was due to leave the local station, the passengers alerted the policeman on duty. The latter began knocking at the ticket office, but nobody answered from there. Then several window-panes were broken, through which they got into the ticket office, where they found the cashier lying on the floor. At first there was a suspicion that the cashier was dead, but when they came close to him it became clear that in honour of the holiday he had been making merry and had not spared any cup...

General meeting of the Zionists.

[Będzin — Zionism, Keren Hayesod, KKL.] On Sunday evening the annual general meeting of the Zionist Organisation took place in its own premises.
The meeting aroused great interest; members came in a number rarely seen at any general meeting.
Mr. Avraham Hampel opens the meeting with a short introduction and recalls the loss of the leaders Dr. Reich, B. Stawski[?] and the martyrs of the Land of Israel, who are honoured by rising.
The chair is taken by Mr. M. Krakowski; assessors S. Petasz, S. Merin[?]; secretary — L. Rozenblum.
The report on the activity to date is given by Mr. D. Hofer. He gives a survey of the time when the Central Committee nominated the outgoing committee, which took over the leadership under terrible conditions: the organisation then had no premises, numbered a minimal number of members, etc. In the course of 1 year — says Mr. H. — the committee created premises that cost about 6,000 zł., carried out a “Keren Hayesod” campaign crowned with success, recruited 161 members, and in general the committee was active in every field of Zionist work.
The report of the “Keren Hayesod” campaign is given by Mr. Marek Szajn. From the report it is clear that 305 members pledged a sum of about 15 thousand dollars for the “Keren Hayesod”. Payments are proceeding normally and, above all, the bills of exchange are not being protested...
Mr. Szajn also gives a report on the relief campaign for the victims in the Land of Israel. 12.500 zł. was collected.
The report of the “Keren Kayemet” is given by Mr. G. Landger[?]; in the course of the year 5689 Będzin gave 8,000 zł. to the National Fund.
Report of “Tarbut” — Mr. Cymberknop[?], and of the treasury — Mr. Brama[?]. It turns out that in the course of the year the budget reached 11.384 zł. 30 gr., and, most important, there are still some hundreds[?] in the treasury...
After the reports come discussions. Speakers: Herszlewicz, Tenenbaum, Podlinski, Suszek[?] and Zaltman. The last-named proposes that the elections be postponed until peace in the organisation is restored. The proposal is rejected. On the other hand, the proposal of Mr. Tyges-Pulwer[?] to express thanks to the outgoing committee is adopted.

Torah-Scroll Completion Celebrations in Będzin and Sosnowiec

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Religion and Community.] On Sunday the worshippers of the minyan A. G. "Adas Yeshurun" in Będzin celebrated the completion of a Torah scroll; the celebration was arranged with a parade, which aroused wide interest among a large part of the Jewish population of Będzin.
The completion and the whole festivity in general took place in the home of Mr. Israel Majtek, gabbai of the above-mentioned minyan. Sewing the sheets and writing the letters lasted from 3 in the afternoon until 11 at night. A marshalik (jester-MC) with a "potatsnik"[?] calls people up to write letters. An orchestra plays a freylekhs, people dance a little, and the modern wives delight in seeing how their "German" (Western-dressed) husbands rejoice with the Torah.
At 11 o'clock the scroll is carried to the minyan room, which is at Modrzejowska Street 44. In front — decorated lanterns, a brass band of former Jewish pupils, "shterkatsn"[?] [unclear word], then the "bride" (the scroll), led under a wedding canopy and accompanied by many hundreds of people from all strata of the Jewish population, from "Aguda" to the "Bund"... Order was kept by the police.
The premises of "Adas Yeshurun" are already decorated with blue-and-white flags and pennants; every worshipper had his pennant. The rabbi speaks on current affairs and dances with the scroll, cantor Żupowicz says "U-venukho [yomar]", and with the singing of "Hatikvah" the religious ceremony is concluded.
Later a magnificent banquet took place in Mr. Majtek's home, at which the marshalik "rhymed", the cantor sang, and after "ve-ha-shtiya ka-das" (drinking as is proper) everyone took to dancing. The "number" was performed in the European manner...
———
The next day, Monday, the celebration of a Torah-scroll completion was held at the Dąbrowa rebbe's. The sewing and writing of letters took place in the premises of "Linas ha-Kholim" and of the "Mizrachi" school. Taking part were the Admor Szapiro of Będzin, a brother of the rebbe, and rabbis from our surroundings.
At 11 o'clock at night the scroll was carried into the synagogue to the sounds of music, where the appropriate prayers were said, and afterwards the orchestra played "Boże, coś Polskę" and "Hatikvah".

A Man Who Likes to Hold "Quiet Weddings" in Sosnowiec, Będzin, Częstochowa and Wherever Possible

[Łódź and the Region — Society and Crime.] How great the plague of "quiet weddings" (religious-only marriages without civil registration) is in Jewish family life is illustrated by the following story:
A certain Gingold of Olminska[?] Street turned to the Łódź Women's Protection Society and asked it to help him look into the papers so that his daughter could obtain civil records of her religious wedding; at the same time he stated that his young son-in-law is entirely opposed to such records, arguing that a religious wedding is enough.
At the society they answered Mr. Gingold that to arrange the papers the young couple must come in person. A few days later the young man did indeed appear himself. His arguments were: no records are needed, it is hard for him to supply the necessary documents, and as proof he told of his biography — miracles and wonders. As an 8-year-old boy a baron adopted him and raised him like a prince. He had finished several universities, commands several languages, and a misfortune brought him to Łódź.
The whole person seemed very suspicious to the chairwoman of the Women's Protection Society; his manner of conduct and speech showed that the man had finished no university and knows no languages, and although a picture-handsome young man, it was plain that he had not grown up among barons; his personal document showed that he came from a small town near Częstochowa. The Women's Protection Society decided to inquire in his home town who the man was, and the first thread unravelled a whole skein of "good deeds" the "handsome" young man had committed. In every other town he had left a wife with a couple of children, whom he did not acknowledge, because he had arranged "quiet weddings" with them, or [printed "adrer"] he had fiancées. In this way he had secret families in Sosnowiec, Będzin, Lwów, Częstochowa and even in several foreign cities. In Łódź too, besides his official wife with whom he lived, he already had 2 fiancées besides. With the wife in Łódź he had performed the wedding ceremony (chuppah ve-kiddushin) before some synagogue beadle, and he did not fancy legalising[?] his marriage officially with civil records.
The police even ordered the fellow arrested for bigamy, but none of his wives could legally prove that he is her husband, and the wondrously handsome "baron" strolls on, and who knows how many more "quiet weddings" he will hold and how many more brides he will seduce.
Important Resolutions in the Manufactured-Textiles Trade to Revive Commerce

From the manufactured-goods (textiles) section of the Central Merchants' Association we have been asked to print the following communiqué:
The protracted crisis in the manufactured-textiles trade, which has already lasted nearly a year and shows no sign whatever of recovery, has now, because of the approach of the summer season, moved the board of the manufactured-goods section of the Central Merchants' Association in Warsaw to convene a larger conference. The meeting, held last week with the participation of the most respected merchants of all branches of the manufactured-goods trade, was devoted to the question of reviving trade and clearing away the obstacles and causes that have brought the merchant class to its present sad situation.
The conference concluded that the main cause of the ruinous state of affairs is the general psychosis of withdrawing credit that has taken hold of the trade, the harmful phenomenon of people losing trust in one another, and the exaggerated fear of the bill-of-exchange obligation, which has led to the undermining of the foundations of normal trade.
The conference therefore unanimously adopted the following resolutions, binding on all merchants of the trade: 1) to combat with the strongest means the wild and harmful phenomenon of withdrawing credit, and to support with goods on credit all merchants, without exception, who pay their bills of exchange normally.
2) to strive to restore the strained[?] relations between merchant and customer, which should rest on mutual trust. These resolutions were unanimously adopted and signed by all the merchants present, who undertook to put them strictly into practice.
