From the chess tournament.
On Monday the chess tournament for the championship of Zagłębie finally ended. First place was won again by the champion so far, Prof. Zawadzki; the strong favourite Szwajcer lost at the last minute to Goldminc, thus ending half a point behind Zawadzki; Goldminc, on the other hand, who had chances of meeting Zawadzki in the final, lost on the second day to Zylberberg and so lost his chances for the championship, and Zawadzki continues to hold [printed "perdigt"] the champion's title.
This year's tournament limped badly in terms of organisation and discipline; the awarding of points mostly took place at the green table, as some players deserved; one-hundred-percent points were earned by Zawadzki, Jasny and Kimelman.
— On the 18th the qualifying tournament for the class "B" championship and promotion to class "A" begins. In February a cup (puchar) match of the extra class will take place in Zagłębie.
— The Sosnowiec class "A" has been enriched by 2 strong players, Ed.[?] Szperling and Ginder; the first a representative of Kraków, the second — champion of Lyon (France).
Useful Popular Work.

(Hygiene among others and among us. — What remains to be done now?)
In Poland a campaign against tuberculosis is now being carried out. In this connection the Sosnowiec branch of "TOZ" [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population] has undertaken to hold a series of lectures devoted to the disease of tuberculosis, which unfortunately occupies a very honourable place in Poland. Evidently it has been realized that one must begin to combat this dangerous enemy seriously and intensively.
This phenomenon, which the population needs so badly, is certainly to be welcomed, but the activity we need here in order to preserve health is still far from exhausted by it.
Although we find ourselves in the middle of Europe, we are still very backward here, so that one must start straight from the ABC.
If we want to raise a healthy generation, one must begin with hygiene; one must simply and openly explain to the masses that first of all one must keep oneself clean. Of course it is no pleasant task, in the 20th century, to explain such primitive trifles, which everywhere in the wider world are self-evident things without which one cannot live or get by; but the hygienic conditions in which quite ordinary working-class families live in Europe cannot be attained here even by well-to-do people.
Congress Poland and the Kresy [eastern borderlands] are in terribly neglected hygienic conditions, thanks to the fact that the Russian autocrats were the masters here, who paid no attention to hygienic and sanitary conditions; therefore the population was raised in the hardest conditions, which can indeed be felt at every step.
We say that here one must begin from the ABC. Certainly that is so. But it is not enough that people will shout that things must be clean and will punish for not keeping yards or rooms according to the prescribed sanitary conditions. Of course, punishing is very easy here; on the other hand no one considers whether the stated regulations can be carried out. For what people in Berlin, for example, cannot understand — how one can live without this or that technical invention — remains impossible here to put into practice.
Let us take a look, for example, at how the people's housing in Vienna looks, in what hygienic conditions the workers live there, what fine, well-equipped bathrooms they have there, and how care is taken that there should be greenery in front of every window and that one can breathe with free nature; when we look around at how in Europe they care for the people's children, who are raised in modern garden cities under the green trees and close to crystal-clear springs — when one looks at all this, one sees that in the wider world care is taken that a healthy generation should be raised, while here absolutely nothing is being done.
For let us not deceive ourselves: what is being done here in this field? "Doing" here already means ordering the population to be clean. For that one has to call and rouse, so that the population will understand the necessity of keeping itself and the children clean. Well, and when the lower masses, the working strata, do understand it — what then? Are they in such conditions that they can keep themselves and the children in the necessary hygienic conditions? Abroad they have modern large public baths, where for a few groszy one can bathe and have[?] enjoyment, and schoolchildren and the masses of the people have all this entirely free; and not only is it free, but it is obligatory to bathe from time to time.
And here? Where is the middling and small citizen to bathe and keep clean? Where is he to send his children to bathe, when he himself lives with a family in a cellar or in an attic room where one cannot turn around? Are such families able to send their children from time to time to the municipal bath-houses, which, by the way, are arranged in the most primitive manner for a handful of people, and to pay as much as[?] 1 zł. for a child?
Yes, there are things that abroad people cannot conceive how one could live without, and here it is still a luxury which few people of the popular and working strata can attain.
More than once we have had the opportunity to hear the teachers of the public schools complain that the parents send their children to school in a most unhygienic state. Of course this shows the low European[?] condition; it looks as though people were still living in the Middle Ages and were still so far from understanding that we live in the modernized 20th century, in which so much attention is paid to hygiene.
But what are the people to do, when they themselves were not brought up any better, and they were also not given the possibility of raising their children in better and more hygienic conditions?
If here in Poland one has at long last come to the conviction that hygiene and cleanliness play such a great role in the human organism, then one must surely give the citizens the possibility to live as life truly demands.
Mere laws, if they are not adapted to the conditions in which we live and cannot be applied in everyday life, will remain only paper laws and will only be a burden for the citizens, who will not be able to carry them out; and such compulsion benefits neither the country nor the citizens. Every country must apply to its citizens such laws as it [sic; read: they] can adapt to.
Be that as it may, one must first of all instil in the citizens the idea that they must use every possibility to raise their children in strictly hygienic conditions; and then, when they understand this and do not have the possibility to carry it out in practice, they will come and demand that the municipal self-governments put it into practice; and the stronger the demands are, the greater the chances that the decisions will be carried out.
"TOZ" could, upon my word, begin to work more intensively in Zagłębie: let it organize free public lectures, let popular lessons be given in the Jewish language [Yiddish], let leaflets be published in which the harmfulness of living in unhygienic conditions is demonstrated. Of course the lectures and lessons must be conducted with the participation of our doctors and intellectual forces, who can also accomplish much in skilled work.
Let the question not be postponed; let us rather take up this useful work, which the people need in their weekday, everyday life.
Y. Sh.
My Friend's "Projects".

[Satirical feuilleton.] (A short feuilleton)
I have a friend. He is a genius at projects. His head is always full of ideas, plans. He only worries about society, only [?] wants to improve, to beautify. In short, had he not been born under a dark star, he would surely have been a great statesman.
Anyway, this week I drop in on my friend and find him in a very agitated state — pacing about the room, eyes flashing wildly, worked up.
I understood at once that he was in a trance of creation, and was about to slip away [?] from him unnoticed.
But he noticed me and gave me a sign [?] to sit.
I sat down and turned to him with a long-drawn-out
— A—a?—
We already understood each other in mute language, and it meant:
— Another project already?
He began talking at once,
— You know, my friend, what has lately occurred to me: we are going entirely down the wrong road.
I nodded my head in agreement [?], giving him the chance to speak his mind. He continued:
— And do you know what is the cause of all our misfortunes? — I shrugged my shoulders.
Inflamed, he grabbed me by the lapel:
— And the World War, who caused it? — He would not let go of me and shook me. To be rid of him, I mumbled:
— Well, let's say, capitalism.
Dismissively he waved his hand and asked further:
— And the recent disturbances in the Land of Israel?
— Luk [?], the Mufti, — I stammered under his burning gaze.
— Nonsense! — he interrupted me and went on talking.
— Listen to the conclusion I have come to. We are all corrupted, the whole world is spoiled, and we Jews no less than others and perhaps even more: take, for example, our youth.
Here I, as a constant friend of youth, could no longer contain myself and blurted out:
— Our youth is unemployed.
— With its feet [i.e. nonsense!].
— A serious drive to learn.
— Playing cards.
— Our youth reads a lot...
— Dissolute boulevard novels.
I wanted to show him how unjustly he judges and told him a fact: I give a lesson to a few young girls; I came in yesterday and found them flirting with a boy. And what, do you think, do our girls talk about while flirting? About books! One asks the young man: "Have you already read today's 'Seven Castles'?" The other chimes in: "I've already finished 'Di Magikovishiske' [?]." The third snatches up: "And I'll have 'The Gypsies' bound, and I'll have a 'table-book'."
— Rags — he cut me short — people have gone completely mad: they take forests, beautiful green forests, slender, fragrant [?] trees, chop them down and make rags out of them. All of life — one big rag. And to blame for all the troubles and afflictions, do you know who? Those very rags, I mean your [?] books. They corrupt our youth, they led to the terrible slaughter of men and all its sad consequences. There is one remedy to save the world: we are already too clever. We must become a little more foolish. You know what occurs to me? It is about a new project of mine that I want to talk to you. I have decided to create a new league; it shall be called: "[Friends] [?] of Illiteracy".
Why are you looking at me like that? I am not mad. It will be of great practical use to mankind. Let me explain:
The greatest plague of society lately is the suicide epidemic. It is a consequence of the crisis, of protested bills and bankruptcies. And imagine that people get rid of the plague of writing: they will stop writing bad books, stop writing gossip about one another; newspapers will go under, politics will go under, wars will go under, bills of exchange will go under, bankruptcies will go under, suicides will go under. — Well, why are you looking at me like that, I am not mad — — — —
Rav Chiya
Mendel Was Helped...

Mendel was having a bad time, a very bad time, so bad that it had simply become unbearable.
Not, God forbid, in business. Business was so-so — may it get no worse.
But with his wife things were not good, not good at all, terribly not good.
He could not get along with her. Simply could n o t. All she did was sulk, puff herself up, get upset every minute, groan, sigh[?], make a sour face, be dissatisfied with everything — on and on like that, always, forever and ever.
What was wrong with her? Mendel didn't know, nobody knew, not even she herself. She was, it seemed, healthy as a rock, strong as an oak, red in both cheeks; never been ill, never suffered from anything, always had the best appetite and the soundest sleep. So why did she groan? Why did she keep puffing herself up? Why was she so irritable[?], so nervous[?], so unbearable?
Mendel consulted various friends and called various doctors to the house — perhaps it's the head? perhaps rheumatism? perhaps gallstones?
No. All the doctors who examined her declared unanimously that there was absolutely nothing wrong with her. She didn't even have corns, and even her corset fitted exactly and didn't pinch her.
So what was missing after all? That was discovered by only one doctor — and a young one at that, a new one, a doctor without a practice and without a livelihood.
"What's wrong with her, doctor?" Mendel asked him with the last of his hopeless strength.
"Your wife is missing an illness," the doctor answered curtly, took out his prescription pad and began writing Latin words.
"What do you mean?" says Mendel. "What do you mean, she's missing an illness? If she's missing an illness, that's good!"
"No," says the doctor and goes on writing. "It's not good. Your wife is too healthy, nothing is wrong with her, she suffers from no illness at all, and that is not good. A woman must have some definite ailment on which to lay out all her interest. When a woman suffers from no illness at all, she imagines she is suffering from all the illnesses in the world. And she stops being a human being. A woman who is too healthy is the sickest woman in the world. In particular, she is missing something: she has nothing to occupy her thoughts, nothing to talk about with her neighbours. Other women tell about their operations, about hospitals, cheeky doctors, bandages, stabbing pains, aches and so on. And she, your wife, stands and listens and has to keep mum[?] like the wall. She simply has nothing to talk about, nothing to tell, nothing to pour her heart out[?] over, nothing with which to arouse sympathy and interest in others."
"You really think so?"
"Of course I think so! Your wife is a very unhappy woman. Just imagine: when a woman suffers from something, she has the best excuse for getting whatever she wants out of her husband. Can you refuse a sick woman anything? At the slightest thing she starts lamenting: 'Oy, my heart!' or 'Oy, my head!' or 'You want to bury me so you can marry a younger, fresher one!' etc. etc. An illness is a very important thing for a woman. A woman can sooner do without a hand than without an illness."
"So what do you want to do, Mr. Doctor? And what are you writing there?" Mendel asked, perplexed.
"What am I doing? What am I writing? First, I am prescribing some respectable illness for your wife. Your wife absolutely must have some ailment on which she can concentrate her thoughts, talk about it constantly and groan about it. That will simply save her! And second, I am prescribing right here a medicine which she is to take three times a day after meals."
"What kind of illness will it be?"
"I don't know yet. It will be either a stomach illness or a heart illness — better a heart illness, actually! Women very much like to feel a little weak at the heart. It makes them look interesting, with melancholy eyes and a suffering[?] pallor on their faces."
"And your medicine is good for that?"
"The medicine I am prescribing for your wife is good for every kind of illness: it can't help anything and can't harm..."
* * *
When Mendel's wife found out that she had a heart defect, she became a completely different person. She became a quiet, loving woman who looked at her Mendel with great tenderness and pity, as if to say: poor Mendel, soon you will lose me and remain a lonely widower...
In a word: Mendel was helped. His wife no longer scolded him, no longer 'ate him up', no longer sulked — because now she already had something else, something more important, to occupy herself with. She had her imaginary heart defect.
Ypsilon.
Questions That Must Be Solved. (IV. What do the members of the professional associations get, and what ought one to have had from them?)

In our earlier chapters we discussed from every side our most topical problems, the most painful[?] questions, which have completely broken the Jewish middle class, and there is almost no way out as to how it might be rescued; and the way out[?] [i.e. the situation] is bad not so much because we are oppressed by the tax offices as because we are socially immature and, on top of that, completely broken.
In what way is the enormous tax screw no worse than the social immaturity and brokenness? This can be explained quite easily: the merchant, the petty trader or the artisan — each one looks in at his association (Verein), in which he naturally has confidence, and there he unburdens his heart, there he sheds a few bitter tears and goes away with the opinion that something will already be "fixed up" (oysklapotshen) for him; and then he feels that a stone has fallen from his heart, he breathes more easily and is almost certain that once the appeal (rekurs) has been lodged the tax will be eased; and meanwhile, meanwhile one pays no tax, and willy-nilly one forgets another tax, and an instalment (rate), and an advance payment (zalitshke). So that before you know it a Jew has to pay a larger sum, which even with the best will in the world he is no longer able to cope with[?].
And here the catastrophe begins: the number of taxes rises[?] and grows, the percentages[?] with the default interest (zvlakn — zwłoka), with the fines chase one another, and it reaches the point where a helpless Jew begins to despair, because he comes to the conviction that, since the sums have become so large, he will by no means be able to pay them; and then come auctions (litsitatsyes — licytacje), bankruptcies, despair; decent, solid firms are lost, and the end is that they go down from the market.
Quite different would our economic situation have looked if we had healthy professional institutions which would serve the interests of their members not after the pattern of the old-time petition-writer (proshenye-shrayber), who used to write after he had heard out his client. A social institution surely ought not to have sunk to this low level, owing to which every member has failed.
There are firms that do not need the association, and although most of them are members there, they do not cross the threshold of the association; this is because for their business and for tax questions they do not need the professional association, since for that they have their own people, officials versed in tax matters, who understand perfectly how to save themselves from a tax danger.
Quite different at the moment is the question for those citizens who cannot even dream of keeping officials for this purpose, and these people place all their hope in their professional associations. Too much faith did the members have in their professional institutions, and the latter were not prepared for all this, and the result was that these small merchants and artisans suffered defeat[?] on all fronts; and owing to all this, it is not enough that they are [—][?], they overpay beyond measure, besides which they do not know whether they are coming or going.
Our professional associations are far from understanding their tasks, and it is too little to say that they do not understand them — merely through their helplessness and apathetic attitude to the most painful questions the members have been brought [to this state] (ibergefirt gevorn).
The heads of the said professional institutions ought to have understood well, and now, after they have had so much practice, they must know even better that they were not what they ought to have been.
It is not enough that the association buys out a licence (patent) for its member. The institution must be set on entirely different foundations. It must be familiar with every member's situation. The member must have complete confidence in his institution, which should be for him a kind of alarm-clock and reminder, an informant and a controller.
It would pay every member to sacrifice a certain fee to his institution so that it should be for him everything he needs. For example: every member should have in his association a separate card-index, where everything is kept in proper order, and from that very association people should come to him and explain: thus and thus stands your question, this and this must be done now, such and such an instalment you have to pay on such and such a date. All tax liabilities, various documents that demand order and about which one must[mmuz — as printed] conduct correspondence, must be under the supervision of his association, and the person in charge of his documents should know everything quite precisely, just as the official of a large firm knows about the matter.
Statistics show us that at a time when the large firms do not overpay a single superfluous grosz for default interest, fines and percentages, it costs these small, helpless citizens an enormously large percentage — and very often not because he does not want to or cannot pay the instalment or the tax, but quite simply because he does not remember that today is his due date. His head is in a whirl: here he has a bill of exchange (veksl) to redeem, and here he must carry out an order, so that his head is burdened from all sides and he cannot take upon himself the heavy load of paying punctually the sum of taxes which he receives both from the Treasury (skarb) and from the Magistrate [municipality]. Moreover, one more thing must not be forgotten: owing to unpunctual payment, because of which he often overpays very much, he becomes even more oppressed because several taxes pile up on him at once, because of which he is toppled and is thus sunk up to his neck.
At least this much must be done: that the professional associations take it upon themselves to solve the question in the sense that, on the one hand, the members should not overpay money needlessly, and on the other hand, thanks to the taxes being paid at the proper time, it will in any case come easier for the citizen to pay them, because they will be paid systematically in proper order.
If this system is carried out, it will be a tremendous[?] gain for the average and small citizens, and the professional institutions will know that they have achieved something for their members.
It is high time that the heads of the institutions finally understood that these are not charitable institutions but professional ones, which must care for the welfare of the citizens in general and of their members in particular.
If the institutions do not begin to care at least for improving the situation of their members, at the very least as much as they are able to, then in that case it will have to come to the point where the institutions will be condemned[?] to downfall, because professional institutions cannot exist when they achieve nothing for their fellows.
It goes without saying that things must not be brought to such a degree[?] that the professional institutions should come to such a catastrophe, which would mean a bankruptcy for productive Jewry; that is precisely why one must look with open eyes at the terrible disharmony that reigns in our professional institutions, which urgently need to be rescued.
R. Les.
Franz Grillparzer. — Consilium medicum

Franz Grillparzer.
Consilium medicum.
(Consilium medicum).

Lady Poesy was ill,
A widow these many years,
Her forehead hot,
Her tongue white,
Her skin now cold and now in a sweat.

Over her whole body a heavy rash.
Her heart beats: tick—tock, tick—tock!
Though her face is fresh and not old,
Yet she grows colder and colder.

Doctors come from every side,
To examine and to quarrel:
Hippocratic,
Homeopathic,
Allopathic,
Hydropathic,
Antipathic,
Philosophically puffed up,
Historically [printed "distorically"] armed,
Dogmatically critical,
Classical, British,
They write prescriptions in long lines,
In vain! The patient can no longer be healed.

Then in comes a village doctor,
Looks the patient over by the lamplight,
He examines the pulse and the tongue,
All exchange a wink.

With a smile he says:
I see no illness here at all,
The lady only needs a husband..!

(Translated for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" by Yosef Perlberger[?])
The Innocent Victim

(A picture of the present day).

When Mary arrived as a shop assistant ["ekspedientka"], she was still a very young girl. The shop where her mother had placed her had a fairly large staff; the assistants[?] were girls serving as shop clerks. There were two men: one employee and a bookkeeper. At first they mostly took advantage of Mary: the older employees ordered her about, sent her [on errands?], and she obeyed them all. Mary, young as she was, understood that otherwise they would not keep her, so she took everything in good part and only consoled herself that it would be just a short while before a younger girl than she would come — and then she would already count among the grown-ups. Mary hoped, and meanwhile envied the older girls who stand at the counter, where they sell and are trusted [with the till].
And the time came when Mary too was trusted; by then Mary had grown up, she had come to know the business better, and she [printed "di"] too began to stand at the buffet counter and sell on an equal footing with the grown-ups. Her wages were raised and Mary was pleased with herself. Her dreams of becoming a grown-up girl had come true; and not only that, but together with her blooming and growing, her beauty and girlish charm blossomed too. This not only raised her standing and compelled her boss to treat her as a grown-up, practical young lady ["panna"?], but her blossoming figure and graceful beauty riveted everyone's eyes, and everyone admired her.
Mary was the prettiest of the whole staff, and the bookkeeper, who already had a wife and two children, cast an eye on her; he liked her very much, and a strong love surged up in his heart. Mary, a fine and decent child of honest parents, knew very well that the bookkeeper could offer her no future [printed "tuge"?]. She therefore did not want to meet him; she avoided him and did not even answer his proposals.
This made him so angry that he sought to take revenge on her. And he did not have to search long. Once, when Mary was sent to the bank to pay bills of exchange — as always, she pays and comes straight back, cheerful and merry — this time she did not come back soon. On the way two scoundrels (sent by the bookkeeper) attacked her, dragged her by force into a nearby gateway, stuffed her mouth with a kerchief and took all the money from her.
When Mary got back to the shop it was already very late. Broken and in tears, she told what had happened to her, but then the bookkeeper stood up and said something coarse[?] [printed "a grande"] to her face. He accused Mary of having deliberately set up the so-called attackers, of having come to an understanding with them beforehand, and of being their accomplice. The bookkeeper declared that he was deeply convinced of this and that everything had been passed on to him from reliable sources.
The boss had no other choice and handed Mary over to the police. There was a trial; the bookkeeper was the chief witness, and on his accusation Mary was sentenced to long months of prison.
Spending a longer time in prison, Mary got to know various types of women; she came to know the underworld of life. When she came out free, she was as lonely as a stone, with nowhere to go. Her own parents were ashamed of her and no longer wanted to acknowledge her as their child. They too would not believe in her innocence. And Mary, having no other way out — spat upon, cast out by her parents, her relatives, her acquaintances and by all of society — went off to a street corner ["rog gas", Polish róg], to her former acquaintances with whom she had sat in prison; and so one more young, pure soul joined the underworld, a soul that had given itself up as a sacrifice...
P. Polier[?].
From the 8 Days of Hanukkah

[Dąbrowa, Sosnowiec, Będzin — Hanukkah; society and culture; sketches.] A stroll by Ben Amotz.
The past Hanukkah was rich in events [?]. From the first to the last day of Hanukkah the posters announced events [?]. The organisation that did not arrange a Hanukkah evening "discharged its duty" with a "Hanukkah ball".
We saw the beginning
in a kindergarten [gan yeladim].
A very young "garden", barely 3 months old and already it has given us some of its "fruits"... The "garden" is very small, some 30 little trees "grow" there, but the shoots promise a lot, a great deal..
In the "gan" mothers and also fathers have gathered. They watch the zest for life of their children, listen with suspense as their children sing and dance Hebrew songs, peculiar dances, and when 5-year-old Rachel Rozenker [?] stands by a "silver menorah" and recites "Hanerot halalu", the mothers lower their eyes for shame... and "console" themselves by promising "on their word of honour" [Polish: pod słowem honoru] that they will take part in the Hebrew courses at "Ḥiza" [?].
And when "Mother Eve", the "gardener" [kindergarten teacher], marches off with the little flock to the buffet, the founder, Mrs. Ratner, gives a short warm speech on current affairs, on the historic day. One must — says the speaker — recite "Shehecheyanu" when one sees that in so short a time it has succeeded that such "assimilationist little souls" understand what is said to them in Hebrew, and she calls on the mothers to join the ranks of "Ḥiza" [?].
After the "vocal-musical" programme the little ones set about eating, the mothers take pride and pleasure (perhaps from the appetites..) and wish themselves to improve by next year.
———
At the "Venus" cinema in Dąbrowa. A crush at the box office, the hall is already overfull, the police threaten that if the aisle is blocked the
Keren Kayemet academy
will not be permitted. The management acts for several minutes. Later — the same again, national Dąbrowa "tears worlds apart", the youth does not abandon its "positions" and the hall looks like a balled-up mass of people.
In the name of the KKL the academy is opened by Mr. P. Lenczner [?]. An orchestra plays the Polish and the Jewish anthem and the floor goes to Mr. Gotlib. He recalls all the martyrs, Abira [?] of Dr. Reich, B. Stachski [?], explains the significance of the "Keren Kayemet" and calls on Jewish Dąbrowa to national deeds.
Then we hear the finely polished lecture by editor [Red.] Heftman. For almost 2 hours the audience swallows the arguments of the speaker, who demonstrates the value of land owned by a people, our historic rights to the Land of Israel, and appeals that in exile too the red Maccabee [?] flowers be planted. During these words a "miracle" happened. A child was heard crying... Apparently the child had "soaked up" the heartfelt words of the speaker and began to cry...
Then comes the "artistic" part. The whole "artistic" world of Dąbrowa united: "Hashomer Hatzair", "Gordonia" and Frayhayt. Each organisation unloaded [?] its baggage, and the organisation that was poor in repertoire made use of "Rebbe Elimelech", and it really was merry...
The evening altogether was rich in "miracles". Nursing babies "wept" and a 16-year-old girl did not "light up"... On the stage a living menorah was displayed [?], Dąbrowa demonstrated its beauties, and one "little candle", and precisely one from a "big field" [a prominent family], "choked" [?] and would not shine.. That is our luck: the joy cannot be complete, in remembrance of the Destruction.
The remaining numbers were successful and the audience went home satisfied.
———
On that evening the Sosnowiec "Maccabi" appeared at
a gymnastics festival.
In the course of the last years "Maccabi" has gone through many illnesses, with various "complications"... The danger has passed and "Maccabi" is getting back its original skin, "the crown restored to its former glory".. We saw the first traces at the Hanukkah festival. For such a face is what "Maccabi" ought to have. First a warm introduction by Dr. Seladista [?], a march-past with the blue-and-white flag (it would have been more impressive [?] in the street...) and then the "feats of strength" of the first men's group. The group's exercises deserve to be crowned with two words: — "beyond competition". The other groups too are good material, but they need to go through a qualified teacher who will train the gymnasts, so that they exercise more plastically and their movements have soul, for "Maccabi" is after all not a collection of trick-performers...
Only, as said, "Maccabi" had such atrophies that hampered its development, and we hope the old-new club will soon get back onto its original rails.
———
On Sunday Dąbrowa again had a celebration. The "Hachnasat Kallah" society held in the synagogue
a Hanukkah evening
performed by the conductor Mr. Kalmus and his choir. The "evening" was prepared according to "the latest fashion". Besides tickets, also "programmes", which announced that "Rom v'nisso" [?] (Ram venisa) would be sung. In the synagogue a policeman strolled about at his leisure, looking like "a Greek in the sukkah"... he had nothing to do; the few dozen gloomy Jews with their pale, worn-out children sat quietly and did not wait for the shammes to make "order" [Polish porządek]...
The lazy one discharged his duty. The choir sang very beautifully. And the organisers had only a moral success.
———
The next day Jewish Będzin had great enjoyment from the grandiose Hanukkah ball
of "Gordonia".
A programme of 14 numbers. Everything successful. There were moments when the spectator forgot he was in the Będzin "Nowości". The ringing Hebrew, the zest for life of little "actors and actresses" made one forget life in exile..
March-past — M. Hampel speaks with enthusiasm on current affairs [misprinted "mesine"] (in Hebrew), Shoshana Kleinman performs "The Miracle of Hanukkah" by I. L. Peretz and a recitation by the same poet — "Hanukkah Candles", very successfully recited by Rachel Zaks. The number "Two Worlds" ends the first part of the programme.
An extraordinary success was had by the first number of the second part, "The Trip to the Land of Israel", a comedy in one act by Yitzhak Katzenelson. Splendid was the dance under the direction of Yehudit Brojner [?]. When the curtain was lowered the hall shook with stormy applause.
The same impression was sustained in the recitation "A New Road", performed artistically by Perach Weissbrot, "Play Me Guitar", a song by Shoshana, and a pioneers' tableau "We Will Not Retreat".
The choir under the direction of comrade Shimon, accompanied by a merry orchestra — sings several Land-of-Israel songs, and with "Hatikvah" the splendid evening ends.
Contributing to the success were the fine stage sets, designed by S. Ferstenfeld [?].
———
In Sosnowiec "Hashomer Hatzair" and "Gordonia" held Hanukkah celebrations. In their own premises, with their own forces, and the members were satisfied. "Gordonia" in particular made very merry; the young folk enjoyed themselves right up to 4 in the morning; they discharged their duty by all opinions, both in honour of Hanukkah and for the "holy Sylvester"...
———
The balls were concluded by the Będzin
Hashomer Haleumi.
All year long they, the "shomrim", spend their time in a small — cellar room, nobody takes any interest in them, they are "as sheep without a shepherd", but when Hanukkah comes, a "Great Hanukkah Ball" is arranged. In reality the 3 words came out very small, and that is no wonder; material there is. Not at all difficult, in fact; only an expert is lacking who would work up the material, put feeling, content and intention [?; printed "vekhume"] into it.
In the great ball the temperamental Dr. Hans Lech [?] took part, who lectured on the subject "The Maccabees of Former Times and of Today". The language — "Reitsch" [Germanised Yiddish], but thanks to the pathos he possesses the impression was a good one.
After the staging of the song "How Beautiful Are the Palestinian Nights", Sholem Aleichem's "Hanukkah Money" is performed; characters — successful (especially Merin, Prower [?]), but Sholem Aleichem took on a different shape here...
Not bad were the stagings of "Carry Me into the Desert" and "Two Creatures".
The sets [?] [—] painted by M. Pelczak [?] — very [—]
The Mice Are Organising...

[Będzin — municipality and sanitation; satirical feuilleton.]
The house-owners of Będzin have been ordered to exterminate with poison the mice in the filthy places in the courtyards.
(From the press [?])

The city president sat thinking about how to beautify the town. Będzin already looks like a real residence-city, a veritable Garden of Eden. "Co prawda" [admittedly], a few things are still missing, but "Nie od razu Kraków zbudowany" [Kraków wasn't built in a day]; another year, another year, and Będzin will be a town one can only wish for — a town at last, if only the head stays healthy and the brain keeps coming up [?] with new plans. Indeed, the "Wydział Zdrowia" [Health Department] has already undertaken an extermination campaign against the creeping creatures, and it will teach them a lesson; it will slip them such a powder [proszek] that they will have to clear out! "A yakushez ey sa begrushe pachenka" [?] [garbled Polish phrase, not deciphered]!
But the city president's sweet dream was torn in the middle by a noise in his room. Frightened, he hastily rose from his chair and saw several four-footed creatures approaching [?] the president.
— "Co wy chcecie" [What do you want]! — he shouted angrily, and as soon as he had said it, all three mouse-delegates, as if on command, leapt up onto the office desk and, fixing their shining eyes straight on the president, the eldest of them, the one on the left, began:
— "Panie prezydencie" [Mr President]! Know that we come to you in the name of an organised mass of several thousand "mouse citizens", among whom 40 per cent are fit for combat, able to destroy and lay waste five times more, ten times, a hundred times more than they need for themselves. The other 40 per cent of our mousy humanity are children, capable of crawling through the crack of a shutter [?] or the gap of a drawer; and then we have another 20 per cent women, who are good at sniffing out and finding all your treasures. And so, in the name of all these brothers and sisters of ours, we, three chosen ones, have come to you, lord of the town, so that you annul the order issued by your "Health Department" to exterminate us. That is our proposal.
The president even wanted to let out a shout: — "Rats, out of here!" But he held himself back, and meanwhile the second "mouse-delegate" straightened his whiskers and drew himself up like a soldier: Lord of the town of Będzin — he began — by what right is a death sentence passed upon us! Have we not the right to exist like every earthly creature!
After all, we all live in an age of civilisation, and in Europe at that, where people are civilised and fight for equality and freedom! Do you think that the harvest and abundance of all the earth's produce this year, in which we have a share equal to yours, belongs only to you and not to us! May our brothers and sisters not even feed on the scraps of what you, privileged little creatures, throw away! And if it rots — will that be better? What do you care that we too enjoy the cheapness [?] and the harvest, the blessing of Mother Earth, who is our protectress! Have we no right to that? Is it all due to you alone and nothing to us?
The president wanted to get rid of the 3 delegates with a "Ja się postaram, zupełna racja" [I'll try, you're quite right], but the young fellow ["bocherek"] would not give in and came out with a speech:
— Dear sir! Do not take our "prośba" [request] lightly; we will not let ourselves be exterminated, and by whom, moreover? By the violators of justice and right! Is it not enough for you that you are already crawling towards "Mars" — must you now go after us? No! You will not succeed with us. Call us "paskudniki" [vermin], the worst creatures — we have a right to exist, we want to exist, as long as creatures like us are found in all your societies too. And therefore we give you, lord of the town, a deadline of 24 hours to annul the order!
The city president wiped his sweat-wet forehead, glanced at the "mouse-delegates" and thought: familiar faces! The same ones from the market, four-footed, two-footed, "co za różnica" [what's the difference]? At last he addressed them:
— I see that you are "people" of understanding. Good — just as with us there must be order: the order was signed not by me but by the Health Minister; you must [?] hand him in writing everything you have told me here, and whatever we are able to do will be done for your underground citizens.
When the three mouse-delegates went off to the Health Minister, it was already late at night, and when the "minister" saw the delegates he flew into a rage and shouted: "Wynoście się stąd" [Get out of here]! I am not receiving any delegations now! This is not my "urzędowanie" [office hours], "a zresztą" [and besides], I do not want to receive you at all, and it will not help you in the least — you must swallow [?] the decree! "You must!
Having received such an ugly rebuff from the "samorodny" [self-made] minister himself, the mouse-delegates at once raised a "trwoga" [alarm]: all the mice from all the holes gathered in one place, heard the report, debated, shouted and squeaked, until it was resolved unanimously that until the danger passes one must hide in a safe place where the decree does not apply; and as the best, safest and most guaranteed place, where no poison will certainly be laid, the whole mass of mice chose — the Magistrate building [town hall]...
Shiele.
A Letter from the Land of Israel

[Land of Israel — the commission of inquiry.] Dr. Binyamin.

(Special for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").

What are people talking about now in the Land of Israel — no, what are they thinking and dreaming about? — About the "Va'ad ha-Hakirah", that commission of inquiry which the English government has sent to Jerusalem to investigate the sad events of the month of Av. What were the "immediate" causes, and what are the means to avoid such events in the future? These are the questions to which the commission of inquiry must find a correct, solid answer. At first it seemed that they would speak here only about what happened in the very last period before the events. But the Arabs did not like that, because if one speaks only of the events and the immediate causes, the Arabs indeed stand shamefaced, for they were, after all, the murderers and the robbers; this did not suit them, and they thought of bringing before the commission of inquiry the whole history of Jewish colonisation, in order to show how harmful it is to the Arabs, and thereby they wanted to justify somewhat the terrible cruelty of the sad events.

No sooner said than done.

Witnesses appeared before the commission of inquiry who supposedly proved objectively that Jewish colonisation harms the Arabs. The days in which this game went on before the commission were hard days for us. It was terribly upsetting to see that, besides the physical murders in Hebron and Safed, there now came spiritual and moral attacks by false witnesses. But it did not last long, and it turned out that the Arab claims are no more than cobwebs. The Jewish witnesses came forward and showed in a calm, objective manner the utter ignorance of the Arab witnesses. And the practical result was that the new turn in the work of the commission served us better than the Arabs had imagined. The plain truth is that we have nothing to keep secret and nothing to conceal, and we can await with the calmest conscience the results of the most thorough investigation.

So far Jewish witnesses have appeared such as Hoofien, the director of the Anglo-Palestine Company, Chief Rabbi Kook, Moshe Smilansky, Sacher, Hartzik [?], Avraham Shapira and other well-known personalities, and each of them spoke quite to the point, without pathos and without regrets. Each of them made a strong impression, precisely because of the facts he presented.

For example: the Arab leaders complain that because of Jewish immigration the country has been impoverished. Then Mr. Hoofien comes and proves that in the last 10 years the Jews have brought in — through private [capital] [—] through the Keren Kayemet and the Keren Hayesod — more than 45 million dollars. [—] Again he proves that imports into the Land of Israel are comparatively greater than in the surrounding purely Arab countries. And here Mr. Hoofien remarks very well: one of two things; either the Jews (as is the truth) made the increased imports, and then they bring wealth into the country; or the Arabs make such enormous imports, and then they cannot say that they have become poorer than the Arabs in the surrounding purely Arab countries (rich Egypt not excepted). And again the famous writer-colonist Moshe Smilansky (38 years in the country) stands up and proves with facts how the Arabs around the Jewish colonies grow rich, while the Arabs in distant places have indeed remained very poor people.

A very strong impression was made by the appearance of the Chief Rabbi, the Gaon Kook. He did not want the commission of inquiry to come to his home (as it did to the Mufti). He said that he wanted the whole world to know "the truth. We have no secrets," he declared, and he recalled that among us even the High Priest used to go to the court to give his testimony. With his truly wise and deep answers Rabbi Kook sanctified God's name both among the English and even among our new generation. One now hears everywhere the old saying: where there is Torah, there is also wisdom.

This is not the place to dwell on every answer Rabbi Kook gave to all the questions put to him. He spoke of the promises we received through our prophets, which can be fulfilled only by Heaven, and of the commandment of settling the Land of Israel, which makes it a sacred duty for every Jew to do whatever is in his power to strengthen the Jewish Yishuv in the Holy Land. When the commission launched into a sea of questions about the shofar which was not permitted to be blown at the close of Yom Kippur at the Western Wall, Rabbi Kook exclaimed with great pain: here they split hairs with great interest about the length and the width of the shofar, as though that were the main thing and not the terrible murders in Hebron and Safed... When the commission was told of the High Commissioner's proposal that the Jews should buy the area in front of the Western Wall, Rabbi Kook exclaimed: "Blessed be He that I have concurred with a great mind!" That has always been my opinion.

Through the appearance of the Jewish witnesses the mood among the Jews in the Land of Israel has risen. Even at the most critical time nobody let himself be discouraged. If there are differences of opinion among the Jews, they concern only the political methods to be used towards the English and towards the Arabs. But fundamentally everyone agrees that all Jews must strengthen the building of the Land of Israel as quickly as possible, both with people and with means, both through private initiative and through national and general institutions. Therefore there are no differences of opinion. Religious Jews and free-thinkers, rich and poor, capitalists and workers are now as united as in the days of the events, when all Jews were united in the "Haganah" (self-defence) without any distinction. Even the disputes between employers and employees have ceased. A more brotherly tone prevails; everyone understands why we came here, what we want to accomplish here, and that this can be achieved only through unity, concord and brotherhood. It also made a good impression that Mr. Hexter, the non-Zionist secretary of the "Jewish Agency", has already come here to work together with the Zionist leadership on the building of the Land of Israel. This is a symbol that the whole Jewish people stands like a wall around our work. On the other hand it is gratifying to see how Rabbi Sonnenfeld goes together with Rabbi Kook on the question of the Western Wall. One hopes that after this first step the radical Orthodox, too, will find the way to join the Jewish "Jewish Agency". And may everything, with God's help, continue onward with luck and joy, and may the fortune of the Jews at last be raised!

—o—

[Żarki — economy.] The house-warming of the "Bank Kupiecki" in Żarki.

Last Sunday the festive house-warming of the new premises of the "Bank Kupiecki" took place; owing to its rapid development the bank has moved into specially renovated, much larger and more beautiful premises.

Almost all the members gathered for the celebration. The head of the bank, Mr. S., gave a speech of welcome in which he pointed out that the bank has developed because suitable persons were appointed as its managers; above all, many thanks were expressed to the chairman, Mr. Tzvi Szparn [?], who has done a great deal for the good of the bank.

In conclusion Mr. S. called on the members to keep to the same direction in the future and to appoint as managers of the bank suitable and honest persons as hitherto, for only thanks to this will the bank continue to develop and gain as much confidence as possible in the wider world.

At a richly laid table the members afterwards spent several pleasant hours.

The house-warming of the "Bank Kupiecki" is a living demonstration that with honest and suitable managers, without any benefit to private intentions, and with good management, a genuine co-operative bank can develop quickly and attain due splendour and respect.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: City Administration Sets the Price and Quota for Water

[Section "What's new in Zagłębie?" — Będzin, municipal affairs.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
Friday, 10 Tevet 5690. — Piątek 10 stycznia 1930 [Friday, 10 January 1930].
Będzin
—o—
City administration sets the price and quota for water.
At Tuesday's[?] session of the city administration the price and the quota of water were set. The price of 1 [cubic] metre of water is 50 groszy. The quota is: for 1 room — 4 metres, 2 rooms — 7 m., 3 rooms — 10 m., 4 rooms 13, 5 rooms — 16, 6 rooms — 19, 7 rooms — 22, 8 rooms — 25, 9 rooms — 28, 10 rooms — 31 metres.
The proposal of vice-president [deputy mayor] Rubinlicht that from 4 rooms upward the quota be raised by 2 metres was accepted[?].
At the session it was decided that the house-owners shall collect the payment for the water, but from the tenants who will pay at the proper time, the magistrate will collect it itself.
A proper number of pumps will be set up in the town; when they are ready, the magistrate will lease out the pumps, and a bucket of water will cost 2 groszy.
Licences Will Be Issued Next Week

[Będzin — trade and peddling.]
This week the chairman Mr. Rubinlicht, on behalf of the "Merchants' Association" [Sokhrim-Fareyn], intervened with the president of the Administrative Court in Katowice regarding the question of licences for peddlers in Upper Silesia.
The president promised that persons who attach certificates from the Będzin "Merchants' Association" will receive the proper documents next week.
A Jewish Girl on the Eve of Apostasy

[Będzin — community and society; conversion.]
In last Tuesday's "Radio" [Warsaw] there was a report from Wilno that the daughter of a local Jewish communal activist ran away from her parents with her beloved, a young Polish artillery officer serving in Wilno.
In connection with this sensational report, the tailor Józef Epsztajn of Będzin, Przeczna 4, came to our editorial office and related that for several days a young Jewish girl, 22 years old, who speaks "Litvish" [Lithuanian Yiddish], has been staying in Zagórze, and that she is about to convert in the first days of next week.
The Jewish press in Warsaw is requested to reprint this report, which arouses great interest.
Grand Keren Kayemet Evening

[Będzin — Zionism; Jewish National Fund.]
The Zionist women's association "WIZO" is holding on the 25th of this month, in the hall of the "Ochronka" [children's shelter] on Góra Zamkowa [Castle Hill], a grand Keren Kayemet evening with a very rich programme.
Grand Sports Event

[Będzin — sport; police.]
The local police commissariat is holding on Thursday the 16th of this month, at half past 8 in the evening, at the "Gnaovshchi"[?] a grand sports event. On the programme: French wrestling, boxing bouts and gymnastic exercises. The sports clubs "Hakoach", "Maccabi", "Sokół", the local police club, the well-known sportsman A. Wracławski[?] and a first-class orchestra have promised to take part in the event.
The entire proceeds are for the bereaved families, wives and children of the police. It is desirable to support the event.
The Gates Shall Stay Open Until 11 O'Clock at Night

[Będzin — municipal affairs and police.]
On behalf of the House-Owners' Association, vice-president Mr. Rubinlicht intervened with the head of the local commissariat that the gates of the houses should stay open until 11 in the evening. The head promised to settle the matter favourably.
A Theft in the Beit Midrash

[Będzin — crime; study house.]
In the night from Thursday to Friday a thief, by breaking open a lock, got into the beit midrash, where he took a pair of etzei chayim [Torah-scroll rollers].
The name S. Rushinsk is engraved on the etzei chayim.
The language of hunger..

A group of unemployed came to the Magistrate [Będzin town hall] and demanded relief or work. When the answer of the town administration did not satisfy them, they began smashing windowpanes. The police soon arrived and dispersed the troublemakers [?].
Guest performance of the Vilna Troupe.

Next Thursday the Yiddish theatre-goers will have distinguished guests. The famous "Vilna" Troupe, under the direction of Dr. Weichert, is coming to us for one guest performance. "Yidn Shtot" ["Jews' Town"] by Aaron Zeitlin will be staged.
It is to be expected that the guests will be received as befits them.
—o—
For electricity — at the Cooperative Bank.
For the convenience of the town's population, the municipal power station has agreed that the charge for light and power may be paid at the "Bank Spółdzielczy" without any special fee.
Meeting of the Charity Society.

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Charity Society took place in the kehilla hall.
Some 400 persons had been invited to the meeting, but only a very small number came. Apparently, the matter of bringing up orphans and supporting widows is at present a scarce article.
The chairman, Dr. Weinzieher, opens the meeting and hands the chair to the vice-president, Mr. Rubinlicht. As assessors: Messrs. Herman Fride [?] and Abraham Liwer.
The report on the year's activity is given by Dr. Weinzieher. From the report we got a clear picture of how useful the society is for the poor strata of the Jewish population.
The society has 80 orphans, boys and girls, under its guardianship. The cost of maintaining the orphans' homes (ochronki) comes to about 35,000 zł. a year; the homes are subsidised by the Magistrate (24 740 zł.) and by the kehilla (3000 zł.); this year's deficit is 7 thousand zł.
Apart from the coal and kimcha [Passover flour] campaigns, the society supports 48 widows, for whom it pays rent and from time to time also provisions.
In the course of last year the Charity Society gave one-time grants for medical treatment (kuracja) to a total of 1999 zł.
The report on the building of the orphanage is given by Mrs. Z. Szajn, who explains that the finance committee has so far collected for this purpose a sum of 113,238 zł. At the same time [?] attention is drawn to the fact that among the donors so far there is not a single one of the Orthodox rich men of our town. But it is to be hoped that they will fulfil their duty towards the building for orphans.
Unemployed, register!

Official circles draw our attention to the negligence of the Jewish unemployed, who are not registered at the proper offices in order to receive government relief.
It is a fact that among 180 unemployed who received urgent winter aid this week there were no more than 2 (read: two) Jews...
The kehilla council will rise at the "Resurrection of the Dead"...

On Tuesday the kehilla council was called to a meeting to consider the budget for 1930. Not a single councillor (parnas) came to the meeting, and the meeting was postponed to this coming Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat).
Meeting of "Menachem Avelim".

Under the chairmanship of Mr. Israel Yitzhak Mintz a general meeting took place on Monday, at which it was considered how to strengthen the institution for giving aid to widows and orphans.
The board consists of: Y. Y. Mintz, Y. Y. Wekslman, H. Zilbersztac, Y. Zawader, A. Y. Sztark, H. L. Jungster, Sh. Parasol, Y. Parasol, G. Grosfeld, H. Micenmacher, Y. W. [?] Margulies, M. Winter, M. Waldman, Y. Drefzurgmajer [?] and B. Kokotek.
It was resolved to undertake in town a "month of pledges" [?].
The "guest performance" did not succeed!..

The thief Marczykowski from Łódź came to Zagłębie. He paid his first "visit" to the Szydłow family in Gzichów. Unfortunately he did not receive the proper "welcome" there, and he was taken off to the Będzin jail.
A ball of the academics

This Saturday the Będzin Association of Jewish Students is holding its annual ball in the hall on the „Góra Zamkowa“ [Castle Hill]. The organising committee is preparing a series of attractions, so that the academic ball, which is always the most successful event of the season, will turn out impressive this year too, and the guests will have the opportunity to spend an evening pleasantly in the best company.
—o—
A lecture by Zerubavel.
This Saturday a lecture by the labour activist Zerubavel [Yaakov Vitkin-Zerubavel, Left Poale Zion leader] will take place in the „Corso“ hall, on the subject „On the paths of Jewish mass culture“.
—o—
A 100-year-old woman has died.
On Wednesday the 100-year-old Dvora Rozenes [?], known by the name „Wolf Lane's wife“, was buried. A few days before her death she asked her grandchildren to pray for her health.
—o—
From the Esperantists' Association.
This Saturday a general meeting will take place in the association's own premises. The agenda will be announced at the meeting.
—o—
Gymnastics festival of „Hakoach“.
Next Monday „Hakoach“ is holding a gymnastics festival in the „Nowości“ [?] theatre. All groups are taking part. Before the festival a parade through the town is to take place.
—o—
At „Gordonia“.
In the premises of the youth organisation „Gordonia“ a festive transfer of the groups (kvutzot) „Shoshana“ and „Giborim“ to higher circles took place.
The celebration was opened with „Hatikvah“, after which Messrs. Liwer, Werdiger, Miss Klajman, Buchbinder and Frajtman spoke as representatives of the other groups.
With Hebrew songs and chalutz dances the celebration was concluded.
—o—
An attempted suicide.
On Wednesday 24-year-old Reuven Fajnski went into a courtyard lavatory and, with the aim of committing suicide, cut his throat with a razor.
The groans of the would-be suicide were heard by the tenants, who took him to the municipal hospital.
The young man had been melancholic in recent days.
—o—
From the „Merchants' Association“
We are asked to announce that: 1) the association's legal adviser, advocate Mitelbojm, is again receiving at the „Merchants' Association“ every Monday and Thursday. 2) All members of the trade section in Upper Silesia must register on Sunday the 12th of this month regarding the question of visas.
Sosnowiec — Festive opening of the evening courses for artisans

The new board of the Artisans' Association is showing signs of life. Little by little [?] the old practices are being removed and order is being introduced [?] in every field concerning the economic and cultural needs of the Jewish artisan.
One of the most important tasks has been taken on by the culture commission, which within a short time opened evening courses for illiterates. The courses are very well attended; 60 pupils are already taking part.
The opening of the evening courses took place on Saturday night. The mood was festive and the audience listened to the speeches with great attention.
The chair is handed to Mr. Bigkowski [sic; probably Binkowski]. Greetings are given by representatives of the Ts.S. [?], the kehilla, the town council, etc. Then Mr. Gancwajch delivers a longer lecture on the importance of culture in general and for artisans in particular. The lecture made a strong impression. Then Mr. Landger [?] recites „Berl the Tailor“ by I. L. Peretz, and Mr. Gancwajch takes the audience on „A stroll through Yiddish literature“.
—o—
Lost both legs.
Not far from Strzemieszyce a passenger train ran over a young Christian and cut off both his legs.
—o—
Butchers' guild against raising the slaughtering fees.
In connection with the kehilla board's raising of the prices for shechita, the Jewish butchers' guild has issued a public protest against the decision.

Suicide of a Jewish woman
At Kusznica [?] 6, in Tafer's [?] house, lives the Knajzler family. On Saturday night a neighbour came in to the family and asked to be given the key to the attic. When the children saw that the key was missing and that their mother Kejle had also been gone from the house for quite a while, the matter became suspicious and they went up to the attic. There they saw the catastrophe: their mother had committed suicide by hanging herself.
The suicide was 54 years old. On Wednesday she was buried.

A young man's foolish revenge.
At the B. family on Targowa Street a wedding took place on Sunday. The next morning a messenger came to the young couple's flat and declared that he had brought a present for the young couple. When the parcel was unpacked, dirty [?] rags and other such „tasty“ [?] objects were found in it. The messenger declared that an unknown young man had given him 50 groszy for his trouble..

A murder and suicide.
On Wiejska Street in Sosnowiec the following family tragedy occurred. At house number 9 on that street lived a Christian couple, just 3 months after their wedding. The couple did not live in peace, and in the end they separated. On Tuesday the husband met his young wife in the street and, after a short, sharp exchange of words, threw himself at her with a knife and wounded her severely; then he went into a courtyard, where he cut open his belly, so that all his entrails came out. The next morning he died, whereas his wife was successfully saved.

Conference of Jewish bank directors in Będzin.
Under the chairmanship of the president of the Cooperative Bank, Director Leon Potok [?], a conference took place at the premises of the "Discount Bank" in Będzin with the participation of the directors of the Jewish banks and the auditor Mr. Szaszkes [?]. On the agenda a number of points of first-rate importance for banking were discussed.
The points were: 1) unifying the rate of commission on bills of exchange, drafts and protests; 2) the time for sending unpaid bills to the notary; and 3) when protests should be handed over to the court.
After a lengthy discussion it was resolved: 1) on the 2nd day the bills will be sent to the notary; 2) within 15 days the debtors are to be handed over to the court and credit to the persons concerned is to be stopped; and 3) the banks are to serve one another with credit information.

"Diamond" merchants have come to Zagłębie.
Mr. Anszel Kokotek [?] of Będzin was walking yesterday along Mandoszewer [Modrzejowska?] Street when a stranger approached him and asked him in Russian: "Where is there a bank?" At the same time the stranger told him that he was from Ukraine and had diamonds to sell. Mr. K. ran home with the "good tidings" to his family and told them of the "luck" that had befallen him. The household, having heard the news, agreed to the deal on condition that the "diamonds" be given to experts for appraisal. The "Russian", however, would not agree to that and vanished.

What's Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — Katowice and Królewska Huta.]
Visit of Lazarus Barth.
The member of the Zionist Executive Mr. Lazarus Barth of London stayed on Tuesday in Katowice, where he gave a lecture in the kehilla hall on the subject "The Present-Day Work in Eretz Israel".
In honour of the distinguished guest there assembled representatives of the Katowice kehilla, the rabbis Dr. Vogelmann and Dr. Chameides, city councillors and a large number of guests.
The president of the local "Mizrachi", Mr. David Erlich, greets Mr. Barth (in Hebrew and in Yiddish) and demands that he, as a member of the Executive, give answers concerning the recent events in Eretz Israel. Then Dr. Bester greets him on behalf of the Zionist Organization, and the floor is given to Mr. Barth, who points out that the accusations against the Executive are groundless; there was no pogrom — says the speaker — but a national uprising, incited by the Mohammedan and Christian leaders. The best proof is that the greatest number of victims was in Hebron and in Safed, where yeshiva students perished. The speaker, speaking about English policy, stressed that we will not give up the Balfour Declaration. In conclusion Mr. Barth says that the Jews in the Diaspora should help in the upbuilding of Eretz Israel, so that they may calmly say "Our hands have not shed this blood".
Rabbi Halpern (Kraków) speaks about the tasks of "Mizrachi" and calls for a strong "Mizrachi" organization to be created in Katowice.
Later a banquet was held in the well-known Jewish restaurant "Piccadilly". Speakers: L. Jungster[?], Lion, L. Buchowicz, Besser (non-party Hasidim), Wajgberger[?] ("Hatikvah"), M. Oppenheim ("Tseirei Mizrachi"), Yitzhak Hersh Winer[?], and finally Mr. Barth.
—o—
Rode into the apartment on his four-legged friend.
A resident of Königshütte, Mr. Głowacz, got drunk and wanted to give his family a "surprise"; for this purpose he rode on a horse into his apartment, which is on the first floor.
The four-legged creature kicked about in the room, climbed onto the sideboard and "put things in order".
From the "surprise" the family fainted. The police, who were called in, led the horse's companion off to the station.

Theatre Notes

[Będzin — theatre.] "The World Is Not Ownerless" (Di velt iz keyn hefker), a grand revue performance in 12 scenes, by the Jewish Dramatic Society "Muza" in Będzin.
After the success that the "Muza" society had with "At Night in the Old Marketplace", it got the urge to stage director's productions, to prove that in this field too "Muza" is able to compete.
And what did we see?
We saw stagings, direction and all manner of delicacies[?], and the upshot is that:
— one saw nothing at all. The big programme, no less than 12 scenes, made no satisfactory impression whatsoever, because it is a fact that "the world is indeed not ownerless"..
The direction of the first number, "Kabbalists", is riddled with ignorance; the rebbe's conduct better suits an old-time village Jew.
"Gentlemen" (Raboysay) — not bad; the same credit can also be given to "The World Is Not Ownerless". Best of all — Mr. Chalfan[?].
"The Bridegroom" really was "obscured"; the "what does it teach us" was in its place, but "what he lets us hear, we do not know".
So-so passed "Zhakim" by M. Broderzon. It was a pity to see Yakov Brzeski when "he became a different sort of person"; Brzeski is material for stage artists, but when he becomes "a different person" one loses the desire to hear him.
The last number, "Muza Khalyastre" (the Muza gang), convinced us that the directors of the revue are also businessmen and understand how "to take[?] the public".. They committed, however, a great fault in not advertising the "enticing number" properly..
A large share in the "moral" success belongs to Mr. Compère. Next time he should be provided with a [?] apparatus that will "tickle" the audience..
And last but not least, the true "yasher koach" is deserved by Moshe Apelbaum for his splendid and successful sets.
Ha-Tsofeh.

10th anniversary of the Czeladź Craftsmen's Association

The small community of Jewish craftsmen in Czeladź last Sunday celebrated the jubilee of the 10-year existence of the Craftsmen's Association. In a big city such a celebration goes unnoticed; in a place like Czeladź, however, a holiday mood reigned. Not only craftsmen, small traders and ordinary Jews (except the only Jewish town councillor), but even the "Czeladźnik" [czeladnik — journeyman, or a Czeladź local] and Christian acquaintances celebrated along, listened to cantorial pieces, Yiddish speeches and recitations, and at every glass of vodka shouted "mazel tov"...
Also "taking part" in the celebration were Yossele Rosenblatt, the artist Gadik, singers, beadles, badkhonim (wedding jesters) and the like.
———
The hall is decorated. Over the presidium table hang the portraits of the President of the State, Marshal Piłsudski and others, which the commissioner lent. (Why not also that of some craftsmen's activist?)
The chairman Sz. Braner opens the evening; town councillor dentist Rotsztejn (Sosnowiec) is invited to chair it, and to the presidium — representatives of the Będzin and Dąbrowa craftsmen's associations.
Mr. Rotsztejn gives a short introduction, the "orchestra" plays "Jeszcze Polska" and "Hatikvah", and greetings follow: in the name of the Będzin craftsmen Mr. Fajgenblat[?] greets, from the Czeladź bank — its chairman Mr. Gelbard, from the library — Mr. Sauerbrucht[?], from the Sosnowiec Craftsmen's Association — Mr. Ganzwajch, and Mr. Jakubowicz greets the delegates and guests in the name of the Czeladź Craftsmen's Association.
Then Mr. Fajgenblat lectures on "The soul of craftsmanship"; he points to the decrees threatening the existence of Jewish artisans and calls on the craftsmen to make their souls healthy too and to work in the field of culture.
On unity in the craftsmen's ranks Mr. Ganzwajch lectures, illustrating with facts that only through unity will the Jewish craftsman achieve victory.
The jubilee gradually turns into a "revue show": after every speech, every recitation the "orchestra" pours forth[?] the "klezmer music" and it's "Layehudim" ["The Jews had light"]...
After the end of the festive programme the crowd pours[?] into the material part. A feast is held in the Jewish manner; in the pause between one "course" (potrawka) and the next a singer of Jewish folk songs "steps up", the gramophone (patefon) is not silent either, and the voices of the singer and the gramophone mix together and compete...
The feast was lavish ("as befits a king"); it is only a pity that the initiators did not at the same time fulfil the commandment of dowering a bride... for at such a meal a young couple could have been married off...
The jubilee was a success and will remain a fond memory for the Czeladź artisans.
