The kehilla representation — The hope placed in it when it was constituted, and what is left of it now

The hope that was placed in it when it was constituted, and what is left of it now.
Who does not remember what joy there was in the Jewish street when the Jewish kehilla representation came into being; when we went to elect our representatives, it was simply a holiday in our little Jewish world. Everything smelled of freshness and of full faith that tomorrow in our homely nest [?] would be finer, more pleasant. Back then we were sure that with the creation of our new representation we would feel more human, that the bent shoulders of our wandering and tormented brothers would straighten. Ah, how beautiful the illusions looked on the Jewish horizon. We imagined, after all, that the Jewish kehillot in Poland would be transformed into a proper self-government, where everything would be concentrated. We believed that here would be the centralisation, where hunger and want, loneliness and helplessness, joys and plenty and cheerfulness would all be concentrated. We imagined that there would be the melting pot in which all of many-sided, varied Jewish life would cook together.
So we thought, so we dreamed, so we were sure that we would reach a higher level in our darkened, abnormal life. We were somehow as if convinced that the institution we were creating would bring a different course into our life, which in this way would become more normal, easier and more modern.
When we recall all this, when we cast a glance back at that short past, only then do we see our failure, only then do we feel how far we have fallen.
Not in vain did we place so many hopes in the newly created Jewish kehillot. Having there the representatives of all strata of the population, we wanted all forms of life to be concentrated there and to be improved from there. We understood that the kehilla representation would stand on guard and protect everything that needed protecting. It would — so we thought — spread its wings like an eagle and not allow a single hair of its members to be harmed.
Not to speak of public life — here no one doubted that the representation had arisen first and foremost in order to take into its domain the philanthropic, religious and cultural institutions. It would maintain them, subsidise them and breathe into them the living spirit, the current [?] of life, and therefore we agreed to be duly taxed, provided we got everything from it. We understood that this institution must stand above all institutions, it must stand above all parties. It must serve the interests of all Jewish citizens in the town, and therefore we gave it so much trust and placed so much hope and faith in it.
Of course we now see the failure and the defeat we suffered with the rise of the newly created kehilla representations, and not only can we get nothing from them, they even disrupt Jewish life.
It is interesting that one kehilla representative has spoken out in the columns of our paper about how they "process" there whatever they like and how they turn the wheel there. Ordinarily we thought that the kehilla administration would show the public that everything it does is for the good of the town, and whatever is not favourable to the town it does not do; so we thought and so we understood it ought to be done. But apparently there they no longer reckon with anyone or anything, and simply do whatever they like, whatever impresses the autocrats; apparently there they reckon very much with the fact that they hold power in their hands, and they hold it fast indeed, as once in the days of Russian autocracy.
Were it not so, had our kehilla leaders understood that they must reckon with the town, they would surely have found it necessary to defend themselves, to give explanations, to submit reports, to convene a meeting when there is occasion, where we might hear a word about how the kehilla funds are administered — funds that are collected in quite handsome sums.
The gmina [kehilla] now knows, as they say, of the dead and of the living. Whom do they not tax? They do not let even the smallest slip by; what more do you need — even professional beggars are found on the tax roll (etat list). Moreover, one must not forget that the levies do not amount to just a few złoty, but to really handsome sums, and we are not speaking of the rich but of ordinary citizens who toil hard and bitterly for their livelihood.
On this account they allow themselves to draw up large budgets, and without regard to their size these people still have the audacity to keep increasing them, so that it turns out that it does not bother our kehilla representatives, because they have a good cow and she gives plenty of milk. What is there to be afraid of — more money will be needed? It is not a poor community, after all. Never mind, it will hold out, Będzin can give more money; and that perhaps it cannot, and perhaps need not give even if it could — if only because the institution gives the town nothing at all [printed "ga nisht"] — of this nobody wants to know. Such trifles, alas for our many sins, are not reckoned with at all; when one has power in one's hands there is nothing to talk about — they do as they please and as suits the business [?] and the politics, which is now conducted with so much wisdom and acumen as they never before understood how to apply.
What more do you need: the kehilla representative Mr Lagdner [?] has, in his last two articles in the "Zagl. Tsayt.", characterised traits of their own, from which we see the absurdity and the lawlessness that go on there, and one can only wonder how people keep their mouths shut as if full of water and say nothing when they see what goes on there. Surely there must be enough honest and clean people in the administration who must not allow public money to be so abandoned and treated with such frivolity, as though Jewish money had been picked up in the streets.
Surely there must be people to whom Jewish honour and Jewish existence are still dear and precious, and they must not allow Jewish labour to be turned into chaff. The people who say nothing, who do not protest, must surely know that by this they consent both to the high budgets and to the tactics practised there, about which so much is said in town.
Well and good, had we known that the money was being used for useful things, such as maintaining chadarim, schools, the sick, orphanages, the aged, trade schools, cultural institutions — it would still have been understandable; but unfortunately the kehilla apparatus in Będzin is so helpless that such undertakings cannot even be dreamed of there. On the contrary: what was managed when the town had 3 dozors [members of the synagogue board] they are not capable of even now, with the great apparatus and the large budgets.
A whole town is taxed with quite handsome sums — what do the citizens get from this gmina of ours? What does it provide, and to whom? Whom does it benefit, and what kind of benefit? Let it speak up, by all means; let us hear clear and lofty words from it. But as long as we hear nothing from it, we do not see what the town gets from the large budgets. Is this heavy money really needed in order to pay pensions to the klei kodesh [religious functionaries] and the office [?] staff?
Possibly they do not know what to do with so much money, so they strive to hand out supplements, regardless of the fact that the pensions are for the most part quite handsome; besides, the gmina has fine revenues from shechita [ritual slaughter] and from the chevra kadisha [burial society], from whom they take the money.
The gmina must not permit itself to pay outright luxury pensions in order to fleece the town, which lives now in such hard conditions. Jewish livelihoods are getting ever harder, and if a Jewish institution in which all strata of the population are represented does not spare Jewish money — then who should spare it?
Besides, let it say its word, let us hear why it needs such high budgets, whom it benefits with them and what that benefit consists of. But as long as we do not hear this, as long as it does not say its word — even though the indignation against it in town is so great and so embittered — so long it must not make any large budgets; on the contrary, the present budget must be reduced to a minimum.
It must not be allowed that a Jewish institution in which all strata of the population are represented, and which must remain non-partisan, should overpower [?] its members.
Nowadays Jews work hard and bitterly to earn a groszy; therefore it must not be allowed that unlimited lawlessness should reign and that Jews should be fleeced of ever larger sums so that they may be squandered [?] on who knows what.
It is no longer any secret that a terrible lawlessness reigns in the Będzin gmina; but even lawlessness must have a limit, after all.
R. Les.
I've Got a "Nadzór" [Court Supervision].

[Satirical feuilleton — Zagłębie merchants and the "nadzór" (court supervision of debtors).] By J. Oberżanek [?].
Good sense is a crawler; it always arrives too late. Only after the folly has been committed [?] do you see that you made a mistake. How many follies a man commits before he gets wise! If young men were, the day before the wedding, what they are the day after the wedding, the rabbinical judges would not have to work "night shifts". There would not be such a divorce epidemic... If the voters' good sense arrived at the right time, many of today's town councillors and dozores [kehilla board members] would still be sitting at home to this day... But good sense is a crawler, and always comes a minute too late.
I think one can recognise [?] the Zagłębie "fortunes" [?]. You are not from Honolulu either, you too are from Zagłębie, so you surely know how a Zagłębie merchant works. The Zagłębie merchant recalls the story of that Jewish woman at the kapores ritual: on the eve of Yom Kippur a Jewish woman stands with a hen and swings the hen over her head, swings once, twice — but it is a hen after all, a living creature.. such an accident can happen.. The woman shouts to her husband:
— Tsadok Ber, just take a look at what has happened here, what does one do?
— What should one do? the husband answers her, wipe it off and keep swinging..
The Zagłębie merchants behave exactly like that woman: wipe it off and keep swinging...
When did all this hold [?]? When one swung it over one's own spodik [fur hat], when putting the woman [?] up for the debt was a rarity — then one really could wipe it off and keep swinging. But today, when it has become a general swindle-swing, when everyone swings, when a time of "there was not a house where there was not one dead" has come, when every merchant from the biggest to the smallest answers "Nadaj mi do daszka" [?], when everyone knows how to get a "nadzór" — that woman's remedy at kapores no longer helps...
Yes, about the "nadzór" in particular: you are not newcomers, you are merchants with a past, you have already been through all kinds of troubles and scares, inflations, stabilisations, stagnations and plain machinations, you have already had various times with various currencies: Russian fivers with "spoons"... zheshkes and banes, you traded in German "millions" and "milliards" and still had nothing to make the Sabbath with... But "nadzór"! Who ever dreamed of such "well-made" [?] novelties? A merchant dreamed of one thing only: — flight! If things did not go right for you, if the "kikhns" [?] started one after another, you didn't ponder any questions, you quickly sang [?] the second verse of the Song of Songs; the bit of merchandise you had [?] — as a charm against the evil eye — you transferred, and the sign was freshly repainted; whatever, whenever — you gave "50 kopecks" and drove on. So indeed your sign was repainted more than once. Once your wife stood on the sign, once your mother-in-law, at worst your servant girl...
That was when things went smoothly for you. But what was the verdict when your creditors were opponents [?] and began to defeat [?] you? When they put you through the wash? When every day they made a black Sabbath for you and stuck names on you: bankrutnik, agwecer [?], bandit, treyf gut, swołocz [scoundrel], parch [boor], sheygets — and who talks about the fact that among your guests there was another Jewish woman too, and every day you had to have other windowpanes put in — then, brother, you were in for chopped troubles, then the business turned out for you like "cupping glasses".
All that was once. Once one had to endure such troubles and calamities. Once they called you: bankrutnik, agwecer, treyf gut. Once you had to repaint the sign and put up your wife. Today the world is cleverer, much cleverer. People have grown wise. Why let oneself be compromised? Who tells me to repaint signs, who? Why prolongations? What do I need bankruptcy for and what do I need "agwecer"? — A "nadzór" — and enough!..
I tell it now with joy: so there I was standing a few weeks ago in my shop. The door does not rest: one creditor in, a second creditor out, each with a "płachta" [?] in his hand. Own [?] and "customers'" (read: "childish"...) — the goods lie in chopped heaps [?], piled up [?] on the shelves, I am thinking about flight, in whose name to register my "majątek" [property]. In the middle of all this an idea comes to me: you fool, son of Pickwood, why should you lie down with a healthy head in a sick bed? What good are all these stories to you? If you go bankrupt, you will have to settle anyway. And where will you get the settlement from? Why shouldn't you do as everyone does — "nadzór"! Ah, but how do I come to a "nadzór"? How does such a little bedbug come to a "nadzór"? It is surely made for the big carp-heads, for those who keep books, who can show the "liabilities" and the "assets". Well, what do I know — nonsense, I thought to myself — a big deal, books, an "important" matter — "assets" with "liabilities".
Why should I tell you much — a few days later I had books with a "balance sheet", with "assets" and "liabilities". Under "liabilities" I entered the debts to my wife's dressmaker, to the butcher for half a year of meat, to the milk-woman, to the pharmacist and other "passive positions". Under "assets" I counted: the credit with the "pomocnik" that I took "na raty" [in instalments] and which will be paid off, God willing, in the year 1932; my wife's fur [?] coat, over which the furrier shouts to this day: the money or the coat; a plot [?] that I will get as an inheritance when my mother-in-law, after 120 years, closes her eyes; a paid-up grave plot I bought myself during my lifetime; and other "ruchomości" [movables] and "nieruchomości" [real estate], all "wartościowe" [valuable] things which must go into the "assets".
Having the finished "balance sheet", I turned to the "sąd" [court] about a "nadzór". I showed "czarne na białym" [black on white] that my "assets" exceed the "liabilities", and both by law and by equity a "nadzór" is due to me.
Now I am already a Jew with a "nadzór" in his pocket. I laugh at and whistle at my creditors, the robbers. The "sąd" appointed a commissioner, a gentile commissioner at that, with a pair of big stiff moustaches. Now I am no longer I. The commissioner with the stiff moustaches has the floor. A creditor comes with a "płachta" — I send him to the commissioner; the sequestrator comes with his briefcase — I give a "przekaz" [referral] to the stiff-moustached gentleman. The kasarnik [?] comes with slips — the commissioner deals with him. What more do you need: even my wife, my own wife, when she comes to me about "drobne" [small] matters, I hand her over to the gentile... The gentile with the stiff moustaches "zastępuje" [replaces] me in all fields. What was supposed to be mine — let it be his. Where is it written that I must talk [?] my heart out and get a swollen heart — the commissioner is [?]!
A fine thing, I tell you, the "nadzór". Only now have I come to my senses. But better late than never.
Small remarks on big matters.

[Sosnowiec — public services, telephone, post office, municipal library.]
Punctuality towards the public
How many times do we Zagłębie citizens get worked up at the telephone: we take the receiver in hand, put it to our ear — and the operator does not answer. How many times, when we lose patience and try to tell her a few harsh words because she allows herself to disregard our time like that, she lets us talk and does not even hear us out — how much disdain that is [?]: that is how clients are treated. It is not enough that she does not perform her function properly; she still has the audacity to belittle the clients by not even wanting to hear the subscriber out.
It is known that the telephone serves for instant handling of matters; but since the clerks pay no regard to this, the telephone company ought to react to it, and since it does not react, the service gets worse and worse — which, incidentally, does not surprise us at all.
Telephone subscribers who are not served properly should therefore turn to the director of the telephone company and inform him what lawlessness reigns among the operators when it comes to connecting one firm with another; it is possible that there [?] they do not know how far this lawlessness goes. The public must not allow the clerks to belittle their subscribers like this.
The telephone company disconnects the telephone as soon as the subscription fee has not been paid by the 15th; so, just as we have duties towards it, so the company must have duties towards its subscribers.
In Poland they want to introduce order in everything: as soon as a tax is not paid on time, one must already pay a fine the next day. They want to teach the public to be punctual in everything — while we do not see the institutions punctually performing their functions towards the public.
If one wants citizens to understand the true meaning of punctuality, the correct sense of the saying "time is money", one must first see to it oneself to be punctual and steady; and only then, once there is a well-schooled citizenry that knows it is served punctually, can one begin to think of adopting penalties against those who are treated fairly and punctually. But as long as this has not been put into practice, not only can one not punish the citizens, but on the contrary — there must be obligation and responsibility, and one must show the citizens that one is punctual towards them, and not demand precisely the opposite...
How does one get a post-office box?
For a good few years now it has been impossible to get a post-office box here. From year to year the question is postponed until after the New Year: when during the year you come to the post office to "intervene" about a post-office box, you are told first of all that there are none. But when the clerk sees that it really matters to you, he takes "pity" on you and tells you to wait until the New Year. When you come at the appointed time, he answers that there is still no box for you, and when you complain to him: what does this mean, sir [?], you yourself told me to wait until after the New Year — you get the answer from him that he owes nobody anything [lit. he owes God his soul]: he merely thought that there would be firms that would no longer keep their post-office boxes, and since nobody has returned the keys, it is a sign that there are no boxes available.
That is how such a matter gets settled. It seems a trifle, and yet it is so important for the town. What does it mean that for several years one cannot get a post-office box — and this is, after all, something that brings the post office clean income. Surely it is not hard to set up a certain number of boxes, by which the question would be solved and the post office would receive a proper income.
And besides, one must not forget that the town is not getting smaller but bigger, and a post office must have a supply of boxes at its disposal, so that one need not wait so long for them and in the end not get them at all.
It is nonsense that over such a trifle one should have to intervene at all and write in the press; abroad this, or similar matters, would look ridiculous. In the big world, in free Europe, one could not comprehend that anyone should have to deal with such trifles.
Upon my life, it is high time that we became a little more agile here, and that care be taken that one should not have to intervene or resort to the system of string-pulling over such trifles.
It is high time that in Sosnowiec one could get a post-office box as easily as one gets a postage stamp.
On the municipal library.
Sosnowiec is progressing; whoever has not been here for several years does not recognise the town. One sees that the town is being managed and that efforts are made to give it a modern European look. We perhaps notice it less, since we are here all the time, but a visitor sees it very clearly the moment he enters the town.
One sees a row of new streets with wide roadways, and even the old ones have been re-cut and look different. Above all they are cleaner, and the sanitary conditions of recent times play a great role.
The 20th century in which we live plays one of the most important roles here. Mankind can no longer live as it lived in former times, decades ago. Time moves on, time cries out that it be reshaped, recast and recarved, for we have entered another period; mankind is being formed differently and must therefore find itself in different living conditions. What was will not come back; we progress and march steadily forward.
Culture too is progressing. Today a person cannot live as in the past without a book and without a newspaper. These have become articles almost of first necessity; it is not as before, when one picked up a book or a newspaper only when one had time, and who allowed himself such a luxury but a rich and well-fed man who no longer had anything to worry about.
Now — who does not need a book? Not to mention a newspaper: it has truly become an article of first necessity, for every sensible person, however poor he may be, must first thing in the morning look through the newspaper, and only then, after reading the newspaper, does he know how to plan his day.
Our municipal self-government understood the importance of this very timely and created a municipal library, which is maintained entirely by the Magistrat [town council].
Of course the Magistrat deserves a "yishar koach" [well done] for this cultural work; but the attention of our Jewish councillors must be drawn to the fact that the library holds only Polish books and newspapers. And since the Jewish population occupies quite a respectable place in the town, and bears the burden of the town together with its Christian neighbours, it would be only fair that there should also be some Jewish [Yiddish] books and newspapers there, where Jewish youth could come and have its spiritual food in its own language.
If one wants to be as cultured as other people, one must suit cultural needs to each according to his spirit and wishes, according to his language and means.
The Jewish councillors must see to it that the municipal library has Jewish books and newspapers for the Jewish population too.
Dr. Papuri.
What I Heard, What I Saw.

By Ben Amotz — caught on the fly and handed to the press.

His Majesty — the Gramophone.
The gramophone, which only recently took the place of honour at every kind of celebration, is gradually losing its station in the larger cities. The enormous progress of technology is pushing out the "magic box" — the gramophone.
But in the smaller places, and among them the shtetls, the gramophone is still a great aristocrat: whenever there is a celebration, the gramophone works wonders[?], for "there is no celebration without a gramophone".
At the 10th anniversary jubilee of the Czeladź artisans the gramophone too played a great role: before the opening, after the speeches, before the greetings, after the declarations, before the meal, after the tsimmes[?] — Yossele Rosenblatt and Garik "delighted"[?] the guests.
Around the "box" bustles Reb Shmelke, the owner himself; his face beams with joy when the public enjoys itself. His good wife too, sitting together with other women on the "gallery", calls out to her husband:
— "Shmelke, turn on that piece, the record[?] with the balloons"...
Reb Shmelke fulfils his wife's wish, puts on a record, out "comes" "Garik with balloons", and the public rolls about with laughter...

A Breakage in the Eggs...
A young man enters the editorial office. On the tip of his nose sprouts[?] a sparse yellow little beard; on his head — a battered[?] peaked cap; on his body hang 2 long garments, a Sabbath kapote and a "weekday" garment.
— What do you want, young man?
— I want to put something in the paper.
— So?!
— That I have a breakage in the eggs.
— Speak more clearly! Are you an egg merchant?
— Give me a little time and I will tell you how great my ruin is.
I am from Wolbrom, a child of a respectable family, I sat in the beit midrash, was esteemed[?] as a fine lad; I made a match from Sosnowiec, a really lucky match; I received a handsome dowry, a house[?], board [kest] and other good things.
After the wedding my father-in-law wanted to secure the dowry. Well, all sorts of plans were considered until we came to the conclusion that the best business is
— to buy up eggs for the winter, because according to the prophecies of the astronomers this year will be a very hard winter, with stronger frosts than in the year 1929, and in such frosts the price of eggs can go up even[?] to 80 groszy apiece...
But "man thinks and the Almighty steers". In Kislev it is actually 5 degrees warm, just like in Italy, and the eggs are sweating in the lime...
— Well, what do you want from our editorial office?
— "I want you to write in the paper that nobody should believe what the 'star-gazers' say; they have ruined me. For when merchants of textiles, leather, haberdashery and other branches suffer from the crisis, they have marketable goods that always keep their value; but what am I to do with my lime-eggs?
— Oy vey, oy vey, that I should live to see such a breakage in the eggs...

He Is "Consistent"...
He is known as a socialist. From head to toe — a leftist; give him just the slightest push and his mouth sprays fire at the editorial office[?] [probably: the reaction], at clericalism; he does not even spare the "notke"[?].
Of the Jewish press he recognizes only the "Folks-Tsaytung" as the sole organ that "opens the minds of the benighted masses" and exposes the lie of "Jewish clericalism"...
Yesterday[?] I meet him, out of breath he is running across the street, clearly in a great hurry.
— Where are you running? I ask him curiously.
— You must excuse me, I have no time to stop with you; I was invited for 3 o'clock in the afternoon, now it is already nearly 7 in the evening[?], and who knows whether I am not late?
— For instance, for what?
— The "Et Yeshurun"[?] society is celebrating a siyum ha-sefer [completion of a Torah scroll] today; well, one must also write a letter...

Reb Yankev Pays...
Hugo Bettauer's work "The City Without Jews" was filmed; in certain countries the characteristic film was not permitted to be shown — they were afraid of the truth there...
— What brought this up?
I was sitting in a theatre where a sports event [impreza] was taking place. The whole hall was almost entirely filled by our brethren, the children of Israel. And who performed the programme?! Hakoah members and Maccabi members; I saw the same gymnasts a few days ago — no comparison with what they, the Hakoah and Maccabi people, showed this time. It was "gevurah she-bi-gevurah" [might within might], especially the Maccabi (1st men's group), first-class acrobats, simply flying through the air and "climbing up smooth walls"...
The 1st women's group of "Hakoah" too performed "paradoxes"[?]. The rhythmic dance with the clubs [maczugi] they had to repeat as an encore at the request[?] of the commander, and eyes stared, lips smacked: "Ach, jak ma śliczne ..." [garbled Polish: "Oh, how lovely..."]...
And I thought to myself — what would the nations of the world look like if they did not have the Jewish people, which has taken upon itself the mission of spreading culture, science, and above all — Reb Yankev pays...
Yes, now I have the answer why the film "The City Without Jews" was banned...

I Am a "Blat" Hasid...
Two Jews get into the tram; the smell of their clothes "tells" us that we have cattle dealers before us; later we also learn that the Jews live in Dąbrowa. Because of the crush in the carriage our 2 personages are separated[?], but that does not stop them from conducting the dialogue out loud:
— Did you do any business in Mysłowice?
— I bought a heifer [jałówka].
— How much the kilo?
— Two złoty; I think she's worth it, the peasant told me the heifer is "wychowana" [well raised].
— Pfui, pfui, pfui, you're going to talk me into believing she's "wychowana"? — A "wypachana"[?] cow has 4...
At this "ethical" expression the faces of the female sex present in the same carriage turn red; they bow their heads in shame and murmur something quietly...
The connoisseur of "well-raised" cows has moved on to Hasidism. I — he says — am a "blat" Hasid [a shrewd, well-connected one]; nevertheless I like the "Aguda" [Agudas Yisroel]; they, the "Agudniks", are also shrewd fellows; I do with them what I want, but they get something from me too: I am a member [członek] of their bank, and every morning, before I drive the cattle out to market, I give a few groszy to the Lublin yeshiva.
— Yes, yes, a fine bunch the "Aguda"[?], shrewd Hasidim — as I live...

A "Children's Performance".
We really are an "Atah bechartanu" ["Thou hast chosen us"] people: in no other nation or tongue does one see such frivolity as among us Jews. We run after every novelty, imitate all foreign customs and usages, and the end is that every good-for-nothing leads us up the garden path...
A small poster appeared in the street: — Sunday morning — a children's performance at the "Corso". Well, well, there began a commotion, a running about, a crush at the box office; mothers gave up their lunch just so as not to be late for the "przedstawienie w Corso", and the hall was, thank God, full of Jewish children.
As for[?] the matter itself? — a word is superfluous. I am only curious what the same mothers would have said if they were taken in by such Jewish "singers" and "keks"[?]...
— A goyish question! At no Jewish performance would there have been such a rush...
Let Us Create a Fund for Jewish Emigration

Heavy, dark clouds have descended low over the great Jewish community of 3 million in Poland.
On all sides the foundations of Jewish livelihood, of the Jewish economic way of life, are breaking and bursting.
The Jewish unemployed worker is dying of hunger; the Jewish artisan is being stifled within his 4 walls [lit. "4 corners"], because of the shortage of work, from competition and from the heavy burden of taxes. The Jewish "luftmensch" roams from fair to fair[?] across empty worlds; things have already become so bad and so tight that even the laths and props that are wedged[?] and set under the tottering edifice of the Jewish economy in Poland are bursting.
And among all these unfortunate and helpless people one single word lies on the mind and on the tongue: emigrate — run wherever one's eyes may lead, if only to save oneself from the locked box that floats without an oar and without a guide[?] over the raging sea-waves.
One must admit that the Jewish emigration societies that we have created stand under proper public control and carry out their difficult work with the greatest seriousness and devotion. They give information and advice, and mediate between relatives on the other side of the ocean. Now, however, one must take a step further and create the possibility for the emigrant to receive also a smaller or larger cash grant towards travel expenses. A people's fund must be created to support Jewish emigrants.
The question of creating a national fund for Jewish emigration has now become very topical, because cases are now multiplying that bring a shocking demoralisation into Jewish life.
It now happens very often that a Jewish emigrant who has somehow already made all his travel preparations and lacks only the little money for the expense sells off during the night a whole shop of goods, borrowed and snatched together; we know of cases in which Jews who had never touched another person's penny "steal" several hundred zł. All because they lack money for the travel expenses.
Such money manipulations, however, become very dangerous, both for the "grabbers" themselves and for dozens of innocent Jews who thereby lose their credit and trust. The "grabber" himself may also suffer from it, since it may well happen that an enemy of his in the new homeland will exploit the fact of the "grabbing" and damage his name and reputation among those around him at his new place of work.
Therefore the idea must penetrate deep into everyone's mind that the matter of emigration has become, for the Jewish community in Poland, a national matter in the full sense of the word. Everywhere the idea of creating a people's fund for Jewish emigration must be proclaimed.
First of all, our existing aid institutions abroad must be interested in the matter. Everywhere, in all Jewish private homes and businesses, collection boxes ["pushkes"] must be hung up[?] for small donations to the emigration fund.
Let us not forget that the vanguard of Jewish emigration is made up of capable young people, or of skilled, able-bodied and work-willing families. Such emigrants have a great chance of quickly establishing themselves in the new homeland and in a short time turning from receivers into givers.
Let us hope that this burning and topical question of creating a national cash fund for needy Jewish emigrants will be placed as the first item on the agenda of all Jewish public institutions.
J. Rykles.
J. W. Goethe — "Found"

[A Yiddish translation of Goethe's poem "Gefunden".]
I strolled in the wood,
hither and thither,
to seek nothing at all —
that was my intent.

There in the shade
I caught sight of a flower,
sparkling like stars,
charming and fair.

I want to pluck it,
then she says with a smile:
why should I wilt,
man, where is your sense?

So I dig and I dig
and take her out with her roots,
and carry it to the garden
of my own house.

I plant it again
in a fitting, quiet spot,
her branches grow fresh,
and she — blooms on still.

(Translated for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" by Yosef Perlberger.)
A discovery that deserves to be welcomed.

Until the year 1930 the accepted opinion was that the Jewish press in Poland plays the role of coming out in public with our demands. Through the press we demand our rights in all fields; with the help of the press protests are made against all the actions done to us, both from within and from without, internally and externally. But that the Jewish press has the task of strengthening Jewishness — that we did not know.
We owe this sensational discovery to the fact that the Agudah organ "Yidish Tageblat" has been privileged to celebrate the jubilee of its hundredth issue.
In honour of this great victory and salvation, greetings were printed in that holy organ on Friday of the weekly portion Vayechi, among which we also read the following very characteristic greeting from the Rabbi of Będzin, may he live long:
[In Hebrew:] B"H. To the editorial board of "Das Yidishe Tageblat". I hereby send my small donation for the strengthening of the journal, for it is a matter of immeasurable greatness, and there is no other way to strengthen Judaism except through the journal, since the other periodicals are a deadly poison even for the old, all the more so for children. And this is alluded to in the verse of Isaiah 44: "Yet now hear, O Jacob my servant, and Israel etc. For I will pour etc. upon thy offspring, and they shall spring up etc. One shall say etc." — that is, through this[?] will be fulfilled: "I will pour etc. and they shall spring up". Through this "one shall say, I am the Lord's" — the Agudat Israel in general and the Cheder Yesodei ha-Torah in particular, which is entirely the Lord's. "And another shall call himself by the name of Jacob" — this is the Beit Yaakov; "and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the Lord" — this is the journal, made in kashrut, without heresy and licentiousness, God forbid; "and surname himself by the name of Israel" — the Tzeirei Agudat Israel and Poalei Agudat Israel. And whoever has a share in this great matter — through him all of Judaism will be strengthened, and there is no measure to his reward in this world and the next. With greetings, writing for the honour of the Torah and of Israel, Chanoch Tzvi HaKohen Lewin, Av Beit Din of the holy community of Będzin and the district.
The translation [into Yiddish] reads as follows:
"To the honoured editorial board of 'Das Yidishe Tageblat'.
I send my small donation for the purpose of strengthening the existence of the newspaper, which is an immeasurably great necessity. And there is no other way to strengthen Jewishness except through the newspaper. For other newspapers are a deadly poison even for the old, and especially for the young.
And this is indicated in Isaiah, verse 94 [sic; chapter 44]: 'Yet now hear, O Jacob my servant, and Israel.' The meaning is that 'name of Jacob' means — Beit Yaakov. 'His hand unto the Lord' means precisely the newspaper that is made in kashrut, without heresy, God forbid. And 'surname himself by the name of Israel' — means the 'Tzeirei Agudat Israel' and the 'Poalei Agudat Israel'.
And whoever supports the newspaper supports all of Jewishness, and there is no measure at all to how great his reward will be in this world and in the world to come.
In the name of the honour of the Torah and of Israel,
Chanoch Tzvi HaKohen Lewin,
Av Beit Din of Będzin and the district."
Everybody Just Pushes!

[Sosnowiec — humour, satirical monologue.] Monologue of a Jew with a cut-off ear. Transmitted by B. K.

There pushes his way into my home a Jew with a blind eye and a cut-off ear.
— [—] take [?] from you a few [—] minutes
— [—] no more than a few minutes [—] you)
— Thank you. I only want to pour out my heart to you... I'll hand my whole life over into your hands, from the cradle to this very day. Listen to me with your head.
Nine months after my father's wedding I felt very cramped in my first dwelling; I really didn't know where to put myself... and the air there wasn't so [—] ["poygldig" [?]] either.. So I thought it over: once and for all, I must get out into the bright world, let there be an end, a finish to it! Enough of being kept in the dark!
When my mother found out [?] what I was planning to do, she started screaming, crying "gevalt", climbing the smooth walls, called a midwife to help, but I listened to her like to last year's snow and with all my strength tore my way out into God's world.
— Already then I understood that freedom is something you have to take yourself...
When I beheld God's world, my father was walking around the house agitated and grumbling...
It was two o'clock after midnight, on a Monday, the nineteenth day of the month of Kislev. In the house there was a bitter cold.
So I burst out crying — my first cry on the sinful earth.
And since my good mother could not bear my crying, she promptly stopped up my mouth with her breast.
That was my first dairy meal..
From that time on a life of pushing began for me:
My mother asked my father to hold me in his arms a little — he pushed me away at once: no thank you, no thank you!
Mother wanted to hand me over to Aunt Pesha — the aunt pushed me away too: she can "manage" ["berreyen" [?]] without me, she said.
When I turned eight, they pushed my father out of the flat together with the household.
My poor father settled in a new flat not far from the hekdesh [?] [the poorhouse], and there a new crowding began — a mere trifle: eleven souls in one room! There was constant pushing: the strong pushed the weak, the weak the even weaker, but me — everyone pushed; I stood in everyone's way.
A little later Mother pushed Father out to go and earn something, and Father, out of great anger, pushed all of us out..
When I once went, on a Friday, to the bathhouse and didn't have a "tsenerl" [10-groszy coin], the bath attendant pushed me out.
I came into the beth midrash to warm up — the shammes pushed me out.
I went to the synagogue to hear the cantor with the choristers — the householders pushed me out.
I presented myself for the "prizyv" [Russian army call-up] — I was sick and pale, didn't have the measurements, neither body nor life — Nikolaike [Tsar Nicholas] pushed me out.
My father saw that I was a shlimazl, a ne'er-do-well, and pushed me out of the house altogether: off to Sosnowiec — he said — and become a man!
So I went — did I have a choice?
I reckoned that here, in Sosnowiec, they wouldn't push me, but I was mistaken.
First I landed here with a fellow townsman of ours, a melamed on Tshasna [?] Street [ul. Ciasna, "Narrow Street"], and it was so cramped there that they pushed me out.
I went to look for work in a factory; I was just about to get work when a gentile worker pushed me out.
I wanted to ride the Magidushev [?] bus ["samochód"] — there too it was a crush — only pushing.
Once I went to the theatre to see the "Vilner" [the Vilna Troupe] — there too they pushed.
I came out of the theatre — they pushed me again.
I walked in the street — they pushed me off the pavement.
When I turned 32, a matchmaker pushed his way to me, a Jew with a tiny little beard and a sharpened "tsigl" [?] [tongue], and pushed into my hands a maiden of 42, sickly, ugly, pockmarked.
They pushed the misfortune in and off they went — as if into water!
Two weeks after the wedding, one fine bright day, a father-in-law and a mother-in-law pushed their way in to me.
And as soon as they had pushed their way in, they started nagging and nagging me, day and night, so long and so wide until... until... they pushed me out of my own home.
I went to the editorial office, wanted to tell of my misfortune — the writers pushed me out.
Strange people, these writers! They hate it when someone pesters [?] them, when someone takes up a little of their time.. There are no decent people among you.. What do you say, huh?..
Well, I saw that there was no end to it, that the little Jew with the cut-off ear could talk and talk like this and never stop, so I slowly opened the door, grabbed him by the collar and pushed him out..
When he was already in the street, he said to me:
There, as you see, that's how one pushes the years along — only they push me..
A Letter from Kraków

Echo of the Zionist conference. — The People's University — Results of the „Keren Hayesod“ campaign, — The Vilna Troupe.
The conference of the General Zionist Organisation of Western Galicia and Silesia has taken place, with the participation of President Nahum Sokolow. Sokolow's stay and his masterly speeches at the conference were a spiritual revival for Kraków Jewry. The conference left a strong impression and serves as the subject of heated discussions. Noteworthy is the position of Dr. Y. Thon on Jewish politics in Poland and his statement on this question. In his speech on the situation in Zionism and on the policy of the Jewish parliamentary representation, Dr. Thon declared: „The policy of the majority is a purposeless[?], irrational policy, and if the policy of assimilation was not honest but healthy, the present one (hear, hear!) is neither healthy nor honest, nor Jewish nor Zionist; all the speeches delivered in the Sejm are monologues that nobody listens to and that nobody cares about at all.“
A great impression was also made by Dr. Schwarzbart's appearance at the conference against „Hashomer Hatzair“. In sharp words Dr. Schwarzbart presented the ideology of „Hashomer Hatzair“, insisting[?] that it borders very closely on quite extreme left-wing groupings. The move — as was to be expected — provoked a reaction. Replies have appeared pointing out that „Hashomer“ — contrary to Dr. Schwarzbart's arguments — stands on the platform of the working Land of Israel, fights assimilation and serves as a constant reservoir for the pioneering aliyah. (This concerns „Hashomer Hatzair“ in Galicia and not in Congress Poland.)
The People's University.
The Zionist academic youth has recently set about organising a people's university, and in this way to fulfil part of its debt to the Jewish population, which with its material and moral support made it possible to build the Jewish Academic House and to found a number of self-help institutions for the Jewish academic youth. The lectures will deal with general scientific and Zionist matters. The first lecture was given by editor Berkelhammer on Jewish nationalism and internationalism. The participation of the most prominent personalities of the Jewish population of Kraków allows one to hope that the university will fulfil its duties.
Keren Hayesod campaign.
The Keren Hayesod campaign, led by the leaders of the local Zionists and members of the Jewish Agency, ended with brilliant success. The number of declarations [pledges] tripled, but in proportion to Będzin the sum collected is still small. Kraków is now preparing for a large campaign for the Palestine Workers' Fund.
The Vilna Troupe.
For some time the Vilna Troupe has been staying in Kraków, enjoying great success thanks to its new repertoire and thanks to the fact that the Jewish public now shows greater understanding for Jewish literature and art.
Eliyahu Gertner.
To Our Esteemed Readers

Our newspaper, which has reached a proper popularity, penetrates all strata of the Jewish population and is read by the simple Jew and by the intellectual — it is therefore required to take a place in the literary world as well. We have a rich circle of readers who are not content with local matters alone, such as articles and feuilletons on Zagłębie life, but want to enjoy literature and art.
For this reason we will also set aside a place for literature, where the best works of our young talents, especially from Zagłębie, will be gathered. In this section literary problems will be discussed, and everything that happens in the literary world will find an echo here.
The first attempt will be made in the next issue, in which a splendid article entitled[?] „Freedom“ by the well-known philosopher and poet Prof. Fleischman will be printed, together with other literary works by local young talents.
—o—
„Varshe“ [Warsaw] — a new monthly.
The first issue of the new monthly „Varshe“ has come off the press.
The name alone already gives the character of the periodical. It is a journal devoted entirely to Jewish economic, social and cultural life in the capital, as well as to the history of the Jews in Warsaw.
„Varshe“ appears under the editorship of Lazar Kahan with the collaboration of the most eminent Jewish historians, economists, publicists and communal workers.
The first issue contains, among others, the following articles: Adolf Peretz: Jan Bloch and the Jewish Question; Dr. E. Ringelblum: When did Jews settle in Warsaw; Dr. Gershon Levin: S. An-ski in Warsaw; Y. Grünbaum: Some memories about Kriastek[?]; Clara Young: My first appearance in Warsaw; Adolf Truskier: The problems of Jewish commerce; Lazar Kahan: Warsaw Jews in finance, industry and trade, etc. There are also articles about „ORT“, the Artisans' Bank, the oldest society (chevra) in Warsaw, etc.
The issue is handsomely and aesthetically produced and costs only 50 gr. as a single copy.
Address of the editorial office and administration: Warsaw, Nowolipki 32, apt. 19.
Theatre Notes

„Yidn-shtot“ [The Jewish Town], a drama in 3 acts by Aaron Zeitlin, [—][?], performed by the Vilna Troupe in Będzin and Sosnowiec.
These are the old differences, the old struggle between the two outlooks of the „heaven-man“ and the „earth-man“, which occurs in the life of mankind; every generation makes and lives through this struggle, only in different forms and other nuances.
And when theoretical considerations meet a real fact in reality, it becomes more prominent and clearer to us.
That is how it happens in every generation: it always repeats itself, the same content, the same troubles, only the forms — different, perhaps more modern — move[?] along with the times.
Powerless, helpless, the „Jewish town“ stands at a loss. Frightened stands the „nest“, stretching out its hands and its eyes to all four corners of the heavens — whence will help come?
In a time of trouble every advice is good, and one grasps at it as at a last[?] rescue.
For the young kabbalist Elikum (the „heaven-man“) earthly sufferings are only a crystallisation for the soul, „and when the evil hour comes“, the whole „nest“ rises together with him to a divine height, where the enemy has no dominion.
But the „earth-man“ (Lipman), who calls on them to straighten their backs and to stand up to the enemy with sticks[?], iron and stones — gets the consent of the „nest“.
The contrast between the doctrines takes shape here, and the author shows us here how wrong both extreme directions are.
Quite different is the path taken by the young kabbalist as an altruist, who already in the first days after his wedding to the young and beautiful Gitkhen[?] sees his personal happiness in sacrificing himself as an offering for the community.
The dramatic moments in the play are not so strong, but on the other hand they are real, such as constantly repeat themselves in life.
Thus we know the „city notables“ as our well-known everyday guests, who bow down before the squire and [—][?], tremble lest the victim who heroically sacrifices himself for them should, God forbid, have regrets, are afraid — the kabbalist may yet become a saint...
The Vilna players distinguished themselves as always with their ensemble, especially Mr. Kamen as the jester, Mr. Weislitz as Elikum, Mrs. Orleska as Gitkhen[?].
And from the heart we thank the Vilna players, who gave us true spiritual enjoyment with their acting.
M. Ts.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: From the Hapless City Council

[Będzin — City council.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 24 Tevet 5690 — Piątek 24 stycznia 1930 [Friday, 24 January 1930].)
Będzin
From the hapless city council.
Jewish councillors get a "lesson"..
On Thursday and Tuesday city-council sessions took place. At the sessions, which took several hours, not a single item of the agenda was dealt with. The reason for this is the "urgent" motions that the "socialists" of the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] push forward, provoking long discussions, and the end is that before the agenda is reached the city council loses its quorum. That is what happened on Thursday and Tuesday. The difference is that Thursday's session was "broken up" by the BB [BBWR, the pro-government Non-Party Bloc] and the Endeks [National Democrats], and Tuesday's session — by our own councillors, who are finally beginning to understand that they should not be "more papal than the pope" and should not always be among the first hand-raisers for the "urgent socialist" motions. At this session the Jewish councillors once again got a lesson that when it is a matter of the tittle of a yod [the slightest Jewish matter], a front forms from the extreme right to the extreme left...
Such a thing did indeed happen at the last session, during the motion of councillor Jakubowicz that the resolution on keeping the "rezures" [barbershops?] open on the second day of their holiday [Christmas] be revised. Well, well, a caterwauling began; not only the "Agudah"-ławnik [municipal board member; ironic label] Hetmańczyk with his comrades, the "democratic" BB[?], but even our ally the director "complained" that "the Jews want to legalise illegal things in Poland"..
The Jewish councillors were apparently frightened by the all-round Catholic offensive and left the session.
———
Thursday's session, chaired by the president Mr. Fürstenberg, opened with an urgent motion of the PPS that the city council should apply to the Minister of Labour to change the instructions issued concerning relief for the unemployed.
Around this motion a discussion developed that lasted about an hour and a half. In the end the Endeks and the BB left the session and no quorum remained.
———
Tuesday's session was "rich" in urgent motions. The chairman Mr. Ehrlich opens the session and announces that the following motions and interpellations have been submitted: 1) from the PPS, relief for the unemployed; 2) an interpellation of the Jewish "club" [caucus] about the fee for trading in the market halls; 3) an interpellation of the same "club" asking why the magistrate [municipal executive] did not exempt the academics [students] from paying tax on the entertainment they organised; 4) an urgent motion of the PPS that the city council should react to the false and tendentious reports on the city council in the "Kurier Zachodni"; 5) an urgent motion of the P.Z. [Poale Zion] faction that the magistrate should carry out a registration of the unemployed who had been employed in smaller workshops; and 6) from Jakubowicz and others, to revise the resolution of 17 December [grudzień] concerning the rezures.
In reply to the Jewish interpellations vice-president Mr. Rubinlicht answers that 1) the matter of the fee on the halls has been settled — the traders will pay the same sum as at the old market, and 2) the academics are not a philanthropic institution.
A heated discussion developed over Rotenberg's motion. Speakers were: Rotenber[g], Feiner, ławnik Goldsztajn, who offers an amendment that the unemployed artisans, who suffer from the crisis and need relief, should also be registered. In the same sense spoke also Garczarczyk[?]. The Jewish artisan — he says — is starving and nobody cares about his fate.
On Mr. Rubinlicht's motion the matter is sent to the committee for general affairs.
The last urgent motion of the Jewish councillors, to revise the resolution on keeping rezures open on the second day of their holiday, set off a fire among the non-Jewish councillors. Hetmańczyk and Laskowski stormed that the Jews want to carry out an "assassination attempt" on the barbershops, and Dir. Błażejewicz shouted that "they want to legalise thefts".
A proper reply was given by ławnik Goldsztajn and (vice-)president[?] Mr. Rubinlicht, who pointed out to the gentlemen that they should not make a "Jewish question" out of such a matter as shaving..
Tempers flared, and the Jewish councillors "broke up" the session.
The comrades of the PPS then threatened that they would take revenge..
The lawsuit with the power station won.

As we have already reported, the management of the power station (elektrownia) in Małobądz brought a lawsuit against the Ministry, which had granted the concession to the local municipal power station.
The case was heard last Friday by the State Tribunal, which upheld the Ministry's decision.
Activity at the Talmud Torah is becoming normal.

At the last meeting of the Talmud Torah committee it was decided that, so that the members may become acquainted with the present normal activity of the Talmud Torah, a balance of expenditure and income shall be submitted every month. The monthly reports will be submitted to the Council and the kehilla board and will also be published in the newspaper.
A „mobilisation“ of Zionists.

As we have already reported, the Zionist women's organisation is holding this coming Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a „Blue-and-White Evening“. For this purpose, as we are told, all the Zionists of Zagłębie and of Katowice have organised themselves to come to this evening, which is to be turned into a Zionist festival.
Besides various spiritual delicacies, a famous Jewish artist will also recite chapters of the Bible (Tanakh) and works by Peretz and Sholem Aleichem.
The „Blue-and-White“ evening has, naturally, aroused tremendous interest.
The Old Market — a sports ground.

A group of sports enthusiasts has created a new sports team (drużyna), which will play football on the Old Market.
The first „match“ took place on Sunday morning...
Spare the post-boxes in the streets.

The local post office has turned to the „Merchants' Association“ with the request that the association should, through the newspaper, appeal to its members to take care that the post-boxes in the streets be spared.
An auction at the community (gmina).

The kehilla leaders have run up a debt of 2000 zł. to the Sick Fund (Kasa Chorych).
Because of this the Fund has placed a distraint (sequester) on the office equipment, such as machines, an iron safe, etc. The auction will take place next Tuesday.
Small traders, register!

On the basis of a circular (okólnik) according to which taxpayers without means can be released from tax arrears — turnover tax, income tax and tax fines — from 1924 to 31 December (grudzień) 1927, a registration of the debtors is being carried out at the local Small Traders' Association.
Registration is open until the 28th of this month.
On granting smaller loans

The manager of the Cooperative Bank, Mr. Taub, has been delegated to the Auditing Union (Revisionsverband) in Warsaw to obtain a certain sum for granting smaller loans, repayable in instalments, to artisans.
A carbide lamp kills a man

In Grodziec [?] the following tragic incident occurred: after finishing work in the coal mine, the worker Nowak went with his friend Koprowski [?] into a local restaurant.
In the restaurant the friends drank „l'chaim“; when they were already tipsy, a sharp quarrel broke out between them and Koprowski struck Nowak on the head with a carbide lamp. The blow was fatal — Nowak died within a few hours. The killer tried to flee, but was detained by the crowd.
Meetings in the public schools

This evening, Saturday night (motzei Shabbat), at 6 o'clock, a parents' meeting will take place in Public School No. 4, at which important educational questions will be discussed and a report will be given on the pupils (girls) who are moving up to higher school classes.
Lecture by Dr. Ferber

At the invitation of the „Tse'irei Mishmorei ha-Cholim“ (Youth of the Sick-Watchers' society), Dr. Ferber will give a lecture this Saturday at dusk, 6 p.m., in Public School No. 8, on the subject „How one should behave in urgent cases of illness“.
From the Esperantists' Society

These days the annual general meeting took place, with 50 members present. After the reading of the report for the year 1929, which was taken note of, the following board was elected: J. Serczarz [?] (honorary president), J. Kowalowski [?] (president), M. Ferens (vice-president), J. Zauberman (secretary), Miss H. Oppenheim (treasurer), A. Szpigler, J. Cwajgenbaum, Miss S. Landkart [?].
The struggle of the Jewish working class and the upbuilding of Eretz Israel

On this subject the well-known Eretz-Israel labour activist, editor of the Kupat Poalei Eretz Yisrael „Yedioth“ and head of the central office of the Palestine Workers' Fund, Mr. Melech Neustadt, who is staying in Poland on a mission of the General Jewish Labour Organisation (the Histadrut), will lecture this Saturday in the „Kursal“.
—o—
Meeting of the leather guild.
Next Sunday evening a general meeting of the leather guild will take place in the premises of the Artisans' Association. Very important questions will be discussed.
To improve Zagłębie's railway communication

The Communication Committee of the local Chamber of Commerce [Sosnowiec], in connection with the Railway Minister's decision to increase the speed of passenger trains, has resolved to come forward with the following memoranda:
To the Railway Directorate in Kraków — that the direct Kraków—Sosnowiec trains of 2 years ago should resume running.
To the Radom Railway Directorate — that motor trains should start running on the Sosnowiec—Kielce line.
To the Railway Directorate in Warsaw — that the number of trains on the Katowice—Ząbkowice line be increased at the hours 13 and 14 and 18 and 19.
The Committee also resolved to approach the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs about building post-office buildings in Sosnowiec and in Dąbrowa, and also about enlarging the telephone lines to Katowice, Kraków, Częstochowa and Kielce.
A Drunk Throws a Man under a Tram — For This He Is Sentenced to 2 Weeks' Arrest

[Sosnowiec — crime, court.]
On Będzińska Street the 24-year-old Jan Gawel was walking in a drunken state. Aaron Gutman came towards him; the drunk threw himself upon him and pushed him onto a tram that was going at full speed.
For this savage deed Gawel stood this week before the district court, which, taking into account that Gawel had been drunk, sentenced him to 2 weeks' arrest.
Demonstration of the Unemployed

[Sosnowiec (?) — unemployment, police.]
On Tuesday morning a crowd of unemployed gathered in the magistrate's [town hall's] courtyard, where they demanded relief payments “with an outstretched arm” [i.e. forcefully].
The police, who were called in, came upon an agitated crowd, part of which threw itself on the police and wanted to disarm them. Nevertheless the police succeeded in dispersing the demonstrators, and several ringleaders were arrested.
—o—
Bread Has Become Cheaper
[Sosnowiec (?) — prices.]
On Tuesday the price commission at the local magistrate fixed the prices of bread and flour. A kilo of bread from 70-per-cent flour costs 40 gr. The price is binding for all of Zagłębie.
—o—
After the Theft She Attempted Suicide
[Sosnowiec (?) — crime.]
From the apartment of Mrs. Radomska, Kołłątaja 11, objects and clothes were stolen. Because of this the owner drank a small bottle of vinegar essence. When the neighbours revived her, she cried out: “What good is my life to me, if I have been robbed?”
“One Fool Makes Many Fools”...

[Zagłębie — imaginary treasure.]
A few weeks ago a certain person from Zagłębie applied to the central authorities with a proposal, claiming that he possessed exact documents showing that in the garden of Director Gadomski there lay buried 10 chests of money dating back to the year 1863. Although the authorities regarded the “treasure” sceptically, they nevertheless set about searching for the hidden treasure. For this purpose several workers were hired, who set to work in the presence of representatives of the administrative authorities, the Treasury (Skarb), the police, and delegates of the Ministry and of the voivodeship.
A pit several tens of metres deep was dug, but the “treasure” was not found.
Zawiercie. — “Because You Drowned Others, You Were Drowned, and in the End...”

[Zawiercie — crime, killing.]
On the Promenade Street [Spacerowa?] a bloody incident took place.
The brothers Paszadło [?] came up to Jaworski, who was out for a stroll, and beat Jaworski with sticks. The latter, wanting to free himself from the attackers, began shooting with a revolver and laid one of the attackers dead on the spot. After committing the killing Jaworski ran away, but the brother of the slain man chased him, tore the revolver out of Jaworski's hands, with which he “treated” him to several bullets and badly wounded him,
A delegation to the "Izba Skarbowa" about income tax

[Zagłębie — taxes.] In connection with the recent distraints, in which even people's bedding[?] and clothes are being confiscated, and also because the [tax] offices do not take into account taxes already paid, which ought to be deducted from the income tax, a delegation went to Kielce on the initiative of vice-president Mr. Rubiglicht [so printed; probably Rubinlicht] to intervene at the "Izba Skarbowa" [Treasury Chamber]. The delegation consisted of vice-president Mr. Rubiglicht, the president of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, and director Garamski.
—o—
"Apostasy" of a Jewish girl.
[Zawiercie — conversion.] In No. 3 of our paper we carried a report that in Zawiercie there is a Jewish girl who is preparing to convert and to marry a Catholic artillery officer. We passed the same report on to the Warsaw Jewish press, suspecting that we had before us the Jewish woman student who disappeared from Vilna.
As we are informed, the conversion ceremony took place last Saturday, and on Sunday the wedding ("ślub"[?]).
—o—
A merchant "must have broad shoulders", but good eyes too...
[Dąbrowa — trade.] A freshly baked merchant came to the fair in Dąbrowa with his little dry-goods stall. His first "początek" [opening sale] was a woman customer, who bought 3 zł. worth of goods from him and handed the merchant a 5 zł. banknote. When the merchant went off to change the banknote, the customer vanished together with several pieces of goods...
—o—
The new master of the Sosnowiec slaughterhouse.
[Sosnowiec — slaughterhouse.] The wresting of the slaughterhouse revenue out of Jewish hands is proceeding at a rapid pace. This week the Sosnowiec District Court appointed Dr. Dobrowolski as sequestrator of the local slaughterhouse. The sequestrator takes all the revenues [misprinted "akhnoses"].
—o—
4 days' holiday in the schools.
[Education — general.] The Minister of Education has decreed that the first half of the school year shall end on Thursday the 30th of this month. Classes in the second half of the year will begin on Tuesday, the 4th of February ("luty").
—o—
An important bureau for the provinces.
[Kielce — trade and taxes.] At the Kielce "Merchants' Association" a bureau has been set up, the so-called "Provincial Department".
Through the mediation of the "Merchants' Associations" in Zagłębie, the bureau will settle all tax matters relating to the "Izba Skarbowa" in Kielce.
—o—
An eye knocked out with a stone
[Będzin — accident.] In the courtyard at Małachowska 8 in Będzin the boys Herszberg and Silberstein "played" with stones. A stone hit Silberstein in the right eye and he has become a cripple.
—o—
Kehilla council and town council.
The gallery will be amused for nothing...
[Będzin — kehilla and municipality.] This coming Saturday night the Będzin kehilla council will consider the budget for 1930.
On Tuesday the Będzin town council will hold a session. The agenda, which has already been "held up" for two weeks, will hardly be dealt with..
—o—
Stadtler's factory burnt down.
[Upper Silesia — fire.] In Żory (Upper Silesia) a fire broke out on Tuesday in Jakob Stadtler's factory. The fire destroyed part of the factory buildings. The damage is great.
—o—
Proceeds of the academic ball.
[Będzin — society.] The ball organised by the Będzin academics brought in a net income of 1,258 zł. and 4 gr.
—o—
Even the fish in the water are not left to live...
[Sosnowiec — court.] Before the Sosnowiec District Court this week the case of the Bauherz firm against[?] the directors of the Myszków acid[?] factory ("zayer-fabrik"), Messrs. Gisten[?] and Domint[?], was heard.
The directors were charged with releasing poisonous gases from the factory, by which the fish of the Bauherz firm are poisoned.
The defendants were sentenced to 200 zł. or 10 days' arrest.
—o—
The whole Rebuke is being fulfilled...
[Kielce region — economy, agriculture.] The trade crisis has also gripped the peasant element. The price of grain has fallen sharply. In the course of the week there was not a single buyer for grain at any of the fairs in the Kielce voivodeship, just as the verse says: "and no man shall buy" [Deut. 28:68, from the Rebuke]...
—o—
Just like in the old days..
[Zawiercie — Zionism, aliyah.] On Wednesday two young people left Zawiercie for Eretz Israel, a "Halutz" and a "Tze'irei Mizrachi" member. Almost the whole youth gathered at the station. Antisemites shouted "Żydki do Palestyny" ["Jew-boys, to Palestine"], the police looked on[?], and the ticket office ran out of platform tickets. But the youth laughed at it all and shouted "Long live the olim [immigrants]"!..
—o—
Unemployment in Zawiercie
has grown again by 400 persons.
[Zawiercie — industry and unemployment.] From this Saturday, the 25th of this month, another 400 workers are again being laid off at the "Zawiercie" textile factory.
—o—
New starosta in Zawiercie.
[Zawiercie — administration.] The former starosta of Zawiercie, Mr. Kowalski, has been appointed starosta in Kozienice. The new starosta is from Liz[?].
—o—
300 zł. a month for... not singing.
[Będzin — kehilla, synagogue.] We have received a letter from a group of worshippers of the Będzin Great Synagogue, in which the worshippers complain about the lamentable management in the Będzin kehilla. The letter points out that for several months now the kehilla administration has engaged a choir conductor, who takes 300 zł. every month, and to this day the conductor has no occupation, because there is no choir.
—o—
Kosher meat 2 zł. a kilo
[Sosnowiec — kashrut and prices.] As the elder ("starszy") of the butchers' guild in Sosnowiec, Mr. Jakob Horowicz[?], informs us, the price commission at the Sosnowiec magistrate has unified the price of kosher and treyf meat, and from today a kilo of kosher meat costs 2 zł. in Sosnowiec.
—o—

—o—

A Society „For Palestinian Produce“ (Lema'an Totzeret Ha'aretz) Founded in Poland

On the initiative of the Polish-Palestinian Chamber of Commerce in Warsaw, a branch of the Palestinian society „Lema'an Totzeret Ha'aretz“ (For the Produce of the Land) has been founded in Poland.
This society has the task of moving the local Jewish merchant to import, instead of articles brought in from other countries, the same articles from Palestine (Eretz Israel). The society will inform him about prices, quality and terms of sale of Palestinian products, and it will also help him establish direct relations with the producers and exporters in Palestine.
Besides this, the society will conduct wide propaganda among the Jewish population of Poland for the spread of the products of Palestine.
The society's office is in Warsaw at Leszno 4, apt. 6, and is open every day except the Sabbath, telephone 34-39. All kinds of information are given both orally and in writing free of any charge.

The lecture at „Korso“ (Corso?) by the emissary of the „Histadrut Ha'ovdim“ (the General Federation of Labour) in Palestine, Mr. Melech[?] Neustadt, attracted a large audience of friends of Labour Palestine. The speaker illuminated in fine form the problems of the upbuilding of Palestine and of the Jewish working class, which has already created much and could accomplish still more if the friends of the Palestinian working class abroad would help it more, morally and materially.
In the presence of the guest from Palestine, Mr. Neustadt, a general meeting of the League for Labour Palestine took place on Saturday evening, at which the immediate work was discussed and a committee was elected consisting of: Dr. Rechtman, Aharon Hampel, Yitzchak Tencer, Shmuel Liwer, Bejtner, Gertler, Arye Liwer, Sh. In connection with the proclamation of the campaign to raise 200 thousand złoty for the Palestine Workers' Fund (P.A.F.), a self-taxation of the earnings of at least 1 working day is being carried out among the members and friends of the League.
This Sunday a house-to-house collection will also be held for the P.A.F., and it is to be hoped that all friends of Labour Palestine will receive the young collectors well.
An Extraordinary Tragic Incident in Grójec(?). Came for News and Was Killed

On Sunday afternoon the 29-year-old Agne[?] Cieślikowa, a resident of Grójec(?), committed suicide by hanging.
The suicide had been ill for a long time with an incurable disease, and taking advantage of a moment when she was alone at home, she hanged herself.
A crowd gathered at the suicide's dwelling, which the police dispersed. At that moment a second, even more tragic incident occurred. While the crowd was being removed by the police, the local merchant Szenkowski fell down the stairs and was killed on the spot.

Olkusz — From the Town Council

Olkusz. At the last town-council meeting, among other items on the agenda, two important points were also dealt with: 1) the sale of a plot to the joint-stock company „Westen“ to build a rolling mill (walcownia), and 2) the fact that the sejmik (district council) does not want to give the house-owners the renovation subsidy, to which the landlords have already had a chazakah (established right) for [—] years. The discussion was long and bore a passionate character. The gallery too (mostly house-owners) took a strong part and reproached the town president that he had been the initiator of the sejmik's decision. The president defended himself, but the gallery would not calm down until they had to be removed with the police. It was decided to send a delegation of 4 men (2 Jews and 2 Christians) with a memorandum to the voivode to settle the matter.
It was also decided to sell the firm „Westen“ 100 morgen of land adjoining the factory at 2500 złoty per morgen, on condition that within 5 years a factory be set up that will employ 3 thousand workers.
Finally it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Wajslefisz, that the magistrate should apply to the authorities to exempt the inhabitants of one-room dwellings from the rent tax.
