The Kehilla Representation.

II.
(What does the internal management look like there? The role of severance payments. — Who gets what benefit from the large budgets.)

And again we find ourselves having to speak about the Jewish kehilla. We say "having to", because in truth we did not want to do it any more; we wanted to have pity on it and leave it in peace. But what can we do when, against our will, we are compelled once again to touch on one and the same question.

The writer of these lines was moved to action by two notices that were printed in the previous issue of the "Zagł. Cajt." [Zaglembier Cajtung], namely: one, that the sick fund had put up the office furniture for public auction, and the second about the conductor, who takes 300 zł. a month and has no employment.

And these two notices give my pen no rest; it begs to be put to use. For these two small notices characterise the order that prevails in the Jewish kehilla. On the one hand pensions are paid simply into the blue, without knowing for what and to whom, and on the other hand the few guilders are not there to be paid to the sick fund, and things are brought to the point that a sum of two thousand zł. accumulates. Is this not sad and at the same time also ridiculous? For what respectable firm would allow that, out of groshen which could quite easily be paid every month, a sum of thousands should accumulate, and that it should come to the point of putting the household furniture up for auction? In this we see the clumsiness, the helplessness, the recklessness and indifference toward what concerns the community, toward what our kehilla leaders are supposed to occupy themselves with.

No one will be persuaded that at a time when an institution has the power to draw up quarter-million budgets, it has nothing with which to pay the few guilders a month for the employees at the sick fund. In this one sees plainly in what a lamentable state the management finds itself; in this one sees palpably that there they have no head to occupy themselves with such trifles, with such nonsense. After all, there is high politics to be conducted there, and at such a time, at such a "serious political moment", one surely cannot occupy oneself with such small matters, which "the party concerned" does not consider worth the trouble...

And the second fact: simple Jews, toiling Jews who work a whole week and on the Sabbath come to synagogue — these very Jews come to the editorial office and point out that the community (gmina) engaged a conductor, to whom, needless to say, a pension must be paid, but he has no work, because he is not given a choir. These toiling Jews see this, while our kehilla leaders have apparently forgotten that they engaged a conductor and that he must be paid a pension and given a choir. Upon my life, these people are a free-for-all, when one looks at what they bring about.

Yes, when we do not want to speak, the street comes and speaks and draws attention to what we would have thought it does not see, does not know and does not feel.

The question therefore arises: do these same leaders of ours behave this way in their private businesses too? Do they also take on people whom they absolutely do not need, or do they not exploit the people who work for them? Do they keep such an order, such a management, at home too? What does it mean to pay pensions to people who are not needed or who are given no work? How can one behave like that? Who told our leaders that this is the most practical way, that this is how one should act?

But why precisely this, when everything goes on so unaccounted for, without knowing what yes and what no. Who can remember it all, and who has the desire to dwell on every trifle separately, when there are only absurdities, only comic episodes about which one could talk and talk, and out of which one could create whole series of jokes and humoresques.

Let us take such items as 500 zł. for droshkies (cabs) and expenses for the rabbinate, or 500 zł. for each moreh hora'ah (rabbinic judge) for making visits to the slaughterhouse. We do not want to start here [discussing] whether the pensions of the religious functionaries are too small or too large; but to us it is ridiculous that, since these are people on pensions, why must one give them separately, for example, for droshkies or for going to the slaughterhouse? If their pensions are too small and they cannot get by on them, they can of course be increased; one can surely take the plain straight road, not crooked back alleys, which look so comic and ridiculous. What does it mean that special pensions are being set for the morei hora'ah for going to the slaughterhouse, in order to see to it that kashrut in slaughtering is properly observed — and what, actually, are the morei hora'ah there for, that they should see to it that it should NOT be kosher? Such tactics cannot be understood, such going with the left hand to the right ear. And if one must set aside something special for droshkies or for kashrut visits, then why — one might ask — should one not also set aside special money for cigarettes (papirosy), for pocket money or for other expenses, a fair question, which a living person always needs?

Now, who does not see what an important role severance payments play in the affairs of our kehilla: for getting rid of a cantor whom there was no need to engage, several thousand zł.; for getting rid of the secretary, who was a stumbling block, so-and-so much; for getting rid of a conductor, so much and so much. Say for yourselves, what firm constantly makes such rotten deals, and on top of that when it is so poor that from instalments of single złotys debts running into the thousands are made, which cause such valuable things as typewriters, fireproof safes, etc. to be auctioned off.

So: on the one hand luxury pensions, severance payments, budgets of millions, and on the other hand poverty, helplessness, and the inability to rise to the level that a representation ought to occupy, as befits such a kehilla as that of the town of Będzin.

The enormous disharmony that prevails in the Będzin Jewish kehilla is simply incomprehensible; however much we try to understand what goes on here, how things are managed here, it remains a riddle. In no way can we make out how this magic wheel is being turned here.

An institution from which nobody has any benefit at all, and when one needs the slightest little thing from it one must pay for each item separately — if at least it had introduced some kind of order into Jewish life, some kind of improvement into our homely goings-on [?]; but for all this it has no time; one must pursue politics on which the world stands, and since that is so, [these matters] are of no concern.

It does not trouble itself over the beggars, it does not lift a finger for the shamashim (beadles); who even speaks of its taking upon itself the competence to improve the necessary institutions, which ought to have proper representation — since they never tried to think about such a thing and do not know at all how to approach such work.

And what does it manage, this municipal institution of ours? Once it managed the mikveh, and it carried on such clumsy activity there that it sought at the first opportunity to rid itself of it.

And since we are already at the mikveh: how much has this building already cost, how many years was it built and rebuilt, and how much money and donations have already been collected for it? And what is the end — that there is neither a mikveh nor any money. Well, is this perhaps bad management? Can anyone have any complaint against our kehilla leaders? Will anyone dare to say a word against them, will anyone permit himself to say that they do not keep exemplary order, that the management is not as it should be? Of course one must not say that, one need not say that, because otherwise they would want to do I-know-not-what to us.

And therefore, therefore it would only be fair to hear what the party concerned itself has to say. We truly cannot point to a single good thing that they wanted to introduce since they began to administer with us and over us.

It is possible that we do not see, possible that we do not know, possible that only W E see differently; perhaps our sight is weak-sighted or short-sighted, and therefore it would surely be good if those who stand at the helm would speak; and they have, believe us, a great deal to say, since they have already stood at the "work" for a number of years, and over years, willy-nilly, much must have been created. And even if we were pessimistic and said that not much was created, still something must surely have been done bit by bit, and when something is done bit by bit over a succession of years, then all taken together it amounts to a great deal.

Be that as it may, willy-nilly one must surely, when the time has come [?], go to the members and give them an accounting and say: this and this we have done, this and this we have created, this and this we succeeded in building and putting into operation. On such-and-such a work we laboured and laboured hard, but we had obstacles from this and that side, and despite the best and most energetic will we did not succeed in carrying it out — as such-and-such facts and such-and-such witnesses can confirm.

Undoubtedly the Jewish kehilla representation has much to tell us, and therefore we would like to hear from it clear and truthful words about what its activity has consisted of through so many years.

R. Les.
Will the Economic Situation Improve?

[Economy — the economic crisis in Poland.]
Only a few months ago the semi-official institutions were still bringing us the glad tidings in their bulletins that the bad times would quickly pass and that a new upswing would begin. But as the signs of a severe crisis kept multiplying, those tidings stopped, and the only optimist left today is the government itself and its declarations before the Sejm. This optimism, however, cannot be taken seriously — not only because a government must officially be optimistic, but even more because one sees no facts at all on which this optimism could rest.
It is a fact that the situation is getting worse and worse, and so sensitive [?] a barometer as the number of protested bills of exchange still clearly points to a storm. It is enough to point out that even at the "Bank Polski", which is very cautious and choosy about its material, the percentage of protested bills keeps growing: in October it amounted to 4.71 percent, in November 5 percent, and in December it already reached nearly five and a half percent. Things are naturally much worse with the other bills. According to estimates, the circulation of bills of exchange in the country amounts to 4 billion zł. Of this, 1 billion 250 million zł. were protested in 1929, i.e. a third of the entire bill circulation. Under present conditions this is no surprise at all, because bills are written out even for such ridiculous sums as 10 zł., and bills are accepted even for articles of daily use, and from anyone who merely has a finger to sign with, without distinguishing whether he is well-off and earning or not.
Trade, it seems, wants to keep up its present volume by all means. But such a way of "financing" consumption is a very wrong and ill-calculated step, because it must lead to bills not being redeemed. This very difficult situation of trade is already being reflected, as was to be foreseen, in very many branches of industry, as for instance in the textile branch, in the tanneries, in the mills, etc. Other causes in turn have brought about a complete standstill in the timber industry, namely the wrong policy of the administration of the state forests and the competition from Russia. Among the exceptions are only a small number of industrial branches, which have not yet felt the general crisis too strongly.
An opinion has now spread that the main cause of our general crisis is the crisis in agriculture; Premier Bartel indeed expressed himself so in his exposé to the Sejm. We will not enter into an inquiry whether other causes, especially the government's economic policy, did not also play a role here; in any case it is more than certain that the fact that the peasant has no possibility to buy was one of the most important causes that brought on the crisis. And despite the government's promises to improve the situation of agriculture, we still see no tangible deeds in this field. The main cause of the low grain prices will not be removed so quickly, because all states have for some years been striving to increase their grain production, thinking only of one thing — how to secure their own livelihood — but not of where to put the surplus for export. This and other causes have brought it about that the downward tendency on the international grain market will persist for quite a long time yet, unless something unexpected [?] happens.
Against [?] this wave of economic weakening, which has gripped a whole series of countries, we are too weak, and at most we can only hope that when there is a better business cycle in the world, we too will be able to benefit from it.
The one thing we could indeed do to save the situation as far as possible with our own strength would be precisely the lightening of the tax burden, and first of all of the turnover tax. It is surely only just that a state which until now has had so much benefit from a good business cycle should now also share in the losses that result from the bad business cycle. This conception has at last found an echo among authoritative government factors, and the bill on reforming the turnover tax has been introduced. Unfortunately, however, the government shows here not the proper energy [?] that it shows in other, in our opinion less urgent, matters. This is a very grave mistake, because this is the only tangible measure we have now against [?] the crisis.
Dr. B. Zeiden.
The Crisis and the Taxes

[Article — economy and taxes.] (The parallel between former and present-day life. — The heavy burdens of the middle class.)
The economic question has never at any time played such a significant role among us Jews as now; never before have we had to debate this question so seriously and so often. Now this matter is for us the most important and most painful, the most serious and the harshest. Constantly we talk about this very problem, which has indeed become the "credo" (ani ma'amin) of our everyday life, the command of the hour.
If we seriously consider, without any bias whatsoever, the importance of this problem, we shall after all, in the end, come to the conviction that life in our generation is very, very hard, very, very burdened.
Before the year 1914, for example, one could not even have dreamt that after the terrible war such hard times would come, such serious moments, which would simply make it impossible to continue our further existence.
People among us often wonder that life has become dry and hard, plain and coarse; we wonder and complain very often that people do not occupy themselves with refined problems, with lectures, with art and with culture in general. We see palpably that all this has become superfluous things one can do without. It is a loss for the Yiddish book, a loss for Yiddish literature, a loss for the Yiddish theatre and for art and for everything that is holy and dear to us.
But one must not forget that this is the consequence of the difficult situation in which the people finds itself, and it is no wonder either — for how can one have it in mind to occupy oneself with second-rate articles when one is hard-pressed[?] (literally "twisted / muddled") and has nothing to pay for first-rate articles?
No small matter how hard life is nowadays. After all, we do not live in the 18th century, when one needed no more than a livelihood, and a livelihood meant a piece of bread with herring and a potato with salt. Today a livelihood demands something more, but even that is not yet everything: we live in a time when one must dress, and have the children taught, and maintain institutions; we also have many duties towards society, and on top of that one must somehow fulfil the civic obligations towards the government — and these very civic obligations are very hard to pay.
It is no news, after all, that taxes occupy the most honoured place in our budget. Of course we know that we are citizens and as such must bear all the civic burdens that the state demands of us; but in this case the pressure is enormous and the burden crushes us, simple, middling citizens.
It has been statistically proven that the greatest number of taxes in Poland are thrown[?] "proportionally" (as printed) upon the middle class, and therefore this element finds it hardest to fight for the existence of life. Worst off in Poland is the middle class. The big man, the industrialist, pays less than would fall to him, and if he were to pay more it would be no misfortune for him either, because he can set his own "stamp"[?] (probably: his price); he then raises his production and so does an even better business. The estate-owner, the landlords (pritsim) and the peasants are, after all, the privileged ones; one does not want to quarrel with them, they are always right. As for the workers, there is nothing to take from them. Therefore everything ends up being thrown on the small merchant and the artisan, who must pay as much as he is assessed at, regardless of whether he can or not, whether he has it or not. If he has goods, he takes them and sells, just so he can pay the taxes without a fine; but if he has no more goods either, they take from him whatever they find in the house.
That the situation of this element is serious and grows ever worse is self-evident; for how can it be good when the tax burden not only does not grow smaller but is constantly increased — from year to year one pays more. It is interesting that when the mass taxes approach and there is nowhere to get the money for the "zaliczki" (advance payments), the instalments (raty), the bills of exchange and the patents (trade licences), precisely in those hard moments voices are heard saying that from now on things will be better and easier with the taxes, that one will pay less; and as soon as the panic passes, one sees no sign of things getting better — on the contrary: then one sees that the taxes are increased and that they constantly look for ways to extract more taxes.
We know, after all, how great the crisis is now in all of Poland; it is no longer a secret that splendid firms have their bills of exchange protested and that the biggest manufacturers are under "nadzór" (receivership / official supervision). So who even speaks of the small ones, of the "flinen"[?] — they have been left entirely without life and without strength to live.
It is known, after all, that because it was summer instead of winter, everything has turned into a ruin and there was no season, so that even articles of prime necessity became cheaper, and with all that there is no buyer. But the burden of taxes will not, God forbid, be lessened here at all: at the tax offices (urzędy skarbowe) it will turn out that the season was a good and a roaring one, and the turnover tax (podatek obrotowy) will surely be increased still further. With them, at the office, all businesses flourish — whether there is a season or not, whether one takes in money or not.
At the office they will certainly not take into account that people beg others to buy goods at half price in order to have something to pay the bill of exchange or perhaps to buy a loaf of bread; likewise we see how people beg [buyers to take] eggs, grain, potatoes, coal — which at the primary sources or at the pit have not become cheaper. It does not matter: they, the big ones, can withstand the crisis, they can wait it out; only the small ones must trade, and if they take in nothing for one day they have nowhere to get a loaf of bread, and they must sell the goods, surely[?] at a loss, just so as to see cash.
Almost always things were better with us in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia than in all of Poland; at a time when we hear about crises in the country, we know very little of them here. Now, however, the clouds are moving towards us as well, and the prospects are pessimistic. More and more, and larger, factories are coming to a halt here, and the number of unemployed is constantly growing.
Of course this casts fear upon the citizens, and upon us Jews all the more so[?].
It is no small matter, after all, when we recall that our great industrial district is beginning to shut down its factories and that the number of unemployed is growing. One must not forget that here everything is tied up and grown together with the working element, from which we draw our sustenance.
The question therefore arises: will our tax offices remember, when assessing the taxes, what a critical winter we are living through and how pessimistic the prospects appear for our near future?
If they pretend to forget this, it will be the duty [to see to it] that the commissions do remember it precisely in these hard moments.
Selekt
A Little Feuilleton. A New Decree.

The decree of forgiving deferred taxes — —
You think I made a mistake, meant to write: the informer[?], the manifesto?
No, no mistake at all. It is a decree, a harsh decree.
You want a parable?
Well, imagine:
A rich man, a moneylender, holds a deferred debt from a poor man. For every week of deferral there is added interest, and interest on the interest. The little ledger grows ever larger, but he never sees a single grosz, because the pauper always comes weeping that he has nothing to put in his mouth.
So the rich man thinks it over: enough, an end to it! He will wipe out the old debts — but for that the debtor must start paying the latest debts — after all, he cannot forgive everything!
And the old deferred bill of exchange he sends him through... the komornik [bailiff], who at the same time carries a second paper as well: to inventory the belongings for the new debt...
That is how our paupers had long since forgotten the old deferred taxes. The sequestrator [tax-distraint officer] too had long ago waved his hand at this "customer". Once he got some certificate of poverty or another similar paper, and that was that — he dunned no more. What can you take from a dead man?
But the balance [saldo] in the books of the tax office stuck in somebody's eye. Bookkeeping figures have a nature: they let themselves be carried over and turned from plus to minus — but you can never get rid of them entirely. Even if the ink and paper cost more than the whole debt, it is lost all the same.
So our Ministry, just like that moneylender, decided to be rid once and for all of the drawn-out illness: to write off the old debt.
This is not the first time. I[?] a few years ago such a "remission" was made. Don't even ask what happened: the world of paupers was shaken up; there, in the little cottages, they again began to see the face of the sequestrator; he came with the good tidings and at the same time began to squeeze out the belongings...
Oh, those deferred debts!
As long as they live, they suck the marrow[?] from your bones, and once they are forgiven, you have to pay a big burial fee.
Well, is that not a decree?
Abi-Ver.
Those Who Want to Take and Not Give.

(Interviews with our communal activists and "providers".)
You probably know them, our communal activists [klal-tuers], who were always so worried and do nothing but think and care about the common good. They have been blessed once and for all with sharpened, smooth little tongues. Their language is a golden one, with diamond phrases. They can hold you for whole hours with sermons and speeches, painting in the most beautiful and splendid pictures all that they are able to do for you. When it comes to elections[?] they are the heroes of the day; golden mountains they promise you then[?] — but hardly have you elected them and they are sitting in the chair, they no longer know you. Then they stand on the highest rung of the careerist ladder, and you are then the "permanent mass", which gazes up at them with eyes wide open, so much that it cannot even see as far as their height and their majestic highness. Then they look at you from above, down, as at people not their equals. Yes, they know you — and do you know when? When you stand below by the ladder and clap "bravo", and your voices echo with shouts of triumph in honour of their "magnanimous" deeds. But beware, should you dare to criticize them, showing that of all their promises nothing came out but pure bluff. Then you will be shouted down and reviled by the handful of busybodies ["cooking spoons"] and toadies [ma-yafitniks] who dance and bustle[?] around our monopolist communal activists...
But the "permanent mass" is little impressed by these few counted shouters, and having, poor thing, no other choice, it comes to pour out its bitter heart to those who write about and check up on the "good deeds" of our "kind-hearted" providers.
And indeed a fair number of "songs of praise" piled up at our editorial office, brought by the "permanent mass" about its guardians, and we decided to delegate one of our colleagues to go and conduct interviews with our communal activists, so as to report in this way on their "activity". The lot fell precisely on me, and I went off to carry out my mission.
So[?], interview number 1.
I went to one of the most respected communal activists, and on entering the anteroom I found a considerable number of petitioners waiting for the activist to finish his midday meal. After the meal I went in, of course, first, and when I informed him of the purpose of my visit, he smiled broadly and said: You have come for an interview — ah, please, do sit down. You surely want to describe the great achievements of my public activity. Well, with the greatest pleasure — and he laid out a sheet of wonderfully crafted plans which he intends to carry out for the common good. Besides that he could not have enough of talking about what he has already accomplished and how great his self-sacrifice is for the poor, the unfortunate and the suffering. I wrote it all down and left. In the anteroom the petitioners had apparently overheard our conversation. And as soon as I crossed the threshold they fell upon me and began to protest stormily: Mister writer [panie], there is nothing to it, it is lies, everything he boasted of is falsehood and deceit; if you want to write, write the truth — that he has never yet done anything; we have been waiting here for days on end and always leave with nothing.
As I stand there arguing[?] with the petitioners, a tall young fellow comes leaping up and shouts: Mister writer, the activist is right, he is a golden man. —
— You are a liar — shout and clamour all the others — we know, you are one of his supporters; he does you a little favour so that you will outshout everyone; Mister writer, don't listen to him. He is one against all of us. — I grasped the game and went on.
Interview number 2.
I am sitting[?] with a well-known city councillor [ratman], a "sweet little mouth", whose sweet sayings everyone licks[?] like liquorice. This councillor, on learning that I had come for an interview, became very angry: What do you mean, you have come for an interview? Don't you know that I am an opponent of your newspaper?
— And why?
— Because you reveal to the public all the things that ought to be kept strictly secret and that nobody except us activists may know about.
— And crying injustices and scandalous facts may not be revealed either? — I ask further.
— Certainly not. What do you mean, you will tell everything? This way one can never be sure of you — what am I to do[?] when every week you raise new outcries about our activity in the city council and you tear down our authority) — we cannot allow it!
— But Mister councillor, what are you so afraid of? Why are you so frightened? When one feels guilty of nothing, one has no fear of criticism. Are you angry that we react to injustices and rouse our communal workers to useful work for the common good? On the contrary, I ask you — you are, after all, a representative of the public — what have we achieved with our victory, winning as many as 16 councillors? Are you defending Jewish interests, or the protégés of the PPS? 16 Jews have one ławnik [member of the municipal executive], and 5 PPS men have 2 ławniks..
You are, after all, like mannequins[?]; our rights are being curtailed from day to day.
— That is exactly why I tell you that you keep asking your blockhead questions, and that is precisely why I refused to give an interview.
— What are you saying, Mister councillor [panie radny], this is a splendid interview; you have spoken clear words that deserve general attention. I thank you for your interview and for your frankness. At least you say that you want to take from the masses and give them nothing, and that is really important to know. Adieu.
From there I went on further, but[?] about the other interviews — another time.
Emitser [Somebody].
"Zangen" (Literature, Life, Art, Science) — Israel Fleishman: Freedom

[Literature — prose poem (translation).] "Zangen" [Ears of Grain] — Literature, Life, Art, Science. (Section.)
Reprinting prohibited.
Israel Fleishman.
Freedom.
Once in a lifetime a person lives through such a moment, which leaves on his whole existence, on his whole being, unforgettable traces.
Once in a lifetime he soars up into the spiritual heights among the ethereal clouds, freed from the yoke, looking down into the valley...
Only once in a lifetime.
And perhaps never in a lifetime.
And then we call it: tragedy, because this moment drives away all the dreary[?] paths and brings joy and happiness.
To the soul — contentment.
Only once can one see and feel liberty, freedom; one cannot compare the enormous height against which you feel your strength — which is in truth your weakness, your "nothingness".
A nothing are the high, strong cliffs that bathe among the clouds, against the wholeness in which you feel your crippledness.
A nothing is the dreadful storm, the mighty wind, before which you tremble like feeble little leaves, like a little fish that has sensed death — — the net...
A nothing is the eternal desert in which hundred-year-old trees remember hundreds of generations, against which you feel a fearfully-hidden[?] time.
For liberty, freedom, is a holy corner — that hovers in its boundless existences — among the stars in heaven, among the hidden depths of the sea — on the highest mountains of its strong cliffs.
Freedom gives fine feeling, a universal knowledge and prophecy! Therefore, he who is happy — once in a lifetime feels that corner of freedom.
— — — — — — — —
And when "she" came, radiant, wrapped and clothed in the spring breeze, you remained bewildered by her splendour and glory.
— So magnificent, blended in colours, like the rainbow[?] in the sky.
— So modest, like a young girl in white dresses..
— So joyful, like the ringing and trumpeting of the singer...
— So beautiful, lovely, like nothing and no one..
She, the great one — Freedom.
The sparkling stars marked out the way for her..
A light south wind sang beautiful songs to her and the old forest trees prayed.
— For she walked splendidly..
— Shining[?] and joyful —
— On beautiful, white angels' wings,
— Accompanied by the harp-songs of King Solomon.
— In merriment.
— In confidence in a better tomorrow.
— Forgetting yesterday.
— And forgiveness to enemies.
— And love...!
— Freedom!!
She walked among a host of singing bells[?], among the traces of the spring-sister...
— In beautiful, dignified holiness,
— God sent her down,
— A gift to mankind,
— As a remembrance for its sufferings...
— As a sign of forgiveness and remission of sins...
— After the day of the verdict — — —
And in the meantime — slavery died.
— The iron rings of the bound were torn apart.
— The loosened chains rang out,
— Doves turned into black night-crows.
— She walked among people —
— Soaked with joy.
— Strengthened,
— Dried the tears,
— Stilled the sorrow,
— Healed the wounds,
— Prophesied the resurrection of the dead!
The beautiful harp-tones rang out from the heavenly voice (bat kol).
— And all the angels sang praise,
— And the whole spirited world, wrapped in laurel leaves, adorned in white and in palm branches, sang:
Hallelujah —"— Hallelujah!
And the soul tore itself up into the heights like a proud and free eagle, soared far, far into the lofty upper realms.
— Like cripples[?] appeared the mighty creations of man's hands.
— Like cripples appeared the high mountains, covered with eternal snow.
— For the soul soared ever higher and higher.
— Into the highest spheres,
— Among the sparkling stars,
— Among the angels,
— To God himself...
— To God in heaven!
— Only once...
The soul circled the ring above the tower,
— Over forests, over sufferings,
— Pains, tears.
— Like a royal eagle!
— Freed from all kinds of worries,
— Armed[?] in freedom
— In a glorious freedom
— Only once in a lifetime...
— — — — — — — —
People gazed at her, were inspired by her, rejoiced in God's work, adorned her with flowers, built her a temple of white marble with slender columns and broad stairs, with a bright, flame-fiery Holy Ark.
— Until the morrow came,
— With the morrow, ill will,
— Disbelief in perfection,
— They sought the flaw,
— In order to repair her
— In order to repair, to complete the bright, holy freedom...
They forgot that God's work is perfect like God himself.
— And they began to uncover the flaws
— This one, and that one...
— Flaws in perfection,
— Flaws, by their own understanding...
— They founded workshops,
— To repair God's work,
— In order to perfect!
— To perfect freedom,
— They drove in nails,
— Into the living body,
— On the fire they wanted to solder the openings that had appeared.
— With files to smooth out the cast-on roughness[?],
— Inhumanly they tore at their living bodies,
— Paying no heed to pain and suffering
— And they ruined a work,
— God's work...
— Without mercy
— Stabbed, cut, filed, bled, slaughtered[?],
— Unto great grief.
— The heart ached.
— Forced to weep.
— Whole veins[?] poured out in tears,
— The wings were torn from the souls,
— From the heavenly All down into the valley.
— Into the abyss..
— Into the depths, where spirits are hidden,
— In order to rob,
— To torment,
— To strangle,
In order to wipe out[?] the free thought and the memory of freedom.
— — — — — — — —
And again one sees before one's eyes an ice-road[?], bloodied and thorny.
And again iron chains have enclosed souls and bodies...
Again the heavy chains clang dreadfully, and the white marble temple with its slender columns and broad stairs, with the flame-fiery Holy Ark — — — lies shattered,
— Like a grave...
— Like an abandoned, sad grave...
— Buried in it is holiness...
— Freedom. — — — —
Translated for the "Zaglembier Cajtung" by Yosef Perlberger.
The Wall.

In our literary balance sheet, imports take up a significant figure, exceeding the number of our own products. And this phenomenon — which is noticeable not only among us — need not be regarded as negative. Bringing the treasures of world literature over into our own is not only valuable in and of itself, enriching the reader's knowledge universally and refining his taste, but it also has an enormous influence on original creation, showing it new paths, momentum, scope.
In this respect we truly have nothing to complain about. The Yiddish reader today, without commanding even any other language whatsoever, can easily become acquainted with the classics of the whole of world literature, with the young poetry of all languages, with the way of life of all peoples: from the rich life of English lords to the life of the Soviet-Russian worker; from the princes of olden times to the heroic life of modern revolutionaries.
But of one literature, of one language, of one land, with which we Jews have some bit of connection, the modern Yiddish reader has no notion. Namely: of the young Hebrew and of Palestine as it builds itself. Let the regrettable fact be recorded here that to this day we do not possess in Yiddish a single translation from the rich young literature of Eretz Israel.
One may take whatever attitude one likes to the Eretz Israel problem, one may view the future of "Altneuland" [Herzl's name for the Land of Israel] through whatever spectacles one wishes, but it is a fact that a new Jewish life is being built there with a distinctive psychology, with its own momentum. A people is being reborn and wants to rebuild a land neglected for a thousand years — how much heroism[?] this holds! And indeed it is gloriously and beautifully sung[?] and narrated by young talents, but the reader who does not read Hebrew has not even an inkling of it.
Our literary journals will not give him the incentive to read such things. He will sooner find an essay on some American writer than on a young Hebrew talent.
A wall has been put up between Hebrew and Yiddish that does not let us look across at what is being created in the glorious land of the East.
They, the well-known zealots, do translate all of Sholem Asch's works into Hebrew; of I. L. Peretz and Sholem Aleichem's there is no need even to speak. Only the Yiddish reader cannot know what has been created by such talented prose writers as A. Reuveni, Kabak, Barash, an exotic writer like Y. Burla; such poets as David Shimonovitz, A. Ts. Greenberg [Uri Zvi Greenberg], Yitzhak Lamdan and many, many more. "Davar" does consider it necessary to publish essays on the newest Yiddish literature, but in our literary periodicals you will search in vain for anything about the young Hebrew literature in Eretz Israel.
The wall must be torn down — in our own interest.
Y. Y.[?]
World and Home Affairs

On Surrealism ["Über-Realism"].
Paris is not only the centre that supplies our women with the season's fashions, but is also the centre of fashion-literature. Paris is the cradle where new literary trends are born, which are soon snatched up in the wide world, just like our women snatch up the new dress style...
Thus a short time ago there arose in Paris a literary trend by the name of: Über-Realism [Surrealism]. Its foundation rests on fantasy and Freud's theory. Surrealism is supposed to be the embodiment of dream and reality, their fusion.
Interesting are the conditions under which, according to Surrealism, [creation] must take place. According to its theory the writer is a kind of psychic automaton who must take in all sorts of thoughts without any control on the part of reason... While creating, the poet must be in such a state that everything that runs through his ideas he should write down, and afterwards correct nothing. To surrender oneself entirely to all-powerful fantasy, and whatever is created, to bring it to the reader that way, without changes or corrections.
The theorist of Surrealism is the well-known writer André Breton.
Besides prominent writers, Surrealism has also influenced the art of painting and other intellectual fields.
* * *
Why Is Jakob Wassermann Against Zionism?
One can possess a great talent, even of world stature, and yet a not very honourable character. Jakob Wassermann, the world-famous Jewish-German writer, depicts, addressing "Eastern Jewry", such ugly insults as are found only in the worst antisemitic pamphlets. He once said from a platform: "The war has thrown up to the surface of life various refuse[?] and abominations of humanity, among others also the 'half-barbarous, greedy grabbers, the Polish and Russian Jews', who through an unfortunate chance threw themselves upon Germany...
So spoke the Jew Jakob Wassermann, the same man who once in in his humility [printed "poverty"] declared that his prologue to the work "The Jews of Zirndorf" was among the most important causes of the rise of Zionism.
Where does such a boundless[?] hatred of Jewry in general and of Zionism in particular come from in him?
Dr. T. Nussenblatt explains it clearly. The reason is neither more nor less than this: the hatred Jakob Wassermann still bears to this day towards Herzl, who did not admit him to the "Neue Freie Presse". Herzl helped many young talents, but in Wassermann, who wanted to push his way into the "N. F. P." by twisted, dishonest[?] means, he saw a spoiled talent. Herzl speaks of this explicitly in his diaries.
And this personal hatred of Herzl he carried over to the entire Jewish community.
* * *
Jubilees.
The great Hebrew poet Shaul Tchernichovsky has celebrated here the 30th jubilee of his poetic work. In Berlin a jubilee committee has been founded, which has undertaken to publish 5 volumes out of the 10 volumes of Tchernichovsky's works and to present the published works to the celebrant as a gift. The committee also includes Nahum Sokolow and S. Dubnow.
○ Also in Berlin, Dr. S. Bernfeld, the well-known historian who has so greatly enriched our scholarly literature, celebrated his 70th birthday.
○ Also Dr. I. Zinberg[?], the great literary scholar, is celebrating his 30th jubilee.
We shall return to speak about the distinguished celebrants.
* * *
A Sudden Abundance...
In Hebrew literature in Poland a deathly silence has reigned for years; rarely did some work appear. Now all at once three whole works are appearing: N. Mipelpov[?] — "Emek Asseret ha-Tmarim" [Valley of the Ten Palms]; L. Hazan — "Ge'ulah" [Redemption]; Al. Tints[?]: "Mi-shirei Hige" [From the Songs of ...][?].

“Eretz Israel Is Exile”

(From the "Blue-Life Evening" [a Keren Kayemet "blue-box" evening] held by "WIZO" in Będzin.) Reported[?] by Ben Amotz.
WIZO in Będzin has won a great victory — over us men. The WIZO activists, with the speakers[?] at their head, are bolder than our father Jacob, who begged his brother Esau: "Give me the souls and take the goods for thyself" — grant me my life and take my property. They, the "Wizonitses", went out into the street with the slogan:
— "Open your purses, and besides that you men shall dance to the beat we play; you men-servants will come at our call."
And so it came to pass: at the appointed time people came to inaugurate[?] [the evening], their thoughts occupied with everyday worries. The feet can barely hold up, but it is lost. One has to pinch one's cheeks and go take part in the campaign for Keren Kayemet, to clatter on the "Góra Waskara"[?], as they called the first "Blue-Life Evening" in Będzin.
— So was the evening "blue-life"-ish?..
The correct answer is: the evening had "yitrum"[?] names:
— Blue-Life evening,
— Dance evening,
— Recitation evening,
— Artistic evening,
— Carmel evening,
— Hebrew evening, and above all
— a Money evening..
• • •
The hall is very beautifully decorated. The "antisemitic walls" are adorned with illuminated, many-coloured Keren Kayemet collection boxes and Eretz-Israel slogans; right by the western wall, beside the "crowned" Herzl, a tent of "Produce of the Land" has been arranged, of Palestine oranges, Carmel [wine] and other delicacies from the "land flowing with milk"..
To drive away "quarrels and envy-hatred" the organizers staged a "joke" like Wilson in his time..
Each "town" received an independent "territory". The great "kingdoms", for example Katowice, received the eastern side with the borders of Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa. The remaining places, of the smallest spot, for instance by the entrance doors, were occupied by Będzin, because the Będzin public has a reputation as people who accept everything with love and do not protest against any wrongs. The same happened here too.
The quick ones, those who came on time, still had a place to rest, and those who "came late" wandered like wounded[?] from one room to the other and were "attacked" by the life-loving waitresses, who echoed with "przepraszam bardzo" [Polish: "excuse me very much"]..
And the in-laws of the celebration excused themselves: "We did not count on such a crowd, wonder of wonders. Wherein lies the magnetic power? All balls end in fiascos, and here such a number of guests, no evil eye — thanks to whom? To Eretz Israel or to the 'Wizonitses'?"
* * *
Simcha starts working wonders[?] with the fiddle, Pieszek with the trumpet, the jazz-band ensemble blares and drums the newest hits, and off one goes to the first mitzvah-dance. At the beginning the atmosphere is strained, boldness is lacking, but it does not last long and the hall "teems"[?] with couples. Some couple grabs a dance in the other room — so long as one dances, like that Jewish woman: when everyone shouts hurrah, she of all people should keep silent!..
And those who cannot dance busy themselves with a game of cards.
11 o'clock at night. The mood — a cheerful one. The temperature rises. The celebration is ablaze. Here appears on the stage the chairwoman of the "Zigerns"[?], Mrs. Ratner, who welcomes everyone who came to the Keren Kayemet celebration with "Bruchim haba'im" and gives the floor to Dr. Rapaport (Katowice). The speaker thanks for the invitation and speaks about the significance of the KKL, which buys up land from foreign hands.
After the short, dry German speech one "proceeds" with a dance — it is, after all, a dance for the sake of a mitzvah; every plastic movement, a jump this way, a jump that way, "increases" after all the income for the upbuilding of Palestine. After every dance it gets lively at the buffet; the public fulfils what is required: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied and bless" — eat and drink and run back to dancing..
Then comes the quintessence of the evening: a concert by Mrs.[?] Alis Lewensohn. Her appearance is announced by the "conférencier" Yehuda Preger, who mentions in passing that a certain talented woman wanted to take part in the evening, but the trouble is that she is a teacher in a school where the number of pupils is close to eighty percent "of our brethren the children of Israel", yet the head is a "baptized one" [convert], and he did not permit a teacher of his school to take part in a "żydowski" [Polish: Jewish, pejorative] ball. He, the baptized one that is, was afraid that the Jewish parents would "take revenge" and withdraw their daughters from the school.
Ms. Alis Lewensohn played better works by Jewish composers, synagogue motifs, but whom did such "nonsense" interest here? The artistic piano tones were weakened by the buzzing and clamour of the dancing humanity.
And last but not least... recitations, performed by a daughter of the town. Among us she is still one of the "hidden ones", whereas in the wide world she is popular — this is Miss Dimant. Her recitations, delivered in an artistic form, are successful on the European stage. Here too the artist showed "wonders": right at the beginning, when "Then sang Deborah"..., the dancing public was "set on its feet" with great attention and listened — chapter 5 of the "Song of Songs", "Shir Ahava" by Bialik, "The Strange Wedding Dress" by Y. L. Peretz, and as an encore a declamation "po niemiecku" [Polish: in German]...
The Hebrew recitations had an influence on the youth, especially on the Revisionist youth. After they had "carried out a revision of the hall" and not found their leader and the local "patent-Zionists", they, the Revisionists, went off into a "hora" with true pioneering fervour; a Jewish mood arose and the evening then took on its true form..
The same impression remained until the very end. The salon etiquette vanished, one already heard "speaking in the language of his people", the orchestra did not spare Jewish "pieces", and the buffet was gradually "wound up"[?]...

[Literature — futuristic story of gas warfare; translated from Esperanto.]
For several weeks rumours had been going around the country about conflicts, attacks [?] and war with the neighbouring state, which lies a few kilometres from the city.
The day came when the people learned from large posters of war with the neighbouring state, and a trembling seized everyone.
But present-day wars will not be like earlier ones; the newspapers had been writing about it for years, men of science had studied [?] the subject, politicians had warned that in the new wars it would not be one soldier fighting another, cannon against cannon, as in earlier wars. —
The new wars will be waged with the newest means of modern chemical murder-science. Soldiers no longer exist; there exist only workers, engineers and technicians on flying murder machines; the workers will be turned into murderers and technical executors of extermination. No longer [do wagons travel?] over the bodies of soldiers who could once be healed in special hospitals. In present-day wars there is only — death. One great common death for all.
For gas there is no difference between military and civilian population, between woman and child.
The newspapers of both states had already some time before begun preparing for the bloody bacchanalia [?] with various fiery articles and appeals, spreading panic among the population of both countries. On the one hand they praised to the skies the engineers and technicians who had invented their own gases and flying machines to defend the country against the enemy — and on the other hand they made themselves out to be innocent and laid the responsibility on the other side in case of an outbreak of war — after all, one must defend oneself.
After the declaration of war, whoever could fled from the threatened places. They thought it would not be so dangerous once they had got away from the threatened places, but the terrible event came sooner. Whole enemy air squadrons appeared over entire towns and villages and did their terrible work — bombing the towns and shtetls with gas bombs of sort Z, type 1950. The gas bombs are invisible when they explode; only their terrible smell brings death to every living being. The first bomb explosions struck the homeless on the roads, who wanted to save their lives by fleeing, and they found death en masse on various roads. The most terrible thing is that when such a gas bomb bursts, one hears no bang, no noise. Thus death did its terrible work without noise or tumult. Whoever opened a mouth to scream — death had already undermined that person's life.
A group of neighbours who had no wish to leave their homes saw with their own eyes, through their windows, the great destruction the gas bombs were causing. And they had in mind that soon we would have the same fate as our acquaintances and neighbours. People began stopping up windows and doors, putting on gas masks. But can any masks help against gas Z, type 1950?
Incessantly the enemy gas bombs burst; the home airmen developed a counter-action against the enemy attacks, but what did it help against the great mass of enemy flying machines.
The gases of 1950 brought to nothing all means of protection, turning everything into a heap of ruins.
In one of the houses a mother sat over the bed of her sick child, whom she loved dearly. Her husband is not at home; he is somewhere on the battlefields. The mother wanted to flee the city together with other inhabitants, but the child's high temperature held her back; a good mother will surely not risk the life of her dear child.
The child fell asleep and the mother thought she had already been saved, her child was already well. What joy awoke in her maternal heart! The mother rested a little, went to the window, wanted to see what was going on in the street. Terrible things she saw: people lie there dead; some living figure of a man swayed for a few seconds and fell dead; no sign of gas at all, no bursting of shrapnel — the air held death within it. The air was gas, gas was the air.
Whoever thought about death was already dead. The rows of the dead lay like cut grain at harvest time; death scattered people like seeds, as a child scatters its toys about the house.
The woman remembered that once, at a lecture on gas defence, the speaker had explained that to protect oneself against gas it is better to be as high up as possible. She took the child out of bed and wrapped it up, and wanted to go up to a flat on the upper floors of the house. Opening the door, she heard the mewing of a kitten lying on the stairs; the woman wanted to take the kitten for her child as a toy, but when she came near it, the white-furred kitten was already lying dead.
Gas! Gaas! she cried out, running up the stairs. Trembling with fright she opened the skylight — so high up the gas will surely not reach; that is what they had told her.
For Z gas 1950 this was no hiding place, and she fell down in a faint. Great was her pain when she heard her child crying. Z gas floated around the window too and struck the mother and her dear child. When the gas [waves?] had drifted off a little and the summer sun shone out, lighting with its rays the dead in the street and in the abandoned houses, it also shone on the dead mother and her dead child. The mother's wax-yellow face was stiffened and her eyes glazed.
Translated from Esperanto by
M. Rozen.

Moshe Trojanowski.

With my head bowed to the ground
I stand weary and lost in thought;
in my brain thoughts drag along
like shadows in a dark night.

Like a [lost one?] who wandered on the way,
driven away from people and friends,

in gloomy loneliness.

And when my weary body
was worn out with longing,

onto my bed, in tears.

No one kept watch at my bed,
no mother — shed a tear;
I lie like a dog and [brood?] all the while,

What’s new in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Magistrat builds new stalls

[Header of the section “What’s new in Zagłębie?”; side boxes: Friday, 2 Shevat 5690 | Piątek 31 stycznia 1930 — Friday, 31 January 1930.]
Będzin
Magistrat builds new stalls
People will dance openly and freely...
At Tuesday’s city council session, which lasted barely 4 hours, a series of statutes was adopted, as were the Magistrat’s proposals that 15 booths (small rooms) and new stalls be put up on the “Targowisko” [market square].
The session is chaired by chairman Fürstenberg. Before the agenda, councillor Szkutnik (N. D. — National Democrats) tables a motion of no confidence in vice-chairman Ehrlich, who “tendentiously[?] conducted the last city council session”. The motion will be on the agenda of the next session.
They proceed to the 2nd reading of the statute on payment for water. Councillor Lewin proposes amending a certain paragraph to the effect that the tenants should pay for water directly at the Magistrat. (As we are informed, the “club” of Jewish councillors has decided that the house-owners should collect the water charges.)
Councillor Rebnic[?] demands that the councillors be called to a special session to discuss the water question. After a discussion, the amendment of councillor Klajnman is adopted, that a conference be called on the matter. The conference is to take place next Monday at the Magistrat.
Without discussion, the statutes on vacant lots, the local (premises) tax, hotel, inheritances, dogs, etc., are adopted as in the previous year. The “worst” fate befell the statute on taxing public entertainments. Over this statute a passionate discussion flared up. It was caused by the interpellation of Mr. Lewin about the Magistrat having taken tax from the last academic ball in Będzin. Vice-president Rubinlicht, alderman (ławnik) Goldsztajn, Błażejewicz, Fajner, Dr. Rechtman and Dr. Jarzębowski stated that when academics, who live in the worst conditions, organise an entertainment, they should be exempted from the municipal tax. Against this came out President [Mayor] Michel[?], who nervously fought this view: academic organisations are not philanthropic institutions, and anyway, whoever wants to dance must pay tax...
The dance debate lasts an hour and a half, and in the vote on various amendments the statute is, on the motion of Mr. Jakubowicz, sent to the committee for general affairs.
Then the Magistrat’s proposals are considered: 1) to allocate a sum of 2 thousand zł. to build 15 booths in the market halls; everyone who rents such a booth will pay 5 zł. a month; and 2) to allocate 15 thousand zł. to put up a row of new stalls, for which the holders will pay 15 zł. a month each.
Speaking against both proposals: Lewin, Gitler, Fajner, who put forward various amendments as to how the square around the halls should be put in order.
Councillor Garczarczyk[?] takes the floor on the question; he speaks about the substance of the question and not about amendments. If — he says — the Magistrat was not able to arrange the halls properly, then the traders[?] should not have been chased off the old market; what did you put up for his sukkahs?[?]
Before proceeding to the vote, Dr. Rechtman makes a statement that he will not take part in the vote. Dr. Jarzębowski makes the same statement on behalf of his “club”.
Both proposals are adopted and the chairman closes the session at 12 midnight.
President Nahum Sokolow Is Coming to Będzin

This week the local committee of the „Keren Hayesod“ received a notice from the Central Committee (Ts. K.) that, on his way to Katowice, the President of the World Zionist Executive, Nahum Sokolow, wishes to honour the town of Będzin with a lecture.
In this connection, continual meetings of Zionist activists are being held on how to arrange a grand reception in honour of the distinguished guest.
The day of the lecture has not yet been fixed. By current reckoning Sokolow will come here in the last days of next week.
Vice-President Rubinlicht Intervenes with the Voivode in Katowice

This week Vice-Pres. Mr. Rubinlicht intervened with the Katowice voivode [provincial governor] concerning the granting of licences to the peddlers („hoyzirer“). The voivode promised to settle the matter favourably; at the same time he stressed that the number of licences issued will be smaller than last year.
„Give Us Back Our Former Water“ — So Cry the Residents of 3rd of May Square

Before the water-mains were installed, 2 water pumps („plumplekh“) operated on 3rd of May Square, and there was plenty of water.
But the moment the water-mains work was finished, the existing pumps were abolished („skasirt“ [skasowane]) and only a single pump was put up. Because of this, terrible scenes take place before one has the privilege of getting a bucket („vyadre“ [wiadro]) of water. Every day there are fights among the servants, and the noise echoes through the air.
120 Halutzim Pass Through

On Tuesday 120 olim [emigrants to Palestine] passed through on the evening express („courier train“). From Będzin the Revisionist Shlomo Fuks travelled with them. In Katowice, at the station, various Hebrew songs were sung.
On the occasion of Shlomo Fuks's departure a farewell evening was held at the Zionist Organisation.
General Meeting of „Malbish Arumim“

Next Sunday a general meeting of the society „Malbish Arumim“ [Clothing the Naked] will take place. The institution, which carries on useful work, comes to the meeting with various reports that should be heard by the members, so that they can see whether the institution properly fulfils its task.
The meeting takes place in the premises of „Ahavat Hesed“.
—o—
Dr. Ostromęcki Appointed to a Higher Post
The head of the health department of the Kielce voivodeship, Dr. Ostromęcki, is leaving his present office and has been appointed to a higher post in the Warsaw voivodeship.
Dr. Ostromęcki is known to us for his decision that the old market should be cleared away.
—o—
The „Khapers“ Plague...
The plague of the „khapers“ [grabbers; apparently street touts] has grown worse again; day after day merchants come and raise the alarm at the „Merchants' Association“, demanding that the association react to this widespread scourge. Therefore an urgent meeting of the board will take place on Sunday, which will consider what measures to adopt so that the „khapers“ will not be so active.
—o—
Meeting of „WIZO“
On Sunday at 4 in the afternoon the women members of „WIZO“ will assemble in the Zionist premises, where current questions will be discussed and a report on the „Blue-White Evening“ will be given.
Sosnowiec — Action by the Merchants' Association

Sosnowiec
Action by the Merchants' Association
Last Sunday the board of the Merchants' Association, Piłsudska 12, called a members' meeting to discuss various current commercial matters.
On the agenda: 1) cooperatives and cartels, 2) competition, 3) taxes. The chairman, Mr. Weigreb[?], reports on the present situation in trade, outlines in bold strokes the severe crisis now prevailing, and proposes that all present express their opinion on how the distress might be eased a little.
Mr. Warman declares that the greatest misfortune brought upon the merchant class is the cooperatives and cartels; we must strive for free trade, and the cooperatives too should pay taxes like all merchants.
Mr. Zendel proposes that the merchants must organise themselves well and that
To Organise Trade Branches.
a kind of „walka z lichwą“ [campaign against profiteering] should be created in the reverse direction, i.e. not to sell more cheaply.
The secretary, Mr. Berkowicz, gives a report on tax questions, reminding the merchants that by the 15th of luty [February] everyone must submit declarations („zeznania“) of turnover („obrót“) for 1929.
Taking part in the discussion are Messrs. Dlutman[?], Gliksman, Honigman and others.
In conclusion the chairman, Mr. Weigreb[?], sums up that no resolution is yet being adopted at today's meeting, but it is established that all present agree that the greatest plague is competition; therefore the first attempt is being made to organise branch sections. For this purpose the members are asked that when they are called, all should come punctually.
Starosta Opposes Mr. Zendel's Resignation

This week the Będzin starosta [district head] notified the kehilla board that the resignation of Mr. L. Zendel as president (prezes) of the kehilla must be confirmed by the voivode, and until the decision Mr. Zendel must carry out his present office.
Paid the Debt with... a Slap

[Sosnowiec — Crime.]
Mr. Ch. Beruszak [?] of Katowice remained owing several hundred zł. to the firm "Szancer and Konopiński" [?]. The latter at long last obtained against the debtor an enforcement clause (klauzula) and then a distraint (zajęcie). For this "impudence" Mr. B. came to Sosnowiec to "settle" the debt.
Mr. B. accomplished the mission "in the best manner": he met Mr. L. Szancer, tore the skirt of his coat, and instead of "interest" handed him a slap...
A police report was drawn up against the "heroic" debtor.
A Meeting of Unemployed Dispersed

[Sosnowiec — Unemployment.]
On Monday a crowd of several thousand unemployed gathered in front of the magistrate (town hall), before whom the Communist Sejm deputy delivered a speech. At that moment mounted police arrived and dispersed the public meeting. Several agitators were arrested in the process.
Inspection of Public Welfare Institutions

[Zagłębie — Welfare.]
The delegate of the Ministry of Social Welfare, Naczelnik Tyrakowski, together with representatives of the voivodeship, carried out in recent days an inspection of the public welfare institutions existing at the municipal administrations in Zagłębie.
The delegate also audited the activity of the labour exchange office in Sosnowiec.
Zionists Celebrate a House-Warming

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.]
This coming Saturday night (Motzei Shabbat) the house-warming (Chanukat ha-Bayit) of the new Zionist premises on Dekerta Street takes place. A member of the Central Committee, Mgr. Goldsztajn, is also to take part in the celebration and will deliver a lecture.
In the same premises a general meeting of the local Zionist Organization will take place the next day, Sunday afternoon.
Today Is the Day of Judgement...

[Sosnowiec — Rabbinate.]
Today, Friday, the Supreme Tribunal in Warsaw will announce its decision whether the rabbinical elections in our town were legally valid, and also whether the 7 votes for Rabbi Englard will be regarded as a majority or not. (15 parnassim [council members] took part in the election; the result was: Rabbi Englard — 8 votes, Rabbi Brodt — 6 votes, and 3 blank ballots.)
It is therefore no wonder that the decision is awaited with great suspense.
A Sad Sunday

[Sosnowiec (?) — Community.]
Last Sunday there were 4 deaths in our town. Such a number of funerals in one day has not occurred here for 5 years.
Death of a Miner

[Zagłębie — Mines.]
At the "Mysłowice" coal mine a lump of coal broke loose and killed 26-year-old Michał Kłaczka [?].
75,000 Złoty or 2 Years in Prison

[Sosnowiec — courts.] Four Christians stood before the local district court, accused of smuggling various colonial goods from Germany into Poland.
The accused were sentenced to pay 75,000 zł. or 2 years in prison.
Success of a Young Artist

[Sosnowiec — culture.] Last Sunday the 19-year-old pianist Szpilman appeared here in a concert. After every number he was showered with strong applause. Szpilman possesses great musical abilities and promises a successful future.
From the Chamber of Commerce

[Sosnowiec — trade.] In connection with the applications for permission to import prohibited goods from abroad, submitted for the first quarter of 1930, the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce announces that those concerned must send to the Ministry of Commerce a copy of the trade licence (patent) purchased for the year 1930.
In the coming days the Ministry of Commerce will stop issuing permits to firms that have not sent in a copy of their trade licences. The copy must bear a stamp duty of 50 gr.
—o—
[Strzemieszyce — community.] Strzemieszyce. — The new kehilla budget.
The kehilla board has completed the budget for the year 1930. The budget amounts to 46 thousand zł. Compared with last year the budget is smaller by 2 thousand zł., solely in the regular (etat) income. Last Thursday the official (referent) of the starosty, Magryczewski [?], carried out an inspection of the gmina's books and found everything in the best order.
—o—
[Strzemieszyce — culture.] A change of name...
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Magawist [?] a meeting of the members of the "I. L. Peretz" library took place. On the agenda was the item: changing the name of the library. By a large majority of votes it was decided to name the library after Dr. Herzl. The meeting was closed with the singing of "Hatikvah".
—o—
[Strzemieszyce — Zionism.] A "Gordonia" founded.
On Saturday night, with the participation of Mr. [K]liwer [?] of Będzin, a "Gordonia" was founded. The elected board has already set about the practical work.
—o—
[Strzemieszyce — culture.] A lecture.
On Tuesday Dr. Kaufman gave a lecture at the "Iluzjon" on an economic subject. The hall was packed full; the proceeds are designated for the benefit of the library.
Mi Yodea.
For the third time...

[Będzin — Kehilla.] Last Saturday night the Będzin kehilla council was called to a meeting to consider the new kehilla budget. One member was missing for a quorum, and the meeting was postponed to Wednesday. But again a "reason" happened, and a mistake crept into the invitations: instead of Wednesday, Tuesday was written; because of this the chairman was angry and did not want to come to the meeting.
The meeting is now to take place next Saturday night.
—o—
The "Warsaw Gehenna" comes to Zagłębie
[Theatre.] Next Friday and Saturday the ensemble of the "Scala" theatre in Warsaw comes to Zagłębie. They will stage the revue "Gehenna" in 10 acts, 12 scenes. The biggest fire in the "Gehenna" will be the famous soubrette Pepi Lipman.
In Sosnowiec "Gehenna" will be seen on Friday the 7th and on Saturday during the day; in Będzin on Saturday night, the 8th of this month.
—o—
Optimism of the president of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce
[Sosnowiec — Economy.] On Tuesday a general meeting of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce took place. President Gardomski[?] dwelt on the present critical situation and said that in 1930 the situation will improve thanks to the trade agreement with Germany. After the report on the activity to date, the project was discussed to begin building, from the spring, workers' houses that will be paid off in instalments. The proposal is adopted.

Festive Opening of the Zionist Clubroom in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — Zionism and public life.] (Sh.) For quite a long time the Zionist Organization in Sosnowiec was homeless, without premises of its own in which Zionist work could proceed normally. With great effort and labour a group of devoted Zionists, headed by Mr. Y. S. Weigrib, has finally managed to create premises in the centre of town (Dekerta[?] 5). Last Saturday night the festive opening of the premises took place.
The mood in the hall is festive; the choir under the direction of Mr. Y. Lejchter sings "Mizmor shir hanukkat ha-bayit", and Mr. B. Rozman, before a packed[?] hall, gives a short speech, after which he hands the senior member of the Zionist Organization in Sosnowiec, Mr. Y. S. Weigrib, the scissors to cut the ribbon. At the presidium table sit Messrs. Weigrib (chairman), Dr. Rieger (Katowice) and Mgr. Goldsztajn as representative of the Central Committee in Warsaw. Taking the chair, Mr. Weigrib greets all the guests and expresses the hope that from this moment on we shall finally be able to get down to normal work. The choir then sings the Jewish and the Polish anthems, and the greetings begin. On behalf of Keren Hayesod, Rozman [and] the president Dr. T. Melodysta[?] give greetings; for the KKL — Sh. Feldman; Dr. Rieger (Zionists of Katowice); L. Jungster (Mizrachi); Prof. Rozenbrak[?] (Tarbut, Warsaw); Klarman (Maccabi); Chlebicki (Hashomer Hatzair); Szmitmana[?] (Herzliya, in Polish) and Nachtwig[?] (Artisans' Association).
The representative of the Central Committee, Mgr. Goldsztajn, takes the floor and gives an hour-long lecture. "When I learned," Mr. G. begins, "that Sosnowiec has its own Zionist premises, I was very glad, because every time I was here — and I have been here perhaps 5 times — the meeting was held somewhere else each time, and I always saw the same people in front of me. Today you already have premises of your own, and I see new people here in the hall. We are here for a celebration, and I would not want to go into investigations[?]. I want to say only one thing: from various sides people are beginning to fight against the Balfour Declaration; we true Zionists are not afraid of that, because if, God forbid, the Balfour Declaration were annulled and 75 per cent of the Zionists were to leave our ranks, 25 per cent would still remain who will believe in our just cause, and in faith lies our strength. Our Zionist flag is blue and white, and it symbolizes something: white — that is purity, i.e. clean hands and a clean conscience; blue — the purity of the sky of the Land of Israel. Such pure Zionists is what Zionism wants. Our ideal is truly beautiful, after all the whole world admires us; I wish you that the new premises may be able to take in the whole idea of our blue-and-white flag." (Applause.)
Then Rozman[?] [and] the president Dr. Melodysta[?] give a longer, successful speech, recounting the various transformations the Zionist Organization in Sosnowiec has recently gone through. "The time when our youth," says Dr. M., "was demoralized because of the war years is already past; we are now approaching an era in which we will not operate with figures, but the main items in our Zionist budget will be Zionist spirit. Our undertaking will have to succeed, because in the blue of our flag I see the hope." (Prolonged applause.)
After Dr. Melodysta's speech Mr. Weigrib closes the official part of the evening, and the public moves to the buffet, where our future "WIZO" leaders treat the guests to a good glass of "Carmel". In very high spirits are Messrs. Feldman and Rozman, who showed great "abilities" in selling apples and pączki (doughnuts); jokers even say they had greater success at that than at collecting for Keren Hayesod.
The unofficial part begins with a concert by young Ziskind, who plays Wieniawski's "Légende" and a romance. The young violinist proves very gifted, and it would be a great pity if such a young talent were to go to waste. The shomeret H. Jasna then sings very beautifully a Hebrew song, "Ro'eh Mehalel" by Engel; the audience rewarded the little singer with applause and called her back for an encore ("bis") — and here something unexpected happened: the commander of "Hashomer Hatzair", Mr. Chlebicki, appears and announces that because of an attack by "Brit Trumpeldor" on the kfirim (cubs) of "Hashomer Hatzair" he must leave the hall with all the shomrim, and at the same time issues a "pekuda" (order) to the shomeret Jasna not to sing any more. This causes a certain consternation (after all, a Jewish celebration...), but it does not last long, because the well-known singer Miss Margot[?] Jasna creates a mood with her very beautiful singing of Shneour's splendid song "Yr Enga"[?], for which she is rewarded with long bravos.
The young crowd draws the old Zionists, together with Mgr. Goldsztajn, into a circle, and they dance a little "rikuda", which drags on until 2 o'clock at night. With "Hatikvah" and "Hithazaknah" (printed "Hatkhokna") the impressive celebration comes to an end.
The decoration of the premises, which made a very good impression, as well as all the technical work, was carried out by the technical committee under the direction of Messrs. H. Rozman and B. Jasny.

The well-known Łódź merchant Natan Lipszyc came to Katowice, where he wanted to obtain some agency. After spending 2 days there, Lipszyc threw himself from the 4th floor of the Hotel "Continental" and was killed on the spot.

An Appeal to the Jewish Population of Dąbrowa.

[Dąbrowa — Zionism.]
In our town a "Grünbaum Jubilee Committee" has been formed, whose task is to join the circle of national Jewry, which fights worthily for a distinctive Jewish national life in the present.
Yitzhak Grünbaum, a self-sacrificing man who has given himself entirely to the altar of the idea in order to serve his persecuted and tormented people — has turned 50 years old!
