The Jewish Kehilla Representation (III)

(What led to the present ruin? — The tactics of the leaders. — The budgets must be reduced. — The classification [for tax] must be an honest one.)
III.
In our earlier chapters we dwelt at length on our kehilla representation; we examined the question from all sides, treated it with full seriousness, and came to the conclusion that the results are very sad. And in fact this is no wonder either, because nobody cared at all; nobody took the trouble to set the institution — which should have occupied the summit of our Jewish life — at its proper height. No one took into account that here, where all strata of the population are represented, this representation should be a strictly non-partisan institution, that it should be above parties, that it should conduct itself with full tolerance on every occasion.
No, this was not even attempted; nobody saw to it that proper loyalty should prevail and that pure honesty should stand as the first item on the agenda. Gradually[?] the institution sank ever lower, and the partisan rabble (lit. 'mouse-swarm') openly and shamelessly plundered every corner of kehilla life. It is therefore no wonder that the highest Jewish representation of our local Jewish parliament has become so petty in the eyes of the Jewish members. And it is certainly no wonder, because nobody cared to maintain the prestige of the institution; and if there were people who had an understanding for something higher and more idealistic, they were pushed out or brought to the point of fleeing from there. And in reality such people — who had an understanding for a brighter tomorrow and a finer today — truly had nothing to do there. And once those who wanted to and could create grand things were removed, the little people began to breathe more freely, and then they began to feel at home. It goes without saying that then began the heyday of phrase-mongering[?], egoistic politics; no one was taken into account and nothing stood in their way. The leaders did whatever found grace and favour in their eyes.
True, at the time one could not have imagined that the institution would sink so low that it would arouse no interest whatsoever in Jewish life; and had we not been taxed so heavily by them, people would have forgotten altogether that they exist here in Zagłębie and that they hold any position at all in Jewish life.
With such a management, such disharmony, such dissatisfaction on all sides, it would have been understandable that the institutions should be dissolved altogether — all the more so when we take into account that their term of office ended long ago. But they have become so hardened that nothing bothers them; they sit firmly in their chairs and, year in, year out, regularly produce one budget after another, behaving no worse than the government institutions, the tax offices (urzędy skarbowe), with higher budgets every year.
It is a self-evident thing and everyone knows it perfectly well: however much he had to pay last year, this year he has more. No account is taken of any crises, nothing is looked at; the officials know only one thing — that every year one must have more revenue, and that is enough.
Our local Jewish 'offices' go roughly the same ways; they too know that from year to year they must have bigger budgets — that they do nothing, subsidise no one, advance at an ox's pace from year to year, does not matter, as long as they make higher budgets.
The Jewish kehillas of Zagłębie are now busy drawing up new budgets, and all of them have prepared higher budgets — regardless of the fact that last year's [assessments] are very hard for them to collect, and they know for certain that much of it they will be unable to collect because the population has become impoverished and is in no position to pay the burdensome taxes.
It is therefore more practical and more sensible to reduce the budget both in Będzin and in Sosnowiec, so that it may be spread over the population in smaller sums that will actually be paid, rather than imposing high taxes on middling and small people which cannot be collected. What comes of the high budgets, when quite a sizeable percentage is nothing but dead capital!!
Besides, our Jewish kehilla leaders surely must look at the Jewish situation with open eyes; they surely must see how grave the danger of a Jewish catastrophe is. After all, they are in the midst of the Jewish throng; surely[?] they [know] the Jewish suffering and the hard Jewish livelihoods, which grow harder and harder from year to year. And what of the present crisis, which reaches every merchant and every artisan — and the prospects for the future are not particularly good either: if not worse, then certainly not better.
Do the Zagłębie kehilla leaders not see all this? Do they not feel it on their own shoulders too? We believe they do; and if so, then the question arises: how can one remain so indifferent and cold to one's own troubles and suffering? Besides, this will serve as a certificate for the [government tax] offices that we can be taxed with bigger sums; they will have proof that the Jewish kehillas, too, have burdened their members with higher taxes, and this will be a satisfaction for them and at the same time a licence (hekhsher) to take more money.
Besides, we have already shown on earlier occasions that we get nothing from our kehillas; it gives us nothing, and we are no longer so naive as to want to demand anything of them, because we know that would be idle talk. Therefore let them maintain the religious functionaries (printed 'pley kodesh' for kley kodesh) and let them touch nothing else — then the question arises: how much does one need per year for the religious functionaries! Moreover there is also income from shechita (ritual slaughter) and other small items. In that case there can be no talk at all of budgets of quarter-millions.
The leaders must by no means show that they rule over us only because they have power in their hands. One must not, and cannot, in today's bitter times take money from the population without the conviction that the sums collected are applied to the most useful purposes. One must nevertheless reckon with a whole town of people; one must enter into their situation; one must consider in what circumstances the people find themselves and whether they are able to pay out money, whatever the amount.
We know, after all, that taxes today are not distributed rationally, each according to his means, but according to protekcja (connections). If one presents oneself (printed 'perzent') before the commission with a good friend, one comes through well; if not, it is bitter — one fails and must weep and pay.
The protekcja system has unfortunately taken hold everywhere. Everywhere it is the ruler and the one with the say; everywhere it stands in first place, ruling and governing.
This system is an unheard-of injustice. It must not be allowed to go on ruling openly and shamelessly without limit. One surely cannot allow one person to pay for several merely because Shmerl or Berl dropped[?] a word. We have plenty of such 'good friends', who do it so artfully, so innocently, that one would think they were pure souls — and meanwhile they are after nothing but deliberately to 'do him in', because they have had an eye on him since old times. There are such 'kosher' little Jews who put on a show of pure holiness, eyes rolled up to the Master of the Universe, only to achieve the aim they have set themselves — to become a communal activist (printed 'klal-tofer', for klal-tuer).
Two cardinal matters must therefore be settled now by our kehilla administrations, in Sosnowiec as well as in Będzin, and they are: unconditionally to reduce the budgets to a minimum; and secondly, the classification must be a rational, an honest one, without any protekcja.
That is all we can still demand of our kehilla representations, as long as they exist and take money from us.
R. Les.
Health or Education?

[Feuilleton — education and family.] By B. Kowner.
(Such a din torah.)

An acquaintance of mine and his wife came to me for a din torah [a rabbinic-style arbitration].
It concerned their little girl of about twelve.
Both of them, the husband as well as the wife, are educated people, and yet they could not come to terms.
The question was: what does their child need more, health or education?
I shall pass their arguments on to you:
He: — My child is a very weak child; she does not eat the way a child should eat, does not sleep the way a child should sleep, and she does not weigh what she ought to weigh; she is perhaps 30 pounds short of the proper weight.
The child is 12 years old and looks as if she were 7 or 8, and who is to blame? — My wife. Whatever she can, she stuffs into the child: you want piano — there is piano; you want writing and reading Yiddish, Jewish history, singing — the mother wants to cram everything into this limp child, and forgets that the child also has to get through school; and all that is too much for such a weak child. The poor thing is collapsing under the heavy load. No time is left for the child to play with other children, to have movement, air and amusement, to go through what a child of her age must go through. When you talk to my child you would think she is already 18. She has grown old before her time, she has never yet had any youth, she is always sad, melancholy, nervous... And now my wife wants to send her to dancing lessons as well; dancing is all she was missing. The child has no strength to live — and go and dance!
Here the wife took the floor:
— I am no more than a mother — she began — but a mother understands a thing better than a father. I say that a child, however healthy, however strong it may be [?] — if it is foolish, that is a misfortune, all the more so a girl. A girl must be more educated, must know music and languages and other accomplishments.
If she is no more than a healthy piece of flesh, that is not good; education adds salt and pepper to life.
We live in different times, in modern times... When a girl grows up and begins to go about with young men, it is much nicer when the young man sees that he is dealing with an educated girl. He has more respect for her; he cannot behave [—] her as toward just a healthy, foolish wench who possesses nothing more than flesh... Flesh alone is nothing. There must be soul, spirit, intelligence — that is weightier than weight [pun: "vikhtiker vi gevikht"].. Am I right or not?
But before I had time to speak, the girl's father snatched the word:
— My friend, my wife speaks, it seems, to the point, as an intelligent woman and mother, and yet she forgets one thing: I do not say that children should not be taught, I do not say that a girl must be mere flesh, mere body... Of course one must be intelligent, of course one must possess education, but when does that apply? When the child is by nature a strong child, a healthy child; but what is the ruling when the child is a feeble child? When all these things are too hard for its health? I say that in such a case education does harm. What use to me is a child with every virtue if the child is not healthy, if she does not eat, does not drink, does not sleep, does not laugh and does not grow? Don't you think that when such a girl reaches, let us say, 19 or 20 and looks like 12 or 13 and has no strength to [?] — that such a girl is more unhappy than a healthy girl who is not educated? Not all children are born healthy, therefore one must not load too much onto such a weak child; the burden must not outweigh her, one must not overstep the measure..
There are children who can absorb everything, they are like sponges... but for our child everything is too hard..
The mother fell silent and the father concluded:
— So, as you hear, we keep quarrelling about our child all the time. And you know our wives, don't you? Once they say yes, it is yes — they must have their way.
And meanwhile the child is wasting away; every day she becomes limper, lighter, thinner, more melancholy... So we have come to you so that you would hear us out and tell us who is right — I or my wife? We consider you a good friend, a man of plain common sense...
— Eh! — I answered — eh! If I were a man of plain common sense, I would not have got married myself... I fell into it just like you, my dear friend... As long as we are the men and they the wives, we shall always remain what we are.. weak, broken, soft as cotton wool... We shall always give away our "I", our pride, our freedom for a smile of theirs, a charm, a caress, a kiss, a stroke. — Those are their instruments, their weapons, which make us what we are... You, for your part, are more right than your wife, although she too is a little bit right... If she were not sitting next to me, I would tell you openly and freely that in the case of your child health is preferable to piano or dancing; but since your wife is sitting next to me, I shall tell you my opinion some other time.. Your wife is a woman who can give good arguments, and it might yet happen that after the arguments she would come out the winner, and that does not become me, it does not suit me; I always want to remain the one who is right, even when I am not right..
Therefore I shall tell you some other time that you are right, not your wife.
And perhaps — I went on — I would hand this question over to our readers. Let them decide the din torah... You are not the only husband and wife who do not agree on bringing up children... If only we had the millions.. Let the readers who can hold a pen in hand answer.
They liked my plan, and they went home satisfied...
"Khapers" (Touts) in a Modern Age

(Grabbing and trade. — The ugliest stain. — Can it be tolerated?)
"Khapers" [touts — street "grabbers" who drag customers into shops]! What on earth is that, what does it serve, who makes use of it? It is doubtful whether anyone in the great world knows it — but what are we saying, that in the great wide world they know nothing of it: even here at home, in Poland, in Warsaw, Łódź, or even in smaller towns and shtetls, people do not know the meaning of the word "khapers" either.
One does not know who wants to grab whom, and why one person should actually need to grab another; but what is known in no town at all is known all the better here in Zagłębie, and above all in our "residence" towns, Będzin and Sosnowiec.
"Khapers", as everyone here knows, are a newly invented apparatus, a kind of magnetic instrument that pulls customers into the shops with tremendous force. The apparatus has so much strength in it that it is capable of dragging customers down into the cellars and even up into the attics. As soon as the apparatus catches people in its paws — oh, then they will no longer wriggle free of it; it can[?] then do with them whatever it wants; then[?] a person is a zero[?] to it, who must, like the clay golem, carry out its commands and its orders.
Who should receive the patent for the apparatus nobody knows, because nobody knows who the inventor was. The instrument has become as ingrained in the people as, for instance, popular sayings and proverbs, whose author no people knows.
Whether it brings benefit or harm — that, too, nobody knows. It is a thing that is hard to establish among us. Of course, among no other people in the world would this have developed. They would have recognised on the spot the danger, the sickness and the harmfulness of this undesirable element, and it would have been stifled instantly.
Quite different, however, is the case with our traders, who know only "shum hayom"[?] — today one must sell, today one must take in cash, because today a bill of exchange is lying presented at the bank which has to be paid [—]; and whatever will be tomorrow — if one has sold today and made a profit, you see, such a Jew has finished worrying about it. For tomorrow we have a great God; let Him worry.
But the little "machine" has acquired such a property that it must get more than its owner. It says to its master: you may[?] not earn; no sooner have I brought you a customer, no sooner have you taken in money, than I am owed such-and-such — and ask no questions, because otherwise I can make myself heard, and then, oh, you will certainly have no more joy of me...
And these instruments have a trait: a word is sacred to them — said and done; nevertheless they have cast a kind of spell on their masters, so that the masters cannot part with them; and that is precisely why all the explanatory articles we have already devoted to the question are superfluous.
Of course it would be quite different if we had before us a healthy merchant element, one that would know how to react to things that must not be tolerated; for what does it mean to introduce Asiatic customs in Europe in the present century? Why do we not stop to consider this harmfulness? Besides, where did we see this, and from whom did we learn these wild customs, to which we have somehow already grown accustomed? But on strangers, on the visitor from outside, it makes a terrible impression. What is this: as soon as people see a fresh face who turns out to be from Upper Silesia, they start tearing at him by the coat-tails and the hands, one dragging him right, the other left, and so on without end.
From[?] whom did we pick this up? Does any of these traders ever take account of how he looks in the eyes of a conscious person, when he watches the way he trades, the tricks by which he wants to earn his living? Is that any finer than the conjurer who pulls ribbons out of his mouth? Does one regard such a person as a merchant, who should conduct himself honestly [reell], in a modern and elegant way? Does such a person not become ridiculous in the eyes of a better person?
Why do we not take a better look at the Upper Silesian firms, which have an understanding for the development of their businesses? They know that their businesses require intelligent salesmen and saleswomen, spacious[?] premises, aesthetic shop windows to attract the customers. They understand how to advertise their goods properly.
They think only of how to create something new and attractive — here with advertisements, there with the good quality of the goods. We would do better to learn from them, rather than letting the "khaper" be the alpha and omega of business. Upon my life, it is a disgrace and a sorrow, and it debases us both in our own eyes and in the eyes of our neighbours.
A trader for whom the essence[?] of the business is the "khaper" cannot get far, neither with credit nor with the development of his business; even among our more intelligent merchants, who are unfortunately still very few in number, he cannot play the role he would have needed to play had he conducted himself like decent people. Such a way of doing business, such tactics, such trade give the impression of cheating and haggling — as the saying goes, "as long as there's trading"[?].
Today, in the twentieth century, one cannot trade in this way, and for these traders we see no future.
Besides, one must not forget another thing: that the ground, the foundation of these traders is rotten through and through. He does not take account of where he stands in the world, how much he needs to earn; he can never work it out for himself, he is far from knowing how to calculate either the goods or the profits. He thinks he has the reckoning in hand from the start when he tells you, for example, that the article costs him 100 zł. and he charges 110 zł. — he has a certainty ["kima lan"] of 10% profit; whereas in reality it is often the other way round: at a given moment he is even adding of his own, because he forgets the small items — he simply does not count dispatch, taxes, administration; and then, when he adds it all up, only then will he see why he grows poorer from year to year.
Of course this "calculation" and the "khaper-traders" do immeasurable harm to the merchants who do not behave this way, those who cannot tolerate such disgusting dealing; but it turns out that they do nothing about it, and perhaps they made attempts, but these proved too weak, too helpless.
Now we see that the "khaper" question has taken on a different character, a more serious and perhaps a more painful one; therefore one must deal with it in full earnest and awareness, so that it can be properly resolved.
One must not put up with it, and it hurts all the more because the degradation[?] stems from ourselves; we make ourselves ridiculous with such hocus-pocus trading, to which no one compels us.
Had we proper professional institutions, had our merchants' and small traders' associations been serious class institutions with a consistent economic line, where everything would find the proper response, they would not have allowed such a sick, harmful trade to develop — one from which nobody gains anything and which harms both our trade and our own four cubits, while these tactics also bring shame upon us before the outside world.
So we must see to it, in Sosnowiec as in Będzin, to abolish the ugly stain that has settled on the shoulders of the Jewish merchant.
With good will, with serious and sincere treatment of the question, our economic professional institutions could find enough means to solve the question radically and remove the ugly stain from the merchant's shoulder.
Selekt.
A Small Feuilleton: Noah's Ark

It is not about Noah's Ark, which floated several thousand years ago at the time of the Flood, that we speak here, nor about the Noah's Ark that has just floated up[?] from the screen [the film "Noah's Ark"], but about the Noah's Ark that is now floating about in the flood of the great crisis.
The flood is extraordinarily great, the whole world is drowning, but in this flood there are nevertheless lucky ones, a chosen few, who have grabbed themselves a place in Noah's Ark and feel at home there..
You will find them, the lucky ones, among all classes and strata — every class and stratum has its own ark.
Let us begin with the manufacturers: the factories stand idle, the manufacturers are drowning in a flood of protests [protested bills], but among these same manufacturers you will find a select few whose wheels keep turning — they have saved themselves in Noah's Ark...
The same with the merchants: the greater part of them is drowning in the flood of taxes and "nakazy" [payment orders], but there are a few individuals who do not feel it; they had the luck to grab a place in Noah's Ark...
Even the workers do not all drown in the flood of unemployment — we do indeed have many thousands of unemployed in Zagłębie, but you will find some who are floating in Noah's Ark..
What more do you need — even in our institutions, societies and banks, which are built on democratic foundations, there are also a chosen few who are inside Noah's Ark, and others who are outside the ark.
As for the flood of our lack of rights, it goes without saying that in this flood too there are lucky ones floating in Noah's Ark!
And that is precisely the trouble: the lucky ones who are in the ark do not take after their father Noah — Noah took into the ark representatives of all species, so that no one should be wronged, but the "sons of Noah" have only themselves in mind...
And one more thing:
Noah, at the very first opportunity, sent out the dove, which brought him a leaf with the good tidings that the Flood was already over; but the "sons of Noah" are not interested at all, they do not care if the flood drags on and on — they need[?] no leaves...
That is to say, there are plenty of "leaves" [Yiddish bletter — also: newspapers], but where does one get the leaf through which we could find out how things stand with the flood?
Onkelos.
Little Letters from Home

[Satirical feuilleton — Dąbrowa.] With God's help, [week of the Torah portion] “ulema'an tesaper” [Bo]..
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
After asking after your good health: I am very glad that I have the privilege of writing you a little letter at least once, from which you will no doubt also draw a bit of comfort for today's daily troubles. After all, “it is a time of trouble for Jacob, but he shall be saved out of it.” The salvation we have merited, with Heaven's help, is not in material matters. God forbid[?] — only that we have become a little “free” of the old mouldy “zabobony” [superstitions], which made our bodies “sick”; [?] we were in the yeshivas, the “prisons”, where one sat — and did not spend the night there. You surely remember how our fathers, may they have a bright paradise, did not let us breathe freely. On winter nights, with a terrible wind whistling outside and snow up to the waist, my father would come up to the bed, where I was sunk in sweet sleep, and shout: “Get up”! It's already 4 o'clock before dawn and you are still lying in bed!
And further[?] I recall: it was at the time when the Dreyfus trial was going on — every day between Minchah and Maariv, by the dim light of the beit-midrash lamp, the “intelligent” of our shtetl told about that world trial. He told, and we, old and young, swallowed his words like the thirsty..
Once our shtetl received a guest from afar; the guest had a newspaper with him, and all my companions prevailed on him to delight us with that gift so precious to us..
But for that lust we paid very dearly: our fathers suddenly came into the beit midrash and discovered the great crime while we sat absorbed over the paper...
We tried to defend ourselves, brought proof from the “Shulchan Aruch” that in times of emergency one may read a newspaper even on the Sabbath, but the defence only increased our sin, and our sentence was a very ugly one...
In later years, when a Jewish newspaper had become a daily necessity, my father still kept to his strictness and did not allow anyone to take a newspaper in hand on the Sabbath. In wartime — he said — one permits reading a newspaper on the Sabbath, but today — heaven forbid...
And at last, R' Shlomo, the “chains” have been torn; the power of culture and civilisation has “broken through” the “dark fears”, and the “[suffering?] sons and daughters in the Orthodox homes have been freed from their sufferings until now, from their fanatical[?]-Jesuitical black fathers”...
The great “turning point” occurred on 18 September in the year 1930.
On that day there appeared in Warsaw the 100th number of the newspaper that is made in perfect holiness: the staff, both of the editorial office and of the administration — before they touch a number of the holy newspaper they immerse themselves 7 times in a boiling mikveh; special guards watch that there be no barrier during the immersion, and until the guard calls out “Kosher! Kosher!” the staff lie under the water..
So it is no wonder that the “day that is wholly good”, the day that brought into the world number 100 of the paper — has been recorded as a great holiday for religious Jewry...
And writers wrote, rebbes[?] sent blessings, and above all — a promise went out that whoever supports the kosher paper will merit both worlds, this world and the world to come...
R' Shlomo! What do you say to the good tidings, eh? I must tell you that when I read through the holy “decree” I recited with full devotion the blessing “who has kept us alive, sustained us and brought us to this season”. The time has finally come when we shall be “freed” of the whole bundle of commandments; to merit a morsel of Leviathan — what good are all the bothers [kłopoty]? Why torment oneself every day with the Daf Yomi, take pains to pray with a congregation, busy oneself with commandments — what for? Until when? Every morning I take the holy organ of the “Agudah” [Agudat Israel] and instead of the blessing over the Torah I say: “who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to read the ‘Yudish Tagblat’” [Dos Yudishe Togblat, Agudah daily in Warsaw]..
The greatest pleasure I have only on the Sabbath: the Chumash and the Midrash are now in the category of Sejm deputies — insignificant... You are — I tell them — “out of fashion”; you have embittered our life enough; in the 20th century there are new “Chumashim” with jokes and caricatures...
On Sabbath morning I sit down at the table and, with the well-known Gemara chant, study the articles of the great men of the generation, interwoven with “holy” words and verses; every word I swallow like Land-of-Israel oranges; even the jokes and caricatures are, after all, like wafers in honey. Oy-vey, oy-vey! What “happy times” we have lived to see...
If you wish, R' Shlomo, I will order such a paper for you; I know, after all, that where you are you surely have no time to fulfil “and thou shalt meditate therein”.. So now you have the opportunity in this way to support[?] the Torah, and above all to be insured for the world to come...
The second “joyful news” is from Dąbrowa [Górnicza], near Będzin. In that town a perfect idyll reigns. The town fathers there are out-and-out “democrats” and hold the position that Jewish interests must not be separated; there must exist general interests for the whole population. Their first step was that all subsidies for Jewish institutions were struck from the budget[?]... Jewish children will get Christmas gifts [gwiazdki], boys will study in the “Macierz”[?] [Polish school society]... etc.[?].
Then they went a step further. The merciful “fathers” could not bear the sorrow of the “żydowskie żebraki” [Jewish beggars] who go from door to door. No — they decided — our “democratic” views do not permit that there be Jewish and Christian beggars; our platform promises equal rights even for Jewish beggars...
A meeting took place; our “righteous women” and “knall-[?]” were invited, before whom the Mr. President [the town mayor] in his own honoured person delivered a sermon: that “[?]”-hearts pine away with grief at the sight of Jewish need, and “please, ladies” [proszę pań], we must see to it that the “poor people” [ubogich ludzi] receive their keep from the “municipal fund” [kasa miejska]...
— Quite right, Mr. President [słusznie, panie prezydencie] — our little wives answered with a coquettish smile — whatever Mr. President “wishes” [sobie życzy] we shall “fulfil” [spełnimy].
— “Thank you” [dziękuję wam] — the President bowed — every lady will receive collection boxes, which are to be distributed “among the shops” [po sklepach] and...
— Goodbye! Goodbye! [do widzenia] Leaving the session, the “ladies” could not stop marvelling that a president, a titled[?] doctor, should be so polite and speak in such a kindly tone to simple women. A rare person — [h]e cannot, poor man, bear to watch Jewish poor people wandering about the streets..
The women carried out the work to perfection. “There was not a house where there was not one dead” — in every Jewish shop there is such a charity box. Our brethren the children of Israel give charity, the municipal fund has an income, and the Jewish poor get a f...
Yes, R' Shlomo, not only in the magistrate's office does such a “broad democratic” order prevail; the local kehilla leaders too are very important[?] “democrats”; to list all their virtues I am quite unable. It will be enough for you to know that the Dąbrowa “dozór” men [kehilla board members] have given away the western wall of the synagogue as a place for advertisements. Not, God forbid, for Jews, but precisely for non-Jews. If a Christian craftsman needs to advertise his products, he turns to a dozór member and the matter is “załatwione” [settled]...
It is a joy — I tell you, R' Shlomo — to read in the synagogue the notices about Sabbath observance, the education of girls, the redemption of the Land, and also that
— “The mason[?] Jan Lempicki lives in Dąbrowa at.. number.. makes tile[?] stoves etc., etc.
— Kazimierz Kasper makes modern shoes etc., etc.
Every notice bears the stamp “The Authority of the Hebrew Community in Dąbrowa”...
Evil tongues murmur that the “authorities” are dealing on the side with the cinema owners, so that they will advertise the hit pictures in the synagogue. Well, what won't a Jewish leader do for “democracy”...
Therefore, I ask you, R' Shlomo, to publicise these reports in the wide world; perhaps[?] the Polish ambassador will be able to prove that in the area of Polish industry there is a shtetl where Jews pay pensions for non-Jewish poor people and kehilla leaders advertise in the synagogue the products of non-Jewish craftsmen...
So have a good Sabbath, as wishes you your
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot: we may perhaps have here as a guest our beloved Nachuml, may he live long; with us he is surely[?] a welcome[?] guest, a pupil of the immortal R' Yissachar Berish of blessed memory, as they say: “better he is not a pupil — [look] who the rebbe was”..
The above.
“Judith” — the Jewish-Polish heroine in Jan Sobieski’s times

“Judith.” The Jewish-Polish heroine in Jan Sobieski’s times.
(A historical legend)

A.
In the remote little town of Białopole lived the Jewish heroine Judith. She was the wife of Reb Avremke the rich man, whom the Christians called “Abramek”.
Among the Polish nobles Abramek was highly respected; he used to do big business with them and sometimes also help them out with an interest-free loan. Therefore the nobles were frequent guests at his house, and Judith always used to receive them very nicely and also to converse with them on various matters.
Judith’s beauty and her grace made a great impression on the circle of Reb Avremke’s Christian friends, so that she became much beloved and admired among the Polish nobility (szlachta).
At that time Poland was just engaged in the unfortunate Turkish war, owing to the treachery of the Cossack hetman Doroshenko [printed “Daratshenka”], and besides that in great civil strife within the country itself, which had the result that the Turks could move ever closer to the Polish borders and occupy Polish towns.
The enemy’s victory also forced King Michał Wiśniowiecki (1669–73) to sign the so-called “Buczacz” peace treaty (1672), unfavourable for Poland, which greatly humiliated the country’s honour. Poland lost Ukraine and Podolia and had to pay Turkey a large contribution as well. Because of all this the Sejm decided, disregarding the peace that had been concluded, to continue the war with the Turks, and handed over the supreme command of the Polish army to Hetman Jan Sobieski, who, after Wiśniowiecki’s sudden death, was then crowned King of Poland (1674–96) on account of his victory over the Turks beyond “Ratshin” [sic; presumably Chocim/Khotyn].
At first Jan Sobieski succeeded in defeating the Turks and driving them out of Poland, but soon the fortune of war turned away from him as well, and the Turks once again began to push ever deeper into Polish soil. Wherever they set foot, they destroyed all the blooming Polish fields, burned the nobles’ property and ravaged the peasants’ huts in pogroms, so that the gentry and the peasants were forced to abandon the village and seek shelter within the walls of the towns, among which was also Białopole.

B.
From Kamieniec, which the Turks held firmly in their hands, to Białopole was quite a small distance, and seeing the danger that threatened the town, they and the homeless who had gathered there took it upon themselves to defend the town. The town walls and the castle were quickly fortified. They armed themselves with all kinds of weapons.
Everyone who was at all able to bear arms had to take his place in the ranks of the defenders, who were commanded by the local starosta.
Reb Avremke had the task of supplying the town with everything necessary; Judith, his wife, devoted herself to healing the wounded and the sick. But at the time when her noble heart was with the suffering, her mind was at the front – she strove throughout to fight in the first ranks of the defenders of the Polish land.

C.
An extraordinarily hard winter came in the year 1675 in Poland, while the Turks held the country under siege. The heavy snows, severe frosts, hunger, want and diseases made it impossible to wage open battle with the enemy; all stores and strength were already on the verge of running out. In Białopole too it was dark: there was no longer anything with which to heal the sick or still the hunger of the healthy, and the despair of the inhabitants reached its highest degree.
Any moment now they were about to surrender the town to the enemy, but the only one who remained steadfast at that critical moment was Judith. With her heartfelt words she consoled the desperate crowd and encouraged them to hold out until victory.
Judith, heedless of the danger that threatened her young and beautiful life, resolved to steal out of the town through a secret little door of the “castle” to the Turkish side, ostensibly in order to surrender the town. Only her husband and the starosta knew of this secret.
And Judith did indeed often visit the pasha and converse with him in a friendly way, but in her mind one single thought burned feverishly: how to free her town as quickly as possible from hunger and want, and above all from the Turkish siege.
When one night, late, she found the pasha sunk in a deep sleep, the feeling of revenge was kindled in her patriotic heart; she beheaded him with his own dagger (kindjal) and, leaving the Turkish camp right afterwards, she managed to return safely to Białopole through the same secret “little door of the castle” and to bring the town the joyful news of the pasha’s death.
With strengthened forces the Poles then set about pursuing the enemy and driving him out of the Polish land. Jan Sobieski, taking advantage of the favourable moment, surrounded the Turks from both sides with his exhausted army.
Judith, “the liberator of Białopole” – the name with which she was crowned – was then driven in a parade on a flower-decked carriage through all the streets of the town, and great ovations were given to her. King Jan Sobieski richly rewarded her for her heroism.
To this day in Białopole (Volhynia) they still recall with great pride the name of the Jewish heroine “Judith”, who saved the town in 5435 (1675) from the Turks in the days of “the gracious and mighty ruler” Jan Sobieski.
Moshe Feinkind.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Bo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected by Y. P.
Parashat Bo.
—o—
A.
"They saw not one another, neither rose any from his place" (10:23).
"They saw not one another" — because no one wanted to see his brother's situation, to help him out of his need; therefore — "neither rose any from his place": they themselves had no rising either, they themselves could not stay standing on their feet.
The Rim of Gur [R. Yitzchak Meir Alter, the "Chiddushei HaRim"].
———
A poor man came before the Baal HaFla'ah [R. Pinchas Horowitz] and complained about his brother, the rich man, who would not even look at him. The rich man is sent for, and he answers: he cannot give too much, for what if he grows old and cannot work — he must keep his capital for himself.
Meanwhile a couple comes in. The wife complains about her husband that he is a spendthrift who hands out too much charity. He answers: what if he dies today, tomorrow — so meanwhile he wants to do good in the world. —
Reb Pinchasl calls out: may God protect each of you from what he fears. — — —
(The rich man, after all, feared he might grow old, and the spendthrift — that he might die...)
———
In Slonim there was a Jew, a miser, a rich man who never gave a Jew a penny out of his pocket. Once, before Passover, the local rabbi, Reb Eizikl [Reb Eizel Charif], sees him shaking his pockets out for chametz. So he says to him: You need not do that. The law is that a place which does not belong to a Jew need not be searched — and you are, after all, a Jew only up to the pocket...
—o—
B.
"Speak now in the ears of the people, and let every man ask of his neighbour, and every woman of her neighbour, jewels of silver and jewels of gold" (11:2).
The Sages say about this (Berakhot 7 [as printed; the source is Berakhot 9]) that God, as it were, begged the Jews to borrow gold and silver from the Egyptians, so that Abraham should not be able to say: "'And they shall serve them and they shall afflict them' He fulfilled for them — the promise that they would be worked God kept — 'and afterward shall they come out with great substance' He did not fulfil for them — the pledge that afterwards they would leave with wealth He did not carry out."
The question arises: and had Abraham not argued so, where is the real justice? After all, it truly was due to them. —
— A young waiter was learning the trade from an old one. The old waiter taught him: you take two little plates with portions, one plate in each hand, and at the table you serve one portion to the one sitting on one side and the other to the guest sitting opposite, and so on in order.
With the fish and the soup everything was in order; only at the meat course they give the young waiter in the kitchen a plate of meat and a plate of horseradish, and the "clever" waiter serves in order: to one guest meat, to the one opposite — horseradish... and so on. In the end half the company had meat and the other half horseradish...
— In fact, God's promise of great substance was meant for the second generation, for those entering the Land[?]. But Abraham will surely argue: to one You give horseradish and to the other meat!? — — — These worked hard and bitterly in Egypt, and to the second generation You will give great substance!?
The Dubno Maggid.
—o—
C.
"With unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it" (12:8)
Maror is, after all, a symbol of the bitterness of slavery, and matzah a sign of liberation, when they fled in haste and had no time to let the dough rise; so one ought to eat maror first and only then matzah. Slavery came first, after all — so why does the Torah command doing it the other way round?
No — maror too is a symbol of liberation, for when they felt the bitterness of slavery, when they saw themselves insulted and humiliated — at that very moment they could already be called free. Slaves they were only as long as they did not feel the slavery...
Therefore matzah and maror are both symbols of liberation.
R. M. of Kotzk[?].
—o—
D.
"Bitter herbs" (12:8)
As maror one eats horseradish; at the beginning of eating, horseradish tastes sweet, only at the end does it bite. — So too the Egyptians at first worked with the Jews "be-feh rakh" (with a soft mouth), with sweet words, and only afterwards "be-farekh" — treated them harshly and bitterly.
The Levush.
—o—
E.
"And ye shall eat it in haste" (11:12 [as printed; the verse is 12:11])
From Egypt the Jews went out in haste, but the future redemption will be a slow, gradual one...
Mekhilta.
———
The beginning of the future redemption will come through the permission of the kingdoms; only afterwards will God put forth His hand and redeem the Land.
Ramban and Radak.
———
"Not all at once will the prophecies promised for the days of the Messiah be fulfilled, but step by step, degree by degree, slowly."
The Shelah.
A Letter from Kraków

“Kiddush Hashem”.
The “Vilner” [Vilna Troupe] gave the Jewish public in Kraków true spiritual satisfaction with their masterly performances. “Kiddush Hashem” made a particularly strong impression.
“Kiddush Hashem” — these are the most terrible sufferings that could be inflicted on us, not only physical but also moral, and the “Vilner” conveyed this with their acting. Wrapped in tallitot and Torah scrolls, the Jews die for their faith with the “Shema Yisrael” on their lips, believing that a generation will yet come which will realise the ideals for which they died — and it has come...
Departure of olim.
This week Kraków bade farewell to a large [group of?] halutzim. A crowd gathered at the station and accompanied the halutzim with ovations and Hebrew songs.
On the faces of the pioneers we saw the responsibility they take upon themselves in building the bright future of their people; they are not going to die for Kiddush Hashem, but to struggle and to build.
In general we now observe a strengthening of the halutz movement. Many young forces from “Dati-Achdut” [sic; probably “Hitachdut”] have joined “HeHalutz”; in the coming days they are leaving for hachshara.
The “Hitachdut” is also considering founding an urban[?] hachshara point (printed “pirugit”) in Kraków.
A Kibbutz HeHalutzi was also founded at the conference of the Right “Poale Zion”, which will be of great importance for the coming aliyah.
Concerning the question of union between “Hitachdut” and “Poale Zion” in the Diaspora countries, the delegates came out against it, arguing that the former are not real socialists, since they do not recognise the class struggle as a dogma.
The PAS [Palestine workers’ fund?] campaign has also been strengthened in Kraków; at the conference of all left Zionist groupings an executive was formed headed by Dr. Terla, stud. Frenkel and H. Welner. In the hall of the Jewish Academic House a splendid festive gathering took place, at which Mr. Geistat from Eretz Israel, director of PAS, gave a long speech discussing the possibilities of increased emigration and calling on those assembled to work for the KPA”Y [Kupat Poalei Eretz Israel], which is of great importance for the struggle of the Jewish worker in Eretz Israel. It is, however, characteristic that at the present moment, when the workers enjoy sympathy, when Kurt Blumenfeld has signed the PAS appeal, the executive of the general Zionist organisation has issued a communiqué not to support the PAS campaign.
An evening of Hebrew poetry.
Last week an evening of Hebrew poetry took place here, at which Mrs. Kahn recited the newest[?] Hebrew works. A fine lecture on proletarian Hebrew poetry in Eretz Israel was given by the lecturer in the Hebrew language at Kraków University, Dr. Ben-Zion Katz, who showed that Hebrew poetry is an expression of the life, the sorrow and the joy of the Jewish halutz in Eretz Israel. “The Hebrew worker” and “the Hebrew poet” have become a synthesis of what is being created in Eretz Israel.
Al-Ger.
The Vilna Drama and Opera Ensemble Will Tour Zagłębie

Next Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, i.e. the 11th, 12th and 13th of this month, the Vilna artists, already beloved here, are coming to us for 4 guest performances: Nechama, Kadish, Kash, Shriftzetser, Litvina, Grodner, Orlak, Sloim and others, who will give 2 performances each in Będzin and in Sosnowiec.
The troupe has been performing for a long time in Częstochowa, where it was invited by the local “Society of Friends of Jewish Art”. The society obtained a whole series of reductions and subsidies from the Częstochowa municipal authority.
The above-mentioned society strives to be in contact with the public and cultural activists in Zagłębie, so that the troupe, which consists of first-class musical and dramatic actors, may from time to time stage the best plays in Zagłębie.
For the first guest performances the troupe presents the following new, very serious[?] (printed “ergste”) musical comedy: “The Persian Bride[?]” (printed “Pale”), from Jewish life in Persia.
The ensemble comes to us with its own scenery, costumes, orchestra and an artistic ballet.

The Man with the Yellow Band

Y. Aberzhanek [?].
(Told by a Jew, a former rich man.)

Do you know the man with the yellow band? Well, yes — who doesn't know him? Especially to us people of Zagłębie he is well known. If you have your own flat with a bit of business [?] — and needless to say if you have been punished with a "patent" (trade licence) — then he is a regular member of your household. You have no say at all. You are no longer master of the house. The wardrobe is not yours, the lamp, the sofas [?], the clothes — over all of this you have no control: the man with the yellow band has the say...

I see that you already understand; you guess that the man with the yellow band is the komornik [court bailiff] — may we never know him!..

Well, who doesn't know him? Will you find a single person nowadays who doesn't know him? Can you show me a single person who has nothing to sing and tell about the man with the yellow band?

May you be guarded and protected from this "Abra-man" [?]. If he gives you a "sholem aleichem" even once, you may as well say a Rabbis' Kaddish in good time; you may take leave of your sideboard (credenza), you must give up on your Sabbath candlesticks. If he has once said to you "moje uszanowanie" [Polish: "my respects"] — the candlesticks are gone [?]..

And this very misfortune did befall me: the first "moje uszanowanie" I had three years ago, and since then the man with the yellow band has become a regular guest in my home. We have both become very good "friends" [?] by now. And what's the wonder? For three years a person has been coming and going. He already knows by heart how many shirts I have, how many dresses my wife has, how many stockings my daughters have, where the holiday dishes are. He knows exactly what my name is, what my wife's name is, how many children I have. He no longer even calls me by my surname, only "po przyjacielsku" [in a friendly way] — "Panie Jasku" [Mister Jasiek]...

May you be guarded and protected from such "przyjaciele" [friends]. A man has set about "clearing out". For three years he has been "clearing", and after every visit the home becomes "airier", "emptier" [?].

I realised that if the "przyjaciel" keeps on "sprzątnąć"-ing [clearing away] like this, in time I will become a Chinaman: — I will have to sit on the podłoga [floor]... So I called my pal aside and began to argue with him (in a friendly way, of course):

"Panie komisarzu" [Mister Commissioner] — I said — "może już będzie dygon [?], ja przecież wychodzę jak świeca" (I am wasting away like a candle). Panie komisarzu. I began to beg him for mercy: "te leskie są od mojego teściowego [?]" (the candlesticks are from my father-in-law), "żeby leciał i prosił" (let him run and plead), "gdzie [?] jest yosher [justice] — panie komisarzu!"

You think he softened? God forbid! "Nie rozumiem" [I don't understand] — he played dead.

I saw it was bitter. What will be the end? How much longer will he go on clearing like this? How does one nevertheless get rid of the man with the yellow band?

As I sit thinking it over, my wife speaks up: You know what? I have — she says — had a good idea.
— Namely? — I ask — what has occurred to you?
— It has occurred to me — she says — that the few odds and ends that are still [—], we should clear out ourselves. Why should we wait until he clears them; let us clear them ourselves.
— Where, I ask my wife, shall we move the things?
— What do you mean, she says, where? Are good friends, family, neighbours lacking? What harm can it do anyone else? God willing, she said, when we "dorobić się" [make good again], we'll put the things back.
— A fine plan. You are right, Sfershte [?]; I will take out the fur coat. He has had big eyes for that fur for a long time.

No sooner said than done. So I took the fur and went out to carry it off to a relative.
I come in to my relative, a Jew, a merchant. Good morning, I say, what's new with you?
— Don't talk so loud — he says to me — I have a guest just now.
— A guest? — I say — who is this guest, that one mustn't speak loudly?
I take a look through the keyhole. Who, do you think, was the guest? — The man with the yellow band...
Of course I grabbed the fur and fled without saying goodbye..

From my relative I went to a good brother of mine. At my good brother's too I did not say right away why I had come. Here too I first asked: what's new? how are you?
I begin to look around the room — a disaster! On the wardrobe a "slip", on the sideboard — a slip, on the scales [?] — a slip, on the piano a fresh "trinket".
— What, is it Shavuot at your place today?
— You are all plastered over with Shavuot paper-cuts.
— No [?], he says, it's the eve of Passover — they're at [?] the "search for leaven".
Of course here too I no longer said why I had come; I took the fur and — "the child is gone" [Gen. 37:30].

From my good brother I went on to another acquaintance. As soon as I step over the threshold I hear a commotion.
— What is this "ruch" [bustle] at your place? — I ask my acquaintance.
— A din-torah [rabbinical lawsuit], he says, is taking place now.
— A din-torah? With whom do you have a din-torah?
— Not me, he says, I'm only a messenger.
I take a look inside. Who, do you think, is having a din-torah? Two men with yellow bands. Both are holding the wife's karakul coat, both are tugging at it; one says: the coat belongs to him, and the other shouts: the coat belongs to him.
— Well, my acquaintance says to me, did you ever study "Two hold a garment"? Go ahead, take and tear the coat in two...
That I made a "and he fled" with my fur I need hardly tell you. I ran as if the black uncle [?] were after me.

What does one do after all? Where do I hide my fur? Where does one find a Jew who has no dealings with the yellow-banded fellows? Wherever you go, everywhere you meet the same trouble, everywhere there are "trinkets" on the wardrobes and Shavuot paper-cuts on the piano. Where does one find such a place where the yellow bands have no power yet?
Think today, think tomorrow. I stand with the fur in my hand and ponder. Suddenly an idea strikes me: I'll take it to Yekele the tailor. Ostensibly for a "poprawka" [alteration]. A Jew who has nothing to do with promissory notes, who has never had a patent, a Jew who sits alone and works, who has no protests to pay — a fine plan.
It would seem, where could it be safer than at Yekele's in the attic room?
So listen to what happened:
This week, while I was still sweetly asleep, there's a knock at the door.
— Who is it? — I ask. I was sure the yellow-banded adversary was here again.
— It's me, Yekele — I got an answer.
— Yekele? What are you doing here so early?
— A calamity, a misfortune — Yekele wrung his hands.
— What has happened? — I went up to Yekele.
— Don't ask foolish questions — he was trembling all over with agitation — your fur..
— What fur? What happened to my fur?
— Taken! — he answered in a broken voice.
— Taken? Who took it? Were you robbed?
— Not robbed — Yekele panted — even worse.
— But tell me already, who took it?
— The ko.. ko.. komornik — Yekele barely stammered out.
— The komornik? — I was beside myself — how do you come to have a komornik? Are you a merchant, then? Do you write promissory notes? Do you have protests to pay?
— One, some pock-marked goy — Yekele swallowed his tears — with a yellow stripe, from the "Kasa Chorych" [sickness insurance fund].
— From the Kasa Chorych? How do you come to the Kasa Chorych?
— May I know as little of evil — Yekele lamented — I once had an apprentice.
In short, you want to know the end? My fur is gone too. Even at Yekele's in the attic room the man with the yellow band got there too...
You see this fur coat? It is my wife's garment. I ask you truly, fellow Jews, perhaps you do after all know of a place where I would be safe from the man with the yellow band?..
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Będzin Kehilla Council 'Considers' the Budget for 1930

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, Tet / 9 Shevat 5690 — Piątek 7 lutego 1930 [Friday, 7 February 1930].)
Będzin
The Będzin kehilla council "considers" the budget for 1930.
Two weeks ago the Będzin kehilla council was awakened from its lethargic sleep. The council was called to its annual mission — to fix the new kehilla budget.
The council had been summoned to the work already ["ush", Polish już] 3 times, and after "great toil[?] and suffering" 6 parnasim came and 14 sat "at home" [printed "ham"[?]]...
The council sessions no longer arouse any interest even among the "gallery"; nobody comes, and one no longer calls the police to make "porządek" [order]..
The so-called discussion was held in the tone of a yored [one who has left the Land of Israel], who cries out in despair: "Free me from this chaos (tohu va-vohu)". All without exception are in favour, since the kehilla's foundation is rotten through and through; even the president himself, in his own honoured person, "promises on his word of honour[?] that 'nobody is nothing against'" [garbled Germanism in the original] the kehilla being dissolved.
—
The budget session opens with the participation of 4 parnasim and 1 "gallery-goer" (later the number grows). After the reading of the minutes of the last sessions that did not take place, parnas Goldsztajn takes the floor and demands that the declaration of the artisans' parnasim, who demand that the kehilla council be dissolved, be sent to the starosta [district head], the voivode and the ministry.
After Mr. Goldsztajn's justification the motion is adopted with the amendment that, together with the declaration, the resignations of the parnasim N.[?] Rechtik, Ch. Szajn and Sz. Frenkel be attached.
Under the item of salaries and other expenses for the rabbinate a discussion developed, from which the "order" in matters of kashrut "shone forth". The point is that, apart from the fixed annual salaries, special remunerations are fixed for members of the rabbinate so that they should supervise kashrut in the slaughterhouses.
The same pay, to the sum of 1000 zł. (apart from a salary of 4 thousand zł.), is provided for the Czeladź moreh tsedek [rabbinical judge]. The "gratification" is defended by the Czeladź parnas Mr. Ch. Szwajcer and by parnas Klajnman, who also has a connection to Czeladź, and it is decided that, so that the minister should not cast an "eye" on the sum, the thousand zł. shall figure under the item of urgent aid.
On this question the vice-president Mr. Prawer touches on the bad management that the rabbinate conducts in matters of shechita. If the rabbinate — says Mr. Prawer — had at least set up the shechita properly, the kehilla treasury would have had more income, to the sum of 25 thousand zł.
On this question the floor is granted to a delegation of several butchers, who came here to complain about the lawlessness (hefkerut) prevailing in the slaughterhouse. The shochtim — they claim — do as they please, as if they had no supervision at all from the rabbinate. If the kehilla leaders — they threaten — do not put an end to this chaotic "order", we will stop the slaughtering altogether.
In connection with this declaration the motion of parnas Goldsztajn is adopted that a conference be called with the participation of the rabbinate, the shochtim, the kehilla leaders and the butchers; at the conference the situation is to be clarified.
The second budget item is expenses and income in the synagogue. Here one parnas, Skurnik, "digs in his heels" and declares that if the president does not treat them to sweets, then — stop, we go no further!
The president, who wants to "drive on" by giving in, hands out sweets to the company, and it becomes a little merrier in the hall...
Under the synagogue item the Agudah parnasim demand that the sum of 2500 zł. for renovating the synagogue be struck out because of the present crisis. The motion is rejected.
The further items: the beit midrash, the cemetery and the office are dealt with "on one foot". It is interesting to note that among the office expenses, which amount to 22 thousand zł. a year, there also figured a meagre sum of 200 zł. for keeping an exemplary[?] kehilla pinkas [record book], but here our parnasim became more thrifty and struck out the 200 zł.
The Agudah parnasim grow tired and leave the session; there remain: Goldsztajn, Hampel, Klajnman and Y. Szwajcer. The latter proposes that the slaughterhouse item not be dealt with now, but that one must await the outcome of the conference.
The motion is adopted and the session is closed.
Recitations by the “Vilner” — not permitted.

On Saturday afternoon a concert of the living word was to take place, performed by the artists Miriam Orleska, Jacob Weislitz and Joseph Kamen. The hall was overfilled; a few minutes before the start the concert was disrupted by the police authorities.
Now that's what you call a “derashah gift”...

On Sunday[?] morning a wedding ceremony was to take place in the local church. When the groom and his “intended” were already right in front of the church entrance, they were met by 3 Christian women, who handed the groom, as a “gift”, an illegitimate child. The groom, and above all the bride, were surprised by this “present” and in revenge threw themselves into beating the “przyjaciółki” (lady friends). The police intervened and took the couple and the guests away to the police station.
General meeting of “Malbish Arumim”.

In the premises of “Ahavat Hesed”, under the chairmanship of A. M. Szwarcberg, the annual general meeting of the society “Malbish Arumim” (Clothing the Naked) took place. The report on the activity to date was given by Mr. Sendisheh[?]. It turns out that this winter the society clothed about 200 poor children, apart from adults. Despite the great expenses on clothing there is 1100 zł in cash in the treasury. The budget for 1930 is reduced from 15 to 12 thousand zł. After it was[?] decided to enlarge the number of the board from 9 to 12 members, elections were held, which gave the following result:
L. Bożykowski, Sh. Zajader[?], H. Shturger, M. L. Sendisheh[?], Sh. Lewkowicz, H. Braner, A. Buchbinder, Sh. Ferstenfeld, M. Rapshik[?], D. Janowski, D. Zilbergold, Sh. Brat, N. Merin, Sh. Markowicz, Sh. Greitzer, Y. Goldring and M. Czerner.
An interesting lecture.

This Saturday afternoon Prof. Kazimierz Kuszyżanowski[?] (Krzyżanowski?) will give a lecture at the “Nowości” on the subject “The Inquisition of Jews and Poles in Soviet Russia”. Prof. Kuszyżanowski, who lived through the upheaval in Russia, depicts comprehensively and in true colours the emergence and the consequences of the Russian revolution.
The lecture, which is very interesting, has had the greatest success everywhere.
Tramway employees receive a raise.

The negotiations between the tramway delegation and the delegates of the tramway employees ended in recent days; the employees receive a raise of 6 per cent. The raise applies from 1 January of this year.
Suit of a milk seller against the tax office.

The following case took place in the local magistrate's court: an official of the “Urząd” (tax office) came into a Jewish milk seller's and found him selling milk at home. On that basis the official already determined that the person concerned needs a 3rd-category trade licence (patent).
The milk seller brought a case against the decision, arguing that the milk is sold not at home but in town; the witnesses also confirmed this, and the court annulled the office's decision.
Tax declarations (zeznania) — by 15 February.

We draw attention to the fact that the deadline for submitting declarations (zeznania) of turnover for 1929 is the 15th of this month.
—o—
A “five o'clock”.
Next Sunday at 5 p.m. an entertainment in the form of a “five o'clock” (tea) will take place on the “Góra Zamkowa” (Castle Hill). There will be various attractions. The proceeds are to strengthen the financial means of the “Dobroczynność” (charity society).
—o—
Lecture by Dr. Perl.
On the initiative of the “Tse'irei Mishmorei haHolim” Dr. Perl will lecture next Sunday at Public School no. 8 on the subject “Tuberculosis”.
—o—
Lost a finger at work.
In the workshop of Moshe Szpigler the worker Herman Niewiem[?], while working at a machine, cut off a finger of his right hand.
—o—
The “touts” question at the police
At the “Merchants' Association” a meeting of ready-made-clothing merchants took place, which dealt with the painful question of the “khapers” (street touts who drag in customers). It was decided to apply on this matter to the head (kierownik) of the local police station.
—o—
Presidium of the school committee.
In the premises of the kehilla a chairman and a vice-chairman of the school committee were elected. Elected chairman was Mr. Gershon Rzechnitz[?], and vice — Mr. B. Pelk.
—o—
The cantor will pray without a choir
This week the kehilla leaders negotiated with the choristers that they should resume their activity. The negotiations led to no result, and the kehilla board is of the opinion that the cantor should pray without a choir.
Sosnowiec — Agreement between the ritual slaughterers and the kehilla

Sosnowiec
Agreement between the shochtim and the kehilla.
This week an agreement was signed between the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) and the kehilla leaders concerning the pensions for the shochtim. The pension of each shochet amounts to 9 thousand złoty a year.
Instead of a „Mi Sheberakh“ — blows...

On Shabbat things were „cosy“ on Dekerta Street. In the middle of the street a brawl broke out between Mr. Wiszliński[?] and one Senderowicz, with their respective sides.
The brawl came about in the following circumstances. Senderowicz's wife, whom her „faithful“ husband had abandoned several months ago, gave birth to a boy, and the brit was to take place on Shabbat. After many interventions the father agreed to come to the brit. But right after the circumcision he left together with his parents. This „retreat“ provoked bitterness among the other guests, who „honoured“ the runaways with hand-gifts. A regular battle therefore broke out, and the police had a lot of work...
A big fire on Warszawska Street

A fire broke out in the paper shop of Mr. S. Langer. The fire also spread to the neighbouring premises of Mr. A. Mangel. Mr. Langer's shop burned down completely. The damage is very great; Mr. Mangel too suffered from the fire.
Rabbi Hager is coming next week

The apartment for Rabbi Hager has already been duly prepared, and next Tuesday Rabbi Hager is coming with his family to Sosnowiec. A committee has been formed which is organising a reception.
This Shabbat Shira [printed „Shura“] the rabbi will deliver a sermon in the synagogue.
Meeting of the Zionist Organisation

Under the chairmanship of Central Committee member Mr. Goldsztajn, a general meeting of the Zionist Org. took place on Sunday in its own premises. Reports on the activity were given by Mr. Wajryb[?], and on the treasury and the technical commission by Mr. Rozman.
During the meeting a telegram of greetings was received from Deputy Grünbaum. The telegram was received with ovations, and it was resolved to create a jubilee committee.
The elections of a board did not take place, because the Revisionists left the hall in protest against the refusal to accept from them the monthly dues, which would have given them the right to vote.
A women's association „WIZO“ founded

On Tuesday the founding meeting of the women's association „WIZO“ took place. A large number of women attended the meeting, to whom Mr. Goldsztajn lectured on the significance of „WIZO“ in the upbuilding of the Land of Israel. A board was elected consisting of Mesdames Rozman, Langer, Horowicz[?], Merin and Miss Goldberg.
The decision on the rabbinical elections — postponed

As is known, the Supreme Administrative Tribunal in Warsaw was to publish last Friday its decision on the validity of the local rabbinical elections.
But a few days before the decision, Judge Makowski, who had sat on the bench in this case, died. Because of this the Tribunal postponed the publication of the decision.
In court circles it is admitted that for this reason it is not ruled out that the appeal concerning the elections will be considered anew.
Cultural work of the "PAI".

Under the leadership of Mr. Yechiel Feiner, a culture committee has been created in the religious workers' youth "PAI" [Poalei Agudat Israel], consisting of: Reuven Bigenshtok [?], Nachman Yaakov Feder [?], Chaim Sternberg and Yeshaya Rubinshtok [?].

The committee has the task of conducting a great deal of [?] religious, and also broad cultural, work among the religious working youth.
A siyum of the Torah scroll.

On Sunday the completion (siyum) of a Torah scroll took place at the home of Mr. Moshe Marianke [?], with the participation of many guests, headed by the great Rabbi R' Arye Tzvi Frommer, may he live long.

At very richly served tables the guests rejoiced until late at night.

The Torah scroll, of very beautiful execution — the rollers (etz chaim) are of silver and the mantle is embroidered with gold — was presented as a gift to Rabbi Frommer.

An Imposing Reception

[Sosnowiec — rabbinate; kehilla.] In honour of Rabbi Hager's arrival in Sosnowiec.
As we have already written, a large part of the religious and national Jewish population in Sosnowiec decided to engage a rabbinic authority for the Sosnowiec Jewish kehilla. Recognised as a suitable candidate for the post was the great rabbi R' Menachem Mendel Hager, until now rabbi in Gisanc [?], who is a great scholar, possesses secular learning and is also a brilliant speaker.
Last Tuesday at half past 7 in the evening the rabbi arrived in Sosnowiec with his family. Already a few days earlier a committee had been elected, which organised the reception.
Rabbi Hager had his first reception in Mysłowice, where about 300 householders awaited him at the railway station. The whole crowd then drove [?] in cars to the synagogue, where the rabbi delivered a sermon of greeting.
In front of the synagogue hundreds of people had gathered who wanted to get inside, but because of the great crush in the synagogue a large crowd remained outside.
The cantor Mr. Yitzchak Lejchter with the choir sings "Baruch haba beshem Hashem" and "Ki mi-Tziyon tetze Torah", and the member of the kehilla board Mr. Y. M. Weinryb greets the rabbi in the name of the kehilla. In his speech of greeting Mr. Weinryb announces that on 25 December ("t. y." as printed) the kehilla board resolved to accept Rabbi Hager as rabbi of Sosnowiec.
Amid tense silence the rabbi then goes up to the Holy Ark and delivers a short but very substantial sermon, which made a strong impression.
"With a pounding heart, with trembling hands," he begins the sermon, "I have stepped [?] into this festive reception. The great honour was granted to me even before I earned it with you, but I hope that with the cooperation of the kehilla I shall raise the honour of the kehilla, the honour of the Torah and the honour of the nation [?]."
In the further part of his sermon the rabbi cites the Jerusalem Talmud in Yevamot, that a community turned to its leader with the question: "A woman without hands — how does she perform chalitza?" (printed "gramit"). "In the present time, when the Jewish people is broken, when 'the hands of Moses are heavy', when there is a struggle on the right and on the left, Jewish homes are being destroyed, the father is a zealot and his children are extreme leftists — at such a moment," the rabbi cries out, "the leader must come 'with his teeth', must act with his voice [?] upon the young generation so that they do not leave the Jewish faith, the Jewish Torah; the leader must play the same role as a yavam — 'to raise up a name in Israel' — by re-establishing the Jewish home; a leader must play the role of Aaron and Hur, bind love together with heroism, and then 'Israel prevails'."
The cantor sings "Hatikvah" and "Jeszcze Polska", and the crowd accompanies the rabbi to his splendid apartment in Wspólna [?] Street. There l'chaim is drunk, while the rabbi speaks words of Torah. The impression is a very good one and a festive mood prevails.
———
This Sabbath afternoon the rabbi will deliver a sermon in the synagogue.
Olkusz. A Lecture on „Keren Hayesod“

Last Sabbath a lecture on „Keren Hayesod“ was held in the local beit midrash by a member of the Keren Hayesod headquarters in Warsaw, Mr. Glauberson. At the appointed hour the beit midrash was packed with almost all the Jews of the town. The Agudah people, wanting to disrupt the lecture, had occupied[?] all the tables and benches[?] in advance with cheder boys, with a commander at their head. When the speaker began to speak, everyone, on command, began to shout, bang and make a racket[?], so that the speaker could not deliver his lecture. This provoked a spontaneous protest from the whole audience, which threw itself upon the Agudah people in every possible way, gave them a good thrashing (lit. „fulfilled the verdict on them“) and then threw them out of the beit midrash. Only then did the speaker deliver, for an hour, a brilliant lecture on „Keren Hayesod“ and its task, which was very well received by the whole audience. It is worth noting that a short time ago an „Agudah“ speaker spoke in the beit midrash for a whole week and abused the Zionists in general and Grünbaum in particular, and none of the Zionists disturbed the speaker; the „Agudah“, on the other hand, decided at any price not to allow a Zionist to speak in the beit midrash. It seems that after their latest beating[?] they will no longer have the courage to disrupt.
In the evening 2900 zł. were collected for „Keren Hayesod“.
A. B.

A Letter to the Editor.
Dear Mr. Editor!
I ask you to give space in your esteemed newspaper to the following letter:
The owners of the notebook („kajety“) factories in Zagłębie held several meetings at the Będzin Merchants' Association in order to arrive at a union. At the first meeting, which took place in the presence of Messrs. Chairman Rubinlicht and Dir. Spengbaum[?], agreement was reached that the union is a necessary thing, because the paper products are being sold below cost price owing to competition, and as a result the existence of several manufacturers is threatened. At the last meeting, when the union was to be created, Mr. Berman did not come, but sent word through a messenger that he does not accept the decision on the union. All the notebook manufacturers then expressed their dissatisfaction that the union had not come about and censured the step of Mr. Berman, who was the only obstructer. The course of all the meetings was recorded in minutes by the Merchants' Association.
Since the notebook manufacturers have already negotiated many times about a union and each time the plan was thwarted by Mr. Berman, I turned to the Merchants' Association asking that it give me a copy of the minutes and that the board state its opinion whether a union ought to be created and who is to blame that the union was not created. The chairman of the Merchants' Association, Mr. Rubinlicht, decided at the last board meeting to issue[?] a letter which presents the whole matter in an incorrect light and avoids naming the chief culprit for the union not having come about; although the majority of the board realised that the chairman's position is incorrect, it did not have the courage to oppose him, and willy-nilly the majority agreed with his opinion.
Therefore I ask: should a merchants' association not stand on the position of rooting out dishonest competition? Should the leader of a merchants' institution be impartial[?], or display sentiments toward a person with whom he has personal business? In that case, to whom then should a member of the Merchants' Association turn for justice?
It is also interesting to note that a board member proposed expelling Mr. Berman as a member of the Merchants' Association, because, besides me, he also strongly attacked the Merchants' Association and its activity with abusive words. The chairman did not agree to the expulsion either. Why, Mr. Chairman? You, as chairman of the institution that has been besmirched with the lowest expressions, ought surely to feel insulted — and how could you pass over this shameful fact to the order of the day?
Mendel Apfelbaum.

For Throwing Out a Bailiff — a Month in Prison.
A bailiff came to a Katowice merchant to collect a tax debt. The merchant asked the bailiff to extend the deadline by a few days. At first the bailiff did not want to, but after the merchant's many requests he agreed to take an advance payment („zaliczka“) from him.
But a few days later the bailiff came again and wanted to carry out a distraint. Then the merchant grew angry and threw the bailiff out of the shop.
These days the merchant „stood“ before the district court, which sentenced him to a month in prison. The sentence is suspended for 3 years.
