Everything Is in the Best Order.

Lawlessness in the houses of prayer. — Lawlessness in our financial institutions. — Lawlessness in the social and cultural associations.
The worst thing is when a people makes a mockery and a laughing-stock of itself, when it ridicules itself and does not care that it becomes a joke in the eyes of others. We ourselves do not want to spare our sacred things, we do not want to pay any attention to our valuables, we often laugh at our best and finest people; we do not care that, through us ourselves, what we ought to protect is spat upon[?] and degraded — what we ought to honour and respect, what we ought to embody as a higher being[?], as a lofty ideal.
We see it, we feel it everywhere and at every turn: whatever we touch among us, we see how we debase ourselves, how we weaken everything that lies solely within our own competence.
Thus we read in the Dąbrowa beth-midrash a notice that the bricklayer Janek makes good stoves, and in the Będzin or Sosnowiec batei-midrash or other houses of prayer we see all sorts of notices: that at Szmerl's or Berl's one buys second-hand goods cheaply, or that at Shloyme's and Moyshe's one can have this or that article repaired. That is what the walls of our houses of prayer serve for. You understand: a Jew comes to pray, and there he has to find out where his wife should buy onions and herring and lemons and who knows what else.
Here no one takes stock of how far the degradation goes, so that [—]. It has led to the point that Christians already have the audacity to demand that their notices be stuck on the walls of our houses of prayer; but we can hardly have any complaints against them, since they see that this is not sacred among us, because our leaders permit it on the spot.
We have rabbinates, kehilla leaders and all kinds of gabbaim and societies appointed to guard Judaism, but this does not concern them: after all, here no one's honour is being touched, here no one has been insulted…
When one debases oneself in such a way that it thereby becomes stamped[?] that holiness turns into something everyday and belongs among ordinary objects, towards which one need have no respect and no reverence — nobody takes notice of it, nobody stops at it; after all it is not politics, one gains nothing from it, it harms nobody, and therefore one need not bother about such trifles, just as one need not bother that the batei-midrash should be clean. Our clergy can tolerate the batei-midrash being as they are, dirty and dusty, with disorder reigning, just as it has been until today; who cares about such trifles, who pays attention to such unimportant matters?
* * *
Not only in this field do we make ourselves ridiculous: whatever one touches, nothing is as it should be. We never have any respect for ourselves; as soon as something belongs to us, as soon as it is merely Jewish, it is at once held in the lowest esteem.
Not long ago we did not know that we would be able to create banks of our own, and once we managed to realise it, it was self-evident that we should be happy with the result. But what do we see? We see that, on the one hand, we turn the great enterprise into tiny little shops; we fragment it in such a way that in time we shall have a great many miniature banks from which competition and intrigue will sprout; and, on the other hand, we do not allow ourselves to keep the institutions at the proper level — there, too, there is no decorum. People have long been accustomed that on entering a financial institution one behaves calmly and tactfully, and as soon as one's business is done one is on the other side of the door. Quite differently do clients behave when they are in a Jewish bank: there people shout and make noise and [—][?] and pass the time and chat over all their business, and in the process, of course, the clerks' work is disturbed. We are often ashamed when we enter a Jewish banking institution; we then feel as if we were in a tavern (karczma) or at a fair.
When at such a moment we compare what a bank of ours looks like with a non-Jewish bank, which is considerably larger — what order and quiet reign there — we turn red with shame. At such a moment we get the impression that our people are still far from well-mannered, and that we ourselves must see to educating ourselves and to behaving more tactfully, more decently and more solidly.
What does it look like when, at the same time, Europeans appear who are used to a different life, and watch how people behave among us in our financial institutions? It makes a terrible impression; it looks as if we were not in Europe. And more vexing still is that as soon as one comes to the squire (the poritz), one understands perfectly well that one must behave more politely. In a Christian bank people know not to disturb anyone, they behave tactfully, they do not speak in a raised voice; whereas in the Jewish bank, where one speaks in Yiddish, one forgets everything; there one behaves, so to speak, not as at home but as in the street: people shout and make noise and come in just to chat and pass the time.
It goes without saying that it would be of greater benefit to the Jewish banks and to our financial interests if we had more understanding for all this, if we did not want to split and crumble the important institutions, and if this were not made a party matter — that each should go to his own bank, just as he goes to his own association or his own shtibl.
This frivolity has caused the degradation and tearing-down of the prestige of the useful institutions that play one of the most important roles in our present hard life.
* * *
In cultural life, too, the same disorder reigns. However poor and petty and meagre we may be in this field, we still find ourselves in no favourable situation at all. When one comes to a Jewish lecture or to the theatre, one feels at home — just as in father's vineyard; the shouting and the noise and the strolling across the hall and the [e]migrating[?] from one seat to another make a dreadful impression on anyone accustomed to going to European theatres.
And further, the same: here too it must vex us to see how the very same patrons know how to behave differently when they come to the Polish theatre: there they know one must keep quiet and modest, take no unnecessary step, walk on tiptoe when coming in and not utter a word.
Whoever else — but the Jewish intelligent ought to understand how to behave in a European manner, not only where he must speak Polish, but even here, where he can speak Yiddish; he ought to serve as a model for those who do not know that one does not go to the theatre merely to laugh.
Regrettably it must be said here that nobody helps to educate the patrons of our theatres and lectures better. Of punctuality[?] there is no question. People manage to come 2 hours later than the poster (affiche) in the street or the announcement in the newspaper says. Going to the Jewish theatre is no small matter for a certain person: he knows that the performance will start much later than [?] midnight.
The reason for this is that both the troupes and the owners of the theatres take the Jewish public lightly; thus they show cinema until 9 30, and around 10 o'clock it turns out that the theatre performance begins. Besides, when a troupe has success, nothing is taken into account; they simply sell as many tickets as possible and pack the hall to suffocation.
Naturally, such tactics only help to demoralise the ordinary theatregoer, who in such a panic sits down on the first best seat, and afterwards no creature is able to take the seat away from him; incidentally, nobody does it, because one knows that one will not get one's own seat anyway.
All this helps to make boundless lawlessness reign; there is no one to keep order, no one to show people to their seats; and so it turns out that the masters of the house are those who push their way in and come with the aim of making noise.
Quite different is the Polish theatre: there one is shown to one's seat at once, and even if that were not done, nobody would dare to sit anywhere but in his own seat.
The upshot is that we ourselves are guilty of everything. We make no effort to improve what is not right; we do not want to educate people who would have understanding of and obligations towards what is better, finer and more imposing.
We must not forget that nothing comes by itself; everything requires to be cultivated[?] and trained. Every single thing must be cared for separately, and whoever thinks that other nations do not take care of every single thing separately is mistaken.
Every little detail must be done carefully from all sides; otherwise nothing would be worth anything.
* * *
We have deliberately touched upon the above-mentioned questions, which embrace all strata of our people. The first is the religious Jew, for whom a holy place is the holiest of all — and yet it has been shown to what extent the houses of prayer are lawless.
The second is the financial institutions, on which the greater part of the population depends; although in the Christian institutions people tremble to touch the door-handle, here among us, where one can speak Yiddish, people have no idea how to keep within bounds, and thus the prestige of the important institutions is debased, and they are turned more and more into small shops.
And the third is our cultural life, from which the intelligentsia and the youth draw their nourishment; among them, too, there is no sanctity for what ought to be their ideal, their reflection of life.
Everywhere, then, education is lacking — the fine feeling for innate intelligence and the taste for something better and finer.
Everywhere one sees lawlessness and ill-breeding running riot, but worse still is that nobody sees it, and people think that everything is in the best order.
R. Lesh.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected by Y. L.
—o—
A.
"And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go" (13:17).
A general sends his servant for fish. The servant is a great shlimazl and brings stale fish. The general flies into a rage and sets him the following punishment: either eat up the rotten[?] fish, or take a hundred lashes, or pay a hundred coins. The servant picks the first, starts eating the fish, gets stomach cramps, but pays no heed — "anything is better than blows and money". At the last piece of fish the stomach pains torment him so much that he cannot bear it and agrees instead to be flogged. They count the lashes, the blood spurts, but anything is better than paying money. At the ninetieth lash he faints and agrees to pay the hundred coins. Had he paid the money at once, he would have spared himself stinking fish and 90 lashes.
Had Pharaoh freed the Jews at once, he would have spared himself both the terrible plagues and the money (the spoils of Egypt), since he sent the Jews out anyway. Mekhilta.
—o—
B.
"And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him" (13:19).
The Midrash says: "The sea saw and fled" (the sea saw and ran away). What did it see that made it flee? It saw Joseph's coffin. One asks: so what — Joseph's coffin?!
— Usually a coffin is escorted by the Chevra Kadisha (burial society), and this society is fond of a drink; they could drink up a whole sea. When the sea saw a coffin, it thought the Chevra Kadisha was coming, and it took to flight ("vayivrach"). A folk saying.
—o—
C.
"And he took six hundred chosen chariots" (14:7).
Why exactly six hundred? — To this the Rabbi of Lemberg [Lwów], R' Chaim Rapaport, said: in war two attackers can scatter ten thousand fugitives ("one of you shall put a thousand to flight, and two ten thousand"). The Jews leaving Egypt were six hundred thousand souls. It follows that in Egypt they were three million, since only a fifth were redeemed and the rest, after all, died during the three days of darkness; and Pharaoh knew of three million — so by the said reckoning he needed six hundred attackers.
—o—
D.
"And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground" (14:22)
"But the children of Israel walked in the midst of the sea upon dry land" (14:29)
Remarkable[?]: in the first verse it says "in the midst of the sea upon the dry ground" — first sea and then dry land — and in the second the reverse, "upon dry land in the midst of the sea". But there were two kinds[?] of Jews. There were the brave, the believing, who jumped into the sea with the faith that a miracle must happen; whereas the cowards, the hesitant, jumped only when it was already dry land. Of the first it is said "in the midst of the sea upon the dry ground", and of the second "upon dry land in the midst of the sea". The Vilna Gaon [Wilno].
—o—
E.
"And the waters were divided" (14:21).
The Gemara expounds: a man's livelihood is as hard as the splitting of the Red Sea. How are they alike? — At the sea the Jews knew that behind them were the Egyptians, on one side snakes and scorpions, and on the other: the sea. Awaiting a miracle they thought: either the Egyptians will die out, or the snakes and scorpions[?] will flee and they will have a way on dry land. But what happened was something they had not reckoned with at all: the sea split. So too with a livelihood: a man counts on this one, on that one — and something completely unexpected comes along. R' Y. of Ruzhin [Ružyn].
—o—
F.
"Then sang Moses" (15:1).
When the ministering angels wished to sing a song, God rebuked them: My creatures (— the Egyptians) are drowning in the sea and you sing a song?!
Living beings are dear to God, even sinful ones. Midrash and Talmud.
—o—
G.
"They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord" (Psalms).
What is the meaning of these incomprehensible words?
Moses and Aaron were two different types of leaders. Moses, the secluded one, spoke only with God and occupied himself little with the people. Aaron, on the other hand, was the lover and pursuer of peace, well-versed with people. When talk came round to Moses, the people grumbled: that is not how a leader should be — aloof. A leader must be in constant contact with the people ("they envied Moses" — they quarrelled with Moses, claiming that he should be "in the camp" — more with the public).
When talk came round to Aaron, the people grumbled[?]: how can it be? A prince lowering himself like that and being hail-fellow-well-met [pan-brat] with everyone?! A leader must stand higher and apart from everyone... must be more — "the saint of the Lord", set apart, dealing only with God. R' N. of Ropshitz [Ropczyce].

Midway...
(The present and the pre-war period. — The "paskarstwo" [profiteering] and competition era. — What does one do next?)

[Article — economy; taxes; the Jewish trader.]
It is no longer a secret that the war demoralized every one of us; there was not a single branch, not a single little corner of prevailing life, that was not[?] infected with the modern disease.

Those days the historian will surely designate by the name: the period of profiteering [paskeray, from Polish paskarstwo]. And if we do not fool ourselves, if we want to be sincere and tell the truth, it will surely become quite clear that back then everyone profiteered. Not only the merchant profiteered; with all their might, of course, the manufacturer and the worker profiteered too, the artisan and the journeyman[?], the journalist and the teacher and the official, and indeed everyone who had any grasp of life at all. We found ourselves then in such a bewitched environment that everything was swept along, everything became infected, and there appeared no way out, no way to free oneself from the magnetic force which, like a kind of hypnosis, encircled everyone and everything. It was therefore no wonder that the government had to create an apparatus at the time to fight the dangerous usury [lichwa — i.e. the anti-profiteering office]; of course this child did not turn out well and brought no good to anyone, but that is a chapter in itself.

While living in that environment, one could not even imagine that one would ever be able to free oneself from this element, but time brings everything of itself, and so this period too, which was so dangerous for mankind, turned over and vanished to its rest.

The abnormal war times vanished, and the times of before the war began to show themselves, when it seemed to us that everything would return to the normal, quiet time, to the period before the war.

But here we were mistaken. The war times did indeed vanish, but the times of peace — the quiet, comfortable times of before the war — have still not come back. And why should we fool ourselves: they really could not come back, because today everything is shaped differently; today one cannot live or get by under those conditions. Today times are different, harder; today one must earn a great deal, a great deal, before one can attain a piece of dry bread. Today the citizens pay enormous taxes. We have colossal expenses, so that if one cannot earn a lot, one goes under. Yet among us people are still accustomed, years later, to make the same calculations as before the war. The psychology is still the same: not "what am I due to earn," but "what am I losing here?"

That is where the crux lies: that is how it cannot be calculated, and one still has before one's eyes the notion: what am I losing here?

The citizen thought that one was fooling the other when he began to sell his products or goods without profit. Time, however, showed them that they were fooling not the other fellow but themselves, and this could no longer be hidden, because poverty appeared here as a witness — and that is such an element. It is so strong a force that it cannot be hidden: from the darkest corners, from the most secret holes it makes itself heard. During this time the citizen had to pay the burdensome taxes, he had to live as well, he also had to send the children to school, so that whoever lived by these false calculations became impoverished, took other people's money, and was himself left with nothing.

A kind of parallel played out between the "pasik" [profiteering] times, when one wanted to swallow everything like a lion, and however much one received it was still too little, and the present time, when goods are sold without any calculation, without[?] any logical reckoning. And we say: just as it was not good in those bitter profiteering times, when everyone profiteered and one could not keep up with the other, just so it is not good now, when the citizens sell more cheaply and without profit.

The present cheapness is a ruin, it is a curse for everyone. After all, things do not get cheaper because the goods are better calculated, but only because there is no buyer, and one cannot hold on to them, because one has to buy bread, pay taxes and bills of exchange, pay a quarter's rent, etc.

Now, when the bitter time is reflected in all its size and splendour, one begins to sober up, one looks at oneself and wants to underline the bottom line [printed ס״ת, probably for ס״ה, "total"]. And at this moment one sees how miscalculated one is, how false the calculations of fooling the other fellow are, and the end is that one fools oneself.

No one will persuade us that one can live from not earning. When one earns, one person lives off another and everything proceeds in the normal, calculated way. On the other hand, with no earnings there is nothing — neither for oneself nor for the other; such a citizen brings no benefit either to himself or to the state.

There is talk of reducing the taxes, which weigh enormously on the population; certainly the citizens can no longer breathe under the terrible pressure; certainly it would be needed and necessary to introduce a little more order and a different system in this field. But to us Jews it must be said that for the time being this is no more than talk, and talking does not yet mean reduced or eased. Therefore one should not go on living in error and believe that taxes no longer need to be counted among our expenses — taxes which occupy such an honourable position in our budget.

And a Jew, as we know, likes to fool himself straight away; to what extent and until when[?] he likes to make a false calculation — no use asking [lit. "a question on a story"]. Straight away Shmerl or Berl can preach in the shtibl or in the mikveh that taxes will amount to a trifle, and on the basis of such a "conversation" one can begin fooling oneself anew. That we are frivolous, there is no need to say — look how one keeps on fooling oneself year in, year out.

It must all be said together: our trade associations sin a great deal against their members, against the broad strata of the population. They should, after all, have been educational institutions for their members, who had no one to learn anything from.

Now, when things have already reached the culminating point, when the water really has reached the soul, when it is already so bitter that it cannot be worse, and one begins to sober up, one sees[?] how lost one is, and the public looks on and wants to hear what its future looks like — precisely at such serious moments our trade institutions must come to their members and give them lessons and guidance on how to act, how to calculate, how they can remain standing on their feet.

One must not let these desperate people lose their balance at such a serious time, when their situation is so bitter and the hope for the future is by no means an easy one — let alone that the desperate should remain standing like this in the middle of the road, not knowing in which direction to continue their life's journey.

Now the better ones of the people must come — those who understand our fate and see that the situation must be rescued by any means, because to remain standing, halted in the middle of the road, is a crime that must not be allowed to happen.

Telex.
The P.P.S. on the Former Minister Sławoj-Składkowski

About the former Minister of the Interior, General Sławoj-Składkowski — who, incidentally, practised for quite a long time during the war years 1917/18 as a doctor of medicine in Sosnowiec — we find in our P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] organ „Głos Zagłębia“ an article entitled „Too Early“.
In this article we read:
„Together with Mr. Świtalski's cabinet, General Składkowski has also gone as minister.
We do not know Mr. Składkowski's abilities as a soldier and a physician; perhaps he is a good general and perhaps an even better doctor. But a minister whose one and only ardent wish is to give all of Poland lavatories is not fit for the office of Minister of the Interior. From a Minister of the Interior we have the right to demand broader horizons...
Finally, perhaps a certain part of the Kielce voivodeship was indeed right when it voiced the opinion that Minister Składkowski came a little too early. This opinion was voiced in the following circumstances:
During one of his inspections Mr. Składkowski visited a village in the Kielce voivodeship, where he ordered a certain number of lavatories to be put up within a month. The minister charged the starosta with seeing that the order was carried out, and indeed a month later the latter established that the lavatories had been built.
— Well, say for yourselves — the starosta addresses the assembled peasants — now you are a civilised village and not some wild Asia. Well, what, perhaps he is not a good one, the Mister Minister?
One of the older peasants scratched his head and answered:
— Good he is, only the „little box“ (lavatory) you gave us too early, Mr. Starosta.
— Why too early?
— Because first they should have given us a minister who would give us something to eat, and only afterwards a minister who would give us some place to ...“
That is the light in which they present the former Minister General Składkowski, who — we have no doubt about it — only some ten years ago was a collaborator in that very same P.P.S. party.
S. Strojch.
The Day of Judgement of the Trees

G. Alkaz[?].
On the day of judgement, the fifteenth of Shevat, the trees and the other plants had been preparing since very early in the morning for the Day of Judgement, on which their fate depended: — who shall blossom and grow, and who shall wither and dry up.
Already a day earlier the beadle of the Heavenly Household had notified the judges that tomorrow, the fifteenth of Shevat, they were to come at such-and-such an hour to a session of the Heavenly Court — and so it was. The next morning the trial had already begun, with a full number of judges and the head of the court at their head. — Let the first one come in, the head of the court ordered. The beadle opened the door, and in came a frightened, childishly naive, many-coloured little soul and remained standing to one side, facing the court. — Well, what have you to say before the court, spirit of the flowers, the head of the court turned to her; have you mended anything in your life? The little soul looks on, poor thing, frightened, and does not know what to say. — Well, why are you silent, one of the Heavenly Household turned to her, say something you know? — I grew — Where[?], the head of the court asks her — Where[?] they sowed me; and nothing more? The little soul stammered something quietly, pleading with mute glances that gleamed[?] like soft velvet. — Well, what merit do you have for her, the head of the court turned to the other judges.
— Her merit is, one of the judges spoke up, that she caresses and strokes hearts, sometimes quite embittered ones; that tired eyes respond to her.
After a short deliberation the little soul of the flowers was set free.
— Let the second one come in, the head of the court ordered. The beadle opened the door and in came quietly, her steps barely heard, the dishevelled soul of the lonely plants that grow somewhere under a fence or in a ditch of a neglected little wood — she stood in a corner and waited. — Well, have you mended anything in your life, the head of the court asked her.
The soul of the lonely plants took fright and did not know what to answer, because for the first time she had heard a voice, the voice of another.
— Why are you silent, one of the judges asked her.
— What shall I say?
— But still, the head of the court repeated to her.
— All my life I spent lonely, alone, never talking with anyone and never seeing anyone.
— Well, what merit do you have, the head of the court turned to the other judges.
— Loneliness, it seems, can atone even for the greatest sin, someone among the judges spoke up.
And the soul of the lonely plants was set free unanimously.
After a short pause the third soul came in: the soul of the willows on which the Levites hung their harps by the rivers of Babylon. The soul came in, and there was heard, as if from under the door, a quiet song that carried as if from far away.
— How did you live, the head of the court asked her.
After a short silence the soul spoke up: — All my life, since the Levites hung their harps on me, I have known no rest: day and night winds blow on the strings of the harps, play out melodies, even quiet ones, but they gnaw[?], they yearn, and the yearning disturbs the rest, makes one so restless that growing becomes almost superfluous. — Have you anything more to say — a judge asked. The soul was silent. — And what merit do you have for this soul, the head of the court asked. — Yearning, the beadle already spoke up, purifies the greatest sin.
Yes, yes, everyone spoke up, the beadle is right; the soul was set free. — Is there anyone else, asked the head of the court?
— One more, the beadle answered. — Let him come in. The door opened and in came the forest-spirit, the spirit of the eternal forests, where no human foot has yet managed to tread. The forest-spirit did not stay in one place; he strode back and forth and hummed fearsomely. — Well, have you mended [anything] this year, the head of the court asked him.
The forest-spirit broke into such a roar that the whole Heavenly Household took fright. — Well, speak, a judge asked him, what do you know? The forest-spirit looks out through wild eyes, and as it seems he did not even understand the questions, because he kept on rustling[?] and humming.
— Perhaps someone can plead in his favour, the head of the court asked the other judges.
— He is wild, but still so whole, so self-contained in his wildness, a judge of the Heavenly Household spoke up.
— Innocent! Innocent! everyone exclaimed, and the forest-spirit came out of the trial clean.
The session ended. Everyone was satisfied with the verdict.
Sheaves (Literature, Life, Art, Science) — Shaul Tchernichovsky. (Thirty Years of Poetry)

[Literature — Hebrew poetry.] By S. Elide [?].

Shaul Tchernichovsky.
(Thirty years of poetry)

With an original harp that gives forth peculiar but strong tones, uncanny to the Jewish ear; along a path not yet trodden — he came thirty years ago into our almost empty hall (heikhal) of poets and at once took an important place at the head.

At that time we were still, on the whole, sitting in the ghetto swamp, and its bacilli were still deeply rooted in our soul; therefore everything we created — be it even under the urge of awakening, of liberation — was breathed upon by the ghetto breath, including the young poetry, which was then still tangled [?] in its baby swaddling. Its scope was: limited, without élan; its language — empty, exaggerated, florid (melitsa), and its content — naive [?], childishly squeaking [?]; streams of wailing [?] tears poured over its face, or simply chattering smiles. Something more: our thousands-of-years-old divine poetry (shira), the generations-old song of the Psalms, hung with its heavy burden on the frail shoulders of the rising new Hebrew poetry. Oh, one does not so easily free oneself from the burden of generations. Our whole new poetry was steeped [?] in holiness. And even when we went out onto new paths, poetry nevertheless remained "shira bat ha-shamayim" (poetry, daughter of heaven), and its mission was understood as raising the material to a heavenly height, refining physicality. Then came a young poet and proclaimed his "Ani ma'amin" (I believe):

"And if you ask about my God:
'Where [?] is He? We shall sing to Him in song' —
here on the earth is He, not in heaven,
and the earth He gave to man as a gift."

His God is here on the green earth, not somewhere in the high heavens. The beautiful tree, the fragrant flower, the high-rising [?] mountain — that is the shape of his God.

"And from despair [?] of the clouds,
from too much gazing at the heights,
his faith [?] passes over to man,
and in the cradle [?] he increases before [?]."

We did not understand him. For thousands of years our gazes stood wholly harnessed towards God, or searching for one. And here comes someone and rebels against the "rebels against life" (mordei ha-hayim), against the human carcasses, and calls to bow "to life, to heroism, to beauty, which the rotten human swarm robbed from Almighty God and bound Him with tefillin straps"... We did not understand him, and regarded him as a stranger. "Goy" we named him. Only in dead Greek literature did we look for the influence of the cult of life. That is how our notions grasped it.

But today we understand him already. The whole young generation of poets interprets for us what Shaul Tchernichovsky sang thirty years ago. Our ear already takes in [?] the full [?], living sounds. And we have already made him a convert (megayer)... He is, after all, the true Hebrew, with the pure Bible language.

His biblical spirit, his genuine Jewish soul, not sooted by ghetto smoke, stood out deeply in his national motifs. H. N. Bialik, the genius of poets, the mightiest herald of liberation, puts such words into the mouth of Bar Kokhba:

"Not otherwise: you must have tormented us too much,
if you have made of us vexed [?] beasts.
An evil beast you have reared
and revived in our blood."

Here the exile's horror of blood cries out: true, he was a holy and mighty hero, but beast-like. True, others reared the beast in him, but still — — — thus wept the heart of his generation, of the exile people. But the young and at the same time four [?]-thousand-year-old Hebrew sees in him: "Springs of heroism were in him, springs of life and light. Our sap, our marrow."

But you have fallen — and been put to shame!
They will honour you! They, the despicable Lilliputian rabble.

And gall pours from his mouth against the generation of the desert, whose "bones will rot in the coffins [?]", who flung mud at their heroes and called the Son of the Star (Bar Kokhba) Son of the Lie (Bar Koziba).
Worldly and Homely Matters

Worldly and Homely Matters

Remarque's new book.
All who have read Remarque's "All Quiet on the Western Front" know that the author devotes much description to the relations between the front and life outside the front. The hero feels completely torn away from home and does not know whether he will find contact again with the world outside the front. The new book "Germany after the War" is appearing from a large publisher in several languages.

Gerhart Hauptmann's new drama.
In Vienna a new drama ("Ghosts" [Spuk]) by the great German poet G. Hauptmann is now being staged. The drama will be played at the Burgtheater. The action of the drama takes place in a fantastic ghost world, of unnatural creatures. Hauptmann has cast off realism (in which his "Weavers", "Carter Henschel" etc. were written) and has gone over to mysticism.

Populism.
Populism is still a quite young literary current, barely half a year old. Its birthplace: Paris; its theoretician: Léon Lemonnier; its motto: a return to naturalism, but in a different form. The war — say the founders of populism — has exerted a harmful influence on our literature. Everything breathes restlessness and abnormality[?]. Against[?] the war's influence a reaction must arise. A calm tone[?] must be brought into literature; a story must be written as a "concrete picture of life" without exaggeration. The writer must be faithful to life — not an analyst, critic or exegete (interpreter). The style must be simple, laying more weight on content than on style. The writer must draw his material only from the people, which has not yet been sufficiently exploited.
Although populism has drawn in such literary lions as André Thérive, it is not liked in literary spheres. Criticism does not foretell it a long life, because at bottom it is only a return to naturalism.

From YIVO.
The latest bulletin "Yedies fun YIVO" has reached the editorial office, in which it is reported that:
The economic-statistical section is preparing a second volume of "Shriftn" with rich content. An economic-statistical commission for Poland has been constituted under the direction of Dr R. Lipowski[?].
— The historical section has received many greetings from great scholars on the appearance of the first volume of "Historishe Shriftn". S. Dubnow writes: "You may be very proud of such work."
— The ethnographic commission at the philological section announces a competition for the best and richest collections of war folklore, which arose in the war years and mirrors the war in all its phases.
The psychological-pedagogical section proposes to carry out a study of the colour sense in children, of the development of chromatic vision in the Jewish child.

The festival of "Literarishe Bleter".
On 31 January of this year the three-hundredth issue of "Literarishe Bleter" appeared — the only tribune we have for culture and creation. The first issue appeared on 9 May 1927, and since then they have come out weekly without interruption. In honour of the jubilee the 300th issue came out with rich content.

Joseph Opatoshu's jubilee.
This year marks twenty years since the well-known Jewish writer from America Joseph Opatoshu began his literary activity. Here the talented writer is known especially for his work "In Polish Woods", which in its time made a tremendous impression on us, both for its artistic height[?] and for its original depiction of the Kotzk court.

Bialik's rejuvenation.
For quite a few years now the great people's poet Chaim Nachman Bialik had fallen silent. This "silence" was a riddle. About two years ago Bialik came forward for the first time with a booklet "Aluf Betzalot ve-Aluf Shum", a masterly creation, original in style. Now Bialik is publishing in the Tel Aviv weekly "Moznayim" (organ of the Hebrew writers) a new legend about King Solomon.

The February issue of "Varshe".
The second issue of the illustrated monthly "Varshe" (Warsaw) has come off the press; it appears under the editorship of Lazar Kahan with the collaboration of well-known Jewish writers, economists, historians and cultural activists, and is devoted to the social as well as economic and cultural life of Warsaw's Jews, and also to the history of Jewish Warsaw.
The February issue has the following interesting contents: From month to month; Eng. A. Czerniaków: The future[?] of Jewish crafts in Warsaw is threatened; Y. Bernshteyn: Warsaw in figures; Nachman Meisel: Jewish folklore of the Warsaw street vendors[?]; Lamed-Kuf: The oldest society (hevra) in Warsaw; the G[—]. ICA in Poland; The credit fund of merchants and industrialists in Warsaw; Teatrikan: Clara Young; M. Burshtin: Warsaw tourists; Lazar Kahan: Warsaw Jews in finance, trade and industry; Rafał Szereszewski, Szmuel Kenigsztajn, L. Milsztajn and M. Prywe[?]. Warsaw cultural activists: Szymon Szenbrun, Warsaw folklore; Bencion Grinbojm: the poets' salon of the Warsaw Art Society; items of interest from the press, business notes, illustrations and advertisements.
Józef Elszade (Katowice). When I Did Not Yet Know You — People...

Józef Elszade[?] (Katowice).
When I did not yet know you — people...

I.
In children's little shoes upon the world's road —
like a just-born dawn upon the morning dew,
so did I stride.
Wrapped about with a velvet-soft web of love,
kisses, caresses reddened my cheeks,
all of them pointed gently at me...
I believed in holy caresses from all sorts of people
as only an innocent child can believe,
not yet sown with lying sin.
In my sea-blue little eyes played
their ever-ready rays of smiles
as in sparkling waterfalls.
And the world, the rose, I saw it
an enchanting one, seductively winking,
in purple roses truly a dipping one.
* * *
When I did not yet know you, people...

II.
Like an autumn tree dried out at the side of the highway —
see: this is my shape today.
It cuts my insides, frosty, cold.
A few times ten years have wrapped around me
— a shroud of pain —
honesty, loyalty — as it means[?] with you,
of which your matter consists.
To man — a locked, bolted heart;
through a side break-in I got through,
and saw: brrr... adders[?], snakes — —
they have already nested in me, the poisonous adders[?].
People's words have already speared me,
so prettily wrapped in coloured garments.
Now I see it, the red-black world,
like a figure of terror,
like the steppe[?]-face of a forest.
— — — — — — — — — — — — — —
When I came to know you, people...

Art and Reality.
In a fragment of J. Opatoshu's work "Frum [?] Grand Street" ("Lit. Bleter" [Literarishe Bleter, Warsaw], No. 5) we read, among other things:
"Before one's eyes there hovered R' Jonathan Eybeschütz, as he stood on the bimah in the white kittel, the tallit fallen over his shoulders. A loose, wide sleeve bent and a white, translucent hand fluttered up and beat 'Al Chet'. The Gaon let the world know that he had not had, did not have and would not have any dealings with the Sabbateans. Had someone then unbuttoned [?] R' Jonathan Eybeschütz's velvet waistcoat and lifted the tallit katan — — — the Gaon wore on his body a c r o s s."
R' Jonathan Eybeschütz with a cross on his heart! Who dares [?] to cast such a suspicion on the well-known historical personalities — we know that it is only the poet's fantasy. But may such a fantasy be printed about a well-known personality?
We shall yet have a talk about this.
H. [?]
“Der Kokh-Lefl” — Figs...

“Der Kokh-Lefl” [The Cooking Spoon] — appears in honour of Tu BiShvat, by Ben Amotz.

Figs...
(In place of a leading article.)
Most esteemed lady readers and gentlemen readers! I confess and admit before you that I am late. It is already a day after Tu BiShvat, isn't it? A Girl's Supplication for the Masked Ball.

(For the coming masked ball we have received the following supplication.)

Dear God
of fashions[?], of dresses,
I stand here by the mirror
for hours[?] on end.

Now I paint my eyebrows,
now I make a “vansa”[?],
of course. It is all merely
a marriage “advance”[?]...

I know the perfumes
of “Coty”, of Dralle

May I have as many years
as the sums of money I squander...

I spare no “finery”,
I do everything and yet —
and what have I achieved?!
No more than a match...

to amuse myself[?] now —
oh, help me that I may

When the merchant finds out that instead of cash the customer has “kugrishe”[?] papers, he opens the door and says:

Go back where you came from.

Among merchants.
Tell me, Reb Getsl, what is the difference between a rejent [notary] and “Khesed shel emes” [the burial society]?
The rejent does the dead bill of exchange (protest) its due when it has not been paid for, and “Khesed shel emes” does the deceased his due when he has already been paid for.

Tu BiShvat Chronicle

A great Tu BiShvat campaign.
At the last meeting of the town administration it was resolved to give up the coal campaign and instead to organise a great Tu BiShvat campaign.
For this purpose the town administration resolved to buy a large shipment of: carob [“bokser”], dates [“teytlen”], oranges and figs.
The distribution will take place as follows:
Carob — it will be distributed among the unemployed, so that they can box [pun on “bokser”/“boksn”]...
Dates [“teytlen”, also “to interpret”] — will be distributed among the well-known town councillors who will take part in the “evening courses” [“wieczorne kursy”][?]...
Figs — will be distributed among the taxpayers who have filed appeals against the housing tax [podatek mieszkaniowy].

From “WIZO”.
At the last meeting of the women's association “WIZO”, after hearing the report on the “Blue-White” evening, it was resolved to elect an auditing committee to check which guests did not pay for the drinks and food they took at the buffet..

Instead of figs..

Stop press.
As this issue was closing we received a telephone report from Sosnowiec that a fruit merchant, a member of the “Agudah”, bought a crate of Palestinian [Eretz-Israel] oranges at the firm of Zendel. We immediately sent out a special emissary, who caught a chat with the merchant: what reasons had caused him to take this step? The Agudah merchant explained that the transaction is connected with the peace between Ger and Aleksander [Hasidic courts].
Worse, Worse.

(To be said with a cheerful face.)

With every day it gets worse —
Zagłębie sinks into poverty
under the mountains of protested bills,
everything is now barely gasping for breath.

Everyone has lost their breath,
everything is ready to come to a halt —
it seems: the Charleston, the Black Bottom,
even those are now danced more sparingly[?].

The winter too, as if out of spite,
came late with its horrors of cold;
the merchants are cutting prices
to get some takings for a bit of coal...

And the carnival — the king —
poor thing, with misfortune[?] on his face,
passes by so "merrily"
that the enemies rejoice...

It's a life like honey cake,
but — nothing to put in one's mouth;
I stick my nose into the ground,
because I am beginning to feel ashamed.

I am ashamed of my human position,
of my pitiful sorrow;
the land of the Inquisition opens
its gate wide to me...

Yakl ben Flekl[?].

Friday, 16 Shevat 5690. — Piątek 14 lutego 1930 [Friday, 14 February 1930].
Będzin
A Metre of Water Will Cost 50 Groszy.
This week a meeting of the town councillors took place at the magistrate [town hall]. At the meeting the statute of the waterworks was discussed. A discussion developed around the statute; some of the Jewish councillors proposed that a metre of water should cost only 40 groszy, and also that the water quota should be reduced, but the non-Jewish councillors declared that the price is not too dear, especially since in the town — or, better said, the residents of Kołłątaja Street — pay as much as 1 zł per metre of water (a familiar song).
On the part of the Jewish councillors, too, there was no great resistance regarding the price and the quota, and it was decided that a metre of water will cost 50 groszy and every room will „consume“ 4 metres of water, that is, 240 buckets of water a month.

On Building Houses for Workers.
In connection with the government campaign to build workers' housing estates throughout Poland, a special conference was held this week at the local magistrate with the participation of a government delegate and representatives of the workers' insurance societies in Królewska Huta and Lwów.
At the conference the question of buying plots was discussed, and it was decided to buy building plots at the „Syberka“ on the road to Czeladź, by the old railway station and at Koszelew [?].
—o—
18 Wagonloads of Coal Distributed to the Poor.
The coal provider Mr. Mendel Radegope [?], as soon as the first frost appeared, set to work and collected 18 wagonloads of coal. The coal was distributed through the „Dobroczynność“ [charity society] to respectable families and widows.
—o—
Tomorrow Is the Last Day to Submit Declarations.
Tomorrow, Saturday the 15th, there is still time to submit declarations (zeznania) on turnover for the year 1929.
Whoever does not submit such a declaration loses the right to lodge an appeal; besides that he also faces a fine.
—o—
Traffickers in Women Arrested.
The local police have arrested a group of smugglers, among them: Krimski, Fr. Maner, M. Maszkowicz and L. Markowicz. Foreign passports and correspondence were found on the arrested, from which it was established that the band was in contact with an international gang (szajka) of traffickers in women. For one piece of „merchandise“ they took 500 zł.
—o—
The Kehilla Council Does Not Ratify the Agreement with the Shochtim.
On Sunday the kehilla council, numbering 4 parnasim, met to consider further items of the kehilla budget. The session began and ended with the shochtim items. The discussion around this point, which lasted about 2 hours, was provoked by parnas Goldsztajn, who demanded an official document on the basis of which the kehilla board had concluded an agreement with the shochtim that they should receive 10 thousand zł a year. The board has no such document, and therefore the council did not ratify the agreement, but rather takes the position that the shochtim should have the same income as last year.
—o—
Conference between the Merchants' and Small Traders' Associations.
On Sunday a conference took place in the premises of the „Merchants' Association“ between representatives of the Merchants' Association and of the Small Traders' Association. At the conference the question was considered that a commission of representatives of both associations should be created.
The commission has the task of settling trade disputes between the two elements.
The proposal is adopted, and each institution delegates 12 members to the commission.
—o—
Spare the Post Boxes.
The Post and Telegraph Directorate in Kraków asks us to draw the attention of the local population that, in its own interest, it should take care that the post boxes in the streets are not damaged by the „secret hand“ that has lately been ruining the boxes.
—o—
Too Little? Here's Some More...!
5,000 zł for a Fifth Shochet.
On Sunday and Tuesday a conference of shochtim, representatives of the kehilla board and council, and representatives of the butchers took place at the gmina [kehilla]. The rabbinate did not take part in the conference.
On the agenda were the conduct of the shochtim in the slaughterhouse and the claim of the butchers, who demand that the gmina engage a fifth shochet.
The matter was settled to the butchers' best advantage: another shochet is being engaged, who will for the time being receive 5 thousand zł a year. Thus [?] we shall now have, thank God, 5 shochtim, who will cost 45 thousand zł a year...
—o—
A „Remedy“ for the „Plague“...
This week the merchants on the main streets at least had some „occupation“: gypsies with bears wandered through the streets, and the merchants, being without customers, ran after the animals, which live more peacefully than people...
—o—
50,000 zł for Smaller Loans.
This week the auditor Mr. Michelson from Warsaw carried out an audit of the Cooperative Bank. After the audit Mr. Michelson declared that the colossal growth of the bank over the last 2 months, since its sanation [restructuring], exceeds all expectations. Because of this the Auditing Union is granting 50 thousand zł for the purpose of issuing smaller loans.
Recitation Evening of Dvora Dimant / Meeting of “Beit Lechem” / The Courses of “WIZO” / 2 Performances by the “Vilner” / Lecture by Dr. Dunai

[Będzin — Culture; Będzin — Society and welfare.]
Recitation evening of Dvora Dimant.
On Wednesday the 26th of this month there will take place at the “Nowości” a recitation evening of Dvora Dimant, who will recite prose and humorous poems, Yiddish and Hebrew.
—o—
Meeting of “Beit Lechem”.
Next Sunday there will[?] take place in the premises of the Artisans' Association a general meeting of “Beit Lechem”. In the present hard times the institution has important tasks; therefore the meeting should be attended in large numbers.
—o—
The courses of “WIZO”.
The Hebrew evening courses of the women's society “WIZO” are developing very well. The number of pupils (female) is constantly growing. Information is given at telephone 2—22.
—o—
2 performances by the “Vilner”.
Tonight the “Vilner” [Vilna Troupe], management Mazo, are staging “Kiddush Hashem” and “Di Taave” (“Lust”). The interest in all, as well as in the performances, is very great; the tickets have almost vanished[?], so that to obtain a ticket one must have a special privilege.

Lecture by Dr. Dunai.
This coming Motzei Shabbat Dr. Dunai will lecture in the same premises of “Tseirei Mishmerei Ha-Cholim” on the subject “Care for the Sick”.

Sosnowiec: The Great Trial of the Left PPS Has Begun / Pogoń Congregation — Peace Concluded / 108 Invited — 3 Members Came... / Representatives of the Socialist Youth International in Zagłębie / Further Persecution of Traders in Upper Silesia / Went After an “Inheritance” and “Paid” Burial Money / A Campaign for the “Keren Aliyah”

[Sosnowiec — Courts and politics; Sosnowiec — Community; Upper Silesia — Economy; Sosnowiec — Antisemitism; Sosnowiec — Zionism.]
Sosnowiec
The great trial of the Left PPS has begun
On Tuesday the great trial of the Left PPS began at the local District Court. In the dock sit the general secretary of the Left PPS, Andrzej Czuma, and his 26 comrades, among them Miss Shprintse Shoymer of Dąbrowa.
The indictment, which covers 93 pages, states that in the years 1926—1929 the accused organised in the Polish Republic, especially in Zagłębie, communist circles under the name Left PPS.
The chief organiser was Czuma, who received money for this purpose from the communist committee and also published the organ “Robociarz”[?].
On behalf of the accused appear the well-known advocates Duracz, Breiter and Dąbrowski of Warsaw.
After the reading of the indictment, which lasted 3 hours, the presiding judge ordered that all the accused be taken back to prison, except Czuma, who is taken for examination.
The presiding judge addresses Czuma with a series of questions about his political activity. Czuma denies that he was in contact with the communist organisation. To the presiding judge's question why he left the PPS, Czuma answers that he could not tolerate their tactics. The PPS — he says — is not following the line of improving the situation of the workers.
At midday a demonstration formed at the court, which then moved on to Moniuszki[?] Street and other streets. Strong police patrols dispersed the crowd.
The trial will, it is reckoned, last about 2 weeks.
—o—
Pogoń congregation — peace concluded.
Ever since the beit midrash was built in Pogoń, disputes broke out there between the gabbaim of the beit midrash and part of the Pogoń congregation, who did not want to come to the beit midrash but had a kloyz (prayer room) of their own.
The disputes reached as far as the District Court, which fined a number of persons 80 zł. each for making scandals in a house of prayer.
This Sunday, thanks to Mr. L. Zengel[?], the dispute was liquidated. The peace negotiations took place under the chairmanship of Mr. Zengel[?] in the premises of the Artisans' Association, where both sides were heard.
The main basis of the peace agreement is that a commission of 5 persons will be elected, which is to manage the whole economy of the Pogoń congregation.
—o—
108 invited — 3 members came...
The committee which is engaged in building a “Moshav Zekenim” (old-age home) called a general meeting for Sunday, at which the question of finding means to complete the building was to be dealt with.
108 members were invited to the meeting; no more than 3 members came — not from among the paying members, but the committee itself, which consists of 3 persons.
—o—
Representatives of the Socialist Youth International in Zagłębie.
On Monday a delegation of the Socialist Youth International stayed in Sosnowiec. At the railway station they were welcomed by the Polish youth organisation “TUR”[?] and by the Right Poale Zion youth “Frayhayt”, on whose behalf Miss Miriam Gajman[?] greeted them. In the evening a festive academy took place in the municipal theatre, where among those giving greetings was also Mr. A. Gancwajch on behalf of “Frayhayt”, who spoke his greeting in French, Polish and Yiddish.
The delegation also took an interest in the life of the Jewish young worker, showed great interest in the building of Eretz Israel, and asked much about the enthusiasm that the Jewish socialist youth “Frayhayt” has for the working[?] Eretz Israel.
—o—
Further persecution of traders in Upper Silesia.
As is known, owing to the antisemitic agitation against the traders in Upper Silesia, they were recently threatened with losing their entire existence up to now. The issue was that the authorities in Upper Silesia did not want to issue to Jews permits for trade. After many interventions the Jewish deputies Wiślicki and Farbstein got the decree eased, and trade was finally permitted.
But no sooner were they rid of one decree than a second arose. Against those traders who do have the proper certificates, reports are being drawn up for trading in the border zone, since within 15 kilometres of the border one may not trade. The authority in charge of the border certificates is the customs office in Mysłowice, which makes great difficulties for the Jewish traders.
In connection with this, the traders' associations in Sosnowiec, Będzin and Oświęcim have undertaken a further action; Mr. Żelanka[?] too was in Warsaw this week about the matter.
—o—
Went after an “inheritance” and “paid” burial money.
Reuven Fuks with his 2 sons Chaim and Avraham boarded at the local railway station a train leaving for Katowice. They got into a 4th-class carriage, which was full of passengers, among them 2 Christians, who did not stop abusing the Jewish passengers and later also beat them.
Thereupon Reuven Fuks called a policeman, who on entering the carriage at once “honoured” Mr. Fuks... Then the policeman took Fuks with his 2 sons, and also 2 Christian passengers, out of the carriage. All were taken to the police station. There the Fuks family was put into a separate room and the Christians were released at once.
As Mr. Fuks informs us, he and his sons were beaten by the police while the report was being written.
—o—
A campaign for the “Keren Aliyah”.
In 2 weeks a group of chalutzim is leaving from here for Eretz Israel. For this reason a collection campaign for this purpose begins on Sunday.
In connection with this, next Tuesday an Eretz Israel evening with a very rich programme will take place in the municipal theatre. The Jewish population of Sosnowiec will no doubt support this important campaign.
General Meeting of the Czeladź Artisans

On Sunday, in the premises of the Cooperative Bank in Czeladź, the annual general meeting of the Artisans' Association in Czeladź took place under the chairmanship of Mr. Feigenblat. Hampel, Ga[?]zweig and Grünfeld spoke on organisation, the guild and evening courses. Then the following board was elected: S. Braner, S. Jakubowicz, S. Lewkowicz, S. B. Feldman, M. Frajer, Isser Rajcher, B. Berman.

From the Zagłębie Chess Club
The return match between the Club named after "Marshal Piłsudski" and class "B" of the Sosnowiec chess club brought victory to the Sosnowiec club by 5:1.
— On Sunday the class "B" championships were concluded. First place was taken by Lejb Kirland[?] with 4½ pts. In second place is Drewniak[?] with 4 pts. In third place — Szlama Warman[?] with 3½ pts., and Buszykowski[?] 0 pts.
— The great international tournament in San Remo brought a brilliant victory to world champion Alekhine, who outstripped his opponents by a full 4 points; second place was taken by Akiba Rubinstein, Nimzowitsch, and only after him Bogoljubow.
— On the 23rd of this month the match between Upper Silesia and Zagłębie will definitively take place in Königshütte. Twelve players will take part in each representative team.
—o—
Attack on a Woman on a Train
Mrs. Fryszták of Zawiercie, travelling from Kraków, was attacked between Maczki and Strzemieszyce by an unknown person, who began beating her with a stick in order to rob her of the belongings she had with her. The woman, however, was not frightened by the blows; she tore the stick out of the attacker's hands and "treated" him to it. The attacker, seeing that he had come upon a "woman of valour", vanished.

Dr. Melodysta's Resignation as President of the Council Rejected.
Yesterday the starosta sent Dr. Melodysta a letter stating that Dr. Melodysta's resignation is not accepted and that he must continue to perform the duties of president of the Sosnowiec kehilla council.

The great trial of the Left P.P.S. in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — political trial.] Up to yesterday, Thursday, i.e. the 10th day of the trial of the Left PPS [PPS-Lewica], a series of witnesses have been heard who play the main role in this great political trial. Apart from the Defensywa [political police] commissioners from Poznań, Wilno, Lwów, Kraków, Warsaw, Sosnowiec, Będzin and elsewhere, the workers' director Sawicka [?] was also examined; she said among other things that she had been present in America at a pacifist congress of Negroes, and that speeches against war had been made there just like those at the congress of the PPS-Lewica in July 1929.
On Wednesday the contributor of the "Folkstsaytung" [Bundist daily, Warsaw], Mr. S. Szwarc, who had been present at the above-mentioned congress, was also heard as a witness.
During Mr. Szwarc's examination an incident arose between him and the presiding judge, who put a series of questions about the difference between the "Bund" [?] and Communism. To this Mr. Szwarc declared that he had been summoned as a witness and not as an expert. The presiding judge thereupon pointed out to him that he may answer the questions put or not, but not polemicize about their content.
According to estimates the trial will be concluded only at the end of next week.
———
In connection with the trial, police patrols in Zagłębie, and in particular in Sosnowiec, have been increased. The district court building is also heavily guarded.
—o—
A group of smugglers arrested at the Czech border.
[Czechoslovak border — crime.] Near the Czech border a group of smugglers from Poland has been arrested, on whom a fairly large number of counterfeit dollars was found. Among those arrested are 2 persons from Sosnowiec.
There is a suspicion that the persons wanted to circulate the counterfeit dollars in Czechia.

A fire at the Dąbrowa railway station.
[Dąbrowa — fire.] On Tuesday evening a fire broke out from an iron stove at the railway station in Dąbrowa [Górnicza]. The firemen who were called extinguished the fire. Part of the goods of the buffet [?] were destroyed.

Solidarity of bank employees.

The staff of the Discount Bank [Bank Dyskontowy] also showed solidarity with the strike action, only in another form: they did not work from 12 o'clock until 1:30 in the afternoon.

Foreign press voices on Dvora Diamant (on her appearance in Będzin on Wednesday the 26th of this month)

Next Wednesday a recitation evening will take place at the „Nowości“, given by the artist Dvora Diamant, who has made a name for herself on the world's stages.
Dvora Diamant has appeared in Berlin, Düsseldorf, Cologne, Prague, Vienna and other great centres. We give here a summary of the criticism about the artist in the foreign press.
About her appearance as Franziska in Lessing's „Minna von Barnhelm“ the „Düsseldorfer Mittag-Zeitung“ writes:
On stage as Franziska, Dvora Diamant surprised with a naive[?] comedy and capriciousness[?] and revealed a strong acting temperament.
About the role of Princess Alma in Frank Wedekind's „König Nicolo“: as Princess Alma, Dvora Diamant displayed high art, which raised the character to a powerfully effective climax.
„...underlined by her who embodied the figure of a king's daughter with quiet grace and majesty[?]; she was in the matter with her whole heart, her acting was penetrating, without being at all sentimental.“
About recitations in Germany and in Prague Dr. Eschelbacher writes:
Dora Diamant gave us great pleasure through her reciting; with grace and spirit she conveyed Werfel's poetry to us, and with power and inner[?] glow she left us unforgettable impressions in the Bible reading.
Max Brod writes in the Prague „Abendzeitung“:
The reciter, well known in Germany, presented a select programme of Jewish poetry. Her manner of reciting recalls the recitation art of Else Lasker-Schüler (a well-known German poetess and reciter), but remains independent in its spiritual and emotional mastery of the poetic material. Heine's „Princess Sabbath“ and Peretz's novellas came off excellently, with controlled authenticity and irony. Very strong form was given to the anecdotes of Martin Buber and two chapters of the Bible, read with tremendous effect in German and in Hebrew.
Oskar Baum writes in the „Prager Presse“:
In the actress and reciter Dora Diamant we have come to know a unique and interesting talent. Her refreshing naturalness, which has now become a rarity, is particularly striking. In the well-chosen programme (Münchhausen, Peretz, Buber, Bible) her organ, capable of modulation, came to expression, carried by a plastic diction and a tender understanding of the poetic and spiritual content. The alternation of humour, pathos and lyrical sweetness in Heine's Sabbath hymn, and Peretz's masterfully rendered novella „Berl the Tailor“, were powerfully moving. A deep impression was made by the mystical anecdotes in Buber's version, delivered with simplicity and understanding. The high point of the evening were the Bible chapters, in which the artist did not, as is customary, rebuke in a thundering voice, but worked through her own pain-trembling prayer, with enchanting originality and with shattering, deep truthfulness.
The applause was strong and deserved.
Strzemieszyce. Police at a house-warming.

(h) In our town the Zionist youth organisation „Gordonia“ has been founded. The founding of „Gordonia“ caused great satisfaction in the local national[?] circles, since it is the only Zionist organisation in Strzemieszyce.
To the festive house-warming of the „Gordonia“ premises, which took place last Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat), came all the local youth as well as representatives of the local branches. Immediately after the singing[?] of the „Hatikvah“ anthem the local commissioner appeared in the premises, accompanied by an armed przodownik [police sergeant] and 2 secret agents, who checked the identity papers of all those present and recorded them in a protocol.
After a [lengthy?] police watch, the opening of the premises was proceeded with, under a heavy impression.
—o—
A lecture!
At the invitation of the „Dr. Herzl“ library, the well-known poet S. L. Shneiderman gave a lecture here on Sunday, on[?] „[?] Paris“, „Black Wings“ and „Spring Eve“. The lecture was a moral and material success.
Mi Yodea.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
„Gmina Izraelicka“ [the „Israelite Community“]...
The board of the Katowice Jewish community has sent out to all local Jewish residents demands to contribute the kehilla tax for the year 1930.
Together with such a demand a questionnaire is also enclosed, which the taxpayer must answer. It is interesting, however, that to this day, when Jewish life in Katowice plays a significant role, the Katowice kehilla does not want to part with its old pedigree — „Gmina Izraelicka“...
—o—
Warsaw Safe-Breakers on „Tour“.
At midday there was a break-in at the instrument warehouse of the firm „Ebeks“ [?] in Katowice, on 3 Maja Street.
The „work“ was noticed by the caretaker, who alerted the police. The burglars are Antoni Batowski [?] and Jakub Baczkiewicz [?], both from Warsaw.
—o—
6,000 zł for Key Money Demanded for a Flat.
This week the trial took place at the Katowice District Court against [unclear word, printed „ersinen“] advocate Wawilski [?] and his wife, who were charged with having demanded 10 thousand zł key money for their flat. The court sentenced the advocate to 4 thousand and his wife to 2 thousand zł fine.
—o—
A „Beach“ at the Station.
At the railway station in Siemianowice a drunk came in who wanted to spend the night there; for that purpose he took off his clothes. When he had already got to his trousers, a policeman came in and invited the „guest“ to sleep in jail.
—o—
Ticket Forgers before the Court.
A group of workers stood before the Katowice District Court, charged with using forged railway tickets. The accused were sentenced to 2 weeks in jail.
—o—
New Danish Consul.
The King of Denmark has appointed Director Aleksander Ciechowski [?] honorary consul for the Kraków and Katowice voivodeships.
His seat is in Katowice.
The 2nd Traditional Eretz-Israel Evening in Będzin.

[Będzin — Zionism and culture.] On 8 March the 2nd traditional Eretz-Israel evening will take place in the hall on the „Góra Zamkowa“ [Castle Hill].
The organisers are making the greatest effort so that this evening too will turn out [?] as it did a year ago, when people spent the time in pleasant surroundings also with a „foxtrot“ and a „hora“ until dawn.
The oriental decorations in Eretz-Israel style are already being prepared by the well-known painter, our friend Moshe Appelbaum.
The oriental music is being rehearsed by the „kapelye“ (band) under the direction of S. Lustig and M. [?] Berenblat.
In general, the evening promises to be very interesting.
The entire proceeds, as a year ago, go to the benefit of the workers in Eretz Israel.
Olkusz. Zionist Activity.

[Olkusz — Zionism.] The „Keren Hayesod“ campaign has been concluded with success. 2 thousand zł was collected in cash, apart from promissory notes. The „Keren Hayesod“ committee consists of the following Zionists and non-party people: M. M. Telerman (chairman), Dr. Y. Kohn (vice-chairman), M. Szwarcberg (secretary), Reuven Damber [?] (treasurer), Yitzhak Rajzfeld [?], Weizman and Mrs. Zylberberg. A strong revival of Zionist activity was brought about by the visit of Mgr. Goldsztajn, who gave a brilliant lecture on the theme „The Process of Realisation in Zionism and Its Norms“. The lecture made a strong impression. The next day a meeting took place in which intelligentsia, youth and artisans took part, before whom Mr. Goldsztajn explained the importance of strong Zionist work and urged that the organisation in Olkusz be strengthened. Up to 40 persons signed up, and a provisional committee was founded consisting of Mgr. Ch. Lender, Szwarcberg, Kerner, Miss Springer, Goldberg and Perelman.

Parnassim and Dictators.

(They crawl ever deeper into the mud. They forget for what purpose they were sent there.)
What is the point of writing, of criticising, of drawing their attention and of telling them an opinion, if they reckon with nothing and with no one? They do their own thing, nothing interests them, they want to know of nothing; apparently they even intend to demonstrate and show before all and sundry. That they were called by the whole people to do whatever pleases them and whatever they want.
Were it not so, had they understood how to act as the general interest demands, they would then have reckoned both with the Jewish population and with the difficult situation in which we find ourselves today.
But it apparently looks as if they want to provoke us and show that they can do what they want, what pleases them, what suits their "politics", and in that case one reckons with no one and with no material sacrifices whatsoever that are loaded onto the people's shoulders.
At present we have in Będzin a total of 4[?] shochtim (ritual slaughterers), who take no more than 40,000 zł. a year. But since that is too little, our kehilla leaders have allowed themselves to engage a 5th shochet, for whom no less than 5[?] thousand zł. has been fixed. And in future it is of course self-evident that his honour will not be lessened compared with his colleagues; that is to say, before you know it we shall need, for the 5 shochtim alone, 50 thousand zł. a year, and it is not out of the question that the sum will have to be raised further, since, as is well known, our gmina (community) has the custom of granting them raises year after year.
That is how our kehilla leaders take care of us, so that the budget is systematically raised every year and the yoke of carrying the kehilla's needs on our shoulders becomes ever heavier.
We are beaten with two rods[?]: on the one hand ministerial pensions are approved for the shochtim, and on the other hand they have to work less and less, so that there should be room for one more shochet. Yet it is perfectly well known that if the shochtim worked as they should, not only would there be no need to burden the town with one more shochet, but even the present number could be reduced. The question therefore arises: either — or; either one gives these people high pensions, and then let them work properly for it and not give private lessons; or if not, let them not be paid so highly, and with the money saved one could afford to take on one more official.
In what business, in what enterprise, at what firm has it ever been heard of that such disorder should be run as it is run in our kehilla? It is unheard of; it does not make sense to any reasonable person; it is incomprehensible to anyone who has the slightest notion of how any transaction at all is made.
It would be interesting to know whether our kehilla leaders also make such rotten deals in their private lives? Do they also behave so lavishly with officials in their own businesses? Of course they will not be able to prove that, because at home people are, after all, exploited to the full. Only kehilla money is ownerless (hefker) — as for reckoning, they do not reckon at all with society, with the masses, for whom it is so hard to pay the burdensome taxes.
In the early days, when the leaders still felt upon themselves the responsibility they had taken on by entering office as kehilla leaders, and could not get along among themselves because of differences of opinion, they came to an agreement only because they were afraid that, owing to the quarrels, the authorities would dissolve the kehilla representation and install a commissioner in its place — something they greatly feared. Now, after so many years of activity, we only now see that the devil is not as terrible as he is painted. Only now do we understand that a commissioner would not have been so terrible; he could in no way have allowed[?] himself to treat a whole town of people so lightly as our elected leaders do on their own initiative. It is unheard of that people should disregard the population to such an extent, but shut themselves up in inner chambers and do whatever finds favour and pleasantness in their eyes.
In what way are their deeds better than the deeds a commissioner would have done of his own will? A commissioner would not have known how to penetrate so deeply into every little corner that concerns the interests of the kehilla members. A commissioner would not have understood how so much over-cleverness and so many political combinations can be applied, as the "sharp-witted" parnassim do.
Their deeds are dictatorial, autocratic. No one can tell them anything, and indeed they pay no attention to it either; they do what they want, what pleases them.
Had they reckoned with the difficult situation that prevails in every corner of our poor life, the whole policy regarding the members and the budget would have been different — more practical, more restrained, more logical. But these people have lost all sense of balance: one reckons with no one, one twists and pushes through whatever one is set on in favour of this one or that one. It does not even occur to them to reckon with public opinion, and therefore one does not want to hear the public, one does not want to be in contact with it, one wants no dealings whatsoever with it, one wants to be as far from it as possible — and so, gradually[?], every line of communication between the parnassim and the kehilla members is broken off.
And that is why the disharmony is so great, that is why such chaos (tohu va-vohu) prevails. Kehilla affairs have become so repugnant in the eyes of all strata of the population that we could never have imagined it could lead to such a degree, to such absolute estrangement and alienation.
The parnassim have turned into dictators and autocrats who do everything without the consent of the members who sent them there and entrusted our kehilla affairs to them.
It is self-evident that they feel comfortable in this role; otherwise they would not have turned into what they are, into what they so longed to become, in order to ride on the backs of the members.
We elected them for 3 years, and all that time they walked on slippery paths until they strayed completely from the straight path and lost all direction, all system. In any case, they could have resigned after their term of office ended; now they are surely entitled to give thanks for the hard mission, whose term ended long ago.
Yes, a few years ago we could not have imagined how far lawlessness (hefkeirut) would reach in our Jewish kehillot. It simply could not have occurred to any of us that elected parnassim would turn into what they are now — because they have lost all respect and trust among the population and their prestige has fallen to zero.
D. Les.
