What I Heard, What I Saw.

[Będzin, Sosnowiec and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

"Arabs" in the "Yesodei Torah" cheder.
The door of the editorial office flies open. In comes a Jew and, after a broad "good morning", introduces himself:
— "My name is Pinchas Florenz, that's my name. I've come here to tell you that in the Będzin cheder 'Yesod Torah' there are Arabs."
— Arabs, no less! You must be out of your mind!
— Just hear me out. It was last week, Wednesday I think; I'm standing at work and I hear a voice calling me:
— Pinchas, your boy is fainting!
— What? My boy, who studies in the "Agudah" cheder, is fainting?
I run into class 5 [division "hey"], and oh God! what do I see — my pearl is fainting. Blood is running from his head and half his face is swollen...
— What happened here? — I turn to the educator.
— There was a mistake — the melamed tells me — your boy took a fancy to peeking outside, so I wanted to give him a rap on the hand with a stick, and by the devil's doing the stick swerved onto his head and...
— Well...!
— You ask "well"? It's not for nothing I called him an "Arab"[?]. I spent 2 years in Palestine and I know the trade with which one of ours gets "honoured" in the eyes — by the Arabs...

He loves "Jewish sparks"...
Hardly had the man from Palestine left when a second one came in. A gloomy little Jew, his face full of wrinkles, his body swaying, barely standing on his feet.
— What is your request, Reb Yid?
— I'm from Sosnowiec [printed "Sasnavtse"?], I've come to the editorial office to pour out my bitter heart. Once, years ago, I was a rich Jew, the biggest millionaire in Zagłębie, but... the dear little war came and turned everything upside down. The old magnates were impoverished and "boils" [upstarts] began to flourish...
I had to give up the grain business, I had nothing to trade with; Reb Poverty spread himself through the house and the breadwinner became my daughter. We bought a sewing machine, she made up a little linen, and I sold the finished linen at the market.
The goods for the aprons I bought in Będzin from a manufactured-goods dealer I knew in the Old Market, a Ger Hasid besides, to whom after a long period of dealing I remained owing about four hundred gulden [złoty].
So he, and especially his only son, started persecuting me; handed me over to various bailiffs to ruin me completely and turn my family into a heap of rubble.
Seeing that the knife was already at our throats, I ran to the Rabbi of Będzin, who also intervened. But my adversary just laughed at it. He sent the bailiffs, who took everything from me, even "the only breadwinner" — the sewing machine too.
And all the while my adversary smiled sarcastically and said:
— Ha[?]! Sparks are flying before your eyes — I get great pleasure from it; my heart is refreshed when "Jewish sparks" fly..

All for the sake of a mitzvah..
At the ball of the "Dobroczynność" [charity society]. The whole "cream" [śmietana] of Będzin came here. Not to have a good time, but for the sake of a mitzvah; with every "l'chaim" — even eating a doughnut [pączek] people said "for the sake of the mitzvah of eating"... Every guest thought only of how to "fleece"[?] the crowd so that the cash box would get fuller.
So Avremel "the White" came out with a proposal: "The vice-president should put a paper crown on his head" — and for that, he said, he'd give such-and-such.
When the president, our Dr. Weinzieher, heard of the mitzvah, he said: "I'll be the 'Ameiser'[?] king", as long as you give money for the sprats...
And the hall "rocked" with delight when the vice-president and the president, crowns on their heads, strolled back and forth.
— A great pity they didn't proclaim earlier: "Thus shall be done" — this is how people act who want to support a needed institution...

Revenge...
Once, in the "old" days, when a boy in cheder or at school had sinned in some way, hadn't done his lessons properly, the melamed or teacher kept him back. When all the children were let out free, the "sinner" had to sit inside.
Today, though, in the age of civilization, when so much "care" is taken over the development of the young generation, revenge is different — "democratic".
The acts of revenge are carried out on a broad scale in our so-called "powszechne" [public elementary] schools. In those schools, where the children pay no tuition fees, a system has been introduced that is in every way adapted to the newest rules of "pedagogy".
For example: "[unclear word]" — for a "przedstawienie" [show] at such a school an "order" [rozkaz] is issued that every child must buy a ticket. The "order" is carried out strictly and harshly, and the child who cannot manage, even by crying for several days, to get money for a ticket from its poor parents is sent home from school by the "pani" [the teacher] — in the worst weather, naturally...
— And the poor mother grieves and weeps over her child's fate. If I — she says — could afford to give my child the gulden [złoty], I would surely want my child, too, to have fun together with other children at the show...!

Pupils...
A Polish proverb says: "Nie ma złego, żeby na dobre nie wyszło" [there is no bad without some good].
This idea occurred to me while attending a lesson at the Artisans' Association, where 4 times a week a large number of illiterate artisans come to the "evening courses" [kursy wieczorowe].
They keep up the courses scrupulously, they don't come late. A decree threatens the hard-working folk: one has to prepare for the examination so as not to have to part with "scissors and iron".
— How old are you, grandpa? — I turn to a grey-haired pupil.
— Oh! close to sixty... I already have, thank God, quite a few grandchildren, and here you are — suddenly lessons, writing "strokes" [pałki] and learning to read "ka-ka".
— When I come home — the old fellow goes on — my children, already real experts, look over my exercise book [kajet], laugh and give me "marks" [stopnie]... Yes, yes[?], times change; once, when they were little children, I examined them on whether they prayed properly, and today they give me "marks".
— Never mind [nie szkodzi], no matter — a little Jew with a little beard jumps in — we'll learn to write; if not for the decree we'd have stayed coarse ignoramuses for ever, but once we can read and write Polish, we have hopes of becoming town councillors too...

Go in peace.
The "Vilner" [the Vilna Troupe], who for several weeks sated us with spiritual delight, who spare no amount of devotion, effort and artistic work and are meticulous about every smallest detail of movement and staging — are leaving us and going abroad.
That the "Vilner" are going abroad pleases us too; on the contrary, let the nations of the world not speak of us with contempt — let them see that we, the wandering people, possess a great number of artists, among them also Yakov Waislitz[?], Miriam Orleska, Yosef Kamen and more and more.
Travel in good health, come back soon with fresh strength and a fresh repertoire. Until that happens we will remember you between "Day and Night"...
One Hundred and Eight Did Not Come — (What is happening with the Sosnowiec "old-age home"? — Does it really remain impossible to realize it?)

A [—] of 3 people are here s"g[?], it seems; what can people accomplish in the public field? And it must be said in praise of the three people that they have done much, very much; they took upon themselves to carry out an ideal, and they have worked devotedly and faithfully; they are dedicated to their idea and go about with the hope of realizing it.
To that end they wished to make their ideal a public cause, and so they created 108 members in the town, which sets a seal on the fact that the institution — which needs nothing more than to be completed — belongs[?] to the whole town and is the property of our entire Jewish population.
We are dealing here with the question of the Sosnowiec "old-age home", which to this very day has not been brought into being, despite the fact that the building already stands and we see before our eyes a work of real substance.
It is no small thing in our times to create an institution such as an "old-age home"; and once such a building has been put up, and it is a matter of nothing more and nothing less than finishing it[?], we ought surely to be proud of it. But what do we see? Unfortunately the chronicle tells us that the committee of the three called a general meeting, which took upon itself the task of creating a fund to complete this useful institution — and what turns out? Something unbelievable: of the 108 members there came — together with the three of whom the committee consists — 3. Can this be tolerated? Must such an unheard-of wrong be passed over in silence? How can one understand such unheard-of apathy? How is such criminal indifference to be explained? Is Jewish Sosnowiec not ashamed to stand aside at a distance and not want to know what becomes of the newly created honest building, which has every chance of becoming a home for old people, something we need so badly? Does it really make no difference to the whole Jewish population whether the institution is realized or, God forbid, not? Is it really all the same to all of you and to us? Do you really possess such coldness, such frozenness, that the whole matter should not interest you at all, as if it were not your cause, your treasure, your property? Where does one get such strength, where does one take so much power?
This coldness is simply beyond the grasp of reason. We must not forget that Sosnowiec is no longer the settlement of old, where a few minyanim of Jews lived. Today, no evil eye, we have a sizable Jewish community, divided into many different classes; and if we draw a parallel between our town and considerably smaller and poorer shtetls, we will see that they have an "old-age home" — while we, modern and in any case better-situated Sosnowiec, are as of the year 1930 without an old-age home.
And the vexation is all the greater because the building stands before our eyes and simply pleads: finish me, complete me, breathe a soul into me, and I will refresh old, worn-out people who need rest in their old age and have nowhere to lay down their worn-out bones.
Some ask themselves: what does Sosnowiec do to this day with its poor old people, who have nowhere to be? It is truly sad: they are made out to be sick and one tries to smuggle them into the Jewish hospital, and how many times do we beg our sister town Będzin to take pity on a Berl or a Shmerl and take them into its old-age home — and, understandably and rightly, it is not so easy to get in there; in such a case every kind of string-pulling is used.
[?] such a kind of beggary befits Sosnowiec. What does it mean that Będzin should take in old people from us at a time when it must itself be restricted, when it has no room for itself? Is it fitting that a town which is no worse situated than its elder sister should have to come, so to speak, for charity bread? Never mind — if there were impossibilities, we would still understand that too; but now it cannot be understood in any way.
What does it mean: a building stands that has already cost about 100 thousand zł., and one needs to have roughly another 30 thousand zł. in order to complete it and finish it. It seems that as soon as citizens have any ambition at all, they must see to it that the realization is accomplished, that the institution becomes an accomplished fact before our eyes.
The said sum could surely be raised easily, without any doubt, in the town; there are enough rich Jewish people who are willing to spend, and it will be an honour for them once they know that their donation decided the opening of this useful institution. It is true, times are now bad, the Jewish situation is threatened, and it is not easy to ask others to give; but one must not forget one thing: the more serious the situation, the more critical the time becomes, the more the town needs to finish the building.
There are in the town many respectable old people who toiled hard and honestly for as long as they had the strength, and now, in their older years, they have nowhere to rest their bones. Must a town not take care that its old people have somewhere to rest their weary bones? Can a town easily bear it when its brothers have to knock about in their old age, as a result of which they fall ill, are deceived[?] and go mad? Is that so easy to bear on one's conscience? Is it not a disgrace and a pain that people who have the means to help build such a building [printed "געביירע"] should look away from it, as if it were not they who are needed for it? Where has one seen that such a question, which is so easy to solve at the present moment, should be treated with so much disregard and despair, as if it were about nothing at all, and whether the institution is created or not were all the same?
How can one remain so cold when it is only a matter of realizing the beautiful ideal that people took upon themselves with so much love and enthusiasm, with so much courage and perseverance? How can 108 people set themselves up like an iron wall and say: eh, what is it needed for, who at the present moment is interested in such non-material affairs? Yes, 108 people did not understand that they should come together and talk things through when it concerns a concrete question. 108 people understood that it is easier to pretend that it has been entirely forgotten and not to touch at all on a question that may come down to money. 108 people did not understand that this is not about raising money in such a way that one would have to break oneself; we know that the present situation is a serious one and the money question is more serious still — but one may surely come together, and perhaps a way out can yet be found.
A practical proposal can be put forward: that each person give according to his means and that even the smallest contribution be accepted; let each contribute a brick to the building, so that he can say: I had the privilege of helping to build the everlasting institution, which can be a glory and an adornment for Jewish Sosnowiec.
But what is the main thing? Yes, the most important thing is first of all to come together, and that the question be considered from all sides. It makes no difference — as long as there is good will, the sum can be raised easily even in the present time.
After all, one must not forget that this is not the kind of institution one can do without. Even the smallest shtetl possesses an "old-age home"; Sosnowiec ought to be ashamed already of the fact that it does not possess one to this day.
The committee of the three must therefore call a general meeting as quickly as possible, at which the 108 members must appear — those who earlier did not come, thereby provoking so much understandable bitterness in the town.

The Fear of the Wife.

A little tale by G.[?] Malar.
One has to be an Arab to be able to understand and feel how great and how luminous is the name Abu Nuwas. They say in Arabia that the man has not yet been born who could withstand the power and the magic of his poems. Such a man would have to be entirely without a heart.
Well, is it any wonder that the famous Caliph of Baghdad, Harun al-Rashid, once spoke thus to the poet Abu Nuwas:
"Abu Nuwas, you have gladdened my heart with your poems. Ask a favour of me and it shall be granted."
"Very well, my lord. I ask of Your Mightiness no more than one thing: may it be your good will to let me wander through your realm and collect a donkey from every man who is afraid of his wife."
"Your wish shall be fulfilled!" said the Caliph.
Abu Nuwas wandered through the Caliph's realm. And when, some time later, he came back to Baghdad, he did not come alone, but with a great, a very great herd of donkeys.
A cloud of dust rose in the distance...
"What is that?" asked the Caliph.
Harun al-Rashid ordered that Abu Nuwas be brought before him. The Caliph was curious to hear about the poet's further journey.
And Abu Nuwas told:
"I have been here and there, I have crossed rivers and mountains, I have met a great number of men who are afraid of their wives, and I demanded a donkey from each of them, by the right which you, most esteemed [?] lord, granted me. I also met on my way many wondrously beautiful women; in the city of Fez, O Caliph, I found a young woman whose beauty is like the beauty of the moon on its fourteenth day.
What a young woman she is! Shall I be able to convey in words the magic of her black eyes, the charm of her curving hips? She is a true wonder, whom Allah sent down from heaven to earth to dazzle and stun us, poor children of men. I do not say who would be worthy of her, if not you yourself, O Caliph!"
"Speak a little more quietly," said the Caliph. "My wife Zubaida is standing behind the curtain and she might yet overhear us."
"Is that so?" exclaimed Nuwas. "Then order at once that I be given a donkey from your stables, and perhaps even two. You are, after all, the Caliph himself — and even you, the mighty ruler, are afraid of a woman. So tell me yourself: what are we to do, we, your poor, weak subjects?"
Tears and Laughter. (A Father's Monologue).

(A father's monologue).
The intelligent young people I cannot understand; somehow they have blind eyes and deaf ears and an irritated [?] mind. Don't think I am just talking into the wind — I know what I am saying. I'll prove it to you, too. Let us first light up a cigarette. When I talk, I have to smoke. What do you say — my words go off with the smoke? It only seems so: you will take back your words when I have finished my story, and so as not to take up your time in vain, I will tell it to you right away:
I am — may it not happen to you — a widower. My wife, peace be upon her, departed from me and from the world not long ago, and I was left a widower with 2 daughters: my Esterl, 26 years old, and the younger one, Maszka, 20 years old.
The elder, Esterl, is prettier than the younger, much prettier, because she takes entirely after me, and the younger takes after her, peace be upon her, my late wife.
Besides being the prettier one, the elder is very intelligent, very well-read in Yiddish, in Polish, in German, while the younger barely got through the public elementary school.
The elder is at home in the best books; she has already read a whole heap [?] of books.
Surely, it seems, it is quite fine when a girl, and a pretty girl at that, takes an interest in literature and music and poetry.
It turns out that it is not so good for her after all, I mean... for a match it is no use.
Because reading serious books has made her serious too... No smile comes to her lips, no merry spark shines in her eyes; she is always sad, melancholy; her face is always covered by a grey cloud... She looks at life through black glasses. Life, she says, is not worth living; everything is false, she says: people are false, their notions are false, and falser still is what people call love.
She utterly denies love; what people call love is nothing more than passion, a momentary joy... Love is nothing more than a word that says nothing, that fools the one who says it and the one who hears it...
If a person shows love, it is love of himself... However much he loves himself, it is still too little for him... because he would like to love himself more than he does... And if a young man says to a girl, "I love you," it is not true. The young man loves himself, not the girl...
That is how she pushes [?] her way into every matter. She wants to fathom the sea — the human mind...
Meanwhile she is going out like a candle. The young men shrink away from her, do not understand her, keep their distance.
Melancholy is truly poured out over her — a Tisha b'Av. She only weeps and laments the Destruction... When someone laughs, it annoys her.
Let the young men shrink away from her! She doesn't care; she is actually quite content. She does not want, she says, to be a doll, a toy in men's hands; she does not want to put on herself the iron chains of family life, to be chained to a house, to children, to pots, to laundry, to quarrels, to a husband who loves only himself.
That means a rope around the neck.
And take the younger daughter, Maszka — she is the exact opposite of the first!
A blaze, a fire, a volcano! She neither reads nor takes any interest in literature, music, poetry — or whatever!
She laughs and dances and eats and drinks and paints her cheeks and her lips and her hair, and smokes cigarettes, and crosses one leg over the other, and she has a sea of young men!
And she goes out with all of them, and rides out with all of them, and kisses all of them!
And the fellows stick to her like flies to sugar... She is always surrounded by three or four young men who never leave her alone. One keeps watch on the other...
Everywhere she goes, and everywhere she eats, and everywhere she dances, and everywhere she kisses...
A flirt!
She is far removed from melancholy; she laughs, makes fun of her elder sister, calls her by no other name than "nun". "Weepy nun"...
And the elder calls the younger "a silly piece of flesh", a little calf...
And yet — young men cling to the younger one by the dozen; she could get ten bridegrooms for one, but she is in no hurry. She wants, she says, to live and laugh before she gets married...
Many times I think: if the young people had my sense, they would surely do better to love my elder daughter; after all she is intelligent, well-read, musical; she understands life, the world, people. Surely it is an honour for a man to have such an educated wife; with such a wife one can talk about everything in the world, and when a wife is clever she can better adapt herself to her husband's character; she studies him, she explores him, she penetrates into his soul, into his heart... And it is precisely from her that they shrink away, the young men!
And the younger one has a sea of young men around her, and she doesn't give a whistle for the whole world... not even for her — father...
That is why I say the same thing I said at the start.
Today's young people I cannot understand; to me they are a riddle...
G.[?] Kowner.
The Jewish Councilmen Must Speak Up.

Actually, this is not about a new tax. This tax has already been in force here for many years. What we want to touch on now is the system and the amount of the tax. We mean the long-familiar tax called „mieszkaniowe“ [podatek mieszkaniowy — the dwelling tax].
For several weeks now the magistrate [municipality] has honoured the population with such „przypomnienia“ [reminders], and in true democratic fashion made no distinction between small and great, poor and rich. We do not mean in the present case to declare war on this tax. Firstly, it is a law, and secondly, our declaration of war would help little. What we want to criticise is only that the magistrate sent out the dwelling-tax receipts [demands] with large payments to far too many citizens who are toiling in raw[?] torment for their daily livelihood[?], and who, as far as they live anywhere, live not in flats but in dens.
The clerk writes, the „posłaniec“ [messenger] hands out the receipts, and the sequestrator [bailiff] will come after them both to collect the tax; but the question is why the magistrate does not know what this payer looks like, how he lives and how he gets by. Writing figures is no great art. Any pupil of any grade can show that. The art is first to think things through objectively and correctly, and only then to set the figures on the basis of truth and justice.
Great want reigns in the town, a tremendous unemployment. All these needy and unemployed people cannot, however, live in the street; they must arrange somewhere a little corner for their bones. But where is the proof that they are liable to a tax on their hovel[?], their poor nests, and moreover such a tax as these same harassed people have never seen even in a dream?
Perhaps it will be answered that those who cannot pay will make an effort and will be exempted. Let us suppose so. But do these people then lack worries, cares and troubles, that they should start lobbying and making efforts at various doors to be granted mercy — and how many of them are rewarded at all for the interventions and petitions[?]?
To all this is added a particularly complicated factor: many citizens complain that the „mieszkaniowy“ tax is not calculated rationally at all. That is, the magistrate assessed their rent too high, and consequently then also calculated the dwelling tax, which follows from the former, many times too high.
From this follows the conclusion that it would be a most desirable thing for the town council, in connection with this tax, to appoint a special commission, in which there must be proper representation on the part of the Jewish councilmen, who need to take an interest in this, since a considerable number of those burdened by this tax are also the Jewish population.
If such a commission was not created before the dwelling tax was assessed, it must at least be created now, so that the appeals or petitions of [—][?] citizens may be duly considered and taken into account to such an extent that the situation of those who are actually unable to pay is greatly eased. In our opinion this is a truly necessary thing.
The initiative must come from the Jewish councilmen.
B. Cwajg.
A Young Man from the Land of Israel Rebukes His Family in Będzin.

Several years ago a certain young man, D. Patak[?], left Będzin for the Land of Israel; he settled there and is very content. His family in Będzin, however, want him to come home, and a correspondence about this is being conducted between him and the family. To show how strongly the builder of the Land of Israel is attached to the Land of Israel, we print this interesting letter[?].
To my dear, beloved brother Abraham.
In reply to your letter of 25 October I want to make my position on your writing about my coming home clear to you once and for all. You may call it politics, fatherland, say what you like, but I cannot write otherwise. First of all — about my health. I work, I earn, and thank God I am healthy. You write to me that things are going well for me, and moreover that I was saved. Certainly it gladdens me that I remained alive, but was I not ready, like thousands of others, to die for the people and the land? You write to me that I take no account of you, that I have „birds in my head“ [fanciful dreams], and that at my age you already had a wife and child. „Fatherland“, „Jabotinsky“, „Messiah-bringer“ you call me, and [you say] that unfortunately we shall not live to see it, and further: come home, you will have a better living than in Jerusalem. I did not want to answer that, but it is my duty to write to you that at a time when the best children of the people of Israel are sacrificing themselves on the altar of people and land, I am a happy man to be among them, and I help with the holy building[?] of the upbuilding of the Land.
You, a son of this people, call on me to abandon my position! How are you not ashamed? You ought to be proud that one of our family is in the Land of Israel — and you call that birds in the head? Have you sunk so low already? That the holiest thing of the Jewish nation you call birds in the head? Draining swamps, building towns, developing a country, creating Jewish villages, tilling the soil, turning idlers into workers, making healthy a people of good-for-nothings[?] and brokers. Yes, my brother! To swindle, to trade, to have no ground under one's feet — that is not called having birds in one's head. Ah! What the exile has made of you, that of day you say night and of night — day.
At my age you already had children, but a Jewish land, Jewish peasants, Jewish workers — did you have those too? I am in the middle of it and I believe that I shall have them, and if not I — the future generations will surely have them; I suffer and struggle, if not for myself, then let my children have it. And you, without „birds in your head“, what have you created — that your child should speak the language of the gentiles, that he should be a free Jew in a free country?
Fatherland — yes! Whoever has been in the Land of Israel for a few years knows what our[?] fatherland is. The generation of the desert also did not believe Moses, and they died before the conquest of the Land. Those who unfortunately say that the Messiah will not come are the same as the generation of the desert, only instead of the desert today there are Russia, America and so on. And further: you write that I would have a living and more joy in Poland than in Jerusalem — my poor Jerusalem! How unhappy you are, that your children laugh at you! Grandchildren of the gabbaim bid us leave you, so that Rome and Moscow may remain... How tragic, how badly off you are, Jerusalem, my holy land!
But know that for me Jerusalem is everything! My home, my father and mother, my sister and brother, my wife and child. — My dear Jerusalem! I shall never leave you, even if your bread is as hard as your eternal rocks... I would rather be lonely and forsaken in Jerusalem like a tree in the desert than own palaces in exile. My dear Jerusalem! It may be that my body suffers with you, but my soul is happy! Therefore, dear brother, tell Mother that she should be proud and rejoice that her child is in the Land of Israel and helps in the upbuilding of the Land. You write that I should come home — on the contrary, you come home, to our old home, back to Zion. Come here, all of you, and here you will help build the great house for the people of Israel... With sweat and blood we are building the house that will one day be called — the Jewish Land.
Dear brother Abrahamele! Nothing will come of our arguments, but nevertheless remember that the Land of Israel is being built and lives!
I wish you all the best, and remember Jerusalem, our holy city.
From me, David Patak.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion

Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion
Collected by Y. L.
Parashat Yitro.
—o—
A.
"Men who fear God, men of truth" (18:21).
Moses was told to choose leaders who would be both God-fearing and men of truth — so it seems there are those who are God-fearing and yet far, far from being men of truth..
Folk saying.
—o—
B.
"Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel" (19:3).
"The house of Jacob" means the women, and "the children of Israel" — the men. Why speak first to the women?
God said to Himself: the first commandment I gave to the first human beings after creating the world, I commanded Adam first and only then Eve; that is why she sinned and brought misfortune on the world. Now (at the giving of the Torah), if I do not give the women precedence, they will now annul the Torah as well...
Midrash Rabbah.
—o—
C.
"Mount Sinai" (19:18).
The mountain on which the Torah was given is called "Sinai" because through the Torah hatred arose (sin'ah, "hatred", sounds the same, especially in the Sephardi pronunciation, as "Sini") of the nations toward the Jews.
Tractate Shabbat.
— Why was the Torah given precisely on Mount Sinai? There were higher and more splendid mountains, Tabor for instance — indeed, because Sinai was the lowest; that is how a man of Torah should regard himself: as nothing at all.
Tractate Sotah and Midrash.
—o—
D.
"I am the Lord thy God" (20:1).
"I" — I am One, without a brother, without a father and without a son...
Midrash.
— A cardinal once asked the Maharal: You believe in God, why should you not believe in His son too? It is the way of the world that a rich man's son is also given credit.
The Maharal answered: Right, a rich man's son is given credit because one day he will come into a great inheritance; but how can one trust the son of such a rich man who will never die...
— A priest asked 3 questions: 1) Why do you say in prayer "God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" and not "God of Moses"? 2) If Jews are beloved of God, why are they poor and the Christians rich? 3) Why do Jews marry early?
The Jew answered all three questions in order:
1) We do not say "God of Moses" in prayer because Moses had a blemish in the family — a priest for a father-in-law... 2) Christians are rich because their God died and left them an inheritance, whereas the Jewish God lives forever. 3) Jews marry early because we already know the reason: on account of one old maid (a word to the wise) we Jews suffer troubles to this day...
Heard.
—o—
E.
"Thou shalt not murder, thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not steal", etc. (20:13).
Why are the rich allowed everything? They may murder, steal, go bankrupt, and a poor man may do nothing? Let a poor man commit a small sin and he is decried at once.
— When Moses broke the Tablets, the people rushed to gather up the pieces of stone, which were of a precious tin[?] and worth a great deal. Naturally, the rich always have luck, so they grabbed the bigger pieces, on which was written "steal", "murder", "commit adultery"... The poor people had less luck and picked up the small pieces, on which were engraved the words: "not", "not", "not"...
Folk jest.
— The Rebbe of Przysucha, R' Bunem of blessed memory, grew up precisely in our Będzin (with the Wardiger family). As a young man he was gabbai of the book-purchase fund in the beit midrash. A poor Hasid came to him who could not scrape together a proper sum. The young R' Bunem took some money by stealth from the book-fund till and gave it to the poor man. It so happened that the "theft" was discovered. An uproar arose in the Mitnagdic beit midrash: how could it be? Such a "theft"? A meeting of the beit midrash gabbaim was called, headed by a certain R' Leib and R' Wolf. They sat down at the table, witnesses told of the "theft", and the last word was given to R' Bunem.
R' Bunem, knowing that he had a crowd of ignoramuses before him, spoke thus: Please, explain to me the verse "I have gone astray like a lost sheep, bakash" (Psalms) — "I wandered like a sheep through a straw" — what did King David mean by it?
(In fact these are two verses, "I have gone astray like a lost sheep" and "seek Thy servant", one right beside the other; only, knowing that he had coarse fellows before him, he dragged "bakash" over to the first verse and gave it another meaning: instead of "bakesh" (seek) — "ba-kash" (with a straw).)
Listen — says R' Bunem — I will tell you a parable. There was once a Jew who took pity on a forlorn little sheep and on a cold day took it into a warm house. The sheep warmed up, began to feel hungry, saw that straw lay in the master's shoes, and chewed up the straw. In the morning the Jew got up and he had no straw.
An uproar arose among the animals: such an injustice! such a murder! The master is so kind and lets you sleep, and you eat up his straw?! — They decided to call a meeting. At the head sits the lion, next to him a wolf; everyone talks about the terrible murder by the sheep. The little sheep calls out: You, lion, how many people have you devoured? You, wolf, how many lambs did you swallow in your youth? — and that is nothing. I, a poor little sheep, when I eat two straws — there is such an outcry, I, a poor little sheep...
I — continues R' Bunem — find myself in the position of that sheep, "I wander like a sheep with the straw": you, lion (pointing at R' Leib), how much orphans' money, how many poor brides' dowries have you swallowed; you, wolf (pointing at R' Wolf), how many people have you devoured, how many bankruptcies have you made — and all that is nothing, quite all right, because you are rich men; only I, a poor little sheep, when I eat two straws, when I give a gift from the book fund to a respectable[?] poor man — there is such an outcry...
—o—
Why did Jethro have seven names?
— He had seven daughters to marry off, and after each wedding he was so cleaned out that he had to go bankrupt and take on another name..
A folk joke.
A Conversation with Deputy Dr. Y. Thon

For quite some time now Dr. Thon [Ozjasz Thon, Sejm deputy from Kraków], owing to his poor state of health, has not taken an active part in Zionist and political work. The public has not had the opportunity to hear Dr. Thon's position on the current Zionist problems. For the Jewish public Deputy Thon is not only a politician and a Zionist activist, but also a great spiritual leader. Dr. Thon is a synthesis of Jewish culture and Jewish nationalism.
Deputy Thon receives me very cordially.
— How does the honourable deputy assess the present situation in Eretz Israel and the possibilities of Jewish-Arab coexistence? — is my first question.
In my opinion — says Deputy Dr. Thon — the situation in Eretz Israel has calmed down; there is only a depressed mood because of the trials and the sporadic attacks on the Jewish population. But they will stop. The work of the Jewish chalutz [pioneer] is already undisturbed now. The „economic“[?] boycott too — Deputy Dr. Thon goes on — is not as dangerous as it seems. On the whole the boycott has not succeeded. Only Jaffa suffered a little; it would be worse if the boycott spread to Egypt and Syria, but it will not come to that. Among the Arabs there are great differences of opinion, and a pan-Arab[?] policy is not even to be thought of. Nevertheless there must come a coexistence between Jews and Arabs, because the Arab people is interested in an immigration of Jews. The Zionist Executive must, according to a definite plan, conduct enlightenment work among the Arabs and negotiate with the Arab leaders who truly represent the Arab people.
— How do you regard the work of the English commission of inquiry [the Shaw Commission]?
— The commission was not objective. It was supposed[?] to establish what the causes of the events were and how to avoid them in the future. Meanwhile the commission debated the Mandate and the Balfour Declaration. What 53 nations, united in the League of Nations, gave us — fulfilling their ethical duty — cannot be subject to any discussion by an English commission.
— What is your position on the action of Dr. Magnes [Judah L. Magnes]?
— I strongly condemn[?] the action of Dr. Magnes. But everyone knows well that Dr. Magnes and „Brit Shalom“ are a small group of theoreticians[?] who do not represent even the smallest part of the Jewish people, which will not renounce its rights. The fact that Dr. Magnes is rector [chancellor] of the Hebrew University has no special significance. Dr. Thon further tells me that Mr. Magnes obtained his position because he is in close contact with the American magnates who finance the building of the University.
— What remains for us to do in the Diaspora at the present moment?
— Other nations sacrifice their best sons on the altar of national freedom. We Jews, however, must bear[?] the donating of sums of money. Eretz Israel must be built up as quickly as possible, and for that a common will of the whole people is needed.
Eliyahu Gartner.

From the KKL [Keren Kayemet LeIsrael, Jewish National Fund] headquarters in Poland we have received a comparative table of the KKL income over the last 6 years, since Tishri 5685, and with great satisfaction we note a considerable rise in the income in the first 4 months of the year 5690, compared with the same months of the previous years.

These figures prove absolutely the warm attitude of the Jewish masses to the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael. The necessity of buying out the soil of Eretz Israel as quickly as possible from foreign possession and of creating larger land reserves for an increased aliyah has become even more pressing after the recent bloody events in Eretz Israel, and therefore every friend of the redemption of the land must receive with satisfaction the news of the rise in the KKL income, and it is to be hoped[?] that Jewish society will continue to support materially the fund that creates the soil for the Jewish people.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Cantor Żupowicz Resigns His Post

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 23 / 23 Shevat 5690 — Piątek 21 lutego 1930 [Friday, 21 February 1930].)
Będzin
Cantor Żupowicz[?] gives notice of leaving the cantorate.
For several weeks there has been no "domestic peace" between Cantor Mr. Żupowicz and the kehilla leaders. The synagogue committee in particular is incensed at Mr. Żupowicz, who does not want to conform to the decisions of the gmina (kehilla).
The culmination was that Mr. Ż. went away without the knowledge of the synagogue committee and also did not want[?] to welcome the Sabbath (lead Kabbalat Shabbat) last Friday.
Because of this a meeting of the synagogue committee and the synagogue worshippers took place on Monday, which censured Mr. Żupowicz's conduct. The latter then pointed to a series of wrongs being done to him: he gets nothing from the "R.Ch.Sh."[?], the gmina owes him several months' salary, and in general he demands a raise. If not — he declared — he will leave the post in 6[?] months.
A protocol was written about this, to which both sides put their signatures.

Secular Subjects Will Also Be Taught at the Talmud Torah

[Będzin — education.]
Secular subjects will also be taught at the "Talmud Torah".
The present board of the Talmud Torah is working intensively and striving to have the Talmud Torah, which for a number of years was neglected in every area and especially in education, raised to the first rank of an educational institution. At the meeting very important questions will be discussed which are of great significance for the merchants of the branch. Delegates will also be elected to the convention of textile dealers, which is set for 2 March.
You Want to Dance? Then Go to the Next World...

[Będzin — crime.]
You want to dance? Then go to the next world...
On Sunday a wedding took place in Ksawera. During the dancing an unknown guest came in who also wanted to dance. Because of this a sharp quarrel broke out between the stranger and the wedding guests; the latter did not think long, gave the stranger a knife in the heart — and that was the end of the matter...
Registration of Apprentices with Metalworkers

[Będzin — crafts and employment.]
Registration of apprentices with metalworkers.
The local metal guild (cech) has received a circular (okólnik) from the voivode, in which it is demanded that the metalworking masters state the exact number of apprentices they employ.
In connection with this a registration is being carried out by the guild, which will last until 1 March of this year.
Income Declarations — Deadline Extended

[Taxes — income tax.]
Income declarations (zeznania) — extended.
The deadline for submitting declarations of income for the year 1929 has been extended to 1 May.
Who Has Lost Something?

From 1 to 31 January [„styczeń“] of this year the following items were found in the trams; they can be collected at the office of the tram depot [remiza] in Będzin.
2 leather bags, 2 ladies' umbrellas, a handbag, 2 pairs of ladies' „hoyzn“ [?, perhaps trousers], a pair of spectacles, a rubber raincoat, 2 ladies' „sakpakes“ [? — probably bags], a bag with school books, an oilcloth bag with exercise books, men's galoshes, a little purse with 30 gr., a knitted shawl, a ladies' purse with 68 gr., 2 packets of rubber for cleaning[?, probably erasers] and 1 cotton[?] kerchief.
At 48 He Was Called Up for Military Service

Mr. Shlomo Pietsh[?], 48 years old, was woken from his sweet sleep on Friday evening. When he woke up he saw before him military men, who informed him that they had come to him so that he should report for military inspection.
— „Panowie“ [gentlemen], is it possible? I am already a man advanced in years...
— True, but you did not report for military inspection in the year 1925.
Mr. Pietsh was taken to Sosnowiec to the P.K.U. [district recruiting command], stood there before a commission, which recognised that he is „zdatny“[?, fit] and registered him as an office reservist.
According to the Old Formula...

The local Jewish porters have begun to use the old methods — terrorising the Jewish merchants who do not want to give in to the tariff for packages of goods.
The method consists of denouncing[?] to the police the merchants who trade on Sunday.
In connection with this a brawl broke out at the premises of Mr. A. Kaplowicz. The latter called the police, who took the „heroic“ porters off to the commissariat.
In the Hands of a White-Slaver.

A few days ago a very elegantly dressed young man made the acquaintance in the street of 2 young Christian girls; the young man proposed to them that they travel with him to Sosnowiec „na herbatkę“ [for a cup of tea], to which the young ladies agreed.
In Sosnowiec the „friendly“ cavalier, instead of [going] to a pastry shop, went with them to the restaurant „Pod Bachusem“, where the company spent the time until after midnight. When the young ladies wanted to leave, saying that their parents would be angry with them, the young man reassured them: your parents — he declared — know me well and will not be angry that you have spent a few hours with me.
From the restaurant the company set off for the station with the aim of travelling home to Będzin, but instead of buying train tickets to Będzin, the gentleman[?] bought tickets to Tarnowitz [Tarnowskie Góry]. This was noticed by a person who recognised the girls as being from Będzin, and he went to report it to the police.
The young man, suspecting that there was an „eye“ on him, suddenly vanished. Hence there is a supposition that the girls had been in the hands of a white-slaver [trafficker in women].
Proceeds of a Ball for „Dobroczynność“.

On the 9th of this month the local charitable society organised a ball on the „Góra Zamkowa“ [Castle Hill], which was a great success. The public spent several hours very pleasantly, and the proceeds too were not bad at all. After all expenses there remained 2 725,06 zł., for which the board of the institution warmly thanks the participants and those who supported the undertaking.
Package-Porters in Uniforms.

This week the commission for general affairs of the town council held a meeting, at which the reform of the porters in our town was discussed.
The reform consists in this: that load-porters must be from 18 years of age, and porters at the railway — from 14 years of age.
The porters must also wear numbers and special uniforms. On the proposal of councillor Feiner, the load-porters are exempted from the uniforms.
General Meeting of „Beit Lechem“.

In the premises of the Artisans' Association, under the chairmanship of Mr. Zawader[?], the annual general meeting of „Beit Lechem“ [bread-for-the-poor society] took place.
Mr. Sendishev[?] gives a report, from which it can be seen that the institution supports 70 families weekly with provisions. Despite this there is still cash of up to 300 zł. in the treasury.
Then a new board was elected.
Sosnowiec — A Meeting of the Kehilla Council.

Under the constant pressure of the Starostwo (district office) that the budget be submitted, the kehilla council met, after a break of a whole year, in order to fix the budget for the year 1930. A large number of onlookers and lobbyists also came, to see to it that the items of the interested parties were not cut. The small meeting hall, which is not suited to such a kehilla, looked like a lump of human mass, so that it was hard to tell who were the "radni" (councillors) and who the "gallery", since everyone stood squeezed together like a ball of yarn; it looked like "a big hut packed with passengers"... among whom there are some who curse [printed "zirlen", misprint for "zidlen"] and swear at each other...
———
The meeting is chaired by the vice-president Mr. Leibish Szwajcer. On the agenda, the parnas David Zylberberg (Mizrachi) takes the floor and says that since the council is not informed about the expenditures and revenues of the previous budget, the meeting should be postponed to another date. The parnas Cieszemski [?] (Agudah) and others agree with this opinion. Against it speak the chairman Szwajcer and the vice-president of the kehilla Mr. Zegrel [?], who declare that the Starostwo threatens a fine [?] if the budget is not ready by the 25th of this month.
After the declarations and after a recess, a discussion began again around the question "to be or not to be". In the course of the discussion the parnasim Cwajgenhaft and Cieszemski treated each other to "jibes". In the end the proposal was adopted that the meeting take place this coming Saturday night, and that every councillor be sent a report on last year's budget.
For orientation, the secretary Mr. Lewenhof [?] read out the report on the budget for 1929. According to the report, the budget (etat) debts amount to about 60 thousand złoty.
"You Can Trade in Palestine".

"You can trade in Palestine" — so says a policeman to a bagel seller.
Since many bakeries have been closed, the Jewish journeyman bakers have lost their jobs. Several of the unemployed, among them Shmuel Leib Zylbersztajn, bought licences ("patents") to sell baked goods [?] in the streets. The selling, however, is being disturbed by the police, and a report was drawn up against Zylbersztajn. When Z. made it clear [?] that he holds a licence, the policeman replied: "In Palestine you can trade".
—o—
The Father an Engineer — the Son a Bandit.
The bandits Orłowski and Argastak [?], who carried out a robbery attack on a woman on a train at Zawiercie, have been brought to the local prison.
Argastak is from Wilno; his father is an engineer at the government technical school in Wilno.
—o—
Further Layoffs in the Coal Mines.
The management of the "Czeladź" coal mine has again laid off 400 workers. From the "Saturn" mine, too, 200 workers have been laid off.
—o—
A Local Young Man Stabbed.
On Tuesday, in Będzin, a local young man, one Smolarski, was stabbed by his companions in a tavern. The wounded man was taken in serious condition to hospital, where he remained for treatment.
—o—
Today — "Day and Night".
The Vilna Troupe, which is playing in Będzin with colossal success, is staging tonight at the Municipal Theatre "Day and Night" by S. An-ski. The play is worth seeing, especially as performed by the Vilna players.
—o—
The 21st of This Month Is Judgement Day.
On Friday, the 21st of this month, the main commission will examine the appeals against the assessment of the turnover tax for 1928.
—o—
Reduction of Municipal Officials.
The local town administration has decided to cut the administrative expenditures of the magistrate (town hall); for this purpose about 30 officials will be dismissed, which amounts to 10 percent of the total number of officials.
—o—
Suicide.
On President Mościcki Street the 18-year-old S. Negas [?] was found dead; a revolver lay beside the body. It is presumed to have been suicide.
—o—
A "Jewish Article" in Gentile Hands.
Some górale (highlanders) miscalculated and brought Purim graggers (noisemakers) to the market. The górale stroll along Modrzejowska Street rattling away nonstop. The merchants are very pleased with this "concert" — in hard times even hearing graggers is good...

Ząbkowice — A Theatre Performance for the KKL.
The local Keren Kayemet committee is arranging a performance next Sunday in the hall of the "Folks-hoyz" (People's House). "Bar Kokhba" will be staged by the drama section of the Right Poale Zion in Ząbkowice. After the performance — dancing.
Collision between a wagon and a tram

[Będzin — accident.]
On Tuesday, in the Alter Mark [Old Market] in Będzin, a wagon loaded with coal collided with a tram. Fortunately there were no human casualties. Some passengers were even injured by pieces of glass from the smashed windowpanes.

At the meeting a resolution was also passed to exempt from tax the society "Dobroczynność" [Charity], which received a house as a gift from the Oppenheim family.

[Dąbrowa — municipality.] This week the budget commission of the Dąbrowa City Council struck out a series of subsidies for Jewish institutions. It is interesting to note that the subsidy for the Jewish community [gmina] for social welfare was struck out of the "budget" by the "Democrats" as well.

The verdict in the great trial against the Left P.P.S.

[Sosnowiec — trial; Communists.]
The trial against the Left PPS [PPS-Lewica], which took place in the Sosnowiec district court and lasted about 2 weeks, ended on Monday. The verdict was pronounced only on Wednesday at 10 o'clock in the evening.
The verdict is as follows:
For belonging to the Left PPS in the years 1926—1929 the following are sentenced: Cwik[?], Burgin[?] to 4 years' hard prison; Gadomski to 3 years; Fałka, Gwałek[?], Kosta and Pieńkniewski to 2 years; Czuma[?], Piłat, Krzeczak[?], Durniewicz[?], Żych to 1 year in prison.
For belonging to the Communist Youth Union the following are sentenced: Bongarenko[?] to 3 years; Lewicka, Płakowa[?], Szwimer[?], Kornelnik[?] to 2 years; Krzyszkowski[?], Szydłowski to 1½ years; Jarek to 1 year.
The defendants heard the verdict calmly.
—o—
The sick fund made him sick.
[Będzin — sick fund; medicine.] 17-year-old Anułowicz[?] of Będzin got a pain in his throat. Being a member of the sick fund (Kasa Chorych), he turned to Dr. Chmielewski in Sosnowiec, who gave Anułowicz help. The next day Anułowicz got terrible pains and stopped speaking altogether. Then the father, Israel, travelled with his sick son to Dr. Besch in Katowice, who declared that Anułowicz showed signs of diphtheria.
On their return from Katowice Dr. Weinzieher was called to the patient; he declared that this was no diphtheria but some illness which had probably been caused by the first doctor who had treated Anułowicz.
Dr. Weinzieher was curious to get to the bottom of the „mysterious illness“, and after a consultation of doctors he came to the patient together with several doctors. The doctors' opinions differed, but the majority stated that Anułowicz's throat had been scalded by the cleansing agent which Dr. Chmielewski had used.
Mr. Anułowicz is handing the matter over to the court.
—o—
Wants to evict the Tenants' Association.
[Będzin — court; tenants.] In the Będzin magistrates' court the case was heard against the board of the „Tenants' Association“, who had been sued by the landlord Mr. Politański[?] on the grounds that in the premises where the Tenants' and Small Traders' Association is located, scandals occur, by which the peace of the tenants is disturbed.
The witnesses rejected the claims, but because both sides produced new witnesses, the case was adjourned to a second date.
—o—
4 million zł. to build cheap flats
[Będzin — housing.] The Workers' Insurance Office in Königshütte [Chorzów] is negotiating with the Będzin municipal administration about selling the magistrate's plot by the barracks. On this plot the company wants to build dwellings for intellectual workers and other officials. The building is to cost about 4 million zł.
The negotiations will probably be concluded in the next few days. According to the plan the building is to be ready in the month of July (lipiec) of this year.
—o—
The small traders sound the alarm...
[Będzin — small traders.] Yesterday the board of the Będzin Small Traders' Association sent telegraphic protest resolutions to the Marshal of the Sejm, the Jewish Club (Koło) etc.
The content of the resolutions is that the government should alleviate the terrible situation of the small traders.

Strzemieszyce.
Meeting of the „Gmilut Hesed“ Fund
Under the chairmanship of the local rabbi, Rabbi Zagrer [?], the annual general meeting of the local „Gmilut Hesed“ (interest-free loan) fund took place.

What Is Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — Katowice: art; trade.]
Wilhelm Wachtel in Katowice.
The name of the painter Wilhelm Wachtel is unfortunately not known to the Jewish public. Wilhelm Wachtel is one of those painterly personalities of whom even the Polish people were proud when they needed them [?] for Polish propaganda abroad. In 1912, when Wachtel exhibited in Paris together with Jewish painters who are famous today, such as Hirszenberg, Pilichowski and others, the Polish art journal „Sztuka“ came out with a large article entitled „Our Polish Painters in Paris“. This is the Wachtel who is now exhibiting his works in Katowice in the hall of the Hotel „Monopol“, and it will be interesting to see whether Silesian and Zagłębie Jewry will appreciate him at least as much as the Polish people appreciated him. Wilhelm Wachtel now comes to us as a purely Jewish painter. He shows us a series of illustrations to the Song of Songs, splendidly composed, very rich in colour and very Jewish in style — above all the ornamentation with which he adorns his illustrations. He also shows us a whole series of Palestine pictures that shine with sun and light. Whoever knows Wachtel's earlier works and sees what he has now brought from Eretz Israel admires the youthful strength that the sun of Eretz Israel gives a creative artist.
Every art lover, and above all those who love Eretz Israel, should use the opportunity: if they do not have the possibility of keeping a little of Eretz Israel with them [?], let them at least visit the exhibition.
The exhibition remains open for two weeks, daily from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Moshe Apelbaum.
