What's New in Upper Silesia?

A small traders' association founded.
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Fridman, the founding meeting of a small traders' association took place on Sunday in Königshütte (Chorzów). The meeting was attended by several hundred small traders, who were eager to see[?] what salvation the association would bring.
Mr. Hershlevitsh[?] (Będzin) spoke on the organisation and the further tasks. Then a board was elected, which sent telegrams to the President of the State, the Marshal of the Sejm and the Jewish „Koło“ (Sejm club), asking that the tax burdens be eased.
—o—
Bloody fight between police and bandits.
The police in Königshütte carried out a raid on a certain restaurant on Moniuszki Street, where several bandits were present. During the raid shooting broke out, in which one bandit and one policeman were seriously wounded. It is suspected that these are the same bandits who murdered the bank director Danziger.
—o—
Car accident.
On Saturday a car accident occurred on Mickiewicza Street in Königshütte. The driver was seriously injured. A few hours later he died.
—o—
Consultations of coal merchants.
In the „Savoy“ hotel in Katowice several consultations of wholesale coal merchants were held.
The aim of the consultations is that the wholesale coal merchants want to found a union which would protect the interests of the coal suppliers. Above all it is a question of how to combat the epidemic of bankruptcies.
Merchants from Kraków, Sosnowiec, Będzin, Częstochowa and Łódź took part in the consultations.

Conference of Jewish and Christian Artisans and Small Traders

On Sunday, on the initiative of the "Small Traders' Association", a conference of Jewish and Christian small traders and artisans took place in Sosnowiec. Taking part in the conference were representatives of all the Jewish small traders and artisans in Zagłębie, of all the Jewish and Christian merchants' associations, of the Starostwo [district administration], the Chambers of Commerce and of Crafts, of the "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office], and others.
At the conference, which had been convened to protest against the tax injustices, an unexpected incident arose over the language question. To blame for the incident is the chairman, who would not or [printed "arer", for "oder"] could not react on the spot to the antisemitic outcries and also settle the whole affair; and also [printed "rer", for "der"] Mr. Ganzwajch, who ought to have agreed beforehand with the organising committee that he wished to speak Yiddish. In any case the Jewish representatives, with the exception of a small number, reacted as was proper and left the hall with pride. The incident will be a lesson for the future that even in purely economic questions we must be independent and not "assimilate"...
———
The chair is handed over to Mr. Witkowski. Delegates of the existing associations and guests are invited onto the presidium. The first speaker is the chairman, who touches on the unjust turnover and income tax. Chamber of Commerce councillor Mr. Aliger[?] speaks on the municipal [taxes] and turnover tax, town councillor Mr. Rotsztajn — on the sad situation of the Jewish artisans in Poland, Mr. Machura — on tax reliefs.
Mr. Ganzwajch is given the floor and declares that, since there is in the hall a certain number of Jews who do not understand Polish, he will speak Yiddish.
But no sooner does Mr. G. begin to speak than a storm breaks out in the hall: "Po polsku!" ["In Polish!"] etc. The "record" in this field was set by Mr. Mazurkiewicz, who bawled "Po polsku, bolshevik!" etc.
Mr. Rotsztajn protests against the shouting; the Jewish masses — he exclaims — know no Polish, because they were under the "Tsarist yoke" and Polish had to be learned in stables [i.e. in secret]..
The chairman tries to calm things down, but when he declares that he is against allowing Yiddish to be spoken, some of the Jews leave the hall and chaos ensues.
Part of the Christian public want to settle the incident, and they succeed when Mazurkiewicz receives a public "nagana" [reprimand]. The Jews regard this as satisfaction, and the greater part come back into the hall.
In the discussion various questions were raised which are a burden on the small traders. Among other things the question was touched upon of health certificates, which are issued by the municipal authorities for a fee of 5 zł., and besides that the shopkeeper has to lose a lot of time before he finally gets such a certificate.
On this question the representative of the Starostwo, Mr. Lechowski, explains that such a certificate need not necessarily be from the town doctor, but is valid from any doctor at all who confirms that the person is not ill with an infectious disease.
After speeches by Eng. Kaliński, the president of the Chamber of Crafts Smuga, Łachnik[?] Goldsztajn and others, the following resolutions are adopted: 1) to apply to the Sejm and the government that from 1 April [kwiecień] 1930 a turnover tax of 1 percent be levied on retail trade, and only half a percent on products of prime necessity. 2) the 10-percent turnover tax be abolished, 3) the tax for 1929 be spread over instalments, and for non-payment on time only 1 percent be charged, 4) the advance payments [zaliczki] for 1930 be paid on the following dates: 1st advance on 1 September [wrzesień], 2nd — 1 October [październik], 3rd — 1 November [listopad], 5) the income tax be paid in 2 instalments.
Also adopted, with certain amendments, were the following proposals submitted by Łachnik[?] Goldsztajn:
1) in order to create new sources of livelihood the government should make larger credits available for building purposes, 2) the economic associations should be empowered to confirm who is entitled to benefit from the circular [okólnik] concerning the cancellation of tax arrears, 3) cottage workers [chałupnicy] should be exempted from buying patents [trade licences] and from paying all other taxes, because the law exempts them from these, even though they employ more than 1 journeyman.)
On this last proposal the president of the Chamber of Crafts spoke up, arguing that with it the Chamber of Crafts would be forgotten[?] — the Chamber, which will control all artisans' cards, and only those who are qualified will be allowed to engage in a craft. He also does not agree with the proposal that the economic associations be empowered to determine for whom tax arrears should be struck off, arguing that the ministry will not agree to it, [—]
When There Is No Consistency

(What can be created when the will is there and the logic is sound.)
In Zawiercie and in Strzemieszyce the free-loan (gmiles-khesed) funds are flourishing.
(From the chronicle).
Nothing can be foreseen in advance; about no institution, or any activity whatsoever, can one say that its fate has fallen out this way or that, that this or that institution will develop well or badly. After all, we see quite often that what one places much hope in turns out a letdown, that we deceived ourselves, that the thing was not worth the effort; and conversely, more than once we notice how something is carried through that was not in the plan, and where one was almost convinced beforehand that nothing would come of it, it turns out that it is going well, that something great and substantial is being created, and a fine monument for generations comes out of it.
So it is in private life, and it is no different in public life. How often, for example, do we see one institution after another fall and leave the arena, despite having had every possible chance to exist and develop well; and then the serious question arises: why is this so? What is the reason that this establishment was not destined to live, exist and create? True, the average Jew, with his worries, has no time to dwell on every detail; he does not know how to consider for what reason it came about. But he who is a public figure, who knows how the public machine must be steered, who knows how it must be operated — he has already found that there must have been understandable reasons, from which an expert will convince you exactly that for this or that reason the institution could not exist.
But whatever reasons we may not take the trouble to look for, we will, on the other hand, always realise [?] that the main defect is that the leaders are not capable, or that they do everything in a bungling way, feet up and head down.
After all, we are now living through very, very bitter times throughout the country, and here in Zagłębie too we feel the seriousness of the moment; we see that from day to day it gets worse, from week to week the situation becomes more critical, so that it would be only fair to think of doing something so as to be able to help, as far as possible, solve the problem of hunger.
Rarely, however, are we called upon here to solve current problems with full seriousness, and that is because we have no understanding of how to conduct purely economic matters; as soon as one merely [?] begins to put one's hand into cold water, politics with honour and patronage immediately starts — and these are the microbes that soon destroy everything. But as long as the microbes do not get in, one can hope that the activity will be fruitful for the good of society.
Unfortunately the dangerous microbe has got into every corner of our life and does damage everywhere.
We are therefore glad to read a report from Zawiercie, where we see that the local free-loan fund has grown so much that, with the help of devoted board members, it has attained some assets and built itself its own school. For this it has its own capital of 16 thousand zł., and from the „Joint“ 14 thousand zł. Besides this, the director of the „Joint“, in recognition, sent 400 dollars for the building of the school.
Also about such a small settlement as Strzemieszyce we read that the local „gmiles-khesed“ fund called a general meeting, and the members heard with satisfaction the report on how splendidly the institution is prospering; it has also collected its assets of 5000 zł. from its own groszy. The public, in Zawiercie as in Strzemieszyce, unanimously demanded that the previous boards be confirmed, in which they have the fullest trust and recognition.
Apparently honest, sincere activity is not lost; it [?] — and in town one feels that it lives and supports those who earn their living thanks to the interest-free loans they receive there.
Can one really appreciate the great value of this colossal undertaking, thanks to which such traders, for whom a bank is closed, stay on their feet? How would such traders manage [?] if they did not have such an establishment, one that takes an interest in making sure that people who want to work and earn a living do not become a burden on the population — only, once they lack those few złoty, they get stuck [?] and vanish from public view. If we look into the situation of the poorest strata, who earn their living with a total of a few zł., only then will one see what great benefit the free-loan funds bring these little people.
Common sense would dictate that if in small towns, where the grosz plays an important role, the free-loan funds develop so nicely, all the more should they develop in the larger towns; meanwhile we see the opposite story: we, the inhabitants of the larger towns, may learn from Zawiercie and Strzemieszyce; it does not matter, we may take an example from them.
After all, one cannot say that Będzin, for example, could not have done more in this field than the above-mentioned small towns, and yet here we have remained so far behind [?]. How then is this to be explained? It goes without saying that Będzin is used to giving; if the institution here does not stand at the proper height, it is the fault of the leaders.
We have almost never written about the Będzin free-loan fund, only because, knowing that they constantly go the wrong way, we pointed out the inconsistency — and then „the heavens opened“: at once there was abuse and threats, so that we avoided the institution and for us it did not exist as such. For the same reason we also do not print all the accusing articles addressed against them that we receive so often.
It is therefore self-evident that the institution in Będzin could have flourished according to the material support it had [?] from the local population; but when would that have been achieved [?]? — had it let itself be spoken to, had they let themselves be guided and not always wanted to play the role of autocrats and dictators, where patronage and honour and politics and seats played the most important role.
They never wanted to take into account that this is a purely charitable institution, that it must enjoy a good opinion not only of this or that party but of the whole town without exception — and that is the reason why the institution began to sink and almost left the arena.
It is therefore no wonder that in town confidence in the leaders was lost; it could not and need not have been otherwise, for one must not treat a town of people with so much frivolity.
Had the patronage system and political wheeling-dealing not played first fiddle there, we in Będzin, as the heart of Jewish Zagłębie, could have had the most exemplary free-loan fund in all of Poland. We had all the best chances for it.
Let this be a lesson for the future: when public workers want to act for the town's interests for the good of „ri“ [sic, for „di“ — those] for whom the institution is created, they must not in that case take a single false [?] step; every move that is not consistent harms the leadership.
Let our public workers therefore remember on every occasion that they must reckon with the public, and if they do not, they thereby harm both the institution and the population. Communal workers must always remember in what society they work, and adapt themselves to the tasks and duties of the institution, if one is truly after its existence.
Selekt.
What I Heard, What I Saw

By Ben Amotz.
„Do Palestyny“ [„To Palestine!“].
At the conference of small traders and artisans in Sosnowiec. A united front against the tax injustices; Jews and non-Jews go on the defensive together to abolish the organs that suck like leeches on the organisms of the already benighted, barely living mass.
In the hall — an idyll. There „exists“ no difference of race or descent, only „the voice of them that cry in the camp“ — it is bitter, the troubles can no longer be borne.
Speakers repeat the already well-known tax absurdities, and the crowd nods:
— That's how it is, he speaks well...
The secretary of the Jewish artisans' association in Sosnowiec takes the floor. He sees that his comrades do not understand what the non-Jews are saying, so he speaks[?] „in the tongue of his people“, stirring the tormented Jewish heart..
And a storm sweeps across the hall; Esau has raised his voice[?]:
— „Do Palestyny!“, „Bolshevik!“
A Jewish town councillor (Ratman) tries to influence the „solidarised brothers“.
— Why are you shouting? Because of Tsarism the Jewish mass simply could not [learn] the Polish language.
But the arguments do not convince; Polish citizens — the gentiles clamour — must know Polish.
An old, familiar formula. The „Skarb“ [the Treasury/tax office] thinks[?] that „citizens must pay big taxes“, and at a conference against the „Skarb“ one hears that citizens must know Polish, and if not, there is a remedy:
— „Do Palestyny“...
„Cold“ coal...
Friday afternoon in the Będzin „łaźnia miejska“ [municipal bathhouse]. In the „waiting room“ a few Jewish visitors sit and wait.
— What is everyone waiting for?
— For the coal to get „warmer“.
And the attendant tells: every Friday something happens in the „łaźnia“. When there is water, there is no steam; when there is barely steam, there is no hot water.
— How long will we wait for the water to get warm? — I ask.
— Half an hour, maybe an hour, who can tell?
Suddenly a signal; the attendant runs to the tap and joyfully cries out:
— Jest woda! [„There's water!“]
The guests „occupy“ the bath cubicles. The attendant gives each one a lesson in how to operate the tap. A turn to the right — she explains — brings hot water, and to the left — cold water. The guest is already at home with the turning, turns this way, turns that way, right, left, and
— cold, cold, co...ld...
Again people run with complaints to the supervisors: how can this be? We waited a whole hour for cold water!
— Proszę państwa, trudno, co piątek tak się zdarza [„Ladies and gentlemen, it can't be helped, it happens every Friday“], just when the Żydki [„little Jews“] come to bathe[?], the coal „goes nieprawny“[?] [unclear Polish-Yiddish word — apparently „gets spoiled / is under repair“] and...
— Oh, how great are the Jewish troubles: even the coal in the municipal bathhouse goes „nieprawny“ in honour of the Sabbath...
A shochet transaction...
The Będzin kehilla is about to close a new transaction. The deal is done behind closed doors. On the table lies a fresh, wriggling little shochet, just out of the eggshell. The pedigree is from a well-known firm. Raised among the Gerer [Hasidim], and[?] because one wants the [?] „presence“ in the kehilla council. Until now the kehilla has „driven“ into the slaughterhouse on a wagon with 4 wheels — no fewer than 4 shochtim are employed in slaughtering — but now they want the wagon to run on 5 little wheels... just so that[?] there will be an even number: 50 thousand zł. for 5 shochtim.
Around the table at which the shochet match is arranged sit the chief in-laws, both from the groom's side and from the bride's side. The difference is that in all other matches the bride's side pays the dowry, whereas in engaging a 5th shochet the „groom“ must give a dowry, and in dollars at that..
In the street people are already wishing each other mazel tov, but according to reports it seems to me that the mazel tov is still premature, because according to the matchmakers' reports the bride's side has dug in its heels: a whole thousand dollars „she“ demands from the groom...
But that is not what we are after; what matters is only that the Będzin kehilla is being enriched by a fresh transaction
— a shochet transaction..
Who is he?
A representative of the Sosnowiec merchants' association complains to us. For years — he says — we „toiled and pleaded“[?] until we achieved that at the hearing of the appeals (rekursy) in the „Izba Skarbowa“ [Treasury Chamber] there should also be representatives of the Jewish merchants' associations of Będzin and of Sosnowiec.
And the result?
A very sad one. To this day the only Jewish representative from Będzin has not taken part in the session of the appeals commission.
If we knew who the Jewish „defender“ is, we would take him by the ear and say: you emissary of the public, why do you play with Jewish livelihoods? Don't you know that not only monetary cases but also capital cases are judged in Kielce?..
That is what we would tell him — but who is he?
Benefactors..
The trustee of the Rabbi Meir Baal HaNes (RMBH״N[?]) charity boxes came to the holy community of Koziegłowy. There the Gerer [Hasidim] received him cordially and then said to him:
— Why should you trouble yourself and come all the way to Koziegłowy for the paltry sums in the boxes; why incur expenses, when we can handle it for you in the best possible way: every month we will empty the boxes and whatever we find in them we will send you to Będzin; so[?], why take the trouble yourself?..
Hearing such fine words, the trustee agreed to the favour — anything[?] not to have to drag himself to Koziegłowy; why not — after all they are „our people“; taking trouble for a mitzvah is something only our people know how to do...
The new month passed; the trustee in Będzin waits to receive the account from Koziegłowy, but there is neither voice nor answer. A few days later he did receive a little letter from the benefactors, informing him that they had kept their promise — the boxes had meanwhile been emptied — only a „small“ change had occurred: instead of for the Chalukah Jews in the Land of Israel, the money had been taken for „Beis Yaakov“...
Help!
With this cry several tenants of the house at Kościelna 3 in Będzin come in to us.
In this house, in one apartment, lives a widow with her children. In that apartment the Angel of Death has „entrenched himself“ and is carrying off victims.
3 years ago — the tenants tell — her husband died, last year — a young man [son], and this week — a daughter...
Doctors say that the remaining souls are also in danger if they do not have a comfortable, sunny apartment. If you can't afford what such an apartment costs — says the doctor — then go sit in the middle of the market opposite the [?] sun, which will warm you for free..
So they come, these people, to the editorial office, asking us to appeal, to rouse the magistrate, the gmina [municipality] and human hearts to help, so that the „remnant“ may get an apartment; the landlord himself also wants to help with a certain sum, and their fate depends on Jewish society.
— Why write much? Whoever saves a single soul of Israel.. and here one can save many worlds... We shall indeed see whether our communal workers will take an interest in this so unfortunate family, which cries out and calls:
— Res—cue—us!..
The Sickness Funds (Why Are They So Hidden from Us? Responsibility, Autocracy, Indifference)

[Opinion — public health; the sickness funds (Kasa Chorych).] Kasa Chorych — the sickness fund: who does not know of this institution, who does not know that such an establishment exists and is active; and yet, just as every one of us knows of the institution, so nobody knows what goes on there, what things look like there and what benefit it brings to the population, to the broad strata of the popular masses.
It is no trifle what this establishment costs the population — and costs it does, everywhere and always, not only [the rich?] and the middle class, the factory owner and the workshop owner, but also the poor man, the [—] [?], the worker and the employee, the clerks and journeymen [?].
[Right?] here the question arises: does the population derive the proper benefit from these institutions? Do they deliver as much as they cost the citizens? Who knows this and who can say it? Who has any notion of it and who can voice an opinion? We know only this: we happen to hear, often and many times, various accusations addressed to the sickness funds. We know, for instance, that many of the doctors treat the patients of the sickness fund with monstrous [?] indifference and apathy; it somehow looks as if they were treating the sick for nothing, as if they were not paid for every visit.
We have heard more than once that a doctor comes in to a patient with rare impudence, often makes a racket and behaves [?] brutally toward the household [?], so that it frequently comes to scandals on both sides. Besides, everyone knows that one rarely gets the doctor on time; we hear not a few comic, ridiculous facts [?] from time to time, and all this when one asks for a doctor from the sickness fund. They apparently think that they are doing the patient a favour. They forget, though, that they never go for free, and that a doctor costs the population more than a private one.
Last week we read that a doctor treated a patient so bunglingly that little was lacking for him to send him out of the world, and in the best case to make him a cripple for life.
The Kasa Chorych is an institution where the doctors work as employees work for a firm; so the question arises: is the sickness fund responsible for its employees as, let us say, a private firm is? Who [?] is the authoritative control over the responsibility of the doctors? After all, this is the kind of work in which human life is put at stake — so in the given case the institution must remain responsible for its employees, to whom human life is entrusted. We hear that in the institution's premises the patients are treated quickly, one after the other, without any delay whatsoever, as if it were a matter of cutting out a shoddy suit. Can people in such a case be examined properly? Can one, so hastily, accurately and diligently ascertain the condition of the sick person? Not to mention when it comes to finding out what the patient is ill with — that, in the course of a few counted minutes, is [?] and impossible.
Public medical aid ought to have been first-class; it ought to have taken the top place in the country; the sickness funds ought to have shone like reflectors, so that wherever one stood one would see the model order it maintains. With good performance [?], with proper management, this could indeed have been realised, for it has every possibility of putting all this into practice.
It is a rare thing for public institutions that are so useful to the people to be run in such a veiled way that one cannot know why the situation is so unsatisfactory, so unsustained.
Why should we not have any reports from the institution that would make clear to the population what is being done there? The revenues come, after all, from the population — so why should it not know where and how the money is spent [?]? Why should one not know in what manner all this is administered and of whom the administration consists?
It is unheard of, after all, to take so little account of those who maintain the sickness funds. We live, after all, in a free, independent Poland, in the twentieth century, when the right to voice an opinion everywhere and to acquaint oneself with everything serves [?] the citizen; and here, when one wants to write about the activity of the sickness funds, about their merits and shortcomings, about their defects — everything is concealed, there is nowhere to obtain the most essential material with which one could work and point out both the good and the bad sides of this establishment, which is so important and useful for those who need public medical aid.
The sickness funds are based on the foreign system, but what a contrast it is — how can one compare it with abroad? We know, after all, that abroad these institutions play the leading roles. From the sickness fund one gets everything there: not only the necessary medical aid, but the cure, too, is properly carried out. People are cured completely at the expense of the sickness funds; they send them to the spas, to recover, to regain their strength. Abroad the sickness funds are [?] the citizen's right hand. There people do not go to the establishment because they have no other choice, because they cannot afford to go to a private doctor; on the contrary, there people know that radical healing comes through the public sickness institutions, maintained by the state, by the government, by the citizens.
With us, too, the tactics of the sickness funds must be changed, where every official is an autocrat and does not want to take the members into account at all. Such an order must be created there that everything is improved for the benefit of the population, for the benefit of this useful institution.
The activity of the sickness funds and the dealings with them must be trustworthy and open to everyone; above all, both the autocratic order and the system of favouritism (protekcja), which plays one of the most important roles in our life, must be eradicated there root and branch.
The same goes for the doctor: let him not treat the patient as though he were treating a charity case, which is precisely why the thing is done hastily, just to discharge a duty.
If we want to turn the sickness funds into first-class institutions called to heal suffering humanity, we must get to know it more closely; we must look into what goes on in the workshop of this people's institution.
Lawlessness in this field, as it exists to this day, must not be permitted: the doctor must not do as he pleases, he must not play the role of one doing someone a favour; the same applies to the officials — they too must not be autocrats and treat the members as they like, as they feel like it.
In the first place, therefore, it is important that the sickness funds bear a truly public character; that we hear what it does for the benefit of its members and what it does not do; they must render an account to the public, so that both the good and the bad side become clear to everyone. Such an institution must not remain clamped shut [?] and concealed from the broad public. Everyone must have access to it, so that he can assess the activity of, and the dealings with, this institution so necessary in the country.
R. Les [?].
Oy... Oy... Oy...

[Feuilleton — the crisis; egg merchants.] (A monologue of an egg merchant).
Oy, oy, who does not sigh today, who does not groan today: oy, oy, bad times, bitter times, crisis.
To today's oy-oy another "oy, oy" has been added, which the egg merchant sighs: oy, oy, oy, a glut of cheap eggs, [people] breakfast [?] on eggs — a bumper egg crop, and when — in "winter"...
The egg merchant sighs and groans: oy.., oy.., oy... oy... Who could have expected such a disaster. Whom could it have occurred to that in March, when by the course of nature there should be deep snows and frost, it would actually be 15 degrees warm outdoors, and the hens would pour out eggs the way merchants pour out protested bills of exchange.
For, as [?] the women gossip, the cheapness has to do with the spring-like winter. The logic is simple: it is warm, so the hens lay eggs; there are eggs, and when there are eggs, people eat eggs; and if today's "magnates" can "afford" to eat eggs, it is a disaster for the egg merchants...
The hens, however, know nothing of sentiments; they do their own thing: they lay eggs, and the egg merchants lay — their gall...
That is how the hens have done it, the Turkish way [?] — this bumper egg crop costs the merchants thousands of dollars.
Oy, oy, every merchant sighs today: oy, oy, but more than all of them the egg merchant groans: — oy... oy... oy...
Exhibit

[Feuilleton — merchants, taxes and the crisis.] (Dedicated to the latest merchants' conventions).
Having learned that a convention of merchants and small traders is coming up these days in Sosnowiec, I decided to make at least a little earning out of it. I am myself a former merchant; I once traded myself and travelled to conventions myself as a delegate; and, as is the way of things, "the end of a thief is the gallows", and the end of a merchant is sometimes even worse than dying... In fewer words: I am out of the game — no business, livelihood — nothing [?] to speak of; but distraints [?], auctions, prolonged protests are not lacking. What, then, does one do in such a time of trouble? Wife and children do ask to eat, often something more besides, and no excuses count with them. So I decided to take the opportunity and arrange ex promptu an exhibition, because time is short and such a moment must not be slept through.
I have no goods on the shelves, I own no factories or workshops either, but from the good old days I have been left such rarities as truly have no material value for anyone; morally, however, they are the best and most interesting material for museums, archives and exhibitions — not to be refused: half a gulden [= half a złoty] a ticket, which everyone can still pay [?] even nowadays, just to see my exhibits [?].
I would be a most unlucky entrepreneur if I allowed myself to list for you here, on the spot, all the rare exhibits of my exhibition; it would greatly harm my new business, by which I hope "to make my fortune" and rebuild myself anew. By way of illustration, however, I do want to give you an idea of the character of my enterprise and its noteworthy exhibits.
Through a wide double door in the new-Polish style, pasted over with notarial [?] notices and auction announcements — of the treasury, of the municipality and of the bailiffs (here the notaries sometimes let their notices be stuck on the doors too) — you enter a special room with empty, dust-covered shelves. The ceiling, as well as the walls, lengthwise and widthwise, are papered [?] with old trading licences, excise concessions and various tax receipts. You must not forget that a practical merchant keeps [?] such papers for nearly ten years, no matter whether he still intends to trade that long or is about to liquidate the business. Willy-nilly you must stop and contemplate the figures of the various sums paid. No special statistical tables, as at other exhibitions, are needed here: without knowing the exact total, you wish you owned nowadays that little bit of property [?] which the state treasury has "tapped" out of the shelf-room (once a business). Our tax inspector always used to reproach me that my missus wears a fur coat. Work out how many fur coats could be made for the money squeezed out of me over the last few years as taxes, and you will conclude that the missuses, mine and yours, are not yet such robbers: you get rid of them with a fine fur once in 10 years, which you are even given a long time to pay off, while the state treasury takes from you 10 furs in one year — and in cash, no less.
Lowering your eyes from the ceiling and the walls, you cast a glance at the bureau (writing desk), which stands at the side still fenced round with wire netting; though it has not seen the shape of a coin for a long, long time, it asks, on its oath, what money is current today: marks, złotys or dollars. You open the drawer — a file of protested bills of exchange from "dead children" [i.e. bad debts], but very lively debtors. Each bill no less than a metre long. Some single bills lie in a specially large file, because they are noteworthy rarities: they bear up to 50, 60–70 and more endorsements, all of which were protested in turn.
The collection costs laid out in claiming the sums amount to 5 times as much as the value of the bills, and each bill separately, when you unroll it, looks like a "perzhagrney" [?] roll of wallpaper. Not far from the bureau the copy-book sleeps, open; I left it open at the time, because on reading the last copy I fainted and took to my bed with a serious illness for three whole months.
Here you have the contents of the last couple of business letters — from me to a customer, and the customer's answer to me.
My letter:
"My friend! I would never have believed that you would commit such a folly and let bills go to protest in your very own powiat [district]. You could rather have grabbed goods in Warsaw, Łódź and the like, and stayed a decent man at home, as most people are wont to do. I advise you, in good counsel, to settle with me, because in the [?] house one does not relieve oneself ('asher yatsar'); such things are done away from home."
The customer's answer:
"My friend! Your letter received. I am greatly surprised at your ingratitude. I truly regret that I did not grab 10 times as much from you. To your parable I can reply that when diarrhoea strikes, one relieves oneself wherever it strikes."
Having read this letter you pass on to the earlier ones — one and all extraordinarily interesting. I reckon, God willing, if the exhibition succeeds and I earn a little money — after paying off [?] for bread, meat and other debts, and also after clothing my family a little — to have the whole of my correspondence of the last few years printed from my copy-book without fail. I think that, God willing, it will sell no worse than Remarque's "All Quiet on the Western Front".
You want to know what else there will be to see at my exhibition? Unfortunately I may not reveal it to you here. For the time being it is a secret. Be so kind as to buy a ticket for 50 groszy. Your gain will be worth much more. One thing I can add, though: I have engaged a whole series of persons — former presidents, board members, judges and secretaries of merchants' and small traders' associations, as well as members of tax-assessment commissions — who will demonstrate in pictures and revive [?] various fine deeds of your providers and [?] philanthropists. It will be of great use to you in future, especially at the convention itself, because there too they will put on the poor little face and set their little groaning machine going. Recognise them in time — right at my exhibition!
No small trader, no delegate should miss the opportunity!
All as one, come and look [?]! Price 50 groszy — price 50 groszy.
———
What do you think? Will I "make my fortune"?
—Lin.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Terumah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Y. P.
Parashat Terumah.
—o—
A.
"Speak unto the children of Israel" (25:2).
"Speak unto the children of Israel" — meaning: speak to the Jews with good, soft and heartfelt words (as in "speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem"), because when it is a matter of taking money from the people, one must use tender words...
Baal ha-Turim.
—o—
B.
"That they take for me an offering" (ibid.).
By the plain sense of the verse it ought to say "ve-yitnu" (let them give), not "ve-yikchu" (which means: take) —
When a Jew, a rich man, possesses a large fortune and is a miser, and cannot bring himself to give a poor man alms, that means the fortune is not his at all, since he does not rule over the estate ("mayontek", Polish majątek), but the estate rules over him.. The generous donor, by contrast, shows by giving alms that he disposes of his fortune; he documents with his donation that he rules over his wealth, and therefore it is truly his.. That is why, regarding the donations for the Tabernacle, it says "ve-yikchu" (take): by giving one shows that the money is in one's possession; only then is it fitting to say "ve-yikchu" — then it means that he takes the money into his possession, at his disposal.
The Gaon of Vilna.
○ The old Kotzker [Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotzk], as a young man, once visited a rich man who owned fields, estates, etc. But he was one who "would let himself be killed for less than a penny's worth", begrudging even himself the spending of a grosz. The Kotzker looks around at the great wealth and asks: With respect, uncle, where do you keep your this-world (olam ha-ze)?
— What do you mean? — answers the miserly rich man — you see so many estates, mills, fields — isn't that this-world?
— Eh, — says the Kotzker — all these houses and fields do indeed amount to a great sum[?] of money, but their value is only for the world to come. Mere wealth, to leave as an inheritance. You get no enjoyment from it, you don't even indulge your own body; so it is in fact your world to come — so where is your this-world?...
—o—
C.
"Of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart" (ibid.).
Solomon too, when he set out to build his Temple, took contributions from all the Jews: "And king Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel" (1 Kings 5). Yet Solomon was rich enough to build a Temple by himself — why did he collect pennies from the Jews? — Because a building that a whole people erects, each with his penny, is more durable than the building of a single individual.
Ahavat Yonatan [R. Jonathan Eybeschütz].
—o—
D.
"And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (25:8).
When "that I may dwell among them" comes true — when God will rest in you, in your hearts, when you meet Him not only in the study house, in the synagogue — then the sanctuary will endure.
Nachal Kedumim [the Chida].
———
— Where does God dwell?
— Wherever one lets Him in, in every heart that is ready to receive Him..
R. M. of Kotzk.
—o—
E.
"Within and without shalt thou overlay it" (25:11).
Surely gold on the outside would have sufficed — why gild it inside as well?
The Ark, where the Tablets lay, is a symbol of a Torah scholar, within whom the Torah also resides. The verse comes to teach that a Torah scholar must be gilded, beautiful, not only outside but inside too .. his inside like his outside. As he is in his heart, so must he conduct himself outwardly. Not play two roles. See tractate Yoma 72b.
○ A certain heretic conducted himself outwardly as strictly religious, went about dressed like a rabbi and sat day and night over Torah and prayer. The rabbis, however, denounced him as a freethinker whose inside was not like his outside, whose piety was merely a pretence. In the end, when his children and many of his disciples converted, the Dubno Maggid told the following parable about him:
— There once was a married couple who had a little shop. And as is the way among Jews, day and night they quarrelled, cursed and threw household objects at each other. Because of the frequent rows ("avanturas") customers stopped coming to the shop. Livelihood is lacking, so they think and ponder until they hit upon this idea: since quarrel they must, and since the takings suffer because of it, the plan is this: they may quarrel as much as they like, only they will change the language. When one wants to say "cholera into your father's father", one will say: "a blessing on your little head", etc. They will understand the hint.. The customers will delight in such an idyll, and meanwhile they will give each other a piece of their minds... And indeed it helped, and the shop was again full of customers, who only ever heard blessings...
Suddenly, during one such "blessing-fight", when he says to her: "may you live a hundred years for me" (meaning: may a plague[?] take you) and she replies: "a radiant paradise upon you" (meaning: may the devil take you) — as they bless[?] each other this way — suddenly: benches. Stools start flying from him to her head and back.. The public is astonished: after so many blessings, they throw benches at each other?...
The moral: so pious, wrapped in a tallit the whole day, and here his children and disciples convert — after so many blessings, benches all of a sudden? It must be that the blessings were in truth curses, and only to draw in "customers" was a pious pretence put on...
—o—
F.
"And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, and make thereto a border" (25:24).
A person's table, from which he eats, is likened to the altar (see Chagigah 27), and just as nothing stolen may be offered on the altar, so a person's table, his food and drink, must also be of "pure gold" — clean, honest money. How? "And make thereto a border" — if he sets himself a fence, does not squander too much, does not live too lavishly, he will remain an honest man.
Matok mi-Devash.
—o—
Shabbat Zachor
"Remember what Amalek did unto thee."
"Yalkut Reuveni" compares Amalek in a parable to a fly. Amalek, the giant — a fly, of all things?
The meaning is this: a fly likes to settle only on a wound, on a place where there is pus; so Amalek, the symbol of the enemy of the Jews, comes only when there is a sore on our national organism, an open wound. If we are spiritually sound, without festering wounds, the enemy of the Jews has no power over us.
Kli Yakar.

A Weekday at the Old Market

A. Lemekh.
(A drama in three acts).
Characters: Grunem Shtaynzakher, Berl Kripnik, a merchant from Łódź, a notary (rejent), a broker, a komornik [bailiff], a researcher, and many others.
Place: the Old Market in Będzin.
Time: Act 1 — 1920, Act 2 — 1930, Act 3 — 1940.
Act One.
(1920, in the Old Market. A tumult, a throng[?] of customers, hard to push one's way through, crowds of gentiles in front of every shop, Grunem Shtaynzakher's shop is overfull, he himself stands all sweaty at the cash-desk, hoarse from shouting, [?] wiping his hands, which ache from measuring).
Łódź merchant (takes up a position at the threshold, unable to get through to the crush[?], shouts across): You will excuse me, I beg your pardon, Reb Grunem, perhaps one could have a word with you about business. I mean, perhaps you will buy something. Fine goods. Dirt cheap, we give two-year credit and six months open.
Grunem Shtaynzakher (agitated): Why are you pestering me [lit. “banging a teakettle”]! To all the black years... spare me your credits! I've long been writing three-year promissory notes. I have no business here! Don't you see how the customers are standing in rows[?]! —
Łódź merchant (humbly): Excuse me, gracious sir, I will give you a year's[?] credit. — I'll certainly come to you at twelve o'clock at night, forgive me (exits).
Grunem Shtaynzakher (with great effort squeezes out to cool off, sees the notary, greets him): Good morning, Panie Rejencie, where are you off to? Surely to protest[?] somebody's promissory note?! —
Notary (laughs): Ha, ha, ha! I've almost forgotten how one writes out a protest, I haven't done such things for a long time. Today there are other businesses. Little Jews are buying little houses.
Broker (wanders about with his walking stick): Not good, Reb Grunem, there's nobody who wants to take any money [on loan].
Grunem: I too would place some twenty thousand złoty. There's nowhere to put it, perhaps you have someone. The interest may be meagre, as long as I get rid of it.
Broker (scratches himself): And an honest man?!
Grunem: Fool son of a [?]! Whom then does one not lend to nowadays?! I have only fools[?] who would want to take it, you fool! (goes back into the shop) Like dogs they are here, the customers! They won't let you grab a bite!
(Curtain falls).
Act Two.
(1930, in the Old Market. Little clusters of shopkeepers standing and yawning, in the middle of the market boys are sliding on the ice, Grunem Shtaynzakher sits by his shop on a bench, dozing).
Berl Kripnik (wakes Grunem): What, are you going to sleep it all off like this, Reb Grunem?
Grunem (starts up in fright): What? What? Maybe a customer is coming? Where is he? Where?
Berl (laughs): Ha, ha, ha! A customer he wants! Since New Year there's been the third customer already in the Old Market, is that too little for you? — (notices the komornik) The komornik is coming! To you, Reb Grunem!
Komornik (at Grunem's in the shop): What is there to write up, Panie Shtaynzakher? Everything's already been written up [i.e. distrained], and here again a clause, everything, the cash-desk, even the window-panes have already been written up. Well, Panie Shtaynzakher?
Grunem (plucking his beard): You've already sucked everything dry enough. Take what you can!
Komornik: And what else do you have? Find something, let it be an old object, as long as there's something to write up — after all, the other party is claiming ten thousand zł.
Grunem: (rummaging and searching) Here, I've found something; this is the firm's rubber stamp! Worth good money! Once I got hundreds of thousands with it. (The komornik writes it up and exits).
(Curtain falls).
Act Three.
(1940, in the Old Market, a garden with a monument [pomnik] to the President who transformed the market into a blooming garden. Next to it, the grave of the well-known merchant; an eternal light burns on it and a very old shammes keeps a guard of honour. All around, all the shops[?] [—]. Next to each shop a gravestone with a protested promissory note pasted on it. A cemetery researcher wanders about, looking for a living business and finding none).
Researcher (reads the text on a gravestone): Here lies the famous magnate Reb Grunem Shtaynzakher, who left a will that shrouds be made for him of protested promissory notes, and that if a Łódź merchant needs to be paid[?], let him come to my grave... (goes over to a second gravestone and reads on) Here lies the magnate Reb Berl Kripnik, who left a will that all paid-up promissory notes be put with him in the grave, to show the Heavenly Court; there were such in the last ten years — all of... two. (Crawls thus from one gravestone to the next, taking notes; a hare[?] jumps out; goes into the garden, notices the old shammes) Aha! Praised be God that I've met a living person! What are you doing here? Perhaps you are a ghost.
Shammes (as if waking from sleep): Thanks to His dear name too, that I see a living person — here is the grave of the well-known merchant. [?] When everything collapsed, the Treasury [skarb] had a grave of the well-known merchant erected and hung an eternal light here, and I guard it.
Researcher: What lies in this grave?
Shammes: Here lie tax declarations [zeznania], payment orders [nakaz płatniczy][?] and the like..
Researcher: What was this place once called?
Shammes: Here was the Będzin Old Market.
Researcher: Who were the buried?
Shammes: The buried were tax collectors (executors), the Magistrate [town council], Łódź merchants and the like, and the like..
Researcher: What is your job?
Shammes: My job is to say Kaddish three times a day for the merchants, may their souls rest in Eden; and right now I have to say it. (Says)
Yitgadal ve-yitkadash shmei rabba —
For those who were magnates
And died paupers,
Rid of the Treasury only
When they became dead —
May they find rest
From all the angels of destruction,
Komorniks, tax executors —
May wrath fall upon them,
AZ"H, AZ"Ch, O"Ch
And say Amen.
(Curtain falls slowly).
Our Leaders Think About Everything — Except a Livelihood.

It is told of an ancient, primitive high state conference of the "Elders of Israel" under the chairmanship of King David; at the conference the question of Jewish lack of livelihood was dealt with. The Jews were then purely an agrarian people, there was not enough livelihood for everyone, and the international[?] trade sector began to develop only later, in Solomon's time.
— The Jews have no livelihood — the elders complained.
— Seek a livelihood from one another, the king answered.
— A handful cannot sate a lion, and a pit cannot be filled from its own dug-out earth.
— Then go out in companies beyond the borders of the land.
Today that would be called emigration.
It seems that our present-day providers ought to study and really think hard about that beautiful, naive legend.
One of our greatest misfortunes in our present catastrophic situation is that we have no conferences and gatherings about livelihood. We have conferences and gatherings about organising the economic associations, about who gets shlishi, who gets shishi, who gets maftir; we adopt sharp resolutions against the government's policy of exhaustion[?], about the horrible pressure of the tax screw, but livelihood never gets a turn.
In order to solve the hard problem of livelihood even partially, one must simply study this matter, just as the Elders of Israel studied it with King David.
A spontaneous mass solution of the question is possible, of course — as, for example, if four million Jews found a livelihood through emigration to America, or if the Polish government suddenly gave us real equal rights and opened to us the gates of all offices, of all the big industries, of parcelled-out land holdings...
That is the meaning[?] of "Go out and spread forth" — help through outside areas.
But we do not at all make use of "Earn your living from one another"...
What does an individual do when he has no livelihood? He looks for a place where one can still open a little shop or a workshop — and he is saved.
In Russia there was once a movement to resettle Jewish artisans in towns deep in Russia, where they were needed. But there could surely also be a similar movement to move people from one town to another, from one street to another, from one branch of livelihood to another.
Who among us thinks about such things.
"ORT" has found a means of supplying machines on instalments. In this way Jewish livelihoods would be strengthened and multiplied. Special mention is made of the shoemaking trade, which is now going under completely among us and could revive in this way. But ORT's action is being stifled in its offices; the public does not take it up; people do not even talk about it.
Hundreds of Jewish factories employ no Jewish workers, or employ few. Who talks about it? Only occasionally, when this Jewish boycott of Jewish workers becomes too crying to heaven.
But not even that. In the most minimal statistics that catch the eye one comes up against the fact — and one can understand it even without scholarly research — that our branches of livelihood are not distributed properly: one branch is swarming as if with flies, and the other is thinly staffed.
Where is the organisation that deals with this, that seeks to regulate among us the distribution of employment opportunities?
Who knows how many thousands of Jewish livelihoods would have been saved if our kehilla providers seriously studied our life, instead of only busying themselves with the "pulverisation" of protests and resolutions, which are an excellent means of squeezing tears from the eyes but not of producing a bite of bread...
We follow the line of least resistance and pour out all their wrath onto paper, which bears everything; and since paper is light and is carried across the whole country, our providers buy themselves a name with their "great" deeds.
But to sit down[?] and think about the problem, as the "Elders of Israel" once did — for that they take no time; apparently they have more important things to do...
P. K.
The Verdict. (A Letter from Kraków).

A particularly important development in Jewish academic life in Kraków is the verdict on the recent events, issued by the highest university authority, the Senate. The uncultured and inhuman conduct of the Polish academics, about which I have already written, was branded by the commission of inquiry as dishonourable and not in accord with Catholic ethics.
That is the only bright point in the verdict. But how else can one describe such "heroic" deeds as beating — while having an overwhelming majority — Jewish academics and — what must be specially noted — women academics, who surely cannot resist the brutality?
The events were sharply condemned, but who the instigators were and who caused several Jewish students to be badly wounded has not been established. The Senate has no means of compulsion, no police, that could punish the guilty by force; it only appealed to the moral conscience of those who took part in the events. But those who had the courage to beat and to agitate against the Jews in the name of religion did not, however, have the courage to come forward. Apparently they are not yet convinced of the truth of the "ideals" for which they fight.
The verdict then turned against the Jewish Zionist corporation "Kadimah" and forbade it to wear special caps, etc. Otherwise the corporation will be dissolved. One can be an opponent of an academic corporation as such; one could accept a Senate resolution to dissolve all Jewish and Polish corporations for introducing feudal methods of the Middle Ages into academic life; but to come out against "Kadimah" not because it is a corporation, but only because it is a Jewish organisation — that is only another link in the chain of the constant humiliation of Jewish honour. Even the opponents of the corporations must agree with this.
These are the basic grounds of the verdict. Despite that, one Jewish and one Polish academic lost a "trimester", and several Polish students received "naganas" [official reprimands].
Al-Ger.
What the Big Ones Think, the Little Ones Hum... (From the Polish Press)

[Polish press — shechita; antisemitism.] The organ of the Endeks [National Democrats], “Kurier Zachodni”, has come out with a fresh sensation: the Christians must support the Jewish communities with their money (!). You will surely want to know how that is possible — well then, hear a tale: the “Eastern” news agency “A. W.” [?] [Agencja Wschodnia ?] has circulated a report that in Wilno a great sensation was caused by the fact that at the local slaughterhouse the slaughtering of cattle is done only according to Jewish law, and the meat is consumed not only by the Jews but by the Christians as well.
Having repeated the well-known refrain that Jewish shechita is harmful to the animals (according to the well-known version of the Endek city councillor Dr. Zawadzki [?] in Warsaw), the author makes a brand-new discovery, namely:
“We forget — writes the ‘K. Z.’ — about something else. For his work a shochet charges a high fee, amounting to 10 to 20 zł. per head. That is much more than the fee of an ordinary doctor amounts to.
A large part of the income from slaughtering goes into the coffers of the Jewish communities. And since not only in Wilno but in almost all of Poland, with the exception of Warsaw and Greater Poland, the slaughtering of cattle is done by Jewish shochtim, it follows as a rule that almost the entire urban population pays taxes for the benefit of the Jewish community.
It must further be noted — the paper goes on — that the Jews have their own self-government and that, in accordance with the laws in force, they have the right to assess taxes for the needs of the Jewish communities. The taxes collected go to maintain their clergy, the beadles in the synagogues and the cemeteries, Jewish religious schools, aid for the poor, subsidies for their institutions, etc., and for all this, besides the Jews, Christians pay too, because the fee from Jewish shechita constitutes a very large item in the income of the Jewish communities.
“On the other hand, despite the Concordat with the Apostolic See, the income of the Catholic parishes is still not regulated. The priests may not collect by compulsion any payments to repair [?] the broken roof of the church [kościół] or for a fence for the cemetery [cmentarz]. Even for the most necessary things for the parish it is likewise forbidden to tax the Christians.”
Shedding a few more sparing crocodile tears, the author ends the article wondering why the Christian population does not react to this:
“Here we have another chapter of the oppression of Jews in Poland! The discovery of the Wilno people does not surprise us; what does surprise us is the apathy of Christian society in the whole matter.”
After the Jewish councillors in the capital city of Warsaw had to wage a bitter fight against the banning of shechita, the painful question now climbs up to us in the provinces. Well [?], yes: “What the big ones think — the little ones hum”...
S. Strojch [Sz. Strauch ?].
A Competition for a Moreh Hora’ah in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — kehilla; rabbinate.] On Sunday the kehilla board in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] held a meeting at which, among other things, the question of engaging a menaker [porger of meat] was also discussed. On this matter 2 proposals were submitted: 1) from the “Agudah” [Agudat Israel], supported by the Rav, may he live long and well, to take on a menaker; and 2) from the president, Mr. Liberman, to announce a competition for a moreh hora’ah [rabbinic decisor], who would also fulfil the office of menaker. Also present at the meeting was the Rav, who argued for the first proposal on the grounds that “a moreh hora’ah may not at the same time also be a menaker.” Because of this a secret vote took place, and by 5 to 1 Mr. Liberman’s proposal was adopted: that both duties, as moreh tzedek and as menaker, should be fulfilled by one kehilla official.
Dąbrowa Unemployed Demand Support

[Dąbrowa — unemployment; kehilla.] A delegation of a larger number of Jewish unemployed came to the Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] community and submitted a written request that the Jewish kehilla allocate a sum of 5000 zł. for the benefit of the Jewish unemployed.
Szczekociny. A Will in the Jewish Language Is Valid

[Szczekociny — law; Yiddish.] In the month of December 1929 a local woman, Mrs. Bajla Rabinowicz, applied to the district court in Kielce for recognition of the will of her late husband. In doing so Mrs. Rabinowicz presented the will written in the Jewish language [Yiddish] and attached translations made by the Jewish community and by a sworn interpreter [?].
The Kielce court rejected the application — that is, did not recognise the will — on the grounds that “the will is written in an unknown language.”
Mrs. Rabinowicz lodged an appeal with the Lublin court of appeal, where advocate B. Warman appeared on her behalf.
Advocate Warman pointed out that the code does not say that a will must be written specifically in the state language or in any particular language at all. The testator may therefore write his will in whatever language he wishes. Particularly strange is the reasoning of the first instance that Yiddish is an unknown language. Yiddish is the language of several million Polish citizens; there is a rich literature in Yiddish; famous works created in the Jewish language have been translated into European literature; the state administration has enough officials who understand and know the language; and therefore the decision of the Kielce court is unfounded. Advocate Warman therefore demanded that the court of appeal confirm the will.
The case was heard two weeks ago. The court decided to postpone the delivery of its decision on this question of principle for a period of two weeks, so that the court might acquaint itself more closely with the question.
Yesterday the decision was finally delivered.
The court of appeal in Lublin recognised that the will is written in “a known language” and that it is therefore valid.
We report the decision of the Lublin court of appeal, which agreed with the argument of the defending counsel, because it has an important significance in principle.

Będzin — Water-charge statute adopted in third reading / Widows and orphans lose 1000 zł. — a link[?] of the kehilla muddle[?] before the court / The "comedy" play of the kehilla board / Small traders' association fights the "grabbers" / Traditional ball at the artisans' / Young man from Łódź dies / From the "Merchants' Association" / "The effect of the surroundings on the patient"

At Wednesday's town council meeting the statute of the waterworks was adopted in third reading, by a majority of 8 votes, according to the Magistrate's [municipality's] draft, i.e. a metre [cubic metre] of water will cost 50 gr.
Councillors Lewin, Mrs. Ratner, Dr. Rechtman[?] and G. Rechnitz demanded in their speeches that a metre of water should cost only 40 gr. Against this spoke the members of the town board, in the course of which it came to a personal insult between alderman (ławnik) Goldsztajn and Councillor Rechinitz [sic; presumably Rechnitz]. All the objections[?] of Lewin, Ratner and Feiner that the price and the quota be reduced were rejected.
On the other hand the President [mayor] declared that far-reaching reductions will be made for those who cannot afford it.
It is interesting to note that at such an important meeting almost half of the Jewish councillors were absent...
—o—
Widows and orphans lose 1000 zł.
A link[?] of the kehilla muddle[?] before the court.
In the winter of last year, 1928, the matzah committee bought 600 sacks of Passover flour from Mordechai Gartler. As a guarantee that the purchased flour would be delivered, Mr. Gartler deposited 1000 zł. with Mr. Dąb. After a certain time the price of flour had meanwhile risen, and Mr. G. did not carry out the purchase agreement with the matzah committee. The committee therefore summoned Mr. Gartler to a din Torah before the local rabbinate, which issued a ruling that the 1000 zł. held by Mr. Dąb should belong to the "Dobroczynność" [the charity society].
Mr. G., on hearing the ruling unfavourable to him, turned the morning after the ruling to a lawyer, who notified Mr. Dąb that he should not hand over the thousand zł.
Then the matter went to court. The "Dobroczynność" came forward with a claim concerning the thousand zł. that the rabbinate had awarded it.
The trial took place last Friday for the third time at the local Court of the Peace. As witnesses for the "Dobroczynność" there appeared Councillor Lewin and Mendel Tenenbaum, who took an oath that Mr. Gartler had not wanted to deliver the flour bought from him.
On behalf of the rabbinate testimony was given by Rabbi R' Chanoch Dawid, who supported the claim in favour of the "Dobroczynność".
As a witness on Gartler's side there was R' Lipa Kaminer, who took an oath that Gartler had wanted to deliver the flour, but the committee had not wanted to take the flour.
On the basis of Kaminer's oath the court dismissed the claim of the "Dobroczynność".
—o—
The "comedy" play of the kehilla board.
The kehilla board drew up this year's budget at a sum of 144 thousand zł. The budget was then sent to the kehilla council, which reduced the budget to 136 thousand zł. At the same level the council drew up the tax assessment (etat-rozkład).
On Tuesday a meeting of the board took place, which approved the assessment and the budget, so as to lay it out for the taxpayers.
But at the meeting the dozorcy [board members][?] Liter and Bauszykowski[?] submitted a protest against the budget. Our readers should not, however, have any doubts and think that the gentlemen submitted the protest "out of love for Mordecai", so that the town should not be burdened with such a budget — no, they protested "out of hatred for Haman": because the council reduced the amounts of the subsidies for the "Gemilut Chesed" fund and for the mikveh...
—o—
Small traders' association fights the "grabbers".
The question of fighting the "customer-grabbers", which we have touched on many times in the columns of our paper, has found an echo with the board of the Small Traders' Association, which on account of this question called a large meeting, at which the matter was considered from all sides and the following resolutions were adopted: 1) it is forbidden to accost customers by means of "grabbers"; 2) all customer-grabbers and callers ("rufers") must be abolished immediately; and 3) for not conforming to the resolutions the merchant concerned will bear the responsibility.
The police too take this plague very seriously, and it is to be expected that the undesirable[?] element [printed "plement"] will no longer have any access among the merchants.
—o—
Traditional ball at the artisans'.
The Artisans' Association is holding this coming Saturday (Shushan Purim) a traditional Purim ball. The organisers are making efforts that the ball be well organised; to this end competitions and many other surprises are being prepared, and even the masks will be "the most beautiful"...
—o—
Young man from Łódź dies.
This week the 18-year-old Fajwel Zalewski from Łódź died in the local hospital. Thanks to Mr. M. Ferens[?] the deceased was promptly taken out of the hospital and was in due time brought to a Jewish burial.

Notice is hereby given[?] to the merchants that those who wish to establish trade relations with Romania must register at the association by the 11th of this month.
— Tomorrow at half past 7 in the evening, at the premises of the "Merchants' Association", the lawyer of the Central Merchants' Association in Warsaw, Mr. Józef Rozenberg, will lecture on current tax problems.
Admission free.

"The effect of the surroundings on the patient".
On this topic Dr. Weinzieher will lecture on Sunday at 6 o'clock at the premises of School 8[?], for the members and sympathisers of "Tse'irei Mishmerei ha-Cholim" [Young Guardians of the Sick].
Sosnowiec

Lapsed taxes are "annulled", but the bailiffs keep doing their work...
Some time ago the Ministry of Finance issued a circular (okólnik) that lapsed tax debts must be annulled when it has been established that the petitioner is poor. But how the circular is carried out in reality is shown by the following fact: from the baker Schwarzberg, who owed 150 zł. in tax, the bailiff took 4 small sacks of flour. The Artisans' Association intervened over this injustice with the naczelnik [district head], and the latter declared that the baker should submit a petition about it, which would certainly be taken into consideration, and the baker would get the flour back.
The naczelnik's promise remained "hanging in the air", and instead of getting back the four sacks of flour, a second bailiff came again and took from the same baker the only sack of flour that was in the bakery"...
Kehilla council approves the budget.
The local kehilla council has finally, after much "self-sacrifice" (mesirat nefesh), approved the new kehilla budget. A series of sessions was held over the budget, some of them stormy, with police interventions. The main "fight" was directed against the pension for the moreh-tzedek Halberstam in Old Sosnowiec.
But Tuesday's session was a lucky one: calm and quiet were the parnassim, who adopted the budget en bloc.
The total budget amounts to 278.000 zł. Compared with last year's budget, this year's has been raised by 14.000 zł. The supplement contains the first subsidy for the new building of the "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home) and an increased subsidy for the "Gemilut Hesed" (free-loan) fund.
Addressed to the price commission.
We receive constant complaints from our Sosnowiec readers about the price commission at the Sosnowiec magistrate. The commission — the complaints say — reduces the price of bread from time to time, but the price of wheat flour is not touched, so that the prices of rolls (zemmel) and challahs are the same as when a kilo of wheat flour cost 85[?] gr.
"Tidings" from the "Agudah" bank-let.
For some weeks now "the birds on the roofs have been singing" that unseemly things have happened at the local Agudah bank. The news reached Warsaw too, the head office of the "Agudah" banks, and from there Mr. Ekerman was delegated here; together with Mr. Adam Branicki he audited the books, in which various embezzlements (malversations) and fictitious money entries were found.
At a session of the board and council the delegate reacted to the abuses and declared that if they did not cover the damage the bank had done, the matter would be handed over to the Ministry of Finance, which supervises the bank.
After a stormy discussion the members of the council and board agreed to settle the damage, which amounts to about 30 thousand zł. The members will also have to lend a large sum.
Because of this "proprietorship" an extraordinary general meeting was called, at which it was resolved that the existing Agudah bank-let be "liquidated".
—o—
Mishloach manot from "Pardes".
The "Pardes" company, Jaffa, has sent its representative Zegal[?] special oranges for Purim, which customers admire for their juiciness and sweetness.
Meeting of small traders

Next Sunday morning the annual general meeting of the local Small Traders' Association will take place at the "Hotel Polski". Very important current matters of interest to small traders will be considered.
—o—
A "war" on the rats.
Next week, on 10, 11 and 12 March, the local magistrate will wage a "war" on the rats. For this purpose the magistrate has provided itself with an extermination agent, which can be obtained at the local pharmacies.
Every house owner is obliged to buy the extermination agent, which must be laid out in the lavatories, rubbish bins etc. on the above-mentioned days.
—o—
Relief fund at the artisans.
The board of the Artisans' Association has decided to create a relief fund, to be used in urgent cases of need among the members. The fund will be created among the members through self-taxation.
—o—
Presidium of the "Merchants' Association".
On Sunday a session of the new board of the "Merchants' Association" (Piłsudski [Street] 12) took place. At the session a presidium was elected: Y. S.[?] Weigryb[?] (chairman), Sh. Warman (vice-chairman), A. Steinfeld (treasurer) and B. Zelinger (house-master/steward).
Board member Mr. Avraham Neufeld sent in a notice that, since he is not a permanent resident of Sosnowiec, he resigns as a member of the board.
—o—
Meeting of the KKL committee.
On Sunday a well-attended meeting of the KKL (Jewish National Fund) took place at the "Maccabi" premises. Reports were heard, from which it can be seen that Sosnowiec holds first place among the provincial towns.
—o—
Merchants are nervous...
In Wojkowice a quarrel broke out in the street between the shopkeepers Kozitowski and Bacia. The quarrel made Kozitowski so nervous that, snatching out a revolver, he fired 2 shots at Bacia; one bullet hit fatally, and before a doctor came, Bacia was already dead.
—o—
A new bank.
These days a "Kredytowa Kasa" (credit fund) has been opened here. The well-known financier and former[?] (abbr. "g.") manufacturer Mr. Adam Branicki has been engaged as director.
The most respected merchants have joined the board and council.
—o—
The first Purim masked ball.
Next Saturday night (Shushan Purim) the women's organisation "WIZO" is arranging in our town the first Purim masked ball, at the municipal theatre.
The ball committee is making an effort for the first ball to be very rich, original, Jewish-national and similar in character to the old merry Jewish Purim plays and entertainments.
For this purpose the best forces of Zagłębie have been specially drawn into the work.
The greatest sensation of the Purim ball will be the election of the queen, "Esther the Queen", as well as a vice-queen; besides this there will be various other attractions.

Committee for Working Eretz Israel.
At the "Hashomer Hatzair" premises a fairly large meeting of the Committee for Working Eretz Israel took place. Taking part in the meeting were "Hitachdut", P.Z. (Z.S.), "Hashomer Hatzair", "Gordonia", "Freiheit" and "Hechalutz".

It was resolved to carry out a "P.S."[?] campaign. For this purpose a delegate of the Central Committee is coming to Sosnowiec, who will help with the campaign.

A Big Fire on Kowalska Street in Sosnowiec / From the Sosnowiec City Council / Lost Items in the Tram / Campaign for Working Eretz Israel / 6 Months in Prison for Forging His Wife's Signature / „The Jazz Singer“ with Ida Kamińska in Zagłębie

[Sosnowiec — fire.]
On Wednesday night a fire broke out in Żmigrod's[?] house on Kowalska Street in Sosnowiec. The fire, which started in the attic from a small candle, thanks to the strong wind instantly engulfed the whole roof. Because of the narrow courtyard the firemen had difficulties with the rescue. Nevertheless they managed to put out the fire at around 2 at night. Of the tenants, Messrs. Józef Englender[?] and Kozłowski[?] suffered heavily. The roof went up in smoke. The damage is great.
—o—

On Tuesday a session of the Sosnowiec City Council took place. The important point of the agenda was to approve[?] the proposal of the city administration that the slaughterhouse should again belong, until the year 1932, to the present leaseholder, Mr. Zweigenhaft[?].
A discussion for and against took place over the proposal. Before the vote councillor Michel („Bendiner Provisent“[?]) introduced a motion that „the magistrate's proposal be taken off the agenda“...
The motion naturally received a majority..

Campaign for Working Eretz Israel.

[Court — forgery.]
6 Months in Prison for Forging His Wife's Signature.
A certain Richter bought furniture from S. Czarnocha[?]. For the sum he gave bills of exchange on which his wife's name was signed. When the bills were protested, Richter's wife only then learned that she had not signed the bills, but that her husband had forged her name.
Richter was punished for this with 6 months in prison.

[Zagłębie — theatre.]
„The Jazz Singer“ with Ida Kamińska in Zagłębie
The latest sensation in Zagłębie was the guest performances of the famous actress Ida Kamińska with her ensemble, which staged (for the first time on the Yiddish stage) the splendid play „The Jazz Singer“. This tragedy of a jazz singer, a cantor's son, is now, as a sound film, a world hit, and is also being staged all over the world as a theatre play. Ida Kamińska, who received the exclusive right to stage the play on the Yiddish stage, gave it a splendid production in every detail: a first-class[?] acting ensemble, beautiful sets and splendid music (arranged by the well-known composer Józef Kamiński). The greatest sensation of the performance, however, is Ida Kamińska herself, in the role of the young jazz singer. She truly bewitches the audience with her speaking, acting and singing.
On Friday, the 21st of this month, „The Jazz Singer“ is playing in Będzin at the „Karso“[?] cinema for the last time.
The same day at 9 o'clock in the evening Gabriela Zapolska's excellent play „Panna Maliczewska“ will be performed in the same hall, with Ida Kamińska in the title role.
