Crisis and... balls.

[Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa — Purim; feuilleton.] A report of sorts, by Ben Amotz.

In the new production of Sholem Aleichem's "The Treasure" ("Der oytser"), which "Habima" is now staging in Poland, the strongest scene is that of the Menachem-Mendel types who hope to find the 12 pots of gold coins supposedly buried in the old cemetery.
The same thought came to my mind as I read the various posters and invitations to the balls, the "traditional" balls and the masked balls that were prepared in honour of Purim in the year 5690.
This is the most glaring symbol of the present critical situation. Exhausted mankind seeks a fleeting pleasure, an opportunity to believe that one is alive, to forget the daily troubles for a few hours; but "dancing and laughing come free when the heart is in it." — So it is. Today's laughter is laughter "with lizards" [Yiddish idiom: bitter, forced laughter]. A dance of resignation, the music blares, merry faces, but the feet are heavy [?], they soon tire...
———
— You should be sorry you were not at our Eretz-Israel ball — an acquaintance of mine told me. — Well, I did indeed "regret" it, waited and lived to see the 2nd "traditional E.I. ball", which took place 8 days before Purim at the "Góra Zamkowa" [Castle Hill, Będzin].
The hall — very beautifully decorated. Apelbaum's hand was evident in the palm decorations. Youth — "yurishe" [?, probably a misprint for "yidishe", Jewish]. The eye meets Hebrew and Yiddish slogans. A splendid kiosk of Eretz-Israel products under the management of Szymon Rotenberg, Polish-speaking waitresses, and yet the joy is a cold one — strong bodies without souls.
Connoisseurs even say that the colour of the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] had a great influence and "squeezed out" the Eretz-Israeli spirit..
The young "Herzliya" was the first to hold a "Purim ball" (neshef Purim), in the "Gwaszczy" [?].
For the first time the youngsters went out into the street; their work is done quietly, modestly. Their task is to protect young Jewish hearts so that they look toward Zion.. to tear Jewish souls away from assimilation..
The "ball" opened with a lecture in Polish by Magister Gajzler [?] (a teacher). He did not speak on current affairs but pointed out that in every new movement in the Diaspora only the Jew suffers. Mr. Gajzler! For your arguments you could after all have used the contents of the Megillah — why bring proofs from Lemberg [Lwów]? — the Megillah tells that, because of Haman's caprice, he wanted nothing other than "to slay and destroy all the Jews"...
"Purim Scenes" — not bad. The same goes for "On Purim Night" (best of all Miss Epsztajn, the mother). Good were: "For the Messiah" and "Moses Wept". The greatest share in the success goes to Moshe Półtorak for his rich, meaningful scenery.
* * *
The little ones, the tots of the "Gan Yeladim" (kindergarten), made merry on Saturday afternoon in honour of Purim. In a large hall of the gymnasium the assembled parents listened as young children spoke and sang little Hebrew songs.
Also taking part in the festivity was Mr. Fürstenberg, who sat down with the children. And one of them, little Lipszyc, presented him with a bouquet of flowers. After the end of the "programme" a "great feast" was prepared for the little company...
On Shushan Purim, after Havdalah, the public began getting ready [?] for the "traditional" Purim balls. Almost every society, organisation and school held a Purim ball with very "rich attractions", so that "there was not a house where there was not a ball" [after Exodus 12:30, "there was not a house where there was not one dead"]. In the streets too it was noticeable [?]; the youth went along enthusiastically [?], hurrying like pious Jews to the mikveh after the last meal before a fast. Later it looked as though people were going to the first Selichot, couples — and on meeting one another they wished:
— "Be well", "ya voypes" [?], "Życzę powodzenia" [Polish: "Good luck"], may we live to see another year.
People went according to a whole system: "each evening after its kind".
The Będzin and Sosnowiec artisans — and their associations; the school youth — at the school; and the youth — at the Sosnowiec municipal theatre, where the "partners" WIZO and Maccabi held "the traditional Purim masked ball".
The theatre hall was steeped in blue-and-white. In a "Diaspora corner", hidden from everyone, stood the bazaar of Eretz-Israel products. The "grand" [?] bazaar, lit with 2 candles, looked like an ohel [a structure over a grave]...
The visitors, mostly youth, with and without masks, danced because they "had to" dance, for one needs the power of restraint not to run to the dance when the well-assembled orchestra under P. Barenblat's direction plays a "tango" or something else.. Though "one doesn't feel like it" and "one doesn't want to", dance one must. But the crisis was visible everywhere: at the buffet it was quiet; one felt "pity" for the waitresses, how they begged the guests to buy something: "Mamy czarną kawę, bardzo smaczną" [Polish: "We have black coffee, very tasty"].. at least drink some coffee, just so we don't go away empty-handed...
After midnight, when the larger half of the visitors had begun to yawn, they proceeded to elect a "Queen Esther". The Revisionist group, which had emptied several bottles of "Carmel", held an urgent consultation (in a box) and decided to form a "Minorities Bloc" for list number 18. Since we are, after all, in exile, there can be no "unity" among Jews — so all the "beauties" intrigued with their admirers, and these submitted a flood of lists...
The election campaign "flared up" and took on a local character: Będzin and Sosnowiec fought each other. The Zionists fought for list 18, on which a Będzin girl figured, and Sosnowiec for its own daughter of the town...
At the election meeting Mr. Klarman campaigned for 18 and appealed to the guests to "defend Jewish honour" and vote for 18..
But just as in the Sejm elections, here too the "Agudah" betrayed, and the "government list 303" "won"... Sala Litmanowicz was elected Queen Esther, and Janka Blumenfrucht-Zendel [?] vice-queen..
The "defeated" candidates muttered: "You don't need to be pretty, only connections [printed 'tsardim'], protekcja"...
The Dąbrowa "Hashomer Hatzair" was late: it held a masked ball for children the next day, Sunday afternoon, in the hall of the Artisans' Association.
In the small hall there were some 70 children (may they multiply) dressed in masks, an "orchestra" of their own played, and the children squealed — it was truly Purim-like...
A Unified Relief Action. (The grave situation in general and the Jewish one in particular. — What about the Passover action in Sosnowiec?)

[Sosnowiec — relief and Passover.]
It is very, very hard to speak at the present time about material support, and it is doubly hard: first, one does not know whom to ask, who are those that can really give; and second, one cannot always ask those who indeed can give, because one must take them into account too. There are some who give all the time, so much so that it really exceeds their strength. Of course, here we mean the middle class, because that is the element one turns to at every moment, and they above all stand in contact with the people, with the broad popular strata. Quite different is the case with the great ones: one can rarely get to them, and moreover the people do not get from them the support that they would want or could give. So it turns out that the greatest burden is carried by the middle element, for whom the times are now very unfavourable.
And yet the situation is a grave one: the people are impoverished, the crisis grows from day to day, and here the holiday is approaching — until [?] Passover arrives, which is so hard to bring into the Jewish home. Well, all year long, when one lives in want and hardship, one can get by [?] from day to day: the hungry man barely earns a few gulden for tomorrow, buys himself what is necessary, and the hunger is stilled.
Quite different, of course, is the case at Passover, when not everything may be eaten and one cannot buy things at any time. For Passover one must prepare in advance, and when the situation is bad, that is certainly, certainly no easy matter.
Usually, every year, a few weeks before Passover, people prepare to carry out a relief action, not only for the poor but also for respectable people who have been brought low [?]; and if this is done every year, this year it would certainly have been a necessity, and of course in a much broader form. So far, however, we regrettably do not hear that such a committee has sought to come into being. One must therefore wonder [?] at the indifference with which our most urgent and painful economic interests are treated here.
One must not forget that from time immemorial the Passover question has been one of the hardest problems for the masses — all the more so now, at a time when the crisis rages so fiercely, and not only are branches torn off, but whole trees with long-standing, well-rooted [?] roots are uprooted and go completely to ruin. A trifle — huge firms go under; magnates are turned into professional beggars; one's hair stands on end when one begins to consider logically the economic situation in Poland in general and that of the Jews in particular.
And since things are so bad, so bitter, one must not remain indifferent and think to oneself: thank God, I can still hold out somehow, I still always have a few gulden turning over, but I am not able to help someone else — I have enough to do with myself until I earn my livelihood. In fact these are true words: earning a livelihood today is no trifle; one may have a livelihood and still not be able to come to the aid of others. In these times one can understand that, yet it would be called egoism, which we must not get used to.
Sosnowiec today has a large contingent of small traders and artisans who find themselves in a very bad situation, and nothing at all is being done for [?] them. Of course this is an unheard-of wrong on the part of our well-to-do Jews; but if until now nothing has been done, it is no more than a wrong — whereas if we left them helpless like this until after Passover, it would be not only a wrong but also a crime and a sin, which must on no account whatsoever be allowed to happen.
Precisely because things are bad all around, because a crisis rages on all sides — precisely for that reason one must approach the action with full energy and with a settled mind. Look at our sister town Będzin, where the Jewish pulse beats more strongly than here: there they started the Passover action long ago. We read in the columns of the "Zagl. Tsayt." the "Products Ring" that the "Beit Lechem" society is conducting, and we see that brick is being laid upon brick until the building is erected. Every week products are collected, and so, one by one, one by one, the action will be turned into a fine work. And we, the citizens of Sosnowiec — what are we doing? How do we intend to come to the aid of our poor and hungry? How, and from where, will they have the means to make Passover, if we, the better-situated, do not take care of it?
Yes, a few months ago we began to carry out a winter action, and for that purpose the editors of the "Zagl. Tsayt." were so kind as to give us space for a "Coal and Potato Ring" — and what do we see? More than once it did not appear at all. It seems that because the winter did not hold, the action was given up — as if coal, let alone potatoes, were not needed even when the frost does not crackle. But with us it is already like this: unless people cry out in alarm, unless they shout so that the walls tremble, nothing at all is done.
Well, if one reckons that when there is no winter one needs no coal and potatoes — one can surely be certain that Passover will quite definitely come; so why is everyone so indifferent, and why does no one consider that one should have set about in good time to carry out this Passover action not so provisionally, just for form's sake, merely so that people see that Sosnowiec too has done what other towns do — but so that it is truly done properly, as they say [?], with the whole heart and with good will, so that both the givers and the receivers may benefit.
When something is done no more than for form's sake, nobody gets anything out of it: it is neither given with eagerness, nor is there anything to distribute. Such an imitation looks nothing but ridiculous, both for the town and for those who look forward to the support.
But turning back the clock is impossible, and therefore the useful action should be taken up now. A committee must be formed of the most respected people in town, who will energetically set about carrying out a broad relief action in honour of Passover. One must not want to do it merely for form's sake, since it can be done properly, especially when there is a necessity — and everyone who has even the possibility of counting himself among the givers will come to the aid of this action.
Sosnowiec must show that it feels with the hungry and the fallen; it must show that it will not be able [printed "umshtand"] to make Passover for itself before it has provided its poor and fallen with the necessary food products.
Let the action be carried out vigorously in town, let it not be neglected [?], let all strata of the population take part in it, so that it may be called with full awareness a "Unified Relief Action in Honour of Passover" for the hungry and the fallen.
Dr. Papuri.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Ki Tisa)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion (Ki Tisa; Parashat Parah).] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.
Parashat Ki Tisa.
—o—
A) — "Then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul" (30:12)
The word "ve-natnu" (and they shall give) also reads backwards: "ve-natnu". It teaches a person: give charity, for you yourself may also one day come to the situation where people will have to give to you... It is a "turning wheel" (galgal ha-chozer); it may come back round to you too.
Kol Eliyahu.
B) — "That there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them" (30:12)
Reb Itzele of Volozhin (Wołożyn) once came to a town to collect money for a good cause; a great crowd came out to meet him, wanting to see the gaon. But when Reb Itzele began to explain to the crowd the purpose of his coming — to raise donations — the crowd began to slip away. Only a small number remained... Then Reb Itzele said the following saying:
— Why did God command Moses to count the Jews by having each one give a half-shekel — were there no other means for a census of the people?
— But just imagine: had God ordered the Jews counted in such a way that each would come and report to Moses — well, to grab a mitzvah that costs no money, everyone would surely have volunteered and even hurried to fulfil it. Well, what a crush, what a shoving there would have been at Moses'! People would have been crushed. Therefore God ordered them counted through giving money, and then "there be no plague when thou numberest them" — there will be no more shoving and crush; where money is involved, people won't be in such a hurry...
Heard.
C) — "This they shall give" (30:13)
On this the Midrash says that God showed Moses a coin of fire, a fiery coin, and said: "Like this shall they give" — such shall they give.
Meaning: fiery, with enthusiasm shall they give their donations, not under compulsion [?]. A heart-flaming coin the donation should be.
[Sur [?]] Siach Sarfei Kodesh.
D) — "The rich shall not give more" (30:9 [as printed; should be 30:15])
The rich shall not give more — the richer one becomes, the more charity he does not give...
Similarly: "Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endureth for ever" (Psalms) — "wealth and riches are in his house": his riches keep increasing, but "his righteousness endureth (stands) for ever" — his charity always stays standing in one place; it does not grow along with the wealth...
Folk sayings.
E) "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less" (ibid.)
The well-known gaon Reb Zalman Margolioth lived in Brody [?]; he held no rabbinical post at all, because he was a very rich man. Once the kehilla imposed too large a tax on him, and he said to the parnassim (community leaders):
— I know very well that you act as the Torah writes: "the rich shall not give more" — from the rich man you do not take too much, from the wealthy you take relatively small levies; "and the poor shall not give less" — and from the poor man you take not little but a lot... The poor man pays, that's how it is. I also know that from a scholar (talmid chacham) you take more than from a coarse ignoramus. Now, I did not know whether I am more a scholar or more a rich man: in the first case you will tax me heavily, in the second case lightly. Now I see that I am more a scholar, and that is why you levy such a big tax on me, even though I am a rich man.
F) "Galbanum" (30:34)
Galbanum — this is a plant [?] that has a repulsive smell, and yet it is counted among the spices of the incense, to show that one must also associate with the dregs of the people, with the criminal elements, and include them in the community — even when it is a matter of divine things such as incense, prayer.
Derash.
• Would that I could love the greatest tzaddik as much as Heaven loves the greatest sinner.
R. Y. of Lublin (the Seer of Lublin).
G) — "And was refreshed" (va-yinafash) (31:17)
The Gemara expounds: "va-yinafash" — "vay, avda nefesh" (woe, the soul is lost — i.e. the extra Sabbath soul has been lost). But that refers to the end of the Sabbath (motzaei Shabbat) — so why do we say it at the welcoming of the Sabbath (kabbalat Shabbat)?
The meaning is different. "Vay, avda nefesh" — when the beloved Sabbath arrives, the Jewish soul loses its "vay" (woe): the Jew throws off all his worries and no longer groans "vay", "vay"...
Rabbi Bunem of Peshischa (Przysucha).
H) — "And He gave unto Moses, when He had made an end" (31:18)
To Moses one gives when everything is already finished... When he [the Jew] has already taken care of everything, of all the luxuries — then he remembers Moses too...
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
• "I am the first and I am the last."
When things start going badly for a Jew, first of all he cuts back on Jewishness: takes the children out of cheder, stops giving charity, etc. That is "I am the first" — God is the first one to save on. And when a Jew falls ill, he runs to doctors, and only when "all the deadlines have passed" does he remember the rescue remedy of charity. That is "I am the last" — God is the last one to be remembered...
Sefarim (books).
I) — "And all the people broke off the golden earrings" (32:3)
Because of the "golden earrings", because of the gold and diamond earrings for the wives, a man tears himself apart entirely (prika): works hard and bitterly, steals, robs — all for a pair of earrings for his wife...
Or ha-Meir.
J) — "Go, get thee down; for thy people have corrupted themselves" (32:7)
"When God told Moses 'Go, get thee down', Moses held the tablets in his hand and did not believe that the Jews had sinned. He said: as long as I do not see it with my own eyes, I will not believe. — Did Moses then not believe God, who had told him 'for thy people have corrupted themselves'?
— This teaches that even when one hears from a trustworthy person about someone's sin, one must do nothing at all until one sees it with one's own eyes.
Midrash Rabbah.
K) — "But a woman among all those have I not found" (Ecclesiastes)
Among those shouting "These are thy gods, O Israel" there was not a single woman. The women did not dance around the calf; the men pulled their jewellery off them by force.
Midrash Rabbah.
L) — "And Moses made haste, and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshipped" (34:8)
Why did he hurry so?
— Moses saw how God was counting out that He would remember the sin of the calf to the third generation, to the fourth — and he was afraid that God would go on counting: fifth, sixth... So he made a bow and thereby cut God's words short...
Yaarot Devash (R. Yonatan Eybeschütz).
M) — "And Moses turned, and went down from the mount" (37 [?]:16 [?] — as printed; should be 32:15)
"Va-yifen" (and he turned) — Moses put on a face... like someone standing before a great misfortune who takes heart... puts on an act...
R. M. of Kotzk (Kock).
N) — "Thou shalt make thee no molten gods" (31:17 — as printed; should be 34:17)
"Molten gods" — a cast god, an iron one, immovable — such a one do not make for yourself.
The aforementioned.
Parashat Parah.
"Wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke" (Chukat).
"Wherein is no blemish" — the pious Jew who sees no fault in himself and considers himself a perfect tzaddik — this is proof that "upon which never came yoke": that he bears no yoke of godliness at all.
Avodat Yisrael.
Jewish Trade 500 Years Ago

[History — Jews at the Leipzig fair.]
(A historical study from the Leipzig Trade-Fair Archive)
By our special correspondent Z. Haber.
In the historical archive of the Leipzig fair one can find out exactly how Jews conducted trade some five hundred years ago. These records are very important, because they form a new chapter in the history of our economic development.
For the first time, at the end of the fifteenth century, it is recorded in the history of the Leipzig fair that Polish Jews had arrived[?] there. "Apart from the Italians — it says there — Jewish merchants from Poland also came in large numbers." The Christians from Germany and other countries who used to come to Leipzig worked mischief[?] [lit. "worked deeds"]. The chronicler tells us that the intrigues of the Christian merchants against the Jewish ones arose only because "they realised that the Jewish merchants were more capable than they and would give them strong competition".
So they began issuing various decrees and taxes in order to embitter the Jews' lives. They introduced a body tax ("Leibsteuer"), land taxes, weighing fees and bridge tolls, which only the Jewish merchants paid; the idea was that they would get fed up and stop coming, but the Jewish merchants did good business at the Leipzig fair even with the taxes. In the seventeenth century an ukase was issued that "one may not rent the Jewish merchants any shops or places facing the street". So the Jews had to set up in the inner courtyards, and it was precisely there that the greatest merchants of the whole world flocked, because they preferred to trade with Jews.
But this decree forbidding the renting of open shops to Jews did not last long, for the first to rent Jews the shops in his big house, which stood in the very centre of the town, was none other than the Leipzig burgomaster, Dr. Wendler... The Leipzig clergy, who owned large houses and plots in the centre, rented them precisely to Jewish merchants, because they paid best.
Only at the end of the eighteenth century, when the Jews declared that they would stop coming to the Leipzig fair, and indeed held a strike for a year and did not come to Leipzig — only then was the decree lifted, and Jews were permitted to rent premises wherever they wished.
Then a stream of Jewish merchants poured into Leipzig from the four corners of the world. From the records of the Leipzig fair office and from the archive of the "Leipzig City Council" we see that five large kosher restaurants had to be founded at that time, in which no fewer than 138 people were employed[?] as waiters, cooks and the like, so that Jews would have somewhere to eat. For these restaurants the "beil-ger"[?] Jews paid a larger sum every year. Besides this they maintained the Jewish doctor Shlomo Hirschel Burgheim, who had to treat all sick Jewish fair-guests free of charge."
The business of the Jewish merchants was very good, and the merchants could not finish within the fourteen days that the fair lasted; they had to begin arranging their goods some time earlier and wind up their dealings again some time later. But since no Jew was allowed to live in Leipzig except during the fair, the town administration issued a permit that a small number of Jewish merchants might live in Leipzig without any hindrance[?] and might "mediate the business between the local merchants and the Jewish sellers".
It cannot be denied that the Christian merchants kept striving to have various taxes and restrictions imposed on Jews, "in order to make coming to Leipzig harder for them"; and if the Jewish merchants nevertheless came and did good business at the Leipzig fair, this is to be attributed to the fact that the rulers of the town were always in need and therefore granted the Jews the greatest privileges for money.
Only in the year 1806 did the permission come out that Jews might come, live and trade at the Leipzig fair freely and openly. Only the Russian and Polish Jews had to have passports from their governments. But a few years later this restriction was abolished, and Jews became merchants with equal rights like the other nations.
Shall We Create a Faculty of Jewish Studies?

[Kraków — university; Hebrew studies.]
(A conversation with Prof. Dr. B. Katz.)
Three years ago, on the initiative of the Senate of Kraków University, the lectureship in the Hebrew language was created. It was the first such lectureship in Poland. The Senate wanted to interest the Polish academic youth and acquaint them with the Hebrew language and Hebrew literature on the one hand, and on the other hand to teach the Jewish academics their language[?] and especially to point out[?] the activity of the Jews in Poland. It wanted to bring about greater coexistence between Polish and Jewish academics and to avoid all the sad consequences that arise from the Polish students' complete ignorance of Jewish life.
The first lecturer, Dr. Rosenman, perished tragically in the Vistula; the second lecturer, Dr. Stein, is now a docent at the Warsaw Institute of Jewish Studies. In 1929 Dr. Ben-Zion Katz was appointed lecturer; in his conversation with me he informed me in detail about the above-mentioned aims of the lectureship. The conditions in the first year — Dr. Katz tells me — were very hard; the Senate devoted only two hours a week to the lectureship. Now we already have 6 hours.
Three courses are run. The first, elementary course teaches Hebrew from the "ABC"; the third course is now studying the creative work of the new Hebrew poetry. Interest keeps growing; as regards the number of listeners, it reaches up to 200 matriculated students.
"And the interest on the part of the Polish students?" I ask.
"Among the listeners there are 60 per cent non-Jews."
"What influence have the recent events had on the lectureship?"
Dr. Katz smiles; he had reckoned with the possibility of such a question.
"The recent events have had no influence whatsoever on the work of the lectureship; I personally was not attacked; the attitude of the university authorities is entirely objective, as towards all lecturers. The lectureship," Dr. Katz continues, "also brings great practical benefit. This year examinations were introduced which allow all graduates of the lectureship to teach Hebrew in secondary schools."
"Will we be able to create a faculty of Jewish studies? Perhaps only a chair?"
"As for a faculty, there is nothing to hope for; to create a faculty one needs many means and, most important, three chairs — and that is impossible.
But one possibility exists and it will surely be realised: out of the lectureship a chair of Hebrew language and Hebrew literature will develop. For that the lectureship must have a tradition, many listeners and other necessary means — but it will surely happen."
"We Jews have patience, after all; we will wait," I say, and thank Dr. Katz for his courteous explanations.
Eliyahu Gertner.

Our National Conscience

By Leo Kenig.
(A bit of fantasy.)
The scene takes place, of course, in heaven. In the great bright conference hall of the “League of the Nations’ Consciences”, where the unrestrained[?] consciences of all the nations on earth sit day and night and toil away.
Beside each national conscience stands a telephone and a great book of records, in which they keep writing down, with big goose quills, the small and great sins of the nations whose consciences they are. Especially overworked, of course, are the tormented consciences of the so-called great nations. They keep ringing on the telephones and calling the representatives of their nations on earth.
But communication with the national representatives on earth is not normal. Apparently they are not so keen to answer them “from below”.
“I want to speak to Hoover about Wall Street,” shouts and rings the American conscience.
“I want to speak to Stalin, to Gorky[?], I must have a long heart-to-heart talk with them,” shouts the Russian conscience.
“Hallo, hallo,” rings the English conscience, calm and composed, “I want Downing Street number ten... I have something important to discuss with MacDonald... yes, about India and about unemployment...”
And so the consciences of all the nations keep ringing and calling from their central building in heaven.
The only national conscience that is quiet is the Jewish national conscience. While all the nations’ consciences are so busy, our national conscience sits and strokes its long, beautiful, prophetic beard... It looks rested and healthy, not like the consciences of the other nations with their worn-out[?] faces and glowing eyes...
The other national consciences envy the Jewish conscience a little for its quiet life, and every moment they call on it to help them in their great and holy work:
“Come, you idler, help us punish, wake up our nations; after all, the children of your people live in our countries...”
“It has already gone against my conscience to meddle in your affairs. Have I preached too little morality to your nations? Too much already, it seems... And tell me, I beg you, dear colleagues, has my moralising helped you at all?”
And the Jewish conscience goes on sitting, stroking its beautiful white prophetic beard and longing for a real piece of work together with all the decent consciences of the normal nations.
And when it gets tired of sitting quietly in one place and watching over the conscience of a people that has no strength to sin, it starts strolling around the conference, whispering every moment to another national conscience:
“Listen, remind your government there to treat its Jews a little more humanely...”
— — —
But lately the Jewish national conscience in heaven has become a little busy.
“My Jewish business,” it jokes to its colleagues, the national consciences of all the other nations, “my little Jews down below think I have fallen fast asleep, and they wake me every time — I’ll be damned if I know what for and when[?]...”
“You are a lucky conscience,” its colleagues answer, “we keep ringing our nations and they don’t answer us... while you get rung from below of their own accord...”
“If only they rang with real, substantial sins...” jokes the Jewish national conscience, “they call me up every time with such empty, foolish complaints... one of my little Jews has some dream or other about sins...”
“You are a lucky national conscience... You are holy, holy...” all the other consciences compliment it.
“I don’t know...” it answers with half a yawn, “I don’t know whether I am as lucky as you think... In any case, dear colleagues, you must excuse me that they ring me through your telephones. You know that I am called from various stations and in all the seventy languages... There, they are ringing me again:
“Hallo, who? Dr. Magnus? Yes, yes, I know you... Shalom aleichem. You are a fine Jew... but I am sorry, I cannot sign your brochure... You understand, what is the use of beating one’s breast ‘al chet’ before the sin... the Arabs, after all, have meanwhile sinned against us... The only thing I can do for you here is to have a talk with the conscience of uncle Ishmael... So give my regards to your American Jews and to those of Eretz Israel. Tell them, in fact, that I am completely calm... Don’t forget.”
“Eh, tovarishch, you are wanted on my telephone,” the Russian conscience calls to the Guardian Angel of Israel, “someone is ringing you on my telephone.”
The Jewish conscience goes over to the telephone slowly, unhurried.
“Hallo... who... ah, shalom aleichem, comrades... I gathered it is the American ‘Freiheit’... like Moscow... But there is no need to curse. Either way: if you believe I am an out-and-out bourgeois national conscience, why do you ring me at all?... If I tell you that I guard the conscience of the Jewish working class too... And your claim that the Jewish workers in Palestine are pursuing an imperialist policy is — I don’t know what to call it... Perhaps you will tell me that my beloved Brenner was an imperialist too... Your conscientiousness, I must tell you, already smells too much of petty-bourgeois sentimentalism... You ask whether Jews in the Orient are an obstacle to the social revolution... I tell you — every constructive work is a value... Let them build Eretz Israel... and you have obstacles enough... Adieu, do svidaniya, auf Wiedersehen...”
The Guardian Angel of Israel is about to sit down when its telephone rings again, this time directly to it.
“Hallo, yes... The Jewish conscience speaking... Who are you? A Jewish journalist. From which paper? Ah, never mind... We rarely read newspapers up here in heaven... So what do you want? An interview? An interview with the Jewish conscience? Good. Ask your questions. What I think about Weizmann, about Magnus, about Jabotinsky, about the Balfour Declaration... All that? Good. To all these questions I will give you one answer! They have not yet disturbed my rest... unfortunately... unfortunately... not yet.”
Recent Theatre Visits in Zagłębie

„Skala“, the Vilna Troupe, Ida Kamińska.
Jewish theatre-goers fall into three elements: the popular masses, the would-be workers' intelligentsia, and the half- and fully-assimilated bourgeoisie. The first lives almost the whole year with worries about making a living. When a theatre comes, it is a holiday for him; he wants to forget himself a little, to amuse himself, to tear himself out of his own narrow four cubits — so he goes to the theatre. He does not ask who is playing[?], what they are playing, how they play; he is the public, he looks for the story. He wants the actor to draw him into the plot, both in laughter and in tears, in full measure. He will not accept compromises; he is no longer an „oylem-goylem“ (a dumb crowd). Woe to the actors who still think the dumb crowd won't catch on and allow themselves anything under the sun. The public has learned to watch and to listen. Give them theatre in a poor form, badly played, and they are immediately dissatisfied. Recently we had a case of this here. There came to bestow upon us true art, oysh[?], from Warsaw, the „Skala“ theatre with „Gehenna“ — a Warsaw theatre with Galician Franz-Joseph Yiddish, „Herz-Schmerz“ (heart-ache kitsch). One had the impression of being in Gimpel's theatre in Lemberg 15 years ago. The hall was overfull, but the public saw[?] the mistake, people began to leave the hall, whistled, made a racket, went away dissatisfied. We know, after all, how such a troupe is made: you put together a troupe, take a few actors who have not played together, and set off across the country with screaming letters: „A tour across Western Europe“ — and you fool the public. Luckily it is only advertising bluff, and the shame of such Jewish theatre remains among ourselves within the country.
The second — the would-be workers' intelligentsia, may they forgive me, have snatched[?] a scanty knowledge of theatre. They want something like modern theatre. Meyerhold, Vakhtangov, Granovsky — names they know from press articles, from individual illustrations, have heard good things about — they want to see the same thing in every theatre performance, and under any conditions. But they do not know when they are given the genuine thing, or at least something a little like it, and when they are given the false, the imitation, often a bad imitation. They forget the main thing: that such theatre was created in a land of revolution, in a land where people broke with yesterday, a land that takes no account of feeling[?] and human weaknesses, that builds everything on a revolutionary economic order; everything is collectivised, everything mechanised, and theatre too is led along that path.
Jewish theatre is a private little shop, without secure means of existence. If a play succeeds and brings in box-office takings — the theatre exists; if not, the private entrepreneur is no worse than a merchant: he goes bankrupt, and that is the end of Jewish theatre. A director comes with a play, a hit (for the director everything he brings is a hit). Even a „Kiddush Hashem“, and the play has more luck than sense, more fortune than any right to success. The public gets „Kiddush-Hashem-ed“; people don't go to the theatre, they run; the public thinks, and so does our would-be intelligentsia, that this is the true modern theatrical art — one sees mass attendance, after all — and incidentally they wave their hands in the air. But they overlook that it is the „Pintele Yid“ staged a little more richly, „revised by a doctor“.
The higher society, the „śmietana“ (cream), is not at all[?] ashamed when it sees the same Vilna players of „Kiddush Hashem“ perform a play like „Ta'ave“ (Lust), a piece without prayer shawls and Torah scrolls, and the actors don't convince — bad casting of the roles, to say it quite loudly, ei[?], this time the actors are no good, they are only fit for Jewish plays; the piece doesn't please them either, they saw themselves a little too closely in their own skin of money-greed and exploitativeness — so they spit on everything: on the actors for bad acting and on the author for allowing himself such things. The Vilna Troupe indeed has all good things, a little for everyone. Their repertoire includes so strong a work as „At Night in the Old Marketplace“; though one could reproach the director David Herman for his restraint in the conception, we know there is a censorship in the country. We do forgive him, and it must be said that it is the strongest production of the Vilna Troupe, except for the jester (Wislich) — somehow he has no place in the staging. The Vilna Troupe broke the record here both in the number of performances and in the number of spectators. The stagings, the frame in which each performance is given, beautiful sets, rich costumes, lighting, music — that is what brings the success, certainly not the acting material, for about the latter a great deal could be said; without any doubt there are capable ones there, less capable, even a real talent (Kamin). But their merit alone would not have drawn such success. One must also credit the director Mazo with great merit for the success: he is a good businessman. He does not skimp on production, travels[?] with technical staff — a painter, stage hands, tailors — puts the main weight on external things and knows how to handle the public. So the Vilna Troupe has in its repertoire something of everything, for everyone: „Kiddush Hashem“, „The Dybbuk“ for those for whom this is Jewishness; „At Night in the Old Marketplace“, „Hershele Ostropolier“, where mockery[?]-derision and despair find expression — that is for the worker-intellectual; „The Singer of His Sorrow“, a heart-rending melodrama (by the way, the finest production of the Vilna Troupe, both in acting and in form. Sklaps[?]) — that is for the man of the people. The Vilna Troupe is thus a theatre for all Israel: all Jews should enjoy it; they have no definite path; another new staging — there will be a living for another couple of weeks. But the theatre does not grow, does not rise higher; it is a group of people with a clever businessman who knows how to run a business; they carry a name, „the Vilna Troupe for 13 years“, and they have a tradition. Therefore we wish you that when you come to us some time, we may be able to say: this is the Vilna style.
Something quite different is a star theatre: when we see a poster announcing just 1 appearance of the artist Ida Kamińska, we know in advance that there is no talk here of a theatre of ideas. Nor of a great ensemble of artists. The advertising speaks only of the star; the play, presumably, is tailored to her in the lead role. One knows in advance that one is going to see the artist Ida Kamińska in a new role, a new staging. And when one sees[?] on the poster a sensational name, „The Jazz Singer“, the „connoisseurs“ and most learned experts begin to turn up their noses: who-knows-what, an American fabrication, surely a melodrama, trash. They read in the press about that same film: a cantor's son, Yom Kippur, Kol Nidre, Negro music — he thinks nothing of it already before he has seen it. But when one sees the staging and Ida Kamińska in the role of the Jazz Singer, one must say that of all the roles in which Ida Kamińska has appeared before us, the Jazz Singer is her strongest. Her subtlety and lightness of acting, which only she possesses in the Jewish theatre, she showed us here in full measure. And how heartfully she sings her jazz songs. It is long since one heard so much soul in a song on the Jewish stage. And how close[?] Ida Kamińska stood, together with the direction, to stumbling into a portion of prayer shawls and kittels. What is in the film — she freed herself from those effects and set the play on its pure dramatic material. Moreover, the cheap effect-material of the Jewish theatre, like prayer shawls, she used for a fine humorous scene (the scene at the cantor's birthday, the gifts of prayer shawls), and how pleased the public is to see, around the great artist, capable young actors; how heartfelt-Jewish, how subtle was the mother (Sterenicka). I cannot imagine at all how Ida Kamińska in the role of the Jazz Singer would have looked in the arms of another mother — a mother of strong emotions and quiet tears, resembling her son. How hard it is today to see such a mother in the Jewish theatre. All the other actors, too, were good in their roles. The main thing: a performance from which everyone — the man of the people, as well as the worker-intellectual or the Jewish „śmietana“ — can have real pleasure. And I wish to conclude with a „yasher koyekh“ (well done) to the Vilna Troupe for their several successful stagings, and to Ida Kamińska for her splendidly crafted creation in „The Jazz Singer“.
A. Teatral.
Tel Hai–Trumpeldor Academy in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.] On Thursday the League for Labour Palestine in Sosnowiec held a grand Tel Hai–Trumpeldor commemoration (academy) in the Municipal Theatre.

After the choir under the direction of Mr. Chlewicki sang "Shuti"[?], the academy was opened by Mr. A. Ganzweich[?], who spoke about the launching of the campaign in our town and called on all sympathisers of Labour Palestine to place themselves at the disposal of the PPS [?, abbreviation as printed]. Greetings were delivered: on behalf of the Zionist Organisation by Mr. S. Feldman; for the KKL (Jewish National Fund) by Mr. Figreich; for the PPS by P. Ruga; for Poale Zion (united with the Zionist Socialists) by Igz[?], Zysman, who also thanked the PPS representative; on behalf of "Hitachdut" by Mr. Milsztajn; on behalf of all Zionist organisations by Mr. A. Chlewicki, who spoke about the significance of Tel Hai and the symbolism of Joseph Trumpeldor. Then the floor was given to the representative of the Central Committee of the Leagues for Labour Palestine, Mr. B. Kruzman, who held the audience in suspense with a 2½-hour lecture, showing with figures what the PPS had accomplished in its 15 years of activity: the greatest guarantee for creating positions in Palestine is given by the working class; without workers' hands capital will accomplish nothing. The lecture made a very deep impression, and the audience gave the speaker warm ovations. Afterwards the "Freiheit" youth performed a tableau entitled "HeHalutz".

After the singing of "Teḥezaknah", the Internationale and "Hatikvah", the academy closed in an elevated mood.

In the evening a torchlight procession went through the town. On Third of May Square, where thousands of people had gathered, several orchestras played and the Strzelcy sang national songs.
On Wednesday at 10 a.m. a festive prayer service was held in the synagogue. The rabbi and the director of 'Yavne', Dr. Einhorn, spoke on topics of the day. Cantor Zhupovitch sings several chapters of Psalms with the choir, and synagogue orchestra no. 2 concludes the programme.
Afterwards there was a march-past [défilade] of the military.
—o—
To provide soldiers and prisoners with kosher food at Passover.
On Sunday and Monday a meeting was held at the community [gmina] with the participation of the rabbinate, the board and the council. On the agenda was the question of raising money to supply the soldiers and prisoners with Passover food. After a lengthy discussion it was decided that the rabbi should take charge of the campaign.
Parnas Landau made the following 'original' proposal: the community should borrow for itself the dollars deposited by the new shochet...(!)
—o—
Dreams are no means of obtaining an eviction...
In Mr. Fink's dwelling at Kołłątaja 24 is the 'Chayei Adam' society. The society has existed in these premises for about 21 years and everything went properly. A few weeks ago Mr. Fink took a fancy to evicting the society; for that purpose he filed a petition with the local court, in which Mr. Fink argued that 'at night he has terrible dreams because of the minyan, he has no rest, and he asks for an eviction'.
The case was heard last Friday. On Mr. Fink's behalf appeared attorney Radzin, who supported the petition of his plaintiff [client].
Against these arguments appeared the gabbaim of the minyan, pointing out that through the eviction Mr. F. actually wants to use the premises to let them to another society which is willing to pay him well for it.
The judge did not recognise the 'dreams' and dismissed the petition for eviction.
—o—
An 'opponent' of sidelocks...
Mr. Yosef Leib Kritzler of Piaski reports the following fact to us: I have — he relates — a 4-year-old little boy, blessed with curly sidelocks, which he had guarded so that not a single hair of them should be diminished. This Tuesday the boy went in to the neighbour, Mrs. Shivek, and she, Mrs. Shivek, made herself a 'joke' and shaved off my boy's sidelocks... Then she wrapped the hair in a piece of paper, handed it to the child, saying 'give this to your father, let him keep it for the holiday'...
When I saw it I felt sick — says Mr. Kritzler — Mrs. Shivek has taken a piece of life from us.
Mr. Kritzler is handing the matter over to the court.
—o—
A 'clash' between the president and the synagogue beadle.
On Friday evening after Kabbalat Shabbat, the synagogue beadle Mr. Kaplan announced, with the rabbi's knowledge, that it is forbidden to trade in pork lard. Because the announcement provoked protests from several interested parties, the president of the synagogue committee, Mr. Rechnitz, ordered Mr. Kaplan to repeat [i.e. probably: retract] the announcement. Mr. K. refused to carry out the order, so there followed between them an 'interrogation'[?]...
In connection with the 'incident' a meeting of the synagogue committee was called, which was to give its opinion on Mr. Kaplan's conduct.
At the meeting, however, it came to a second 'clash', between the cantor and the conductor[?]. Because of this the meeting was broken up.
—o—
'It's not as bad as people shout'...
In connection with the appeals submitted to the 'Izba Skarbowa' [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce against the enormous tax assessments for[?] the year 1929, the head of the Chamber came here to acquaint himself with the actual situation.
As we are informed, the head inspected a number of businesses and afterwards expressed the opinion that Będzin has not been impoverished[?]; the shops — he said — are full of goods and the protests against the taxes are exaggerated...
—o—
The public pays for water.
Since Monday the water pumps in the town have been put under concession; at every pump stands a concessionaire who sells the water at 2 groszy a bucket. Meanwhile various comic scenes take place between the water buyers and sellers...
—o—
The 'Days of Awe' have already begun...
Since yesterday the 'experts' [assessors] have been at work on the assessment of turnover for the year 1929.
The Jewish commission members are duty-bound not to miss a single session, because otherwise Jewish merchants and artisans may suffer.
—o—
A 35,000-złoty claim dismissed.
At the Sosnowiec district court this Tuesday the case against the board of the 'Yavne' gymnasium in Będzin was heard. The board was sued by the former director Mr. Grinberg, who is claiming 35,000 zł. because the board dismissed him from the post of director.
On the gymnasium's behalf appeared attorney Pawles[?], who showed that at the time when Mr. G. was director of the gymnasium he had been negotiating with another school, so that Mr. G. can have no claim whatsoever regarding compensation.
The court agreed with this view and dismissed Mr. Grinberg's claim.
—o—
Apprentices! Today is the last day to register.
The magistrate sent out notices to 1,200 apprentices to come and register, so that, according to the voivode's circular [okólnik], they may have a representative in the examination commission for artisans.
By yesterday 700 had registered. The deadline was Wednesday, but we obtained an extension of the deadline until Saturday, i.e. one can still register today.
—o—
It's 'raining' appeals...
By Monday about 100 appeals against municipal taxation had been submitted. But on Tuesday and Wednesday the number grew sharply, so that in those two days another 200 appeals were filed.
As people say, the number of appeals has grown thanks to the agitation of well-known board members.
—o—
'Contra Zhitlowsky — contra Gruenbaum'.
A lecture on this subject will be given this Saturday at the 'Korso'[?] by the well-known speaker Mr. Zerubavel. The subject is very interesting and topical.
The lecture has aroused great interest.

Sosnowiec / Kashrut Matters Under the Authority of the Kehilla Administration / The Name Day of Marshal Piłsudski / Tram Conductors Get a Raise / The Telephone Operators Don't "Hear"... / 115,000 Zł. for Building Purposes / The Starosta's Proposal to Elect a "Sub-Rabbi" / A Brawl Over a Donation / Fell into a Cauldron of Boiling Water / Terrible Death of a Young Schoolgirl

On Thursday evening, under the chairmanship of Mr. Zendel [?], a conference was held in the premises of the gmina (Jewish community) of Sosnowiec with the rabbis Rabbi Hager, the Koziegłowy rabbi, Rabbi R' Dovidl Halberstam, and the kehilla administration.
Rabbi Szwarc did not come to the conference, declaring that because of the fast he was not able to come, and Rabbi R' Yehoshele did not come because of the Purim festivities.
At the conference the proposal was discussed to found a kashrut committee, which is to deal with the matter in general and with Passover certifications (hechsherim) in particular.
After a discussion Rabbi Hager's proposal was adopted, that the committee, which the rabbis also join, [stands] under the supervision of the kehilla; all income from certifications flows into the gmina treasury, and afterwards the kehilla administration can distribute the income at its discretion.
The second meeting of the kashrut committee took place on Tuesday evening; at the meeting a presidium was elected of: Rabbi Hager (chairman), Rabbi Frommer (honorary chairman), Rabbi Halberstam (secretary).
—o—
The Name Day of Marshal Piłsudski
was celebrated with a great parade. On Tuesday a march-past took place with the participation of the army, police and firemen, accompanied by a great crowd. The procession stopped at the "monument" of the Unknown Soldier; Professor Nawrocki [?] delivered a speech on topical matters.
The next day a solemn prayer was held in the synagogue. The synagogue was packed full; the kehilla administration came in corpore. Rabbi Hager and Dr. Seladysta [?] appeared with speeches rich in content. Then the cantor Mr. Lejchter sang appropriate chapters of Psalms with the choir.
—o—
Tram Conductors Get a Raise
The negotiations between the tram management and the conductors, which began at the start of 1930, were finally concluded this Tuesday.
The tram conductors get a raise of 6 groszy an hour: instead of 1.04 zł. they will get 1.10 zł. an hour. The raise applies from the 1st of January (styczeń) of this year.
—o—
The Telephone Operators Don't "Hear"...
The local merchants draw our attention to the phenomenon that the telephone operators at the local telephone exchange are "deaf" and do not hear the requests of the telephone subscribers.
It is high time that the merchants' associations intervene, so that the telephone operators take their duties more seriously and flirt less during their working hours.
—o—
115,000 Zł. for Building Purposes
The local municipal administration received from the government a credit in the amount of 115 thousand zł., which was divided in the form of loans among a number of house owners for building purposes.
Among the "lucky ones" there is also one Jew, Mr. Rajcher, who received a loan of 10 thousand zł.
—o—
The Starosta's Proposal to Elect a "Sub-Rabbi"
The kehilla administration received a proposal from the starosta (district head), who proposes that until the rabbinate question is settled, the Koziegłowy rabbi should fulfil the functions of a "podrabin" (sub-rabbi).
Since a rabbinate board has been created, in which the Koziegłowy rabbi is also represented, the proposal is no longer relevant.
—o—
A Brawl Over a Donation
On Purim morning an unknown Jew came into the minyan at Pańska 29 and asked for support of a few gulden. Upon the request a worshipper of the minyan turned to the gabbai, asking him to give 5 zł. from the machatzit ha-shekel money. Because the gabbai rejected the proposal, a quarrel broke out and then a brawl, in which Mr. Kożuch was lightly injured.
—o—
Fell into a Cauldron of Boiling Water
On Monday the following terrible accident happened in the municipal slaughterhouse. The worker Bank, while working with the pigs, fell into a cauldron of boiling water.
He was taken out of the cauldron in serious condition.
—o—
Terrible Death of a Young Schoolgirl
On Saturday during the day, at the public school on Żytnia Street, a schoolgirl fell into a courtyard latrine and drowned.
The police and firemen were alerted about the terrible incident, and with great effort they took out the tragically perished child.
Olkusz / From the KKL Ball / From the "Dobroczynność" Ball / Arrests / A Couple Aged 200 Years Has Died

On Saturday night a ball for the benefit of the KKL (Jewish National Fund) took place in the "Workers' House". At the ball there were many fine attractions and surprises, which is a rarity for Olkusz. Almost the entire youth of Olkusz attended the ball, guests from Zagłębie and the local veteran Zionists; the net income was 715 zł.
—o—
From the "Dobroczynność" Ball
On 8 March a ball took place for the benefit of the "Dobroczynność" (charity society). The ball, which was attended by the local intelligentsia and youth, was arranged with a rich programme and, together with the previous collection, brought in an income of 1000 zł.
—o—
Arrests
Last week the police noticed communist leaflets on Szpitalna Street, on account of which several young Jews were arrested. After the interrogation they were released, except for one, who was sent to the investigating judge in Sosnowiec.
—o—
A Couple Aged 200 Years Has Died
Last Friday Wolf Zeliger, an old man of 105 years, died here. Eight days earlier his wife, an old woman of 95 years, had died. The deceased were healthy and fit for work until the last year. May their souls be bound up in the bond of life.
A. B.
On Cancelling the Municipal Loan.

[Sosnowiec — municipality.] At the last session of the Sosnowiec town council a resolution was adopted to apply, through the mediation of the Izba Skarbowa [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce, to the Ministry of Finance, asking that the loan which Sosnowiec took in the years 1926, 27 to employ the unemployed be cancelled.
—o—
From the Sosnowiec Brit Trumpeldor
The Brit Trumpeldor held a Purim evening in its own premises on Saturday night (motzei Shabbat). After the literary part the real merriment began, which lasted until the morning.
— On the 30th of this month the Brit Trumpeldor is holding a lecture by Dr. Felrshua[?].
—o—
A Dance Evening at the Jewish Gymnasium.
This Saturday night a large dance evening with various attractions will take place in the splendid halls of the gymnasium named after "Fürstenberg".
The proceeds of the evening are designated for the needy pupils of the gymnasium, and it is to be hoped that those who have been invited will take part in the ball and support this important cause.
—o—
Catastrophe in an Upper Silesian Coal Mine
In the "Szarlej" Biała[?] coal mine beyond Katowice a pillar collapsed. Two workers were killed on the spot and one was injured.
—o—
Suicide of a Railway Cashier.
Yesterday morning the baggage[?] cashier at the Sosnowiec railway station committed suicide by shooting himself.
Lord Balfour Has Died.

[Zionism — mourning.] Together with the whole Jewish people, Jewish Zagłębie was shaken by the terrible news that Lord Balfour has died.
A great soul has been extinguished. The great friend of the Jews is gone — one of the most splendid and noblest figures of our time. Lord Balfour stood like a giant among the rare Righteous among the Nations, who shine with their great, humanity-loving souls in this coarse world, and this splendid figure will forever remain in the memory of coming generations, surrounded with gratitude and love.
———————
On Wednesday at 6 in the evening the radio announced Balfour's death. The news spread with lightning speed and made a heavy impression on the Jewish population of Zagłębie.
The Zionist organisations have decided to hold mourning assemblies ("academies") dedicated to the passing of Lord Balfour.
Imprint (Colophon)
[Colophon.] Editor and publisher L. Szpigelman, Będzin. — Printed in its own printing house. (Imprint line at the foot of page 8, in Yiddish and Polish.)
Zaglembier Tsaytung — Masthead

Zaglembier Cajtung / ZAGŁEMBIER CAJTUNG. No. 13. „20th year“. Price 25 groszy. (Postal stamp: Opłata pocztowa uiszczona ryczałtem — „postage paid in bulk“.)

Fight between tram passengers and bandits / To the address of the Będzin power station / On prices of articles of prime necessity / Brother-in-law of the Radomsko Rebbe becomes a rabbinic judge in Łódź / „Matzot need not be clean“... so a baker explains / Będzin is becoming like other people... / Lecture by Dr. Kruk

On Tuesday at 11 in the evening a bloody fight between passengers and bandits took place in the tram that runs from Siemianowice to Katowice.
As the tram was approaching in the direction of Maria-Hof, 6 masked bandits got in; some forced the motorman to stop the tram and the rest threw themselves on the conductor, intending to rob him of the ticket money.
When the conductor tried to resist, he was struck on the head with an iron, from which he fell unconscious.
Then the passengers came to the conductor's aid, and a fight broke out between the passengers and the bandits.
The result was that 3 bandits were arrested and tied up, and 3 escaped.
—o—
To the address of the Będzin power station
We often receive complaints from our Będzin readers about the improper conduct of the officials of the power station (elektrownia) towards the subscribers. The complaints point out that the power-station officials cut off the light without any reason.
Yesterday Mr. Meir Szenwald, Kołłątaja 27, came to the editorial office and related that the fitter of the power station came to his flat to cut off the light; then[?] he explained to the official that the light had already been paid for and that Mr. Szenwald had the receipt. The official paid no attention to these words and cut off the light.
—o—
On prices of articles of prime necessity
From the commission for fixing prices of articles of prime necessity at the Sosnowiec magistrate (municipality) we have received the following communiqué.
All merchants are obliged to hang up in their shop, in a visible place, the price list (cennik) drawn up by the price commission.
For charging higher prices the merchant must be brought to court.
Complaints concerning the charging of high prices should be reported to the statistical offices of the Będzin and Sosnowiec magistrates, or to the alderman (ławnik) of the Sosnowiec magistrate, Dobrowolski, 6 Warszawska Street.
—o—
Brother-in-law of the Radomsko Rebbe becomes a rabbinic judge in Łódź
The brother-in-law of the Radomsko Rebbe, R' Moshele (son of the Komarno Rebbe), has been admitted as a member of the Łódź rabbinate. Yesterday the moreh-tsedek (rabbinic judge) left for Łódź accompanied by the Łódź communal leader (parnas) Mr. Mincberg. At the Sosnowiec and Będzin stations he was greeted by a large crowd of Hasidim.
—o—
„Matzot need not be clean“... so a baker explains
A policeman entered the bakery of Mr. Lipner in Sosnowiec and found that matzah baking was being carried out in unsanitary conditions.
When the policeman wanted to draw up a report, the baker explained that matzah baking is not subject to the hygiene regulations but is under the supervision of the Jewish community (gmina).
When Rabbi Hager was informed of this, he went to the bakery and saw to it[?] that the matzot should be baked in the proper manner.
—o—
Będzin is becoming like other people...
Since Wednesday the reform has been introduced at the Będzin telephone exchange. When telephoning Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa etc.[?], one must, when stating the town, at once also give the requested telephone number.
—o—
Lecture by Dr. Kruk
The new evening courses for workers in Sosnowiec are holding next Sunday evening a lecture by Dr. Y. Kruk on the subject „The bankruptcy of married life and the new social conditions“.

Notes of the Week

The Australian government has issued an order to stop immigration for Europeans.
—o—
In Lemberg [Lwów], Endek [National Democrat] academics (students) carried out antisemitic excesses against Jews.
—o—
A fire broke out in the port of New York. The damage is estimated at 30 million dollars.
—o—
Outside New York a passenger train ran onto a car in which 4 men and 4 women were sitting. All were killed on the spot.
—o—
Rabbis in Soviet Russia have permitted baking matzos from "khometsdik"[?] flour (flour not guarded for Passover).
Dąbrowa

Session of the City Council.
This coming Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a session of the local City Council will take place. Among other things, the Magistrate's proposal to take a loan of 10,000 zł. to build a public (folk) school will also be considered.
Meeting of Polish merchants.
A meeting of Polish merchants was held here. At the meeting it was decided to apply to the city administration, which should issue a ban whereby foreign merchants (read: Jews) shall not be allowed to trade in Dąbrowa at the bazaar on market days.
Dąbrowa is getting an "honoured guest"...
From 1 April an "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office] begins to operate in Dąbrowa.
Olkusz. — Protest meeting against excessive prices for matzos.

On Saturday evening[?] a protest meeting took place in the premises of the "Craftsmen's Association" against the excessive price for matzos (140 a kilo) set by the partners who have taken over the kehilla's oven.
Several speakers pointed out that last year, when flour cost almost double what it does today (likewise fuel and wages), at private bakers it cost no more than 140 a kilo, and today at the kehilla itself it is to cost 1,40 a kilo; and at the time when private bakers wanted to bake matzos at 1 zł. a kilo, only the Rabbi, may he live long, would not kosher the oven for them. It was decided to send a delegation to the Rabbi and to the gmina [municipality] to have the prices reduced. It is worth noting that before the kehilla set up its oven (two years ago) all the local bakers formed a partnership and practised profiteering ("pask") on matzos, which is why the kehilla set up an oven with its own money — and today these[?] want to do the same.
A. B.
—o—
Book chain of the Jewish Socialist Workers' Party "Poalei Zion" (united with Ts. S.) in Będzin, Modrzejowska [Mandzhever] 64.
We have received the first 50 books from Mr. Yehuda Prener, who challenges Yaakov Erlich, Aharon Hampel[?], Gaten[?] Gutman and editor Leibish Szpigelman.
—o—
Campaign for the Jewish secular school in Zagłębie
On a mission from the Central Yiddish School Organisation, the labour activist and speaker Mr. M. Mandelman of Warsaw is now staying in Zagłębie; during the coming week he will conduct in Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec a campaign for the Yiddish secular school system in Poland. In Będzin the campaign opens with a conference of all public institutions and prominent public activists who stand on the ground of Yiddish secular schools. The conference takes place on Friday evening in the hall of the Będzin City Council.
—o—
Intervention of the Chamber of Commerce concerning the advance payments (zaliczki).
The local Chamber of Commerce has applied with a memorandum to the Ministry of Finance, that from merchants trading in textiles (manufaktur), leather and grain only 40 percent advance payments of the turnover tax be taken in the year 1930.
—o—
Literary evening of "Hitachdut" in Sosnowiec.
On Saturday night "Hitachdut" arranged in its own premises a literary-musical evening for members and sympathisers of "Gordonia". Ch. Filsztajn opens the soirée and invites Messrs. Fajnrajch and Frajberg to preside. Then Mr. Frommer plays "Techezakna". Mr. Filsztajn describes the great loss that Zionism has suffered at such an important moment in Lord Balfour, and he is honoured by rising.
With the "Living Newspaper" and a "hora" dance the first part is concluded.
In the second part Gawrilowicz sings with his sister Chava "What will be the end, mamele", then Miss Yagna[?] sings "Zey a shuk mir"[?], and Gawarilowicz and Konopinski sing "Moishele".
—o—
Intervention of the Director of the Royal Academy in Antwerp on behalf of a young man from Będzin
The young Abraham Goldkorn of Będzin studies at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp. His father Berish decided that his son should break off his studies. Because of this the son informed the director of the high[?] institute that his father wants him to break off his further studies.
This week the director turned to Mr. Goldkorn with the following letter:
Mr. Goldkorn!
Your son Abraham has informed me of the decision you have taken regarding him. Allow me, Sir, who stand up before you on his side, to beg of you permission for him to continue his artistic studies at the highest institute in Antwerp, in which he is indeed one of the most outstanding pupils. It would truly be regrettable to put an obstacle to his studies at the moment when he has already found his right path, and to hinder him from attaining a career which promises him to be fruitful and famous. Believe me, Sir, that my intervention is due to the interest aroused in me by the fine artistic works of your son, who works with great enthusiasm and undoubted success. I see in him a full development of artistic talent on the way to absolute flowering.
Please accept, Mr. Goldkorn, the expressions of my esteem.
Director Opsomer.
What's Happening in Upper Silesia?

Paid with... slaps.
Hirsz Benczkowski came to a debtor in Radzionków[?], a certain merchant Mr. Y. When the debtor declared: "I have no money," Benczkowski demanded the goods back.
To this proposal the debtor at first agreed, but later he "honoured" him with... slaps.
Benczkowski, covered in blood, went off to the local police commissariat, where he asked for help. There he was answered that he should sue the assailant in court.
About the vanished Szczelczuk.
4 weeks have passed since the moment when the 45-year-old Katowice merchant Szczelczyk disappeared in a mysterious manner.
The Katowice police, which is investigating the matter, has to this day not the slightest trace of the vanished man. According to existing conjectures there is a suspicion that Szczelczyk was lured by unknown persons to Germany and perished there.
Public anti-Jewish incitement.
In the village of Michałowka[?] huge posters hang in public places with the following content: "Do not buy from any Jews"..
Unemployment grows
In the course of the week the number of unemployed increased by 800 men. Altogether there are about 33,000 unemployed in Upper Silesia.
Zawiercie — A Vice-President and an Alderman Elected

[Zawiercie — municipality.] The last session of the Zawiercie city council, at which elections were held for a vice-president [of the town] and an alderman (ławnik), aroused great interest. All the councillors were present; the gallery was full.
President Wolf points out in his speech that the previous city administration had managed affairs badly and left a deficit of 1 million 100,000 zł.
After a series of matters had been dealt with, they proceeded to the elections, which gave the following result: elected alderman was Mr. Barensztajn [?], who had been removed by the voivode.
The election of the vice-president produced no result. The candidate Cichocki [?] received only 13 votes.

Public Representation.

(After the completion of the kehilla budget. — The irresponsible tasks. — What led to the present state.)
The Będzin Jewish kehilla board has informed its members that the budget for the current year has already been drawn up, and yet, before anything else, before one even had time to examine the budget, rumours had already spread in town that it was not drawn up with deliberation by committees, but[?] that everything was carried out dictatorially by the vice-president of the kehilla board alone.
That the rumours took on serious forms can be seen already from the fact that the budget committee found it necessary to announce publicly that the rumours are unfounded.
We do not intend to analyse the matter, we do not want to conduct here an investigation of how things are in reality; for us it is enough what the public says, what the street talks about, and this very talk shows at what height the kehilla board stands, to what extent we should esteem and respect its representatives.
It goes without saying that if[?] the institution had stood at its proper height it would not have fallen so low [printed גידריג for נידריג] and given explanations that amount to: God, look, we are utterly blameless [lit. „we owe God the soul“], we have taxed nobody, that was done by the representatives of your economic organisations — i.e. quite simply, plainly: if you have any [complaints], those are to blame, but in no way whatsoever we, the kehilla representatives. So one wants to throw [the blame] onto the other — from which we see that somebody is to blame nonetheless.
Thus has fallen the institution from which we had hoped to have so much, to benefit so much. Suffice it to say of it that beyond making budgets, beyond taxing the Jewish population, it does nothing anyway. Well then, the whole year, if there is no occasion to rummage in „politics“ and scheming, people in town do not even know that we possess such an institution, for it gives us nothing, and as soon as[?] one needs it during the year one must pay well for every trifle.
The Jewish kehilla board cannot be compared even with the smallest philanthropic institution, which does something for the pennies we pay every month. The Gmina costs every average Jewish citizen a great deal of money, and it gives nothing either to him or to his poor brother, for it neither maintains institutions nor supports such. At first glance one might think who knows what obligations it has towards the Jewish population. In truth, however, this is an institution that does nothing beyond taking. It has already reached the stage where it has itself become so accustomed to this that it has forgotten that it was called to something else, and that we hoped for more from it than to have a „meysim-shtibl“ [house for preparing the dead] and to pay the annual budget — beyond that we get nothing from it. It is therefore no wonder that it has fallen so deep; with all possible means it pushed out the people who wanted to clean off the mould there and adapt the institution to the people and to the times.
We said earlier that the kehilla board provides nothing more to the Jewish population, only takes money. But if one looks deeper it turns out that even for taking money it is not competent; it does not know how the work is done, for after all everything must be done according to a certain system, according to proper order — which we do not see among the kehilla representatives.
So we see that everything and everybody has been taxed. Last year, for example, they taxed even professional beggars; this year we do not know how it looks, but since they learn nothing, they have surely [printed אורעי] made the same mistake again. The same also with unmarried young men: they are regularly taxed, without regard to the fact that they live with their parents and do not pay separately.
There are thus many items [„pozycje“] that are not paid and certainly will never be paid — so why tax such people of whom one knows in advance that they will not pay? Why create unnecessary work when one knows that nothing will come of it?
There is a large contingent of taxpayers who complained last year that they had been wronged, and since they were not reduced they do not pay at all [printed לגמרא]; now they remain indifferent, it does not interest them how much the budget for the current year amounts to, they did not even want to look at the list. That means all these are people who will not pay — so why, on the one hand, tax such people with too-high assessments and, on the other hand, burden a beggar and poor people, when it is self-evident that nothing will be collected from them? Had there been order, had the budget been approached according to a system, there would have been no need at all to tax those who cannot pay — on the contrary, one would have had to give them something, since they have nothing for a midday meal; whereas[?] those who do not pay only because they are not in a position to — one would not have needed to burden them too heavily, so that a small sum they would have tried by all means to pay; and so the kehilla gets nothing from either category.
This is what it means that they do not even understand how to collect monies, for what stands on the list in the kehilla office is still far from being paid. The kehilla board surely has enough such debts — so why must it keep people who should deal with the unpaid items, and collectors who are kept busy walking back and forth?
Even the government has realised that on such debtors it loses money [lit. „adds from its own“], that the officials dealing with uncollectable debtors have endless work, so that in the end the assessed sums are written off. And one must not forget that the Jewish communities are not as strong and powerful as the government institutions.
Besides all this — what regard and respect can the members have when they see that the kehilla leadership treats public activity lightly[?] in an extraordinary manner? Today it is not what it once was some years ago; today everything is done in such an artful way, with so much frivolity and indifference, that it is no wonder at all that the public lacks the respect and deference that ought to be due to the kehilla representation — they make themselves a laughing-stock [printed „חוכה וטלולה“].
We see that the kehilla representatives themselves are far from agreed on the matter of the budget; we know that many of them say[?] [הייסן] they will protest against the adopted budget. So one pulls this way and the other — that way.
Does all this not look like a Purim play, as if one were making fun of the other? So why wonder that the population has no regard for the kehilla representatives, when they themselves have no regard either for themselves or for the body they have the honour to represent. It is an old rule: if you want people to respect you, if you want to be esteemed and honoured, you must first of all know how to keep yourself at the proper level, and [here] you show no example of how one should relate to what ought to stand higher and how to appreciate the merits of public workers, of the kehilla representation.
R. Let.
