She Does Not Grow Older

[Feuilleton — war and peace.]
Ploni ve-Kohen.
There is an old Oriental little tale of how a witch once blessed a young fifteen-year-old prince that he should live out[?] hundreds of years, but never grow old[?].
The prince was very[?] pleased with this blessing and had the witch given a medal and many gifts.
And the blessing was indeed fulfilled: the prince outlived twenty lifetimes and old age had no power over him. The passing of the years left not the slightest impression on him. Until his death he remained a young lad, kept the same stature, the same appearance as at the moment the witch had “blessed” him.
But all his days he felt extremely unhappy, because this blessing caused him terrible sufferings and turned out to be the greatest curse that could ever have come from a witch's lips.
Firstly, there was a law in that country that a king must have a big, broad, long beard, and as long as an heir to the throne did not have such a beard he could not receive the crown.
Well, the prince turned twenty and no “seal of a beard” appeared. He turned thirty, forty, fifty — and not a sign of a beard.
So the kingdom passed to the prince's younger, bearded brother, and when the younger brother had lived out his years and died, the prince in question still had no beard and was not worthy of the throne.
And so it went on and on. Centuries passed and no beard came to the prince; he was still a young stripling.
Secondly, there was a custom there that a bridegroom must be a good few years older than the bride and must look it. Well, with his fifty-year-old[?] appearance he could not attain any match. No respectable father wanted to marry his daughter off to such a young boy, and even non-respectable fathers were not keen on him either.
But the prince was set on marrying, and once he even humbled himself so far as to ask for the hand of a simple shepherdess, but she too refused him.
And so the years ran on and the prince became a very old man, a hundred and fifty years old, but he still looked like a young whippersnapper[?], and a bachelor he still remained.
Until at long, long last a certain beggar, a drunkard, took pity on him and gave him his daughter, a twelve-year-old girl. But only now did new troubles begin: the girl grew and became a fully developed woman, while he stayed as he had been, a young boy who still ought to be playing with hobby-horses.
Then children came. At first it still went not too badly. The children played with their father as with an equal companion. But soon they left him behind; they outgrew him, became tall and broad, well-developed young men, then men. And the father was a laughing-stock to them. Instead of him managing[?] them, they managed[?] him. Instead of them obeying him, he had to obey them, or else — they would beat him.
The same spectacle repeated itself when grandchildren came. As long as the grandchildren were little they still had a good time with “grandpa”. But when they grew older and outgrew him, they would laugh and mock him: “Some grandpa for the table!”
And he died a great-great-grandfather, but into the grave went the body of a boy.
This moralizing little tale awakens in me the suspicion that some terrible witch once favoured all mankind with this kind of “blessing”. For although mankind is already an enormous old woman and has already — as the scientists would have it — put behind her a stretch[?] of hundreds of millions of years, in intellect she is still a young stripling; old age has no power over her. She has, it seems, gone through such an abyss of experiences and still behaves as when she lay in her primitive swaddling clothes.
She has gone through, for example, such terrible experiences with wars, especially with the last World War, which has truly left a lamentation for generations, deep wounds that cannot be healed — and in the end she still has the same understanding as before, in her primitive childhood years.
And when they finally get down[?] to carrying out a little bit of the programme of the prophet Isaiah's prophecy of peace, they kibitz away weeks, haggle, argue how much to reduce the fleets of destruction, and nothing comes of it, so that you must perforce conclude that none of the conferring parties is serious.
For if they truly and honestly wanted to reduce the quantity of weapons and thereby reduce the danger of war, they would come to an agreement in a jiffy. That is, every government would agree to be at one level of armament, proportionally, like the others, and nobody would want to out-diplomat[?] the others and remain stronger than them. For as soon as one wants to remain stronger, it is surely the best sign that it is saddling[?] its horse[?] for war.
I remember, when I was a little boy, two cheders[?] in our shtetl waged wars with each other. Moshe the melamed's cheder was the Turk and Bertzik the melamed's cheder was the Russian. I belonged to the Turkish army. The rebbes of both camps were pacifists and hated wars; they would thrash the “soldiers” together with the “generals” and slay[?] them every time they got a whiff of “mobilization”... Our fathers too were pacifists and on their part also chopped away as into cabbage and tried to drive out of us the appetite for war. But it did not help: we warred over field and meadow, over hill and dale, until once a real war flared up among us and several of us got split heads. Then everyone resolved, “they voted and decided”, that the war game could go to the devil, and that from this day on we would no longer mention soldiers and generals, Turks and Russians, “rifles” and “swords”.
So we, the foolish Jewish children of a small shtetl, had the sense to learn a lesson from bitter experiences: a couple of knocked-out eyes, a few split little heads cured us of war. But highly civilized mankind lost twenty million souls and inherited millions of cripples and terrible economic ruins — and that has still not brought her to her senses.
Ah, if I were, say[?], a MacDonald! I would serve them there in London, at the conference, such a portion that it would stick in their throats. I would tell them: Down with the masks, enough[?] of hypocrisy! If you are really out to prevent war, then take the military hand off the [?]... and cut the fleets as is proper, break up at least sixty percent of the cannons — otherwise, the [?]... take you, go home and say openly that you are still the same as before.
Help, Jews, when will our civilization at last begin to grow older?! When will at last a bit of true intellectual[?] [—] begin to grow in the human race
The Season of Our Bankruptcy [a pun on 'the season of our freedom', i.e. Passover]

[Humour — anecdotes; the economic crisis and bankruptcies.] A. Lemech.
(Anecdotes and jokes about today's most burning, most topical "pleite" [bankruptcy] problem...)
"We are bankrupt!"
"When a Jew is hungry, he sings," and when his heart is pounding, when his brain is whirling, when troubles darken his eyes — he cracks jokes, he laughs; nobody like the Jew can make such fun of his own misfortune, let out a ringing "ha-ha!" over his little woes. Perhaps the Jew has created as many jokes as lamentations [kinot]. If I were a painter (I have the urge) and wanted to paint a picture of Israel going along its road of exile, it would come out like this: a bloodied, tormented little Jew with a finger set against his shrewd forehead and a crooked open mouth with the tongue stuck out: ha, ha, ha!
I think that of all the good things attributed to the Jewish endurance of the bitter exile, the main one is his talent for laughing off — "let it be an atonement" [?] — all sufferings, for showing the fig [the fist gesture] to bitter fate..
And if philosophy it must be, I want to state a paradoxical truth (don't be alarmed): if all the books of Jewish life were lost, and only the Jewish jokes and anecdotes of all generations were carefully preserved, one could form from them the best idea of Jewish life, because the Jew has always painted his life with a brush of pointed sharp wit [?] dipped in a [?] mocking paint.
Polish Jewry now suffers terribly from the economic crisis and, as its consequence — bankruptcies and "pleites". And an abundance of quips and jokes is being created around it. We want to gather a few, and let the esteemed reader (and to every writer a reader is esteemed) not think that we wish to give a whole lexicon of jokes; we had indeed set ourselves such a "[?]" of dozens of anecdotes and sayings, but we limited ourselves to the theme: we are bankrupt.. Still, we pay at any rate a few percent, and that in "cash" — here, we are already counting it out, here you are..
I. Come Along to the Wedding...
A small-town rabbi of former times fixed the wedding date of his daughter for a certain day. The rosh hakahal [head of the community] apparently knew nothing of it, and when he set the wedding date of his only daughter it fell, as bad luck would have it, on the same day. At the rosh hakahal's they began preparing for the wedding of his only daughter with great preparations and invited all the town's rich men, who were, by the way, his customers. Only at the end does he learn that the rabbi is holding a wedding on the same day. Fearing that all the rich men would rather be the rabbi's wedding guests and that only the paupers would dance at his, he quickly summons the rabbi and presents him with an ultimatum: to call off his daughter's wedding date. Hearing [?] such words from the mouth of the rosh hakahal, the greatest magnate and strongman of the town, the rabbi feels a bitter taste in his mouth. It is, after all, a great disgrace to call off a wedding date. But a Jew, a Torah scholar, finds a solution: the rabbi will proclaim under ban and prohibition that no rich man may come to his wedding, only poor people; consequently the rosh hakahal will have all the rich men as guests and all will be well.
Evening of the wedding day. At the rosh hakahal's, tables are laid fit for a king, as only such a magnate can afford, a full band, everything in order — only the guests don't come.. It is already getting dark, quite late, and the town's rich men are neither seen nor heard.. The rosh hakahal grows uneasy. He takes a servant and sends him to see what is happening at the rabbi's. The servant comes back with the news that all the rich men are gathered at the rabbi's. The rosh hakahal is furious: how can it be?! The ban broken?.. He runs quickly to the rabbi and, standing on the threshold of the rabbi's home and seeing the rich men, shouts in anger: "[unclear: 'haz Moshe zagne'?]!? There is a ban that no rich man may come here — and you, Berl?!" — — —
The rich men stand up and swear every oath that they are not rich men at all.. that they are stark-naked poor people, they are "under themselves" (bankrupt, in plain language).
"If so," exclaims the rosh hakahal, turning pale, "if so, then I too am a pauper: my whole fortune is spread out among you, and if you are bankrupt, then I too am a pauper.."
"Then come along," they all cry, "to the paupers' wedding! Come along to the wedding! By all means, wash your hands with us [for the meal].."
II. So That He Shouldn't Forget...
A Jewish merchant who went bankrupt only half a year ago and has now pulled the trick again is asked [?]: "How can it be, Berl! Did you really need [printed 'bearapst'] to go bankrupt a second time? It seems the business wasn't so bad —"
Berl replies: "I'll tell you a story. A tailor, as is well known [printed 'kirua'], likes to filch a bit of cloth from every garment he is given to sew. Such is his nature. After the season, when there is no work, the tailor usually sews garments for himself and his children. Once his wife notices that while cutting a garment for their boy he takes off a piece of cloth and hides it.. She asks him: 'Fool, what are you stealing from yourself?'
"'Listen, my wife,' he answers, 'I'm afraid that during the workless days I'll meanwhile forget how one steals, and so that I shouldn't forget, I filch meanwhile [?] from myself..'
"Yes, my dears," Berl concludes, "I am going bankrupt now once more, although I don't need to, so that I shouldn't, God forbid, forget in the meantime..."
III. "Since You're Already Playing..."
In olden times there was a custom that when someone went bankrupt, an organ-grinder would come with a barrel organ [katarynka] and play a special song in front of the shop. Once a false rumour was spread about a merchant that he had gone bankrupt. The organ-grinder knows nothing about business and goes off to play there. The merchant comes out in a rage: "What impudence? I haven't gone bankrupt!"
"But," he reconsiders after a while, "since you're already playing, so be it.. never mind.. play on.. so now I'm bankrupt..."
Help Build a Sanatorium for Jewish Academics!

(On the campaign which begins in Zagłębie next week).
In March 1923 a committee was founded in Lemberg [Lwów], which set itself the task of leading the work of building a sanatorium for Jewish academics [university students]. In that same year the committee bought a plot for the building in Worochta [?] (Carpathians) and wanted to start construction. But from the very first minute one ran into difficulties that were very hard to overcome. Because of the economic crisis in the years 1924, 1925 it was impossible to collect the necessary financial means to begin building. Only in 1927 was the work begun, and it was interrupted several times for lack of funds. At the present moment the sanatorium is still not a reality; we still cannot open its gates to the sick student. The idea came from us; our achievements so far [?] are great. We show the public what we have created so far and demand help and support in the further work. We demand of the public that it fulfil its duty and enable the completion of this splendid building. It is remarkable and sad that the public in Congress Poland has so far contributed the least to this useful work which is being created.
The hygienic and sanitary conditions in the life of the Jewish academic compel us to build the sanatorium as quickly as possible. It springs from reality; it is the greatest necessity of the moment. Statistics show a great deal of tuberculosis and other diseases among Jewish students. The Jewish student, who runs all day from one lesson to another in order to earn his living — and often does not even have that — who studies at night in a small attic room or in a damp cellar. The Jewish academic now comes to the Jewish public and asks for help. Whoever wants the coming generation to be healthy, whoever does not want to allow the physical degeneration of the future Jewish intelligentsia, will not refuse. Come and help the sick Jewish academic, come and wipe away the tears of the mother who can give her child nothing more than motherly love. We believe in your human conscience, we believe in your Jewish heart. Our victory and yours will be the first academic who regains his health in the sanatorium.
Stud. A. Gertner.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The PPS Wants to Express No Confidence in the Chairman of the City Council, Mr. Fürstenberg

[Head of the local page; Będzin — City Council.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 6 Nisan 5690 — Piątek 4 kwietnia 1930 [Friday, 4 April 1930].)
Będzin
The PPS wants to express no confidence in the chairman of the City Council, Mr. Fürstenberg.
At Tuesday's session the PPS "club" (faction) submitted a motion to express a vote of no confidence in the chairman of the City Council, Mr. Fürstenberg. The matter will be dealt with at the next session. (It should be noted that although our councillors[?] knew in advance that the PPS was preparing such a motion, they came to the session when the matter had already been taken off the agenda.)
Then the statutes of the municipal power station (elektrownia) and waterworks were discussed and adopted in second reading.
At the session it was also considered, for the first time, to levy road tax (podatek drogowy) on the owners of new houses. Vice-chairman Rubinlicht was against, but the majority was in favour.
—o—
[Będzin — Taxes and Trade.]
Będzin merchants are "defended" in the "Izba Skarbowa" (Treasury Chamber).
Hundreds of appeals are simply ignored.
A few weeks ago we drew attention in our paper to the fact that at the sessions of the "Izba Skarbowa" in Kielce, where the various tax appeals are dealt with, the Będzin merchant community had no representative who would support the grievances of the hundreds of afflicted[?] merchants.
For 10 years the fight was carried on for Będzin and also Sosnowiec to obtain a seat on the appeals commission; finally this was achieved, and, as we are informed, at the last sessions in the Izba the representative[?] of the Będzin merchants was not present. The result is self-evident: hundreds of appeals were not defended at all.
—o—
[Będzin — Economy and Banking.]
Annual general meeting of the Discount Bank.
On Sunday the general meeting of the members of the Discount Bank took place in the hall of the Będzin City Council. The board had hoped that the 400 invited members would come and hired[?] the large hall of the City Council; but only a little over a hundred members came, who were very comfortable sitting and strolling about the hall..
The chairman of the supervisory council, Mr. Lidzi-Barski (Lidzbarski), opens the meeting with a short introduction, and on his proposal the chair is handed over to Mr. Meir Cimberknap[?]. As assessors: Herman Fride, Herman Pinkus, Meir Berdi[?], Kalman Hejde, and secretary Icchak Granek.
After the reading of the minutes of the previous general meeting, reports are given. On the activity during the year 1929 the bank director Mr. S. Jakubowski reports, illustrating with figures the growth of the bank during the past year. For example, shares (udziały) reached 60,566 zł. in 1929. Bills of exchange[?]: in 1928, 245,870 zł., and in 1929 — 593,206 zł. Collections (inkaso): in 1928 — 6,901,065 zł.; in 1929 — 9,611,122 zł. Net profit 20,000 zł.
Report on the activity of the council — D. Gutensztajn. He declares that the council fulfilled its task properly, supervised the activity and carried out all its functions.
After the reading of the report of the Audit Union[?] a discussion develops. The discussion did not concern the reports, but the fact that the balance sheet is solely in the Polish language. Because of this, Mr. L. Rozenblum stresses, a large number of members did not come, since they were not aware that the balance sheet concerned the meeting.
Explanations regarding the reproach are given by Messrs. G. Tenenberg and S. Jaki-Bawski [sic; = Jakubowski]. But an end to the discussion is put by Mr. Lirzbarski [sic; = Lidzbarski], who cries "Selach na" (forgive us)!.. and promises that next year the Jewish language (Yiddish) will not be forgotten... The audience is satisfied, and all with one voice express thanks to the chairman Mr. A. Tra-Pojer[?] for his great achievements for the bank, to the honorary president Mr. Pinkus, to the director Jakubowski and to the whole board and council.
The profit of 20 thousand zł. remains, by agreement of those assembled, as reserve capital. The budget of about 25[?] thousand zł. is adopted. Then it is resolved: 1) the bank has the right to rediscount up to 1 million zł.; and 2) the credit per member — up to 10 thousand zł.
The elections of 3 members to the board and 4 to the supervisory council gave the following result:
Board: Szaul Fridler, Nachman Tenenberg and Józef Rus.
Council: Herszel Stopnicki, Dawid Gitler, Z. Zygelbojm and Abraham Isachar Rechnic.
—o—
[Będzin — Crime.]
He made a mistake in his accounts — and accused a Jew.
The cashier at the local notary (rejent) Mr. Czyszek[?] made a mistake in the till on Friday; he was short a sum of one thousand zł. On the same day an employee of the textile (manufaktura) shop "Tekstyl", Mr. Fruchtbaum, had paid a bill of exchange for one thousand zł. When the cashier saw that he was short such a sum, he suspected that he had not received the thousand zł. from Fruchtbaum for the bill. He therefore turned to the police and demanded, on his own responsibility, that he be arrested.
The demand was carried out and Fruchtbaum was arrested. Later the cashier found that he had made a mistake, and F. was released.
—o—
[Będzin — Passover and Matzot.]
Many bakers — 1.20 zł. Fewer bakers — 1.40 zł.
This year, before matzah baking began, the bakers held a meeting at which it was calculated that the price of matzot should be no more than 1.20 zł. per kilo. The calculation was made when a large number of bakers who had the intention ("bre'ah" [sic; = de'ah]) to bake matzot figured on the list; but when the number of those baking matzot became smaller, the price immediately went up to 1.40 zł. per kilo.
—o—
[Będzin — Charity and Passover.]
The traditional tea gift from the Wysocki firm.
The well-known tea firm W. Wysocki, which distributes tea for Passover to Zagłębie institutions, has this week too informed us, through its representative Mr. I. S. Nagenhajch[?], that tea has been dispatched which is to be distributed by the editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
On the quantity and the distribution — in the next issue.
—o—
[Będzin — Institutions.]
Reorganisation of the Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund.
The board of the Gemilut Chesed fund, seeing that it is losing more and more the confidence of the population, has now set about reorganising the institution. For this purpose a report conference was called for Sunday the 6th of this month, to which representatives[?] of the local economic organisations and public workers were invited.
The conference will have the task of examining the activity so far, creating a council and so on.
It is desirable that all those invited should come to the conference, so that the institution may be set[?] on the proper level.
—o—
[Zagłębie — Politics.]
Premier Sławek as leader of the PPS Central Committee in Zagłębie.
Concerning the biography of the present Premier Sławek we are given the following details: Walery Sławek was elected in 1902 as a member of the PPS Central Committee (C.K.) in Zagłębie. In 1903 he is arrested in Będzin, where he sits half a year in prison. From Będzin he is transferred to the prison in Sieradz, from where he escapes to his parents in Ukraine.
—o—
[Będzin — Charity and Passover.]
Many needy — little money.
The Kimcha [de-Pischa] commission is receiving very many letters from respectable needy people asking for Passover support. Therefore everyone who is able to give for this purpose should hurry with his donation, for "the time is short and the work is great".
Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — education; followed by ten short news items: trade, accidents, charity, Zionism, rabbinate, excursions.]
Jewish landlord wants to evict the Jewish gymnasium
As we learn, Mr. J. Grigbojm [?] [probably Grünbaum], the owner of the house in which the Jewish gymnasium in Sosnowiec is located, has obtained at the Warsaw Court of Appeal an eviction order against the Jewish gymnasium. We cannot believe, however, that there should be a Jewish landlord who would permit himself to throw a Jewish school out onto the street and thereby ruin an institution that is now the pride of Jewish Sosnowiec.
—o—
Action of the Small Traders' Association against the „grabbers“
The board of the Small Traders' Association has turned with a memorandum to the Chamber of Commerce concerning the fight against the so-called „customer-grabbers“ in the town.
—o—
Tragic death of a child
At the „Mak“ [?] coal mine in Zagórze, 4-year-old Jandrusik fell under a cart loaded with stones. The boy was killed on the spot. The horses of the cart were being driven by a brother of the tragically killed boy. After the catastrophe the brother wanted to commit suicide.
—o—
Collection of old clothes
The Women's Committee of the local Charity Association has, as last year, organised a collection of old clothes, linen, shoes, etc., which will be distributed among the poor population for the holiday.
In connection with this we have received from the above-mentioned association an appeal to the Jewish public in Sosnowiec to [?] support this important campaign.
The donated clothes are accepted at Mrs. Dr. Grudzińska's, Kowalska 2.
—o—
Academy of „Herzliya“
In connection with the 5th anniversary of the existence of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, the local Zionist youth organisation named after Theodor Herzl is arranging on Tuesday, 15 April, at the Municipal Theatre a grandiose festive academy with a very rich musical programme. Several prominent Zionist personalities are to take part in the academy.
—o—
Elections to the district conference
Next Sunday, from the afternoon on, elections of delegates to the regional conference, which takes place during Chol HaMoed Passover in Kielce, will be held at the premises of the local Zionist Organisation.
—o—
A sermon in the synagogue
This Sabbath afternoon Rabbi [printed „hib“] Frommer will deliver a sermon in the synagogue. In the morning Rabbi Hager was to deliver a sermon, but since Rabbi Hager is sitting shiva for his late mother, he will not deliver the sermon.
—o—
Tried to „stop“ the tram
On Wednesday, on Żeromskiego Street, a young Christian tried to „stop“ the tram. From the blow he received he was thrown onto the pavement. Luckily he came out unharmed.
—o—
A three-day excursion to Warsaw
The Jewish Society for Regional Studies (Land-Knowledge), Zagłębie branch, is organising a 3-day excursion to Warsaw on 19, 20 and 21 April.
More detailed information is given in Będzin by Miss Mitlis [?], Kołłątaja 45, and in Sosnowiec by Mr. Kamps [?], Kowalska 10.
—o—
A lecture
The Cultural Committee of the Zionist Organisation is holding on Sunday, at its own premises, a lecture by a member of the Zionist Central Committee, Magister Polakiewicz, on the subject „The situation in Polish Zionism“.
—o—
Found murdered
A certain Swoboda, 28 years old, was found murdered on the „hałdy“ (mine waste heaps). The police have established that comrades murdered him.
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — education; followed by four items: KKL, town council, murder, fire.]
A „Jewish“ elementary school
Here we also have 10 public elementary (powszechne) schools, and among them there is not a single school where only Jewish children would study. On this question councillor Rechnic conferred with the president [mayor] and the chairman of the town council, who promised that for the new school year a separate elementary school will be opened for the Jewish pupils.
—o—
A film of life in the Land of Israel
On the initiative of the local Keren Kayemet committee, a Jewish film entitled „Spring in Eretz Israel“ will be shown from next Monday on. The picture acquaints the audience with the life of the Jewish colonists, blossoming towns and villages, schools and many interesting moments of the new Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel.
—o—
From the town council
At the „annual“ [?] (printed „shnasdiger“) session of the town council a number of statutes were approved, among them the statute on railway loadings. Against the statute were several councillors of the Endecja, who stressed that the tax would cause products of basic necessity to become more expensive. The speakers therefore proposed that the statute should not apply to articles of basic necessity.
The proposal was rejected by the B.B. majority.
—o—
A woman planned to murder her husband
On Saturday at 3 before dawn a murdered man was found not far from the railway station. The police, who energetically set about investigating, established that it was 41-year-old Michał Kuc, a laid-off worker.
About the mysterious murder we are given the following details. Kuc lives in the village of Panki near Częstochowa; Kuc's wife has a lover in the same village, and the two of them worked out a plan to get Kuc out of the world. For this purpose the „woman of valour“ gave her kochanek money to buy a revolver with which he would murder her husband. The kochanek bought a revolver, and when Kuc travelled to Dąbrowa he travelled along with him. Arriving on Kościuszki Street, the kochanek fired 5 times at Kuc and murdered him. After carrying out the murder, the kochanek went home to inform the „woman of valour“ that their plan had been carried out.
The police went to Panki and there arrested the murderer together with his kochanka. Both were brought before the local examining magistrate and then sent to the Będzin prison.
—o—
A fire
On Wednesday at midday a fire broke out in the courtyard of Mr. Greitzer's house; the local firemen put the fire out.

HIS MOTHER,

express their deep sympathy. (348)
Died at the Market.
[Upper Silesia — sudden death.] In Nikolai (Mikołów), the horse dealer Bibi[?] Kizman died suddenly at the market. Doctors established that Kizman had suffered a heart attack.
“Hashachar” in Tarnowitz.

[Upper Silesia — organisations.] In Tarnowitz (Tarnowskie Góry), on the initiative of a group of young people, an organisation “Hashachar” was founded. The organisation, which was led by Rabbi Dr. Ribner[?], developed well within a short time, but among the members, who consist of “Polish” and “German” Jews, a sharp conflict arose over the leadership, and the result is that the “Polish” members have for the time being left the organisation.
Tram Collision.

[Upper Silesia — accident.] On the Świętochłowice—Hajduki line a collision occurred between 2 trams. The front cars were damaged and several passengers were injured by glass from the smashed windowpanes.
Brawl in Court.

[Katowice — court.] At the Katowice district court a trial took place against several criminals. While the judges had gone off to deliberate, the accused began to make a scandal and threw themselves at the court guard to beat him. The police, who were called in, put an end to the brawl.
The Liability of the Italian Insurance Companies in Poland.

[Insurance — economy.] Not long ago a report appeared in some daily newspapers that the Italian insurance companies in Poland are not liable in Poland with their foreign assets for their obligations towards the insured in Poland. Elsewhere[?] in this issue is the content of the resolution of the united life-insurance companies in Poland, which deny the said rumours and establish that the Italian companies are also liable with their assets located outside the borders of Poland.
—o—
Theatre Repertoire for the Coming Holiday.
[Będzin — theatre.] The coming Passover brings Jewish theatre-goers unexpected[?] guests. An artistic event is the visit of the world-famous “Habima”, which will stage next Tuesday “Keter David” (The Crown of David), a tragedy by Calderón. It goes without saying that the news about “Habima” has aroused enormous interest.
* * *
The Będzin “Muza” is giving a premiere for the holiday. We shall see: 1) “The Golden Chain” by I. L. Peretz, 2) “Rags” (Shmates) by Leivick and 3) “Elijah the Prophet” by Peretz Hirschbein. The performances will be given on Monday in Dąbrowa and on Wednesday in Będzin. We wish to hope that the audience will leave with the same impression as from “At Night in the Old Marketplace”.
* * *
On Saturday the 19th we shall have a very distinguished guest in Zagłębie. The actor Jonas Turkow, beloved in Zagłębie, is coming here with his good ensemble to perform “The Cause” (Di sibe), a famous psychological drama in 4 acts, which made an impression in the European centres and is being performed for the first time under the direction of Jonas Turkow.
* * *
For the holiday the cinema “Nowości” is showing the latest world hit “4 Devils[?]”. First-class actors take part in this picture, and the technique too stands at a high level. Besides this a lively supporting programme is given.
— The “Kameo” too has prepared a rich programme of pictures and an interesting supporting programme for the holiday.
Social Notes.

[Będzin / Sosnowiec — society and culture.] 4716 zł income from a ball.
The supervisory board of the “S. Fürstenberg” gymnasium organised last month a ball for the benefit of needy pupils.
Great interest was shown by the chairman of the board, Mr. Fürstenberg, who sold among his merchants tickets to the sum of 1,608 zł. In total the income was 4716 zł.
A collective lecture.
On Monday the 14th of this month the “Poalei Zion” (united with the Z.S. [Zionist-Socialists]) is organising in Będzin a collective lecture with discussion by: Moshe Nusman[?] and Yehuda Frener on the topic “Our Credo”. In the name of the Revisionists David Hofer will appear. All political groupings will be admitted.
Academy of “Herzliya”.
On Thursday, the 3rd day of Chol HaMoed Pesach, “Herzliya” in Sosnowiec is organising a rich academy in honour of the 5th anniversary of the opening of the Hebrew University. Besides the varied musical-vocal part, there will take part in the academy the Sosnowiec rabbi, Rabbi Hager, Rabbi Dr. Chameides, Dr. Meladista[?] and Magister Polakiewicz.
A Letter to the Editor.

[Dąbrowa — taxes and trade.] Esteemed editor of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung”!
We ask you to print the following letter in your newspaper.
As is known, an “Urząd Skarbowy” (tax office) is being created here; in connection with this we were called upon by our headquarters to send lists of candidates to the tax office, since we, as an economic organisation, must have our own representatives; above all the small traders in Dąbrowa, who languish under the tax burden, are vitally interested, because until now we have had no representative of our own in the tax offices. But we were astonished when, a day before the sessions for assessing the turnover tax for the year 1929, someone went round in Dąbrowa to every merchant with a list on which figured the hitherto members of the assessment commission, and every merchant was told that “there exists in Dąbrowa no merchants' and small traders' association” and that only these persons and no others must be the public representatives in the new office being created. Those who did not want to sign were threatened that they would have something to remember[?]... Against such conduct we protest most strongly, and against the methods by which people push their way into the tax offices; we are firmly convinced that the Jewish small trader, who groans under the tax burden, will no longer let himself be terrorised and will know how to react to the conduct of such “public representatives”...
Respectfully,
Central Small Traders' Association, Warsaw, Dąbrowa Branch.

The Chamber of Commerce. (Which section should interest us? What can and what must be done there by us?)

Jewish merchants have several times drawn our attention to the fact that the "Izba Handlowa" [Chamber of Commerce] located in Sosnowiec does not bring the proper benefit to the Jewish merchant community in Zagłębie, i.e. it could do considerably more for the commercial world if we had a Jewish vice-president here.
Because the institution that has been created[?] is beginning to penetrate more and more into commercial circles, and because it is very little known to the Jewish merchant, it would therefore be desirable to dwell on the question and to deal with it.
It is therefore important to give some explanations about the institution. In the "Izba Handlowa" there are several sections; what interests us here is the commercial section. Each section has its president and two vice-presidents; it goes without saying that the commercial section too has the same number of presidents. The president, a Christian, is in Sosnowiec, and the two vice-presidents, of whom one is a Christian and the other a Jew, both live in Częstochowa. On top of that, fate willed that the Christian vice-president should resign from his office, so that at present there is only one vice-president, and even that one is as if he did not exist, especially for the population of Zagłębie.
The Jewish vice-president is the Częstochowa owner of an optical warehouse ("optyk-skład"), Mr. Gutfeld[?], a very honest man; but firstly, we do not have him in Zagłębie, and secondly he is an elderly man who is moreover ill, so that he was operated on not long ago and is now staying at a health resort, and is therefore not able to act for our economic interests.
From this one can see that even Częstochowa gets nothing out of him.
So it turns out that the commercial section, which should have been the most capable and the most important, does not have a single vice-president. It is therefore self-evident that the work there cannot be carried out properly and that the necessary matters cannot be settled to the best advantage of the merchants. It is thus, first and foremost, a terrible wrong that the members of the commercial section take it so lightly that they work with one vice-president, at a time when there ought to be two. Such an important question must not be left hanging in the air like this. One must see to it that first of all the board is complete, so that the whole work can be conducted in a planned way.
The section must therefore have, like all the other sections, two active [vice-]presidents, with whom it can work jointly — and that is not such a great matter either. As it is, the Christian vice-president has resigned his office, so another can come in in his place. As for Mr. Gutfeld, it should be explained to him that under the prevailing conditions it is impossible for him to remain effective for the time being; he should therefore resign, and another Jew should take his place. Mr. Gutfeld will no doubt accept the request, so that the board can be completed.
Now then, about a Jewish candidate. Just as the Christian is a Częstochowa man, the Jewish one must be from Zagłębie. The candidacy is due to us for several reasons: firstly, one must not forget that not a single meeting may be missed on our side, and a Częstochowa Jew will not be able to attend to them as well as a local man, a Jew from Zagłębie. After all, one must not forget that from Częstochowa to Sosnowiec and back the journey takes about[?] 6 hours, whereas we here are always at home, where every meeting can be attended on time. And secondly, Jewish Zagłębie has priority, because the number of Jews here is greater.
It is self-evident that Zagłębie has no benefit at all from a representative who lives in Częstochowa. Imagine that a Jew from Będzin, Sosnowiec or Dąbrowa has a complaint to make and for that purpose needs the Jewish vice-president — in that case he will have to travel to Częstochowa. Is that reasonable? Is it logical, sensible, practical? Of course this is a cardinal fault, from which the Jewish population of Zagłębie has no benefit whatsoever, and therefore such faults must be corrected. The change must therefore be carried out as quickly as possible, so that it may be for the good of the Jewish population, for the good of Jewish Zagłębie.
As regards Zagłębie, the mandate ought to go to Będzin, because — the same thing again — Sosnowiec has the president, and secondly Będzin is the heart of Jewish Zagłębie, so it should have priority.
At the same time, however, one must not forget that this is not yet everything. With Będzin getting the mandate the question is still far from solved, for we do not mean prestige alone. In economic questions honour is not everything; the main thing is activity, orientation, ability, being well-versed, and knowing how to defend and guard our vital positions.
As said, the "Izba Handlowa" now plays a very important role in the world of commerce, and the prospects for the future look as if they will become even stronger. Therefore one must not remain indifferent to this important institution. If we remain apathetic at the present moment, we harm Jewish commercial interests. Already because of the Christians our representatives must not display their indifference. Let them not think that we hand everything over into the hands of their fate. Let them see that we are on guard, that we protect our interests, that we are capable and can defend ourselves, can guard our positions ourselves.
Only at that moment will the Christians reckon with their Jewish colleagues, when they see that they understand their tasks, that they do not want to sell the birthright for a pot of lentils, that they know exactly their tasks and duties towards their brethren.
Everywhere we are represented, and everywhere we can help solve and ease our conditions of existence, we are obliged to do so. We must not let any opportunity slip by; we must always[?] and everywhere stand on guard, protect our interests and ease our conditions of existence.
We must show the Chamber of Commerce that we have something to say there and something to demand, and for that purpose Jewish Zagłębie must have its own vice-president in the merchants' section, where it undoubtedly plays a significant role.
Let this position not be let slip by us, let it not be neglected, at a time when it has the right to play the most significant role.
Y. Sh.

I Laugh at the Crisis...

[Feuilleton — Passover humour; the economic crisis.] Why am I so cheerful? What has come over me, this grandeur? Why shouldn't I be cheerful? Why shouldn't I rejoice, why? A trifle, a small joy — you throw off the yoke of earning a living; and that a Jew like me is already provided for the eight days of Passover — is that a small pleasure?
Yes, gentlemen, I am a happy man. Who can compare himself to me? What is Szymon Fürstenberg to me, or even Rothschild; what is the crisis to me, and when is there a crisis for me? I laugh at the crisis, and basta! Thanks to the crisis I have become a free bird, a man without worries, a man without troubles and without headaches. I know [?] nothing of bills of exchange, of protests, of sequestrators with bailiffs (komorniks); I laugh at the creditors with their clauses — I laugh at the crisis, and enough!
What, so to speak [?], did I have before the crisis? I had a drapery (manufaktura) shop; day and night I had to deal with taking bills and giving bills, books, bookkeepers, balance sheets, discounters, "reyentn" [?], banks, a din [?], a hullabaloo — my head spun like a windmill, always late, always toiling, and always I was a gulden short of a rouble...
And when you have a shop with laced (officially sealed) account books and balance sheets, you must after all have a respectable flat. So my missus indeed "furnished" herself a flat befitting a Jew with a wallet: a "salon" [?] with a "bedroom", with a "children's room", with a "…-room" [?], with a "…" [?] and other "conveniences". And when you have a flat with such "conveniences", you must after all have "appropriate furnishings". So she indeed "furnished" herself with wardrobes [?], with "pomatsnikes" [?], with "…" [?] beds, "kovetkes" [?] with Turkish and Chinese cushions and other trinkets. And when you are so "furnished", when you have "…" [?] beds with Chinese and Japanese "cushions", you must after all have servants, chambermaids and governesses. And when a Jewish wife has servants, chambermaids and governesses — you already understand that the home is a hell: every month a different servant, every week a different chambermaid, every few days a different governess. And when you have such a "comfortable" flat and every month different servants, you must after all invite guests, and when the guests come [?], you must after all "entertain" them...
So indeed I had neither day nor night. By day in the shop, taking and giving bills; when I came home I had to "entertain" the guests and "calm down" [?] my wife, the Madame, about the servants, the chambermaids and the governesses — I did not have a single quiet minute.
Now I am a happy man. The bit of merchandise was taken by the "Treasury" (skarb); the wardrobes with the "pomatsnikes" [?], with the "kovetkes" [?] and with the Chinese and Turkish "cushions" I handed over "for safekeeping" to the Magistrate for the "rent tax" and "income tax". The "comfortable" flat was taken by the landlord. I am left with my old "estate", as my wife calls it, and I lead a decent life... I have nothing to do with any bills of exchange, I need no bookkeepers, no discounters, no books with balance sheets; my little wife doesn't tear her heart out with the servants, the chambermaids and the governesses. A worry is off her head: watching whether the shikse nibbles from the pots and whether the governess is not a little "dasig" [?] towards me.. At night I don't come home "tsepakhmeter" [?] (worn out) and I don't have to "entertain" the guests. I am a free bird, I have no troubles, and I laugh at the crisis!..
What do I do, where does one get a living from? Who says I have a living at all? And when did I ever have a living? In the days of the wardrobes with the "pomatsnikes" [?], with the Chinese "cushions" and the governesses — did I have a living then? Ah, you ask, what does such a [?] Jew do about his stomach? Utter mockery [?]: if my wife has got out of the habit of squabbling with the servants, the stomach can get out of the habit of eating...
But the worst of all was with Passover. Well, all year round one gets through somehow — eating, not eating — nonsense; as you say: the stomach isn't made of glass — it must [?] not what it is given.. But the worst of all was with Passover: how does one bring in Passover!
That very question my missus asked: tell me, Hersh Ber, what will be with Passover? You've completely forgotten that Passover is coming — how shall we make Passover?
Laugh it off! I reassured my wife. You'll see that, God willing, we will make Passover together with all Jews; you'll see, Yente-Gele, that I shall be a king, as is right and proper.
On the contrary, she says, I am really curious to know how, from what business.
If so, I say to her, I will tell you a little story. Just listen to me carefully:
A Hasid came to the Rebbe around Purim and complained: bad business, Passover is pressing, what does one do?
Don't grieve, the Rebbe reassured him, go home in life and peace — with the Almighty's help there will be Passover.
Two weeks [?] went by; the Hasid comes again to the Rebbe: holy Rebbe, what does one do? It is already two weeks to Passover.
Go home, I told you once that there will be Passover.
When it was already right before Passover, only a few days left, at other neighbours' there were already matzos in the house, the Passover borscht had already been set — the Hasid again runs to the Rebbe with a cry: holy Rebbe, Passover is already at the door, what does one do?
Go home in life and peace, the Rebbe said again — there will be Passover.
Well, well, my wife grew curious, did the Rebbe's words come true?
Of course, I say, they came true. On the morning of Passover eve the Hasid went off with his wife's little gold watch to the pawnshop (lombard) — and the Rebbe's words came true — the Hasid made Passover.. You'll see, I said to my wife, there will be Passover. Not only will it be — it is already here. As for Passover, I have no more worries.
Who needs to worry, when [?] I am registered with "Beit Lechem", my wife has registered with "Dobroczynność" (Charity), and since my daughter has a "military education" she has signed up for the soldiers' seders. Well [?], I ask you, am I not provided for Passover with every good thing, and am I not a king and my wife a queen!
Yes, gentlemen, thanks to the crisis I have become a free bird — without troubles, without worries, without business, without a "comfortable" flat, without servants, without chambermaids, without governesses — I laugh at the crisis, and basta!..
Ab Nek.
Our Economic Interests

(Taxes, taxes above everything. — How are the positions guarded on the part of the authorities, and how do we guard them?)
To speak now about the economic situation in Poland in general and about our own position in particular is undoubtedly the hardest thing under the prevailing conditions[?], when everywhere the difficulty of existence shows itself, when at every step one sees nothing but economic ruin, when the most solid firms go out of business, when the pillars of Polish industry, which employed many thousands of workers, leave the arena entirely.
The economic ruin penetrates[?] into every corner of everyday life. Systematically one gets used to the cruellest conditions. Had someone come, say, a year or two ago and said that the first-class manufacturer X or Y would within a year not be worth a single shilling, that person would without doubt have been considered out of his mind; such a one would have been taken for mentally ill. Now that the bombs explode one by one[?], people have become as indifferent to it as to the explosions on the battlefield; one gets used to the troubles and the persecutions and forgets how bad things are now and how much better they once were...
One does not notice at all that things have reached the stage where one is afraid[?] to let the piece of merchandise out of one's hand; and of course, living in such an atmosphere one cannot achieve much, one cannot trade properly, earnings have stopped altogether; one trades just for form's sake — because one wants to live, because one has an open shop, because one employs people, because one pays taxes and because one must keep turning with the round dance. Who is even talking about making turnover properly, as the business or the enterprise requires.
But when one goes into the offices [urzędy][?], one is beside oneself on hearing there how well the citizens of the country are doing; and regardless of the stagnation in all branches, of the unemployment, it turns out, according to the naczelniks[?] [office heads], that turnover in the country is growing from year to year, so that the turnover tax must be larger every year. Is that not ridiculous? Does it not look like a comedy? One could split one's sides laughing, were it not so tragic, did it not cost the livelihood of thousands of citizens. What does it mean that last year bigger banquets[?] were held, at a time when the crisis and unemployment and the turnovers[?] forgot [—][?]? Is it not ridiculous that at such a moment, when the citizens are under the heavy yoke of the taxes, which they can no longer drag along, people come forward with proposals to raise the taxes? What happens? Since there are now (with the constant "failures"[?]) fewer taxpayers, those who still exist must carry on their shoulders the taxes that the firms which have now dropped out would have had to pay.
Only now do we see how naive[?] we were in thinking that at last the government would realise that it must loosen the tax screw a little, which the citizens can no longer bear. Only now does one see that this was nothing more than a dream of people with great fantasies, for how could one think of such a thing when even now, in this terrible crisis, one can come forward with proposals to raise the turnover tax. Of course this exceeds every limit; of course logically thinking citizens understood that at a time when a crisis reigns in the country, when posts are being cut and first-class officials and workers are being dismissed altogether, it is self-evident that at such a time business interests do not flourish, and therefore[?] the taxes too must be reduced. But it turned out otherwise: instead of reducing, one actually has to fight and stand on guard so that the taxes are not raised. Can simple people from the world of trade understand such tactics, such calculations?
Watching this "righteous" conduct on the part of the tax offices, one only then understands how necessary a "citizens' guard" is, which would stand and guard the citizens' interests. We know perfectly well that many mistakes are made because our representatives do not understand their tasks and do not guard their interests.
A year ago, for example, the population of Będzin was badly wronged in the income tax, because our representatives took the matter lightly and hardly came to the sessions, and those who did come now and then were so poorly informed that they might as well have stayed at home; as a result many in town were badly wronged and a great deal of Jewish money was squeezed out[?].
We thought that the lesson, which cost the Jewish population so dearly, would teach the representatives for the future; but apparently we were mistaken, and now too an unheard-of injustice has been done to the population of Będzin, which must not be passed over in silence.
For years Będzin has been trying to be represented in the "Izba Skarbowa" [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce, where the tax appeals are examined. At last it succeeded, and Będzin had the opportunity to have its representative present when the appeals were dealt with — but here something unheard-of happened: Będzin was not represented at all. Although it had the opportunity and the right to have its representative on the commission, nobody went, and of course in that case the appeals were looked at through the fingers, since there was nobody to report on them.
Must such injustices be tolerated with indifference? Is this the way to defend painful public questions which touch our economic interests?
So it turns out that, in the opinion of the offices[?], we must pay as much tax as possible, and however much one pays it is always too little — that is from their side; and from our side, further, there is nobody to point out the injustices, nobody to defend the hard position of the Jewish citizen.
And what impression does the whole matter of appeals make on the naczelnik[?] in Kielce, as soon as he sees that the town does not find it necessary to send its representative there? In this case they surely reckon in Kielce that writing appeals is done merely for form's sake; as someone says: what is he risking here? That is how our most painful problems are brushed aside, our most vital ("bloodiest") interests, which quite often cost the livelihood of this or that merchant, this or that petty trader and craftsman.
On the other hand, we have seen more than once that when conscious Jewish representatives sit down at negotiations and defend the interests of their brethren with truth and integrity, they achieve a great deal for the community. We have already had the opportunity to establish this more than once. Hence one sees that we must stand on guard and protect our interests. One sees that not only must we protect our interests, but we must wage a stubborn fight so as not to let ourselves be ruined. So what can we call such representatives, who take it upon themselves to defend — it is their mission — and do not do it? Must we take lightly such ignoring of our most vital interests? Let the Będzin "Merchants' Association" say why the position which had to be represented in Kielce was not filled. What is the reason that there was no delegate there, who might possibly have saved a great deal of Jewish money?
Why should our economic interests be ownerless? Who is responsible for them?
R. Let.

A Seder of Apostates

Moshe Feinkind.
(The tragedy of modern „anusim“ [forced converts]).

The historic Seder, with its symbolic customs, has always held a kind of secret power to awaken Jewish feelings even in Jews who had already fallen away, the apostates, and the great desire to celebrate the „Seder night“, the „leyl shimurim“ [night of watching], in a Jewish way. Just as if they had been Jews all year round. —
And much, very much has our „martyrology“ to tell us of those anusim, of the Spanish „Marranos“, who made great sacrifices and often even paid with their lives on the pyres so that they could hold the „Seder“ according to the customs of their fathers... With self-sacrifice they held the „Seder“ in secret; in dark cellars and caves they sat and told of the „Exodus from Egypt“ and sang the holy prayers in terror and torment, fearing the „inquisitors“ lest they find out about it, for a cruel death at the stake awaited them for it; yet regardless of that, they, the Marranos, who all year long strove to erase from themselves every trace and every sign of their attachment to Judaism, when Passover time came, began to feel braver and simply sacrificed themselves for the sake of the historic Jewish festival!..
This tragedy of the „hidden Jew“ has not yet ended. That was not yet the last act in Spain; the tragedy lasts to this very day.
When dear Passover arrives, the spring festival of the Jewish people, it draws back to the Jewish people also the modern „apostates“, who could not withstand the hard trial of not converting for the sake of a bit of career, or even just for a fancy. Today too there are apostates, present-day „anusim“, who try somewhere, in a hidden place, to quietly hold the „Seder“ according to Jewish custom and law — and such places they seek out abroad, far, very far from their home.
True, their „holding of the Seder“ is no longer bound up with such self-sacrifice, nor with such danger of being burnt at the stake as once in Spain; yet they too have to endure great moral torment — and in a certain sense also self-sacrifice.
They hide, these present-day anusim, their longing for Jewishness. Here too they keep it hidden from the whole world and above all from themselves, from their own families...
They come from afar to a foreign country with wife and child, and „officially“ it is called a spring trip abroad, but in truth they come here to hold the „Seder“, to celebrate the Jewish festival together with all Jews.
It is interesting to see such a „Seder“ of these apostates, gathered from afar, which takes place regularly every year in the calm, quiet German town of W—n.. Already 2—3 weeks before Passover these apostates notify, in writing or even by telegram, the local Jewish restaurateur, who is under the supervision of the rabbinate, of their coming as guests for the festival, and they book places in the „closed company“. Each of them registers under a false name, and by that name he is also called the whole time.
When Passover eve comes, these apostates, old and young, are already here on the spot. They usually stay, with very few exceptions, in first-class Christian hotels. In the evening, around 8 o'clock, before the Seder, they gather one by one; like frightened sheep, in the splendid hall that has been reserved for them, and announce themselves by their „pseudonyms“. It is enough for the owner of the kosher restaurant to open the doors wide for the guest; he leads him into the guest room and — at once shows him the place, already assigned to him in advance with a label — bearing his pseudonym.
Soon these guests, in black morning coats, and the ladies in white evening gowns, sit down at the festive table, adorned with fresh splendid flowers and flooded with a sea of electric light, each in his place, and before each one stands a bottle of „Carmel wine“ with a cup, a Seder plate with three matzot, on which lie karpas, maror and haroset, and a Haggadah beside it.
The owner of that restaurant, a former Austrian corporal, who all day long does not take his skullcap off his head, himself in person conducts the „reign“ at the Seder and orders his „Obers“ [waiters] to pour wine into the cups, and in an elevated mood he chants the Kiddush with its melody for his guests. The old ones still say a few words along with him, but the young ones look at one another in astonishment, and so he conducts the Seder with these lost souls.
As for hearing — one hears the whole time only the voice of the „king“. He recites the Haggadah from beginning to end, and his guests listen to him with devotion. During the Seder they also eat all the bitter herbs that the Obers serve them. Especially interesting and moving is the moment when the host calls Fritz, the „Ober“, and tells him to open the door leading out to the courtyard, and begins to say aloud: „Pour out Thy wrath upon the nations that know Thee not“... pour out Thy anger on those who do not acknowledge Thee, God. It is interesting then to look at the faces of these modern „anusim“. Many of them shed tears at that point, quiet tears of remorse and repentance... And so the Seders of these „present-day Marranos“ come to an end. Quietly they disperse as they came, almost like [?] — with the others they do not speak at all; they do not even know of one another who they are and where they come from.
The next day they are already again the same as they were...
Last night's „Jewish princes“ soon turn back into gentiles again, with gentile thoughts and a gentile life, and this two-sided[?], double life — outwardly a gentile and inwardly a Jew — this is also the most tragic thing about today's apostates, as about the „anusim“ of former times...
Across the Great Beautiful World — XII) The Egyptian Treasures in the Paris World Museum, the "Louvre".

[Travel notes — Paris, the Louvre.] (From my travel notebook.)

7.
It has always been accepted in the world that Paris is the city of sin and licentiousness, of luxury and chansonnettes. True, that kind of thing also occupies a quite honourable place, but it is still not the main thing. One must not forget that Paris is the centre of Europe, the heart of the world.
What does one not see and what does one not have in Paris? The Eiffel Tower — the tallest building in the world — is the symbol of Paris. It catches all the phenomena of the air and the radio sparks that travel through the atmosphere of the planet Earth, and sends them out again to all parts of the world. In Paris lies the magnetic ball whose threads stretch out into every corner of the globe, and the same is also true the other way round: the threads of the world wind together in the world-city that we call Paris.
Like a sponge Paris absorbs the dull-yellow Chinese and the nimble, agile Japanese, the hot-tempered Italian and the calm Scandinavian, the taciturn Englishman and the shrewd American, the Negro blackened by the sun and the Siberian hardened[?] by the frost. They all come to Paris; all peoples, races and colours send, year in year out, tens of thousands of representatives into the great cauldron-pit called Paris. Everyone is drawn to the city of fine taste, elegance, grace and refinement.
Travellers and tourists, art lovers and artists, scholars and pleasure-seekers, diplomats and people with nothing to do — everyone and each one is drawn to Paris. One seeks there the alluring licentiousness, another the atmosphere of art, another is interested in the extraordinary historical riches, for Paris is through and through art and history, chronicle and antiquity. At every step you see history and art in Paris, every stone breathes them, everywhere you are surrounded by art and by ennobled, polished taste.
On what a high level[?] art and history stand in Paris — these priceless treasures are, after all, beyond any price. Paris possesses them without measure.
It is no trifle, what antiquities, what priceless treasures are found in the famous "Louvre" museum — the whole world does not possess the like. There is, after all, an inexhaustible sea there, holding many thousands of treasures.
I would very much like to describe the Louvre museum, but how poor my pen is for it, how much strength one must take upon oneself, what means one must have for it and how much understanding one must grasp for it. The more I walked through the labyrinthine halls of the gigantic Louvre museum, the more I became convinced of the impossibility of this difficult task. The more I toured the Louvre, the more I strained to grasp what I saw, the more I became convinced of the impossibility of seeing everything, understanding everything and describing everything.
The Louvre has a unique power: it wears the visitor out. Every time I was there and wanted to measure myself against it, in order to exhaust the whole sea that is meant for the human eye, I felt that I was eating in portions too large, which do harm. The Louvre, it seems, likes to be eaten slowly, piece by piece, studied unhurriedly — and it apparently has a magical power.
About every little corner one could write endlessly. Here we see the historical-archaeological excavations of all times and eras, which together form living monuments. All forms of human creation, of all cultures and civilisations from the very oldest times, from the prehistoric ones down to our very latest days. Who will undertake to study all this and give even a pale miniature, a reflection of everything seen?
And therefore in the present chapter we will look at only one corner — the Egyptian-Biblical department, which holds colossal treasures from archaeological excavations of very ancient civilisations, and at them we will cast a glance, because more than a glance one cannot give even in this chapter; to examine each thing separately would be too heavy a task, except for specialists in the field.
* * *
Egypt is counted among the oldest primitive civilisations that history can tell of. Some 6—7 thousand years before Christ, "garmaric"[?] peoples settled in various places in the upper reaches of and around the river Nile and formed half-civilised communities. Then for the first time cities, temples, systematic irrigation and signs of a social organisation appeared in Egypt. From that time, then, begins the great history of Egypt, which stretches over many thousands of years, down to the times of Rome's expansion over the world and the beginning of our era.
We owe the Egyptians, after all, the ancient script which they invented, writing on a special kind of clay[?] found in Egypt and preserved for our generations. Only not long ago were the hieroglyphs deciphered in their language; the one who discovered this was the French scholar Champollion, and we see his portrait in the Louvre among the living remnants of those dead worlds and civilisations.
Many of these inscribed stones are in the Louvre, and from them it is possible to reconstruct the history of their religion and traditions, which is remarkable for the times of idolatry.
When one looks closely at this stroke-script on the stones, one notices a strong resemblance to our Hebrew script. Apparently the Jews then inherited the script from them, just as they inherited other traditions which they took with them when fleeing the Egyptian yoke in the days of Moses our Teacher.
The pictorial hieroglyphic script was, it seems, the property of the rich and the magnates; we see this in the decoration with this script of the old tomb monuments that are in the museum.
———
As is known, the Egyptians were then an idolatrous people. Of monotheism nothing was yet known then, and so every family had its own god, besides thousands of other gods which filled the specially built temples, served by a caste of priests. The latter, besides the religious function, also performed the function of science, medicine and astronomy, which were the property of the priests. This caste held power in the land. Above them, however, there was one more supreme authority — the king, the Pharaoh, who was, incidentally, the god. And therefore these kings had built for themselves enormous gigantic tomb-pyramids and sphinx-monuments, which are to this day the greatest wonders of human labour. Their art consisted in general of building for eternity, because according to their belief true life begins only after death.
As soon as one enters the first gigantic hall of the Egyptian department, the human eye is riveted to the giant sphinx made of deep[?] pink granite stone, polished so fresh and gleaming as though it had just come from the artist's hand — and yet the sphinx is already about four thousand years old. According to the inscription it was built by Memptah[?] of the ninth [sic] dynasty, that is, at the time when the Jews were enslaved in Egypt. The sphinx was found in Egypt, in the city of Tanis.
Of the same pink granite, which counts among the strongest stones, a little further on stands a six-metre statue of King Amenophis the Third, who was of the 18th dynasty, i.e. even older than the Pharaoh of Moses' time. This statue is broken, and we see the giant head separately and the feet separately.
We also see here, from the same 18th dynasty, a sphinx of the goddess Sekhmet, made this time of black granite, as is the characteristic feature of most sphinxes, whose faces are for the most part animal-like: when the body is that of a human, the face is that of a dog or a lion; when it is animal-like — the face is that of a human.
At the end of the 18th dynasty we see the figure of King Aman [sic], the successor of Tutankhamun, who was excavated only a few years ago.
It is interesting that the stone[?] turban on the head of King Aman is made in the shape of our Tablets of the Law — who knows whether Moses did not take them as a model.
