Longing

[Literature — story.] Róża Jakubowicz.
The Rabbi's hand, resting on the broad volume, is pale and shot through with an unnatural gleam. The book is a quite unusual[?] work: in it the great men of the generation argue at length whether a woman must undergo halitza when she is left after a man of whom it is not known whether he perished in the fire.
His hand trembles; it has felt a light breeze that comes rushing in through the open window of the court-room and mixes up the pages.
— How have I lived out my years? The Rabbi leans out of the window, as though he wanted to ask someone for an answer to his question.
In [?] tones and colours the spent summer day plays[?] outside; veiled in a dull haze, the air seems to conceal many passions.
He draws back his gaze, unused to the freedom outside, and looks around his court-room. Here the golden ray of the sunset appears like a stain, gliding over the [?]-silk curtain cloth of the Ark that moves on the eastern wall.
From high bookcases, on which whole cases of books stand displayed, look out book-spines in a [?] print of three hundred years ago and with an age of content[?] from far earlier still.
On one-legged[?] lecterns lie appeals of Jerusalem charity societies, proclamations in which it is announced and made known that a village wants to break away from the town, a covenant[?] of Christians, because Jews had wanted to use the Christian cemetery.
In a small wall cupboard, polished inside, lie old record-books of the synagogue and of the burial society, a halitza slipper, a little box of Land-of-Israel earth, a shofar. Set apart lie invalid bills of divorce and old wills.
In his other litigants' room sit various litigants: a sunburnt Yemenite Jew with a striped kaftorban[?], saying to everyone: "Abbra bikhni arbi[?]" (I speak Arabic). He tells that he left his seven belongings on the ship that sank between Port Said and Jaffa — just like that, into the water! He cannot bear the air of the Cairo alleys[?]; after the stormy surging of the sea he has come to the court-room to ask for a letter stating that he is "full and overflowing" [deserving], so that he may travel from town to town, from country to country, and scrape something together.
A tall, red-haired Jew is waiting for a din-torah with his son, also an estate dealer, because the son snatched a business deal from him.
— Rabbi — another man steps up to the Rabbi's feet, a tall "straushnik" [guard, Pol. strażnik] with Jewish gestures — what will be my end? As a child I was taken as a cantonist and converted, and now my grandfather comes to me in a dream every night and says: Do you know who you are? You are a Jew! —
— But they will persecute you to destruction, the Rabbi says to him. — The cantonist answers: let me live but one hour, so long as the soul is saved!
Uriel, the beadle, passes by the house with a big tallow lantern and talks to himself: When I see a little calf[?] go still under the hands of those who examine it with wickedness, murder, treifot — I cannot bear it, and my entrails rumble within me.
— What else does one hear in town, Uriel? —
— In the forest they found a twin[?] of the couple who got married last week — Jews sitting in prison eat treif — a lad in a black shirt went up today in the synagogue onto the bimah to preach before the morning prayer.
And every time it grows harder for the Rabbi, in his loneliness, among the kehilla [?] [probably: kehilla bosses], to be able to do something for his people Israel. Ruling on questions of kosher and treif, he sees his hope of mending the people vanish, creating nothing, and he is drawn to the book. And when he tries to withdraw with the novellae of Torah that God has granted[?] him, he feels guilty towards the town, which needs his supervision so much. The synagogue, he hears, is to be closed, because the roof does not hold; the mikveh too is about to collapse, and so he sees himself wandering[?] between this and that temporary dwelling, having nothing to show for himself, because he had nothing to hold on to.
Now he sees the summer evening outside, like a stranger's well-being. Under the bright evening sky shadows hide and die away in the glow of twilight and in longing.
Some incomprehensible remorse gnaws at him, and I — how have I lived out my years.
— — — — — — —
The Rabbi knows that the silvery laughter of life — these are false tones, opposites of the Shekhinah, that conceal within them an ugly vanity, and that they want to overpower him and defeat him..
He shakes them off and remembers his children.
His daughters have become estranged from him, and his son is doing practical work in Eretz Israel.
— What have I failed to do for my vineyard, that it lies waste?
And the father longs for his son — let him come even with those foreign words of his with which he used to frighten his father; let him come and say something, perhaps it will be easier for him to die. But the evening is so quiet and lonely, and before the window of the sick Rabbi the polish [vestibule] of the beit midrash now looms black, with the chain where people used to be locked for every sin.
And below the beit midrash appears the very old cemetery, the unfenced one, where one still finds an iron pot of a certain dead doctor, who left in his will that after death he should be cremated and the ashes buried; single human bones that do not want to pay their last debt by giving[?] themselves to the earth and lie still; golden spangles of bridal veils, which have not rotted all the time the cemetery has stood.
And a great trembling seizes the walls of his heart: to whom shall he reveal the murmuring of his tormented[?] soul, to whom shall he tell the wondrous visions now revealed to him. And he feels ill with the sobbing[?] that no longer lets up.
He sees that the last consolation, which his heart had promised him, that should let him die in peace, will come no more. And it seems to him that he had been[?] — for nothing? —
He sees how his long body, with all its unfulfilled desires, lies beneath the covering of black thought on the ground, and over his dead head the memorial candles, how they flicker —
And the sick Rabbi's pale, bony hands rise over his head with a despairing cry: God, where are You? —
But soon he sighs long and heavily and repents that he could for one minute turn away from his trust in God — which is like the sin of "taking one's own life". And with a movement that shakes off, like road dust from a clean garment, this life with its unstilled "I want" — he sits up straight, washes his hands and begins to prepare himself for "there".
Mendele's Conspiracy against the Kingdom

[Feuilleton — Passover, domestic satire.] Y. Oberżanek
If the whole year were Passover, how good it would be for him, for Mendele. The best holiday for Mendele is Passover; at Passover Mendele feels that he too is something of a "Mannsperson" [a man], that he can command, that he is an independent person. At Passover Mendele tastes the flavour of "and he shall rule over her" [Gen. 3:16]. Not for nothing does Mendele pray the whole round year for the "season of our freedom", for the beautiful, dear Passover.
For what, as they say, does Mendele know of life the whole year, what does Mendele know of manliness? He is as big as a yawn, as thin as a plucked broom, green and [?] like an old withered etrog, and he has a womanish little voice, and on top of that a hiccup together with a crow's caw.
That is the "Mannsperson".
And what does his wife look like? [?] His wife is the very opposite of Mendele: tall as a pine, strong as an oak, a pair of hands, each of which could make six Mendeles and maybe more, a square figure; more than once she has quarrels with the tram conductors, who demand that she buy two tickets because she takes up two seats.
Which of the two is master of the house is surely superfluous to tell. Who knows of a Mendele, who hears of a Mendele; it is enough to take one look at the "he" and the "she" and you are sure that the say belongs to Rivke Rokhl and not to Mendele; you look at the "pair" and you see before you Shabbat ha-Gadol [the Great Sabbath] with the short Friday.
So our poor Mendele laments his bitter fate: Where were my eyes! Mendele complains — wouldn't a wife [?] like me have sufficed for a fellow like me: a short one, a thin one, a dried-up one; let her [?] also hiccup with a whistle as a bonus [dodatek] — what would I have cared? I wouldn't have such a "scarecrow" [straszydło] going about the house, before whose one glance all my limbs die within me; I must needs have a conductor and I have to dance as she conducts.
So Mendele complains the whole year, so he complains his whole life; since he got to know his Rivke Rokhl he feels like a bird in a cage, and worst of all is that his nine children have all taken after their mother: tall and broad, healthy hands and feet, and if they take him into their circle he is nullified one in sixty; when one looks at the eleven wreckers — who would ever believe that the tiny Mendele is their father, that the little creature holds up such a gang of gluttons on his little shoulders!
But everything has its time, and for our Mendele too comes a time — Passover. As Passover approaches, Mendele becomes quite another man; right after Purim his Rivke Rokhl becomes soft as butter, and Mendele? Mendele, on the contrary, becomes stern, serious; he grows from day to day, from minute to minute he becomes bigger, grander [?] in his own eyes, he begins to find his tongue; Mendele's word is holy, a law; the big, broad, healthy Rivke Rokhl looks little Mendele in the eyes, serves him the finest and the best — and what is the wonder? The future king!
When the eve of Passover comes, Mendele is truly raised to greatness; the eve of Passover is the finest day of his life. With the greatest deference the whole household treats its "Majesty" the "king"; the "queen" goes about in the soft house slippers, the "king" is excited; the tall, healthy, broad-shouldered Rivke Rokhl wants today to find favour and kindness in the eyes of Mendele the "ruler".
And what to say of the evening at the seder — Mendele is a true king, an autocrat, a despot; the queen submissively makes up for him the reclining-bed, a whole throne; Mendele sinks into the mountain of pillows, one command follows another: "Prepare the throne!" goes Mendele's first command, and at once there appears the embroidered matzah-cloth that Rivke Rokhl herself crocheted while still a bride. Mendele "arranges" [strojić] the seder: sets down the shank bone, the bitter herbs, the haroset, lays out in order the "Kohen", the "Levi" and the "Israel", shows each one its place; obediently everyone carries out the "command" of the "king". Mendele says the Haggadah with the melody. The queen shuffles the pages [?]; Mendele sets down the cup — the queen also sets down the cup; Mendele drinks the cup — all drink with him; Mendele makes a blessing — Rivke Rokhl answers "Amen" devoutly. Mendele rules and commands, Mendele's word is law. All and everything is subject to Mendele; Mendele is a king, an autocrat, a despot, and Mendele makes use of the opportunity — it is not always Passover; once a year Mendele feels his manliness... Not for nothing does Mendele pray the whole year for the beautiful, bright holiday — Passover.
So it went all the years, since he got to know his Miriam Rokhl [sic; earlier Rivke Rokhl]: the whole year he lay in the ground [i.e. was miserable] and baked bagels, and prayed for his "kingdom".
But all this comes to an end, and in Mendele's rule and Mendele's "kingdom" too there came an upheaval. Since the thrones began to shake, Mendele's throne too began to tremble. Since the crowns of other rulers began to fall, Mendele's crown too began to move.
It was a year ago, as every year before Passover: Mendele began to prepare for his "kingdom", became stern, tried to command, began to rule over Miriam Rokhl. But somehow it was not the same; somehow Mendele does not feel the "royal respect". Miriam Rokhl listens to him like to last year's snow. Somehow she does not go about in the soft pre-Passover slippers; somehow she has her chametz-[?]. Mendele feels that "in the kingdom of Denmark something is not in order".
Mendele suppressed it within himself and kept silent — did he have a choice? He did his own thing, and Miriam Rokhl did hers; — she made [?]. Not a hair different from the whole year.
But Mendele did not expect all this — that his "throne" is in danger, that a [new] royal order is being prepared; that is Mendele's luck. Mendele would never have reckoned that his own queen is preparing a conspiracy against the existing royal order; it never entered Mendele's mind.
In the evening, for the seder, Mendele comes home from the shtibl [Hasidic prayer house] — what is this? Where is the queen? Where is the reclining-bed? Passover [?] — guests at the seder, of all things? When one must prepare for the seder, they are playing the piano? What sort of news is this?
Miriam Rokhl! — Mendele let out, in "king" fashion, a shout and a hiccup — have you quite forgotten what day it is today? At once the reclining-beds must be made —
You surely think she was frightened by Mendele's commanding tone? — She burst out laughing, and when Rivke Rokhl [sic] laughs the windowpanes tremble. Look, just look — she choked with laughter — a poor wretch, and Mendele a king! What do you think, what, — Miriam Rokhl came out with her [?] tongue — that I'll forever be making you "vesper-beds" [?]? Enough of being a fool; you can wait until I make you haroset and maror — that I can give you as much as your heart desires.
Mendele saw that it smelled of gunpowder and began to speak kindly: Don't make a fool of yourself, enough joking, it's getting late, enough, enough, get ready for the seder.
— What are you thinking of, — the eldest daughter came to her mother's aid, — it's high time to throw away your "superstitions" [zabobony]. We are, after all, somewhat educated people.
— "Shame and disgrace" [Polish: wstyd i hańba], — chimed in the younger daughter.
— Because the Jews went across the sea, — joked the youngest kid [?], — must we today eat grass like cattle?
What happened next you can guess for yourselves. Mendele, all alone in a corner, said the Haggadah, and the poor man wept over his lost kingdom. He was pained by the disloyalty of his "queen", who betrayed him in his older years.
This eve of Passover Mendele goes about confused; an end to his dynasty; Mendele no longer commands, no longer rules and no longer disposes [dysponuje]. This year Mendele is preparing to celebrate his "kingdom" at a stranger's table.
Poor King Mendele — in Wilhelm [Kaiser Wilhelm II, deposed 1918], Amanutahn [sic; Amanullah Khan, King of Afghanistan, deposed 1929] and other homeless kings may you, Mendele, find your consolation.
The Old Haggadah in a New Staging

[Passover feuilleton — Haggadah parody; satirical play in three scenes.] By A. Lemech.

By way of an introduction.
A theatre management turned to me asking that I write some beautiful and interesting drama of Jewish life in Poland. So I pondered the written invitation and asked: what does "of Jewish life in Poland" mean? Do Jews, then, live in Poland? Jews die in Poland, lie in their death throes, go about like the slain — but do they live?.. But joking aside, one does need a subject. So I searched for a country as similar to Poland, and an epoch as similar to the present one, until I came upon the traces of — the Jews in Egypt. And I set about reworking the old, well-known play: "The Passover Haggadah". After all, don't they re-use old ministers and form new cabinets? And secondly: are Tam, Rasha, Pharaoh, Laban the Aramean etc. not living types of today? — And the main thing: I don't mean the Haggadah, after all, but the kneidlach...

FIRST SCENE.
Pharaoh with his friends.
(In the streets of the capital it is announced by posters that the Egyptian king Pharaoh is arriving, visiting Poland for a short time. The well-known antisemitic writer A. Kawaczyński hurries to the hotel where the king is lodging. They treat each other like two old acquaintances, and the following conversation takes place between them:)
KAWACZYŃSKI: — I am amazed at you, Pharaoh, that you let such a Moses grow up in your court, who freed the Jews. Ah, if not for him we would have no Jewish Question today, the accursed Jewish Question. How can one let such a Moses grow up in one's own court?
PHARAOH: — My mistake was made because I saw that little Moses was "heavy of mouth", a stammerer. And I knew that Jews are great doers with the mouth, they only know "mouth-work". When it comes to deeds they are great idlers [?]. So, seeing such a stammerer, would it have occurred to me that such a one would be a Jewish leader? And who would make fine speeches? — That did not occur to me. — — —
KAWACZYŃSKI: — Pray, explain to me the sense of your decree: to throw all Jewish children of the male sex into the water and to let those of the female sex live — why not throw them all into the water?
PHARAOH: — My decree was well thought out, better than your bakery mechanisations, monopolies and the like. Imagine: if the old Jewish parents had born and raised only daughters, and had no one to marry them off to — for all the boys had been drowned — they, the grey-plaited old maids, would have wandered about the Jewish houses without bridegrooms, without husbands... Ah! Nobody would have envied them any longer, the Zhidkes [Polish slur for Jews]; they would all have buried themselves alive...
(There is a knock, and a Tax Director enters. Pharaoh, recognising in him one of his own, asks him to sit down, and the conversation begins at once.)
TAX DIRECTOR: — Perhaps His Excellency could serve us with his information and explain in what way [?] our arrangement of tax collection limps compared with the former Egyptian tax repressions? What do we lack for perfection?
PHARAOH: — Yes, please. I'll tell you. You surely know from the Bible that "they set over him taskmasters" [Ex. 1:11; lit. "tax officers"] — the meaning is that the Jews themselves were appointed as tax collectors. Jewish tax dunners, you see — if the Polish Jews had that too, they would be finished..
KAWACZYŃSKI: — I don't know; the Jews keep complaining that they are not admitted to government posts — why not indeed make only Jews the collectors? — Then they would really have something to complain about, the Zhidkes...
TAX DIRECTOR (noting the plan down for himself): — But did it achieve its aim?
PHARAOH: — And how! See what the Haggadah's author says: "and thou wast naked and bare" — naked and bare they remained, like an "at" ("thou", feminine) (the word "at" is feminine). Like a woman, that is: naked like a modern-dressed girl of today...
TAXES DIRECTOR: — How did you then drive out the handful of Zhidkes when they had already been emptied out and were no longer useful?
PHARAOH: — It is written: "And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities" [miskenot, read as "of poverty"] — they built themselves arrest-houses and ghettos with their own hands, and "they sighed" — they sighed.

SECOND SCENE.
The Haggadah-master with the Four Sons.
(The master of the Haggadah, an elderly Jew, sits hunched over an old Haggadah. In comes a thin, emaciated young man, a real skeleton, ragged and worn out. A mouth without teeth. The Haggadah-master looks at the newcomer in astonishment.)
HAGGADAH-MASTER: — Who are you, man?
WISE SON: — You don't recognise me? I am indeed your Wise Son, the Wise Son of the Haggadah — a fine eye you have, I must say. —
HAGGADAH-MASTER: Is that so? How you have changed! Oy, I have no joy of you, my son. Ragged, worn out, starved, abandoned by all.
WICKED SON (a red Yevsek [member of the Jewish Section of the Soviet Communist Party] enters): — "What is this service to you?" Why are you sitting like this [?] — surely you are studying; I'll report at once that you are carrying on counter-revolutionary work.
WISE SON: — And if one studies...
HAGGADAH-MASTER (cutting him short): — You wise guy! With whom are you getting into a debate? For them, those hooligans [lobuses, Pol. łobuz], I long ago worked out only one remedy: no discussions will help, only "blunt his teeth" — a slap in the mug... Only that can convince such a one..
SIMPLE SON (enters, goggling a pair of calf's eyes): — What is this, eh?
HAGGADAH-MASTER: — And how are you, my child? How is the world treating you?
SIMPLE SON: — Not bad at all. I hold the most honourable posts in the Sejm, in the government, in the kehilla and in the city council..
HE WHO DOES NOT KNOW HOW TO ASK (a little Jew, a merchant, enters sweating): — Perhaps I could get a small interest-free loan, Jews? I've already run all over town and got nothing.
HAGGADAH-MASTER: — There's the real "one who does not know how to ask" — he doesn't know how to borrow [pun: Heb. lishol = to ask / to borrow]..

THIRD SCENE.
The Balance Sheet.
(At a desk sit a few Jews, merchants, doing their accounts.)
R' YOSI: — Do you know how much the "finger", the finger, has brought in?
— Yes. By my reckoning a whole fifty thousand.
R' ELIEZER: — Eh, how he reckons it [?]! "Trouble" he didn't count. "A mission of evil angels" — not either; that's why you get such a sum. Take it all together: "wrath, fury, trouble, a mission of evil angels" (names of Łódź firms) — and you'll see it is a whole two hundred thousand.
R' AKIVA: — You're mistaken too; add it up properly and you'll see it is a whole two hundred and fifty.
HAGGADAH-MASTER (enters): — And what are you quarrelling about, children?
ALL: — About the credit we have "drawn".
HAGGADAH-MASTER: — The sums you just named — what do you mean? Money?
ALL: — Look in the "Haggadah" and you'll see; we are counting the plagues that we have been left with.
HAGGADAH-MASTER: — Is that so? Does the "Haggadah" [?] mean the present time?
— How else? You write it yourselves: "In every generation a man is obliged [hayav]" — today everyone is indeed in debt (hayav)... And: "Who redeemed me [and] will redeem our fathers" [as printed] — today we are all gall [Yid. gal = bile]... And: "Had He given us their wealth and not split the sea for us" — today, until one gets some money, doesn't the sea split?...
HAGGADAH-MASTER: — And how do you manage?
ALL: — We play your "Had Gadya" game. "For two gulden [złoty] (a week, to be paid in instalments) Father buys a coat from the 'abtsoger' [?] [instalment pedlar] and doesn't pay" — comes the abtsoger to Father to dun him and bangs on the table. Comes the warehouse-keeper to the abtsoger to dun him and bangs on the table. Comes the Łódź merchant to the warehouse-keeper to dun him and bangs on the table. Comes the manufacturer to the merchant to dun him and bangs on the table. Had Gadya, Had Gadya.. I'll sell you the whole of today's life for two zuzim...
In Honour of Passover — commentaries, remarks and sayings on the Haggadah

Commentaries, remarks and sayings on the Passover Haggadah.
Collected and adapted by Y. P.[?]

a) — Ha lachma anya ("This is the bread of affliction")
There are readings "Ha lachma anya" and there are readings "Kha lachma anya" ("like this bread"). What is the difference?
A poor beggar was suddenly made fortunate when he found a precious windfall. He threw off his beggar's clothes with the beggar's bag and began to lead a rich man's life. Out of gratitude for his good fortune he made the day he found the windfall into a memorial holiday. On that day he put on the beggar's clothes with the bag as a reminder of his former poverty and handed out gifts and sweets to the children. But money is a turning wheel, and years later he becomes a poor man again. Having no choice, he goes back to his old occupation, puts on the beggar's clothes with the bag and gets ready for the road. The children, knowing that when their father hangs the beggar's bag on himself they are due gifts and sweets, now crowd around him and demand theirs. The father puts on a sad face: "Once, my children, my beggar's bag was only a sign of remembrance, so I handed out presents; today I am a real beggar, a poor man"...
Once, when we lived in the Land of Israel as free Jews, the matzah was only a reminder, a symbol of the Egyptian bondage. Today, in our bondage of exile, it is no symbol of the past but a real beggar's bag, not merely for remembrance... not "kha" ("like this") but "ha" ("this is")...
Emet le-Yaakov.

b) Next year in the Land of Israel... next year free men
We pray to find ourselves in the Land of Israel and to be free men there, free — for if we are to go on being slaves, then what is the Land of Israel for?...
— We say the prayer "Next year in the Land of Israel" in Hebrew, not like the rest of the passage, which is Aramaic, because those of little understanding, women and children, have no longing at all for the Land of Israel: why wander off to some distant land when here such a rich Seder is laid out?... And so that they should not understand it and have their holiday spoiled, it is said in Hebrew, which they will not understand..
Birkat ha-Shir.

c) — On this night, only matzah
"On this night" — this night of exile eats us up with nothing but "matzah" (strife; nothing but quarrels and disputes devour us.
Olelot Ephraim.

d) And because he excluded himself from the community, he denied the essence of faith
There are six hundred thousand letters in the Torah, and six hundred thousand Jewish souls. When someone wants to separate one Jewish soul from the community, it is as great a crime as erasing a letter in a Torah scroll, and he is a denier of the essence of faith. But see: when the Torah is not in sheets sewn together but in separate Chumashim, one may already erase individual letters. So too when Jews live apart, they lose their Torah holiness, and one may already erase and scratch them out.
R. L. Y. [Levi Yitzchak] of Berdichev.

e) — The simple son, what does he say?
"The simple one — a simpleton — what does he say": he declares by himself what he is; you need not pull him by the tongue for long to convince yourself that he is a simpleton...
Folk saying.

f) — And it is this that has stood by our fathers and us
The Jew raises his cup and says: "And it is this that has stood by us" — this very cup has stood by us, so that we exist as a people. Other nations, when they were defeated by an enemy, immediately began to drink and carouse with the victors, clinked their cups against the victor's cup, and so assimilated and perished. We, however, may not drink together with other nations and may not intermingle — and therefore our national integrity has been preserved.
Kesef Nivhar.

g) — Lice, wild beasts
"Arov" was a plague in which all the cattle and wild beasts gathered together and wanted to destroy Egypt; according to the Midrash, the lice came along too. One asks: the lice had already had their own plague — so how do they come a second time?
A rich man celebrated his son's wedding with a seven-day feast. On the first day the relatives were invited, on the second — Torah scholars, on the third — poor people etc. There was one man who came on the first day, and on the second, and on the third. A servant asks him: How can this be? Each day is set aside for others! He answers: the first day is for relatives, the second for Torah scholars — I am a relative, and a Torah scholar, and a poor man, so I come on all three days...
First the lice came as specially invited guests; afterwards, when all the wild beasts and cattle were mobilized, the lice came as in-laws too, as beasts too...
Ohel Yitzchak.

h) — Boils
Why does one say "even a scabby one counts for a minyan"? — Because a sixth worshipper completes a prayer quorum, even though four of the ten have already prayed; and boils is the sixth plague..
From the mouth of the people.

i) The plague of the firstborn
Why is "the plague of" not mentioned for blood, frogs, etc., but only for the firstborn?
The explanation is: "makat bekhorot" — the firstborn struck their parents so that they would send the Jews out quickly, so that they themselves would not croak like dogs.
Yesod ha-Emunah.

j) — D-Tz-Kh, A-D-Sh, B-A-Ch-B
What did Rabbi Judah earn here?
— By Rabbi Judah's mnemonic the word "makot" (plagues) is saved, for it really should have been "B-A-Ch-M-B". So he earned what every Jew earns — blows ("makot")..
Folk saying.

k) And these are: the Passover offering, matzah and maror
We place on the table a piece of shankbone (in memory of the Passover offering), matzah and horseradish, a remembrance of Egypt. So why do we not put some money on the table as a remembrance of the spoils of Egypt and the spoils of the Sea?
— Because of the bitter herbs much is left to us even today, whereas of the spoils of Egypt, of the gold and silver of those days, we have long had no trace...
Rav Mordechai of Brisk.

l) — This bitter herb that we eat, for what reason?
Maror is also a remembrance of freedom, a symbol of liberty —
Once there was a king's son with whom his father became angry[?], and as punishment he sent him off among beggars. So he lived for years, and with all his senses he became a beggar. Some time later the king sends a messenger to him and orders him to ask what he lacks. — "A pair of shoes and a new beggar's bag" — was the answer. His comprehension reached no further.
We Jews too sink so deep into the swamp of exile[?] that we ask only for a new beggar's bag. Our comprehension no longer reaches as far as redemption.. Therefore, when one feels the taste of maror, when one dreams of deliverance, that is already called redemption —
The Rim [R. Yitzchak Meir] of Ger.

m) — To seat me with nobles, with the nobles of His people
When someone becomes rich, then everyone becomes his relative; each wants to prove his kinship. When he is "seated with nobles", sitting with nobles, then everyone in his family is one of "the nobles of His people". With a poor man it is the other way round.
Folk saying.
Charoset — Next Year!

Charoset
Satirical supplement
in place of the koshered-for-Passover "Kokh-Lefl" ["Cooking Spoon", the regular humour page]
by Ben Amotz.

Next Year!
by Leonidas.

And again there is merriment,
and again there is a Seder,
and everyone is a king —
the rabbi and the bathhouse keeper.
And who is the rich man now?
And who is the beggar?
When everyone eats matzah
and everyone eats bitter herbs!
Passover unites
with luck and blessing
an old, torn-apart,
beautiful family.

We hear at the Seder
the same men of lineage,
the same "free men",
the same anusim [forced converts]...
We hear the same
"Mar bar Rav Ashi",
we all ask
the same questions...

And all of us offer
the same answer:
"We were slaves!"
Respect, respect!
Respect, you gentiles,
for former slaves
who know the taste
of good and of bad.

You can no longer, gentiles,
surprise us with anything —
we have already eaten
all kinds of dishes.
Stuffed necks and gizzards,
both bitter herbs and charoset,
and we have drunk liquor
from all sorts of cups...
From the cup of blessing
and the cup of consolation,
from the cup of tears
and from the cup of blood.

From the cup of sorrows
and the cup of poison —
yet we live
for ever and ever, selah!

* * *

The Passover Seder —
a very precious fashion:
all Israel recites
from the same Haggadah.
When does such a kind of wonder
happen among Jews?
With us, after all, always,
every party is separate...

We call ourselves, supposedly,
comrades and brothers —
but every Jew has
his own Seder...
his own synagogue
and his own cheder —
only once, at Passover,
do we have one Seder...

Together we count
the plagues and the miracles —
for we all come
from Raamses and Pithom.
What is the difference,
whether Joachim or Chaim?
We all come, gentlemen,
from the same Egypt.
So raise, brother,
the cup of Elijah,
and call out with confidence:
— Next year!..
Laws of the Search [for Chametz].

For Będzin.
a) Climb up to the Będzin "Zamek" [castle] and from there fulfil the commandment of searching for chametz. First of all study the list of the Zagłębie merchants, in case there is one among them who does not suffer from "constipation"... If you manage to discover such an antique, place him among the Four Sons of the Haggadah, next to the "Simple One"..
b) Pop in for a search in the office of the President [mayor], look there for the documents about clearing away the old market; if you come across in them the names of well-known public figures, sweep them off with the feather duster and say "Kol chamira"...
c) In the hall of the City Council do not make any search, because the law is that in a "bedroom" one does not search... On the other hand, some of the councillors should have a search made in their stomachs, lest, God forbid, there is still left there a remnant of the "watery feast"...
d) Eavesdrop on the "political conversations" between the kehilla president and the leaders of the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel], to find out to whom and how many dollars the fifth shochet [ritual slaughterer] has to pay...
e) Audit the minutes of the "Merchants' Union", to find out who is the delegate who, instead of sitting in the "Izba" [chamber] in Kielce, sits instead in Będzin...
f) Leave the institutions in peace, because the "dead" must not be disturbed in their rest..
g) The same also applies to the political organisations. Of their platforms no trace has remained for a long time...
For Sosnowiec.
h) Make the first search in the premises of the former "Bank Ludowy" [People's Bank], of blessed memory. Check well and find out whether the director said "it is all mine" or whether they studied there "two hold [a garment]"...
i) If you find the fine Yissakhar ["dem feynem Yisokhern" — perhaps a pun on the surname Fein], go with him into the flat of Fein's R' Shlomo, and there search in all the corners. As soon as you find the historic agreement, put it — the agreement, that is — into a little bag of Land-of-Israel soil and keep it for generations.
j) A third search must be carried out in the same street, that is, in the Small Traders' Union. Search the books and get a clear account of how much part of the former board "took"...
k) From Targowa street jump over to Modrzejowska street. In that street there once existed an artisans' cooperative. Search there (if there is anything at all) and establish where the "tur"[?] has got to and where the "kop" [head].
l) It is a duty upon every Jew to make a search of how many Jewish conductors there are on the trams.
Our Haggadah with a New Interpretation.

Kadesh. If you still own 2 groszy, buy a bucket [wiadro] of water from the invalid, throw in a little "redness" from the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] and make Kiddush.
U-rechatz. Pour out all the cups; with the rest wash your hands and make no blessing.
Karpas. Take the "mute" councillors, dip them in the filtered water and say the blessing: "Creator of the fruit of the earth"...
Yachatz. Divide the few protested bills of exchange: use one half for the holiday and hide the other half for the "kumen"[?] [the future?]...
Maggid. Talk today, talk tomorrow — what one "hammers in" is what remains..
Motzi. A young man of today can dance, whistle, and cannot say the Hamotzi blessing...
Matzah. Patients treated by the dentists of the Sick Fund are exempt from eating matzah...
Maror. Young and old cry: the situation is bitter, but the chiefs [naczelnicy] of the "urzędy"[?] [government offices] say that
Shulchan Orech. The situation is not bad: people eat, drink, go to balls, dress according to the newest fashions.
Therefore, since we still have something left over for a few kilos of matzah —
Hallel. One must give praise to His dear Name for the great miracles...
Ka-ha.

Take 2 matzot from the Council of Rabbis and 1 matzah from the bakers, put them on the Seder plate and say: "Ka-ha" — such is the shape of the Sosnowiec kehilla; "Kol ditzrikh yeitei" ["let all who are in need come"] — every side comes with its grievances; "Hashata hakha" ["now we are here"] — today a mish-mash still reigns; "Leshana haba'a" — in a year — "benei chorin" ["free men"]: we shall be freed from the plagues.
Mah Nishtanah? (Why Is It Different?)

Here a heated discussion developed. My little son [„bnak“] asked for the floor „formally“ and categorically demanded that the Questions be dealt with in Yiddish.
Against this my only daughter came out with great enthusiasm — a pupil at Krzymowski's school and a member of „Herzliya“. She, the little daughter, shouted: Hebrew! Hebrew!
My woman of valour, a member of „WIZO“, was „opposed“ [„przeciwna“] and said that it is „desirable“ [„pożądane“] that the „questions“ [„pytania“] be „explained“ [?] „in Polish“ [„po polskiemu“].
When I wanted to put the question to a vote, my son submitted an urgent motion that his 3 comrades from the Haggadah (except the Wise One) should also take part in the vote...
It goes without saying that as head of state I rejected the motion; after all I cannot allow such types as our city councillors to take part in so important a matter... and I referred the matter to the management of the CISzO branch in Będzin.
Ma'aseh be-Rabbi — here an error crept in: instead of „be-Rabbi“ it should be „Grav“ [?]. It happened at the rabbinical elections in Sosnowiec: ve-hayu mesaprim — the community told stories for long months, ad she-ba — until Israel Moshe came ve-amar and said: children, higi'a zman, the time has come for us to adopt the system of Ger [Gur?]..
Yakhol me-Rosh Hodesh — perhaps you think I mean we should wait until new elections; talmud lomar ba-yom ha-hu — you should know that one must already answer with deeds, be-sha'ah, at the time when matzah and maror lie before you, while the whole material still lies in the hands of the State Tribunal.
Ve-hi she-amdah
(Cover the forbidden [?] matzot; in your right hand hold the cup, in your left hand the „Vey-geshrey“ [Cry of Woe] of the „Group of Householders“ in Sosnowiec, and say): Ve-hi — these are the very same ones who are out to stir up quarrels in every generation; in every town and shtetl there are such destroyers, but the Holy One, as it were, saves us from their hand.
Put down the cup and on the „Vey-geshrey“ let fall 3 drops of wine, according to Rabbi Judah's mnemonics: DeTZaKh, ADaSh, BeAHaV..

In Sosnowiec we call the ten plagues by the following names:
a) „Elections“,
b) the Tax Office,
c) the Magistrate,
d) the Gmina,
e) kugel [?] grabbers,
f) communal busybodies..,
g) the rabbinate,
h) bailiffs,
i) and institutions,

Had the Będzin market-tax collectors been driven away and not paid for water — Dayenu.
Had the Jewish city councillors come to the sessions and not had a „club“ — Dayenu.
If the Starosta accepts the resignation of half the parnassim — Dayenu.

That the market-tax collectors pay for water, the councillors have no „club“ and do not gather for the sessions.
The Starosta does not accept the resignation of the parnassim.
Institutions flourish [?].

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 13[?] / 13 Nisan 5690. — Piątek 11 kwietnia 1930 [Friday, 11 April 1930].)
Będzin
The PPS began and the BB finished...
The secretary of the city council threatens the Jewish councillors.
Wednesday's session of the city council again proved that the present city council was "born in an unlucky hour". Instead of positive work they busy[?] themselves with acts of personal revenge..
After the minutes, the first point on the agenda is the motion of the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] to express no confidence in the chairman (prezes) Fürstenberg. Councillor Lewin makes a counter-motion to pass to the order of the day. Lewin's motion is adopted. Then the BB [BBWR, Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government] puts forward a second motion of no confidence in the whole presidium. Here the PPS want to save their "prestige", and the "Agudah-ławnik" [alderman] Hasmanczyk[?] declares that [lit. "dz", misprint] as a protest they are leaving the session and recalling their secretary from the presidium. The said secretary Łaskowski also speaks about the matter and declares that they, the PPS, will take revenge on the Jews over the budget...
During the discussion of the budget of the power station (elektrownia) the BB proposed that the supervisory board be abolished. Against it spoke: alderman (ławnik) Goldsztajn, Lewin, Klajnman; for — Dr. Rechtman and the BB councillors. Thanks to the absence of several Jewish councillors the BB's motion is adopted. In protest the Jews break the quorum of the session.
—o—
An order from the starosta: the dozors are to go "into the cheder"..
The starosta has sent the kehilla board a letter (letters) to be handed to the 5 dozors [kehilla board members], Messrs. S. Fürstenberg, Icchak Chinadzki[?], Szmul Fajgski[?], Nete Landner[?], and Jekl Najmark, who are to inform the starosta by the 20[?]th of this month of the reasons why they do not come to the board meetings, and whether they intend not to take part in kehilla activity in the future either. If — the letter goes on to say — no answer is given by the above-mentioned deadline, the starosta will consider that the dozors resign their mandates.

For the 10th anniversary of the founding of the 23rd Regiment the Jewish kehilla presented a costly electric clock to the regiment.

On Saturday night at 9 o'clock in the evening, as 22-year-old Moshe Machtinger was walking along Małachowskiego Street, a passenger car ran into him, breaking Machtinger's leg and badly injuring him. The unfortunate man was taken to the municipal hospital.

Before starting to bake matzot the bakers calculated that the price of matzot should be no higher than 1.40 zł. At the beginning of the week, when the demand for matzot became great, the price was raised to 1 60 [1.60] zł...

Petitioners from 10 o'clock on.
The city administration has introduced the "reform" in the magistrate: petitioners are received in all departments from 10 o'clock on.

Academy for the Hebrew University.
Last Saturday a festive academy devoted to the 5th anniversary of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem took place in the "Nowości" theatre. A short opening speech is given by Mr. Eliyahu Gertner[?], who announces that the academy stands under two slogans: to expand the university to the scale of all European universities, and to remove Dr. Magnes, who disturbs our work of building with his treacherous activity. After honouring the late Lord Balfour, councillor Mrs. G. Ratner gives a witty Hebrew speech.
A long and fine speech is given by the member of the Zionist Central Committee Snr.[?] M. Polakewicz[?], who speaks about the great importance of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem for Jewish youth. Mr. P. devotes a few warm words to the unforgettable Balfour and calls on the assembly to work for Zionism.
The academy made a strong impression. "Herzliya" was the only one in our town that did not forget the role the university plays in the building of Eretz Israel and the regeneration of the people.

From the municipal court.
Last Tuesday the case against Dr. Ferber, who had been sued by the Welgrin[?] children for allegedly refusing to give help, took place in the local court. After hearing the statement of the inspector of the health-insurance fund (Kasa Chorych) Dr. Rider, that Dr. Ferber had been on night duty in obstetrics that night and that Dr. Dugaj had immediately gone to the patient, the court dismissed the charge.

Extraordinary meeting of "Malbish Arumim".
Several weeks ago a new board was elected at the annual general meeting. But from the very first day the board had no stability; instead of activity various intrigues multiplied, until... the matter reached the "high windows", from where it was ordered that new elections be held.

This week the town physician Mr. Wasserzweig[?] left for Paris, where he will stay about six weeks. During this time he will take part in medical courses and perfect himself in them.

[Sosnowiec — local news.] On Monday a big trial of communists began at the local district court; they were accused of conducting communist activity in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia. In the dock sat: Szwarcman, Pszyszowski, Władysława Wroszka, Winiarski, Targasz, Józefa Tajchner, Dora Kisler and Szyhała.
The hearing of the witnesses lasted until Wednesday[?]. Afterwards[?] defence speeches were delivered by the advocates Brajter (Warsaw), Barczykowski[?], Landau, Krzymowski.
After deliberation the judges handed down the following verdict: Szwarcman and Pszyszowski 5 years of hard prison, Wroszka 4 years, Winiarski and Targasz 2 years. Kisler, Tajchner and Szyhała were acquitted.

Suspicion fell on an employee of the bookkeeping department, who has been arrested.

The inspector's opinion of the girls' gymnasium.
Not long ago the inspector of the Kraków school curatorium inspected the Jewish girls' gymnasium in our town.
In connection with the inspection the school administration of the gymnasium received a report that was very favourable to the school. It is interesting to note that the inspector stressed that Jewish tradition is cultivated in the school...
But how sad it is that such a school, which after long years of work has been brought to such a level, is threatened with eviction[?] — and by a Jewish landlord, of all people...

Tuberculosis ward at the sick fund.
Thanks to the initiative of Dr. Zamieński[?] a special ward for tuberculosis patients has been founded at the local sick fund (Kasa Chorych). The newest technical equipment has been installed in the ward, so that this important ward is on the same level as all other similar institutions. The new medical institution deserves to be welcomed.

Artisans must join the guilds.
In connection with the regulations of the guild law, which will soon come into force, we remind all Jewish artisans in Sosnowiec that in their own interest they should join the relevant guilds as soon as possible.
Under articles 116 and 120 of the guild law, artisans are obliged to conclude contracts with the apprentices they employ. The chambers of crafts will admit to the journeyman's examinations only such apprentices as have at least 3 years of practice with a master and whose contracts are registered in the chamber of crafts.
So that the influx of young Jewish craftsmen should not be stopped[?], all artisans who employ apprentices must immediately conclude contracts with them through the relevant guilds. Failure to conclude contracts with apprentices is punishable by a fine.

A mass meeting.
On Tuesday, the first day of Chol HaMoed [Passover intermediate days], a mass meeting will take place at the Artisans' Association, at which very important matters will be discussed.

Tax declarations (zeznania) — by 1 May.
We draw our readers' attention to the fact that the final deadline for submitting declarations on "income" (dochód) for the year 1929 is only[?] until 1 May. Failure to submit declarations is punishable by a fine.

The last transport of Palestine emigrants.
The Italian government has forbidden the "export" of emigrants to Eretz Israel through the Italian border. The last transport of emigrants to Eretz Israel was held[?] this week by the firm Zendel[?] in Sosnowiec; no more transports beyond this one will come.

From "HeChalutz".
For over a year now a "HeChalutz" organisation has existed in our town.

Bloody events in Olkusz.
On Wednesday a meeting of unemployed took place in Olkusz. The workers then led the director to the starosta (district head), who only then prevailed on them to release the director.

The calculation in the declaration (zeznanie) of income tax (podatek dochodowy)

For merchants, who now have to submit declarations (zeznania) concerning income tax, it is of the greatest importance to pay attention to the calculation of income.
One should not write in the declaration only the sum of the income; rather one should give a calculation of the income — from where and in what way the income flowed in.
Every merchant should state in the declaration in detail what percentage of profit he made on his turnover. Since in no branch is there a uniform profit — there are some articles on which one earns 10 percent, on other articles in the same branch one earns no more than 5 percent, and on quite other ones less — one should therefore divide the turnover according to the profit groups. In doing so one should state the general name[?] of the goods groups and the profit.
For example, a textile (manufaktura) merchant: had a turnover of 100 thousand zł. Of this, from „beynkhl“[?] goods (perhaps: cotton) 60 thousand zł. with a profit of 10 percent — income 6000 zł.; and 40 thousand zł. from white goods (linen) with a profit of 5 percent — income 3 thousand zł. Together 9 thousand zł. profit.
And so one must state it in all branches.
Submitting the calculation of income is of colossal importance. The assessment commission cannot reject it so easily without reasons, and thanks to this one can defend oneself successfully."
Two weeks of propaganda for Polish cretonne

On the initiative and with the cooperation of the American adviser Dewey[?] a propaganda campaign for Polish cretonne is being organised throughout Poland, which will last two weeks.
The campaign will take place from 27 April to 10 May.
All textile (manufaktura) shops, even the largest and most splendid stores in Warsaw and the provinces, will display cretonne in their shop windows, and a special large campaign will be conducted for wearing cretonne.
In all theatres, cinemas, restaurants and cafés (kawiarnie) it will be shown how beautiful dresses can be made from Polish cretonne. The actresses will appear in cretonne dresses.
Besides this, all radio stations and the newspapers will campaign for Polish percale.
The textile merchants should take note of this and also prepare themselves for the campaign.
To the Jewish estate owners in Poland!

The circle of Jewish agronomy students at the University of Wilno appeals to the Jewish estate owners in Poland to assist its members in their studies by enabling them to do summer practical training.
Summer practice is an absolute necessity for agronomy students, because without practical work agronomic studies are impossible. The university does not provide the students with practice, and they must see to it themselves. Until now the situation of the Jewish agronomy student has been very hard. He lacked the practical side of his studies, because there were no proper bodies that would look for summer practice for him and mediate for him. Now that the circle of Jewish agronomy students at the University of Wilno has been founded, it decided, as one of its first steps, to turn to the Jewish estate owners in Poland with the request that each of them should undertake to grant summer practice to one of the circle's members.
We believe that the Jewish estate owners will help us in our studies and grant us whatever help they are able to grant us.
The board of the circle of Jewish agronomy students at the University of Wilno.
The address of our circle: Koło Rolników Studentów Żydow U. S. B Wilno Ludwisarska 4.
The “Westen” factory in Olkusz has been closed. 2000 workers left without work

On Tuesday, under the chairmanship of the Olkusz starosta, Mr. Stamirowski, a conference took place in connection with the events at the “Westen” factory, about which we already wrote in the previous issue.
Taking part in the conference were the chief inspector from Kielce, the labour inspector from Sosnowiec, directors of the factory and delegates of the workers.
The factory management declared categorically that because of the crisis and difficult production conditions the factory is being closed for an unlimited time.
The same announcement appeared a few hours later on the gates of the factory.
2 thousand workers have lost their bread.

The Dangerous Disease. (Can it be tolerated that irresponsible lawlessness should run wild freely and openly over the Jewish bodies?)

A curse, a damnation, a bewitched poison lies poured out over Jewish work, over the Jewish "praca" [Polish: work]. Our "harowanie"[?] [Polish: drudgery] has lately become unbearable; earning a piece of bread costs the Jew a hard parting of the Red Sea, and it is really no wonder that the taxes and administrative expenses devour more than what the Jew sets out to earn. He makes himself a calculation that he will lick off no more than a taste, and at the same time he does not[?] bear in mind at all that to this "licking" he adds quite a sizeable coin.
It is, after all, self-evident that with such false calculations one cannot get far[?]; a certain time passes, a hole appears[?] in the pocket, and then[—]: bankruptcies, distraints, one loses[?] one's place and the firm goes under.
So[?] it is when things go "normally", systematically and in a calculated way[?]. Quite different, however, is the case when one hits an obstacle, when a firm is over-assessed [Polish szacować] and when one starts to pile taxes on it beyond all nature; in that case the firm is smashed in one-two and there is no more remedy for it. At such a moment one runs into the "skarb" [the treasury/tax office] to intervene, but by then one can already write[?] "alive and well" and nothing helps any more — it is written and sealed and lost. But a Jew is still a Jew; one cannot get rid of him so fast: he will — he says — not budge from the spot until they show him in black and white why and how he was taxed so highly. But then, you see[?], they will not be able to prove[?] to you on what grounds they taxed you with such a high sum; they will answer you short and sharp that the commissions did it so, and the commissions — say the officials — know[?] very well what they are doing, and if they have pronounced that you can pay so-and-so much, there is no further room for doubt.
And in truth it is indeed, in reality, quite correct too, because they [the officials] will not at all accept [anything] from our representatives here[?] when those do not order payment; but when they do order payment, then, without any inquiry or investigation, one must take as fast as possible and as much as possible.
Be that as it may, we have various representatives. There are some who give themselves no account of their representation; they are not up to the task of knowing how far they are able to serve the public interest, and consequently they do not understand how much harm they can bring the community by not reacting when they see that an injustice is being done to this or that citizen, to this or that oppressed[?] firm. That is to say, then, that such representatives harm the community unwittingly, because, as we see, the "urzędy"[?] [government offices] rely very heavily on the naivety of the public delegates, and they watch[?] for every favourable opportunity to exploit it for themselves. For that very reason the offices wish to have among them such representatives as will not be stubborn, so that every demand will be accepted by them on the spot.
From this we already see how far our public delegates must not be yielding, how far they must fight and be stubborn, because otherwise position after position is[?] lost, and this causes the community enormously great harm.
All this has been said about representatives who do not understand their tasks, who do not know how the problems to which they have been invited ought to be solved. It goes without saying that it is a great wrong both on the part of the people who take the mission upon themselves while knowing that they are not qualified for it, and it is also not right on the part of the public institutions when they send such representatives, who are not capable of performing what should lie within their competence. This is one of the greatest wrongs that the people can never forgive, because the public sins in this case are enormously great and painful.
But there are sins whose stains will never be wiped away. We have, to our regret and to our greatest shame, such representatives — both in the commissions and in the offices — who are out only for their own good and for the other man's harm. They go there in order to do harm to this or that Jew; that is their only goal. They want nothing more than to undermine their competitor, whom they mean to "chop in" — so that they shall know. When that moment[?] arrives they fight right and left only so that their competitor gets as large a portion as possible; then they are incomprehensibly capable, and their stubborn ambition reaches the very highest degree. And in order to do another man harm it need not necessarily be a competitor of his: it may as well be the competitor's customer, or merely an enemy of his on whom he always hoped to take revenge — and now he settles accounts with him. Just as a bloodthirsty beast needs ever more victims to sate itself, so these "people's representatives" [printed "folks-pereter"] need to take ever more revenge, and then they reckon with nothing and with no one; they lose then the whole image of God and become plain bloodthirsty beasts.
This is no news: it has been known too well for years and from even earlier, and now one learns of it more and more; the later it gets, the more horrible are the deeds we hear of from those who come to disrupt and take revenge.
It was thought that the disease would be eased, that people would somehow realise that their work is not a noble one, that it is a criminal one, because it is not honest from the civic standpoint — for the government does not aim to break a citizen only[?] because he happened upon another citizen's enemy — and also from the national standpoint the tactic is a criminal, a loathsome, a disgusting one, which no honest person will want to touch. Unfortunately, not only is the disease not eased, but on the contrary it takes on an ever more dangerous character. Wherever we go and wherever we stand we hear that unheard-of[?] deeds are becoming more popular, so that the sickness is taking on an epidemic character. It is unheard of to be able to exist in such a way, for which person has no enemies? It turns out, then, that he will have to tremble and quake lest his enemy have an eye in the "high windows", or else he can make him miserable. Within a short time he can be smashed as a victim.
It is therefore clear as day that the sickness is taking on a dangerous character, that the question is growing ever more disgusting and frightening, and for that reason we must not remain indifferent to these criminal deeds. Our economic institutions, our honest and upright public delegates, must take a stand on this question. It must be shown[?] to the authorities once and for all that one cannot rely on information that comes from a competitor and an enemy, whose only aim is to push the other man out of his place.
Nor may such people be sent to any public institution or government institution as representatives, as delegates of the people. On the contrary: not only must they not be people's delegates, representatives of any stratum whatsoever, but one must strive to have an investigation carried out, and if the investigation proves that the information was given with the sole intention of clearing one's competitor out of the way so that one's own situation should be improved, then these people should be punished by the authorities, and in the Jewish camp they should be branded as traitors who wanted[?] to destroy people because those others wanted to live and exist just as they do.
The irresponsible lawlessness must no longer be allowed to run wild freely and openly in the Jewish street. There must be a limit to everything, and everything must come to an end.
Selekt.
In Honour of Passover

[Passover — collected Torah sayings, anecdotes and remarks.]
Short Torah sayings, anecdotes and remarks relating to Passover. Collected and adapted by Y. L. [?]
a) A Passover without a "she'elah".
A Hasid came to the Radomsko Rebbe, the author of "Tiferet Shlomo", to take leave before Passover. On parting the Rebbe wishes him: "May you have a Passover without a she'elah [a ritual query]." The Hasid stares wide-eyed and thinks the Rebbe is giving him a simple blessing — that Passover should pass for him without a question about hametz. Well, for a Jew who is a Hasid such a blessing is worth a great deal. But the Rebbe smiles: I mean that Passover should pass for you without a she'elah — that you should not need to borrow for Passover... (In Yiddish "she'elah" also means a loan.)
b) "Only by wickedness does he give matzah" (Proverbs 13:10).
In Prague [?] there was an upstart rich man, and like all upstarts he occupied an honourable communal post, although he was a great miser who never gave a Jew a penny [grosz], and on top of that a thorough villain. At Passover, when the kehilla distributes matzot to the poor, the management of the distribution was handed over to him. No doubt he showed all his wickedness in distributing the matzot to the poor; he gave them burning troubles. Of him the "Noda BiYehuda" quoted the verse: "Only by wickedness does he give matzah" — the matzah that he hands out, not from his own pocket, even that he does with malice, with ill will. (The true plain meaning of the verse is: through ill will comes "matzah" — strife.)
c) Ma'ot hittim — in the Torah.
The custom of collecting "ma'ot hittim" [Passover wheat money] and distributing matzot to the poor is found in the Jerusalem Talmud, Bava Batra, chapter 1, and it is cited in the glosses of the Rema, siman 429 [printed "ס״ו"]. The Vilna Gaon, however, found an allusion to it in the Torah.
In the portion Bo matzot are mentioned twice. Once: "Seven days shalt thou eat matzot (מצת)", meaning: a duty upon a person to eat matzot. And the second time: "Matzot shall be eaten" (מצות יאכל), meaning: not only you yourself — you must also see to it that the poor have matzot.
The Gaon remarked on this that in the first verse, where it speaks of the person himself, "מצת" is written without a vav — for himself a person may be sparing with matzot; but where it speaks of the poor it is written in full, "מצות" — the poor you must provide for without [?] stinginess, with an open hand.
d) Passover — the day for our children.
The essence of the Egyptian exile concerned our children: "Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river" — so Pharaoh decreed. And at the time of the redemption, too, it was the children who first perceived God and said "This is my God and I will glorify Him" (see Sotah 11), and therefore at Passover we hold a spiritual review of our children: "The Torah speaks of four sons."
Strictly speaking, if there are four sons, it follows that the wicked make up twenty-five percent of our children. But further on we see that for the simple son, for example, it says "And when thy son asketh thee" — in the singular, and likewise for the wise son and for the one who does not know how to ask; only for the wicked son does it say "And when your children shall say unto you" — in the plural. Proof that the wicked are the great majority.
Something more: for all the sons it says "when thy son asketh thee" or the like, always in the language of a question. Only for the wicked son does it say "And when they shall say" — because the wicked son does not ask; he wants no debates, he comes with ready-made formulas; for him his corrupt ideas are certain, beyond doubt.
Drashot El Afi [so printed; probably "El Ami"].
e) "Banim" is also a plague...
A villager, reciting the ten plagues at the seder, made a mistake and instead of "kinim" [lice] said "banim" [sons]. His son catches him on the slip [?]: "Father, not banim but kinim!" The rural Jew answers: You hear, my son — sons are also a plague..
f) "Ve-ata kalbeta"...
A band of young men decided to play a "trick" on a great rabbi and burst in on him in disguise during the seder. Just as they burst in, the rabbi was saying the words of Had Gadya: "Ve-ata kalbeta" (in came a dog).
Shevi'i shel Pesach [the seventh day of Passover].
g) The splitting of the Red Sea and eating.
As is known, a festival is more lenient in law than the Sabbath in that on a festival one is permitted to do work needed for a person's food ("okhel nefesh"), and interestingly: the permission of work for a person's eating is mentioned only for the seventh day of Passover (and the other festivals are derived from the seventh day of Passover), because that is when the splitting of the sea took place, and a person's food comes to him with as much hardship as splitting a sea.. Thus a confirmation of the saying: "A person's sustenance is as hard as the splitting of the Red Sea." — R. Tz. of Zhidachov [Żydaczów].
h) "And Israel saw... and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14) [printed "בד׳"].
At the Red Sea the Jews saw such supernatural wonders, and yet from "and they saw", from seeing everything, they had to arrive at "and they believed", at simple faith. One can see everything clearly and yet not have faith. — R. Y. M. of Ger [?] [Góra Kalwaria].
i) "And they believed in the Lord and in His servant Moses" (ibid.).
After "and they believed in His servant Moses" came at once "Then sang Moses", because the leader can sing, create, only when the people believes in him, when it stands firmly behind him. — Degel Mahaneh Efrayim.
j) Parnassim and parnassah...
It is an old custom among Jews to elect all sorts of communal heads, dozors [members of the kehilla board], members of the Hevra Kadisha and the like on the seventh day of Passover. Where does the custom come from?
In the Gemara the communal heads are called "parnassim", because according to how they administer, according to their order, so is the livelihood (parnassah) among the people... Therefore they are called P-A-R-N-A-S-S-I-M, because the well-being of the people, its livelihood, depends on their leadership; and the seventh day of Passover is connected with livelihood, because "a person's sustenance is as hard as the splitting of the Red Sea" (see above, letter yod [so printed; should be zayin]). Therefore all sorts of parnassim are elected then. — Bnei Yissaschar.
Jewish Social Work

(Special to the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".)
Ten thousand Jewish orphans, who are maintained and provided with food and clothing in 124 institutions and in private homes; 3,170 children who are learning a trade, and nearly 4 000 children who have already become self-supporting — these are the results so far of the activity of the Federation for the Care of Orphans ("CENTOS").
33 thousand school-age children under constant medical supervision; 22 thousand cured of various illnesses; 7.700 patients being treated in 12 institutions for tuberculosis; 20 child-advice stations; 10 advice stations for mothers; 22 dental surgeries; 31 outpatient clinics, 4 hospitals, etc. — this is the present state of the "TOZ" organisation.
Some 14 thousand professionally trained adults and young people, a number of craft schools and supplementary courses, factory schools in the country[?] and the like; agricultural cooperatives; 1,060[?] Jewish families who live from working the land and are served by the society — this, in very brief strokes, is the widely ramified work of the "ORT" society, which has set itself the goal of the productivisation of the Jewish masses in Poland.
And if we also take into account the 150 thousand people who were served over the last 5 years by "JEAS"; the reduction of emigrants' travel costs thanks to its intervention, and loans granted to a sum of 110,000 dollars; the first 200 Jewish families settled on the land in France — we can get a picture of the great work of the Jewish Emigration Society.
The budgets of the four societies together amount to 10 million złoty a year. Quietly and modestly these organisations have carried on their activity, founded schools and workshops, provided light, knowledge and education to thousands of children, prepared tens of thousands of people for the struggle for existence and developed in them faith in a better future. Without noise and fuss, with a deep understanding of the tasks that weighed on them, the boards kept away from all political games and personal ambitions, steadily increasing the scope of their work and the number of people whom they kept in a healthy physical condition and prepared for a productive life in Poland, or in a distant, foreign land.
But the work of the societies mentioned has until now relied mostly on help from abroad. Polish Jewry contributed only from time to time to the purposes of these societies; life in the struggle for existence, however, called forth a stronger, or greater interest; a large network of institutions, schools and workshops was built up and developed, and now it can no longer be maintained. The subsidies from abroad are steadily shrinking, and if Polish Jewry does not now show its understanding, does not contribute with a generous hand and does not bind itself to these societies — everything may go under.
A gigantic work has been accomplished. If we analyse precisely the past years and the most varied fields of activity of the said societies in the field of social aid, we must admire the colossal energy, initiative and devotion of the Jewish communal workers.
This gigantic work is now threatened by danger. Foreign help is steadily shrinking; the severe crisis in Poland does not allow a longer and more serious consideration[?] of the most important problems of life. But one must not keep silent. The duty of the devoted workers in every town and shtetl is to awaken the Jewish population and interest it in the work of the societies. This is our core question; this is the means of holding out in the hard struggle with life. And we must hold out and endure.
In time the state and the municipal institutions will increase their subsidies and cover the greater part of the budgets. Until then Polish Jewry will create the necessary means.
Jewish social aid work is in danger, and it must and will be saved!
Arye Cytlin.
From the "Hazamir" Library

"Hazamir" — the largest Jewish library in Będzin and also in Zagłębie — has recently renewed its activity and embarked on an intensified campaign to popularise and cultivate the Jewish book. The external appearance of the library (after the renovation carried out), its internal order (the new catalogue on the card-index system) and the freshly bought books are all sufficient proof that the library is rising to a new life. In the last 2 months alone nearly 200 new works have been added, most of them the newest things in Yiddish literature, belles-lettres as well as popular science, and also the best translations from world literature.
It is only regrettable that the circle of readers has not grown in parallel with the growth of the library, despite the accessible conditions. One may hope, however, that this apathy too will in time be broken.

A Letter to the Editor.
[Będzin — Kehilla.]
Esteemed Editors!
Please print the following letter to the board of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin, for which I give you my best thanks in advance.
To the Board of the Jewish Kehilla in Będzin.
Two years ago I turned to you with a letter in which I declined to remain active as vice-president and as a member of the kehilla council in Będzin. Two more members of the council did the same and resigned, but to this day we have received no answer whatsoever from the board, and we assumed that our resignation was being accepted, for "silence is tantamount to admission"; otherwise[?] we would have counted on an answer.
It turns out, however, that we are again counted as parnassim (communal leaders): budgets are set which suit, on the one hand (as to the sums), Łódź or Warsaw, and on the other hand (for cultural purposes) Zgierz or Sagdżew[?]; and on top of it all the president of the council calls sessions to consider the budget. Naturally, the first time there is no quorum (there is no quorum at all...), so the session is set for the next day, to be "valid with any number present", and then the president comes with another 1—2 persons and fixes the budget. The public (of the council) is satisfied — it has done[?] its duty; and when the town's public is not satisfied, it shouts and swallows[?] —
The purpose of my letter is — since[?] the "Zaglembier Cajtung" reported that the Voivodeship did not take our resignation into account:
1) That the town, that is, our voters, should know that we have resigned from our posts.
2) The budgets are passed irregularly, since the number of council members is incomplete.
3) The board was obliged to inform us whether or not it accepted our resignations, and since it did not do so, it must bear the consequences.
4) The term of office expired long ago; I already consider myself released from my post, and therefore I bear no responsibility whatsoever for the activity of the board and council.
Respectfully, Szlama Frenkel.

"Habima" in Sosnowiec.
At the railway station the "Habima" actors were awaited by a delegation of Hebraists. The delegation received the guests with a reverent silence. From TsYShO.
At the last board meeting of the TsYShO branch in Będzin it was resolved to turn to the Central Committee with a request not to delegate any more delegates who, like Mr. Magrelman[?], make use of Hebrew verses...
A Flood Danger.
Because of the collective "lectures" which the P.Z. (Poale Zion) organise, there is a threat of the Przemsza overflowing.
The councillors[?] of the Left P.Z. faction have submitted[?] an urgent motion to the municipal board that rescue measures be adopted for the inhabitants there.
"Depression".
Lately it is very noticeable how deeply depressed the Agudah leaders in Sosnowiec are.

Today, on Shvi'i shel Pesach, a conference of the Revisionist organisations in Będzin and Sosnowiec will take place.
The conference will discuss starting an action to discover: 1) a Jewish pharmacist who cheated the kimcha (Passover flour) committee in Będzin, 2) carrying out an audit at the Sosnowiec kehilla council in order to find the stamps of the gmina, and 3) the 100 zł. which a Będzin religious functionary took for a "needy person" for Passover..

At the last minute we are informed from Olkusz that a fact has occurred there: a poor Jew received a loan from the "Gemilut Hesed" fund after only one month of running around..
A Fine Donation.
The Passover campaign of the Dąbrowa "Women's Society" was brilliantly successful this year. A special impression was made by the donation of a local rich lady, who "understood" the present situation and donated as many as 3 eggs and a whole kilo of potatoes..
He Is Already Sweating.
(A Sosnowiec tale.)
A Sosnowiec rich man fell ill. The doctor prescribes him a medicine with the remark that if he sweats he will recover; if, God forbid, not — it will go badly. The patient took the medicine several times and did not sweat; he took fright and called to him "a communal worker" in order to pledge donations to charitable societies[?]. When he began to write down a hundred for the Jewish hospital, and two hundred for the old-age home [?], he broke out in a sweat.
Seeing that he was sweating, he said to the communal worker:
— Cross out the donations, I'm already sweating.
The Ma Nishtanah for the Second Days [of the holiday].

What makes you different, Miss Sonia?
You're a girl of marriageable years...
So I have questions to ask you —
just give me a clear answer...
Tell me why, when morning comes,
you have wrinkles on your face...
Green[?] cheeks, blue lips —
the signs of a corpse...

Your eyes, like the glass panes,
have the colour of curl-papers[?]...
and your "charming[?] coiffure"
gives the impression of a... rag...
Your little teeth — the lathe-turned ones [i.e. false] —
are pearls, a real wonder...
and they lie in the night-table
in a little pot of their own...
Look in the mirror: then you look
like a "forty-year-old" [—][?]...
You have a face like my grandmother's
when she comes home from a masquerade...

But later, Miss Sonia,
when you go out to your rendezvous...
you have a completely different face
in the quiet evening hours...
You have a little face like a toy,
on your little lips — lipstick...
and your eyes as yellow as
citron lemonade...
and your little mouth adorned
with platinum and gold crowns...
Whoever sees you would give you no more
than twenty years, honestly...
———
I'll give the answer myself:
it all depends on the make-up...
You walk into a "skład apteczny" [drugstore]
and there you turn from a brunette into a blonde...
Fishel.

A shameful denunciation against a member of the Rabbinical Council, Rabbi Frommer.

Yesterday morning we received the news from Sosnowiec that a search had been carried out at Rabbi Frommer's on the basis of a base denunciation.
Later we received the following information about this villainy:
From a certain quarter a denunciation was submitted to the starosta, the voivode and the ministry with the following content:
„There is a Jew by the name of Frommer, a melamed by profession, whose purpose is to extort money by means of blackmail. He introduced his first blackmail in Koziegłowy, where he extorted from the local Jews the title [?] of rabbi. From Zawiercie — the denunciation says — Frommer moved to Sosnowiec, where he follows the same ways“..

Bloody events between police and workers. Bread or work — a clash. — Dozens wounded

On Tuesday a bloody clash took place here between the unemployed and the police. The result: 3 workers were seriously and several dozen lightly wounded.
The course of events was as follows:
Already from 9 o'clock in the morning masses of unemployed gathered in front of the magistrate [town hall], demanding relief for the holidays.
At 11 o'clock the number of unemployed reached 8 thousand persons.
A delegation went to the town president Hilger; the latter had a telephone conversation with the voivode, who promised that the relief payments could only be given the next day, Wednesday.
When the delegation came back with this answer, the crowd was not satisfied and began singing „Czerwony Sztandar“ [„The Red Flag“].
At that moment a larger detachment of mounted police arrived, which was met by the crowd with stones, bricks, etc. The police dispersed the gathered crowd by force, and on the spot 3 workers were seriously wounded; the ambulance [pogotowie] of the Health Insurance Fund took them to hospital.
The lightly wounded received medical help on the spot.
At the same time a delegation went to the district starosta, demanding that the term of the relief payments be extended.
The starosta promised to deal with the request properly.

Four masked bandits broke into the property owner Skotnicz [?] in Grabaszyn [?] and, threatening with revolvers, robbed him of 4 thousand zł. The victim reported the attack to the police in Kazimierz, which arrested 1 bandit an hour later.
Under interrogation the bandit „told tales out of cheder“ [gave the game away], thanks to which the others who took part in the attack were arrested.
Another 3,245 zł. was found on those arrested.
Not „a foot for a foot“, only 1 month in prison.
