A Fitting Monument

(On the 17th yahrzeit of Rabbi R. Yissachar Berish Groibart, of blessed memory.)

Year after year, when the yahrzeit of Rabbi R. Yissachar Berish, of blessed memory, comes round, we remember him; we recall his greatness, his beauty; others remind us of his virtues, his genius, his sharpness, his good character, his fine manners and his aristocratic bearing. Anyone who knew the personality of Rabbi Groibart at all closely can recall for his yahrzeit one of his sharp-witted sayings, a quip, a pointed characterization aimed at some communal busybody. All his students still remember with what fervor they sat over the Gemara, under the direction of that luminous figure.
More than once we have heard great men envy us, saying: among you the seat of the rabbinate was occupied by a great man, an important personality — you had R. Yissachar Berish as rabbi. Yes, we had R. Yissachar Berish as a rabbi, but did we know at the time what sort of personality we had as our spiritual leader? Did we know how to appreciate his greatness, his lofty idealistic thoughts, with which he carried himself and sought to illuminate the Jewish world? He always strove to unite into one strong organization all the religious elements, which in those years were not only splintered and petty, but still raw, had as yet no system, and did not know how to step onto the public arena.
At the rabbinical assembly held in those years in Petersburg, Rabbi Groibart played a significant role among the great Russian rabbis. Then the religious parties were not yet crystallized and did not play such a role as in today's parliamentary era. Then parties were not born and did not die every Monday and Thursday through people of no merit in any movement; and yet one looked upon the leaders, upon the spokesmen, differently — one knew that these were personalities for whom the ideal and the truth stood above all else in the world, and perhaps that was indeed the reason they were given full trust, were held fit to stand at the height on which they then found themselves.
Those were altogether different times; then one could not even imagine that partisanship is approached in a petty way, and that the main nerve of this or that party is falsehood and hypocrisy — something that has, alas, penetrated so deeply into the marrow of the bones that people no longer understand that it can be otherwise, that one can make do with the innocent naked truth just as it is. Then the world was not yet so refined and had not yet even begun to walk the ways of 'modern partisanship'; then everything was still so primitive and innocent that one can hardly imagine it today.
Today both communal-political life and private-egoistic life have been altogether changed; the whole system of life has been completely transformed, so that humanity in general and we Jews in particular have entered an entirely different phase, and the conditions in which we now find ourselves are entirely different. An entirely new world-outlook has thus arisen. The European war introduced an entirely different system into the conditions of our way of life, so that our outlook and train of thought are entirely different, founded on other foundations in our life today.
It therefore happens quite often that we would gladly take a stroll through the corners of that former life, when before the war we were so closely bound together; we would gladly pay a visit there and draw from the wellspring of memories that breathed into us so much hope for the future. For all its shortcomings and moldy staleness, we would know how to appreciate the simplicity and naivety of those days, of which, alas, we have so little today.
And here is what is interesting: we notice that, despite humanity having hoped so for new times and having therefore forgotten the pre-war world, after a certain time a longing for the past set in, and people began to study the fine customs we lost in the bygone pre-war world. This is a sign that humanity is now not much more content, and perhaps even less so than before.
That is apparently also the reason why we here in Będzin had forgotten to observe the memory of the departed gaon. It reached the point that the town even forgot the yahrzeit of the deceased; and it is interesting how instinctively Jewish Będzin roused itself and with strong fervor began to long for the spirit of the great religious leader, and only then did it awaken and begin to take part so massively in his yahrzeit, so that each year the number of participants grows and the memorial becomes more imposing. Only now, years later, does one begin to appreciate the greatness of the departed rabbi.
There is an old rule among us: 'After death — [they are called] holy'; after death one begins to enumerate the virtues, while in life we see nothing. When our great ones are among us we do not appreciate their greatness, and not only do we not know how to appreciate their greatness and beauty, but we pay no attention at all to the personality that lives and works among us. The same happened with Rabbi Groibart: however much reverence and respect we ought to have had for him, we were far from knowing how to appreciate what a gaon then occupied the Będzin seat of the rabbinate. Only now do we begin to understand him, only now does the great spirit hover before our eyes, now we begin to grasp whom and what we had in Będzin as a spiritual leader.
It would therefore be just to immortalize the memory of the great gaon. A leader who was rabbi in Będzin for 20 years deserves that a fitting institution be founded in his name, by which his spirit would be sanctified, and by which religious Jewry would show that it knows how to appreciate its personalities, its great men.
On the 17th yahrzeit one ought to speak seriously, so that the aim may be achieved and the proposal become a reality. It makes no difference — Rabbi Groibart had merits enough for the town, so that he has honestly earned a fitting monument; this we see on the day of his yahrzeit, when various strata of the population gather together to honor the memory of the great spiritual leader. Let the question therefore become topical, and let it be treated with the full seriousness and sincerity that such a matter deserves.
R. Let.
A Fortress of Yiddish

There is a city in the world that constitutes a veritable fortress of Yiddish.
When you enter this city, it is at first simply hard to get your bearings, to know where you are. Is this Eretz Israel? — for Hebrew is spoken all around. Soviet Russia, or Ukraine? — but there are no Bolsheviks here. The streets of Manchester? Then where are the Jews, in their kapotes? The New York East Side, or London's Whitechapel? You walk through whole quarters and see on no shop any sign other than a Yiddish one, you hear no language other than our mother tongue. You are immersed in the Jewish quarters, for of the 1.2 million inhabitants that Montreal counts, 60,000 are Jews. The 60,000 Jews are its [—] element, so that whenever the city administration needs to turn to them with any kind of appeal or announcement, it prints it in Yiddish too. The journalist Mr. Firszt, who writes about Montreal, asks himself a question: whence did Yiddish draw such strength as to spread through the largest Canadian city more than in any other city in the world?
And he finds an answer himself:
Montreal is a city of French and English, who for many years have been carrying on between themselves a game, a war, over stamping a new cultural imprint on the city. Both groups command here the same forces — if the French are more numerous, they nonetheless stand on a lower cultural level (the Canadian French descend from peasants). So, after all, England remains the ruler of the land [Canada].
By [—], to this day neither of the groups has managed to vanquish the other, and meanwhile the Jew profits from it — he does not let himself be assimilated by either side and goes his own way — Yiddish!
He speaks Yiddish at home and in the street, and a pure, juicy Yiddish. The sign over his shop is Yiddish, and he keeps the books in the shop itself in Yiddish too. He reads a Yiddish newspaper and a Yiddish book, the old generation as much as the young. One pities only the young Jews and the women from Poland, Romania and other lands, who in the old home were not accustomed [—] to speak a Yiddish word, and here must, poor things, break their tongue...

Our stage is broad and great: the entire globe. In it lies our power, our power-of-exile, which brought us to the Balfour Declaration, to San Remo, to the glorious labor in the Valley [Emek], to the holy paths and the [ingathering] [?].
Should the Passfields and MacDonalds bar for us the gates of Eretz Israel, drown with pioneers' blood the holy paths of pioneers' sweat, we shall play the very same play in all the corners of the world with Bar-Kokhba fire, which once already cost six hundred thousand Jewish souls and saw the fall of the Roman Empire.
That epilogue was played out on the mountains of Judea, mingled with red fire, as the singer — Rome has fallen, Jerusalem lives — we shall play that epilogue, [—] headquarters, in all the remotest corners of the British Empire.

The Inexhaustible Wellspring (On the [—]th Yortsayt of the Gaon R. Yissochor Berish Grojbart z"l), Collected and Transmitted by Sz. Lewkowicz

[Religious column / anecdotes.] 'The inexhaustible wellspring' — a collection of the ever-refreshing, sharp-witted sayings of the Będzin rabbi R. Yissochor Berish Grojbart z"l, on his yortsayt.
1. From a neighboring rabbi the rabbi z"l suffered frequent 'troubles,' insults and even deeds unbecoming of a rabbi. Those close to him advised him how to be rid once and for all of that man's doings... The rabbi shook off the 'good advice,' would not hear of it and said: — Heaven forbid! Of the sons of Jacob it says 'and such a thing is not done' (ve-chen lo ye'ase); they too could not avenge themselves on Shechem son of Chamor with the same weapon as his... — If that rabbi wished to win his community's favor with finer deeds than mine, with a better sermon than mine, I would have a counter-weapon — I would have to strive for even finer deeds and a finer sermon. But with ugly deeds I cannot avenge myself on him. — 'And such a thing is not done.'
2. The rabbi z"l delivered his last sermon on Shabbat Shuva 5684 (1923). At that time — as Będzin Jews surely recall — support-posts (slupes) had been standing for a while in the synagogue for repairs. Just then the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha asked the rabbi to mention in the sermon that the wall around the old cemetery needed repair. The rabbi said: — It is written, 'A stone shall cry out from the wall, and a rafter of wood shall answer it' (even mi-kir tiz'ak u-chefis me'etz ya'anena). What does 'shall answer' mean — the beam answers it back? The plain sense is this: 'even mi-kir tiz'ak' — the cemetery wall cries out to be repaired; 'u-chefis me'etz ya'anena' — the wooden posts answer it: Why are you crying out, cemetery wall? You, whom people see so seldom, no wonder you are forgotten; but I, a wooden post in the synagogue, seen every day and still left in such a state — how much more must I cry out!
3. An author came to the rabbi z"l wanting him to buy his book titled 'Avraham Yagel.' When the rabbi took the volume in hand he quipped: — 'Avraham Yagel' is already off the press, 'Yitzchak Yeranen' too is already off the press, only 'Yaakov u-vanav' — Jacob and his sons — are still in the press (still in print/in a jam)...
4. Once — it was on the eve of Sukkot — there was a great glut of etrogim in Będzin; the prices fell from hour to hour, so that by nightfall one could get a fine 'specimen' (geshtel) for half a ruble. A market-trader who had snapped up such a 'bargain' rushed to the rabbi to ask whether the etrog was kosher. When the Jew left joyfully that his 'merchandise' was kosher, the rabbi laughed and said to those present: — People come to me with all sorts of questions, but it has not yet happened that someone asks me the law of 'tzedek and a just hin' (eifa tzedek ve-hin tzedek)...
5. Of a well-known 'respectable' Będzin magnate, who had a reputation as an honest man but of whom unflattering things were told about his earlier conduct — when the rabbi z"l heard this, he said ironically: — How much a poor man robs, plunders and steals in the course of his life, so as to remain a bit of an honest man...
6. The day before the eve of Passover a grave lung-question (she'elat ha-re'a) arose in Sławków, which could have caused a great financial loss, besides the 'danger' of the town being left without meat. The then rabbinic decisor, a great scholar, sent his son to Będzin, to the departed [rabbi], with the question. The rabbi z"l studied the question at length and then told the messenger these words: — There is only one authority who permits it, and your father and I will also say 'gesht'... The verse in Psalms 'For this let every pious one pray to You at a time of finding; surely, when great waters overflow, they shall not reach him' the rabbi z"l expounded with a legend: In the days of the Destruction the enemy took captive 400 children, boys and girls, to apostatize them. As they boarded the ship, first the girls and then the boys leapt into the sea. Because the girls had sanctified the Name first, it was decreed in Heaven that the girls' souls would descend to the world again and their reward would be 'and she shall rule over him' (ve-hi yimshol bo) — that they would rule over the men. This is the plain sense — said the rabbi — 'for this let every pious one pray': a pious man prays that at the 'time of finding,' when he takes a wife, 'surely the overflowing waters shall not reach him' — that he not receive such a wife from those who drowned in the water, i.e. that he not have 'an evil wife, more bitter than death.' For the most part — the rabbi z"l added — the gentle men receive the worst shrews...

[—] are greatly mistaken about this chronic sickness, [—] that one can help it only through reforms of the [tax] system, of [—], by freeing the [—], by placing the Jew on an equal footing with the rest of the [strata] of the population with regard to the various means of earning a livelihood.

These questions concern in equal measure all strata of the Jewish population — whether the merchant, whether the small trader, whether the artisan, and whether the worker.

We deliberately do not touch upon the national-cultural questions; we mention only those present-day points which at the present day can be solved through decrees.

If we were to take a look at the matter of the Jewish communities, we would come first of all [to the conclusion] that the question of how a rabbi is to be elected and how long the term of office of a community should last plays a very small role in comparison with the general community problem, which consists in this: that the community must be a Jewish autonomous corporation, which concerns itself with the whole complex of [general] Jewish problems.

In no more than a few weeks' time the [entrusted matters] [—] can be changed by way of decrees.

It is an ardent wish of the entire Jewish population that this should finally come to pass.

We have already been waiting for it for 10 years.

Will the answer come now?

Dir. J. Rozenblat.

But Joséphine was not frightened by his strong fist. When she read the letter over, she burst out laughing; since she happened just then to be spending time with [Talleyrand], the former secretary of the Paris city administration, she showed him the letter and, with a smile, said:

We Got Rid of the First Election Fair

[Feuilleton/satire.] [Our][?] first election fair is the one that [—] before us, that we have already [—] had, and we got rid of the first election fair — after the Sejm elections. [—] the Sejm elections were a kind of holiday[?], like Simchas-Torah. [—] with the [—], it has already become a holiday '[—]' on [—]; a Senate voter, compared with the Sejm voter, has [—] less temperament [—]. We do see [—] how impetuous and full of temperament the Sejm elections were; [—] the [—] people don't sing [—], and how sleepily-sleepy the 18th bloc ran[?] its campaign. True, that is why the youth drove in three times as many votes. But what do I get out of it — that with nearly 8,000 votes we nonetheless remained mute as a fish… and I was left with a headache from the day-and-night domestic quarrels.
[—] it burst forth [—]; [someone] almost said outright that such a little shopkeeper might perhaps [—] vote [—]; a candidate says [—] '[—]', [—] credit to all the shopkeepers and [—] all the taxes. [—] let someone [say it]. My [neighbor][?] tells me: — [—] I lost[?] the [—]; take my advice and vote 17; I am a Sabbath-observer, I'll get a certificate — I'll travel to Eretz-Yisrael, and I'll also demand [it] back, and you will all become colonists, it will be 'each under his vine and under his fig tree,' and we'll forget all our troubles.
Listen to my disputant, who hurls back: — Indeed, far more for you than for us[?] [—].
[—] fortunes, how far [—] one [kills off?] the [—], for to choke; here, heed [—], vote on the one side[?], perhaps [—] the squire will yet do you some favor for it [—], keep [—] hold a [—], let all see — [—] the Rebbe has commanded…
That is how we began, and little by little a war flared up, for life and death; [—] one called me: Messiah![?] 'mah-yofis'-[—]! he called me [—] a crawling flatterer[?]! My opponent[?] called me: Lemeshke [a schlemiel]! and I [—] face!
An uproar arose, a commotion [—] until I fled the house. In the street the war went on [—]. And even more heat: wherever I go, wherever I stand, [people] only torment themselves, only mean [me], a dust 'rose' right up to heaven.
I already wanted not to vote at all[?], but they would not let go of me with my opponent[?] and his [—]; they must come with me to the ballot box[?] and see which slip I put in.
The end was this: on election day we ran about a whole day, did not get through, and when we finally reached the officials[?] they would not let us in — too late already!
But thank God, it's over! A clamp off the head.

Trifles, Defects

[Feuilleton/op-ed.] (What sort of attitude do the officials have toward the citizens? — In Poland, and how does it look in other countries?)
It often happens that a citizen comes to some institution or office and is not treated properly, then leaves in frustration, convinced that 'we are very far from the cultured world' — even though Poland lies in the center of Europe and strives by every means to stand at a proper cultural level. Instead of informing and instructing the citizen how to fulfill his civic duty, the official snaps at him or ignores him, and the citizen must stand and 'knock' (klapn) before him so he will deign to grant a word. Such an attitude is not seen in the cultured countries of Europe, and in Poland it is not official policy — government circles insist that officials treat citizens courteously and provide the needed information. Things sometimes reach quarrels and formal protocols, and the offended citizen must then prove he meant no harm. After such an 'operation' the official grows even more arrogant and acts as an 'autocrat.'
The writer gives examples: the telephone operator (telefonistke) who fails to connect the right number, deliberately delays, or answers that she is 'busy,' and if you reproach her does it 'out of spite'; and another: a citizen asks at the post office how many stamps an express letter abroad needs, is told, affixes and mails them — and the next day the letter returns as insufficiently franked, so he must pay a surcharge. To the official this is a 'trifle' not worth discussing.
Abroad, says the writer, such a wrong would be treated with more respect, and an official who gave wrong, damage-causing information would be punished and perhaps even dismissed; there every official is responsible for his department and serves the public by clear regulations.
Another fact he read in the 'Zaglembier Tsaytung': a respected merchant from Będzin recounts that abroad he could not pay for a telegram in the local currency and offered the official a Polish banknote as a pledge until he could exchange his money — and the official took offense; and at home too, at the post, they refused to accept a pledge from him. The difference: abroad, where he is not known, he felt ashamed before the official; while at home, where he is known, he was shamed — because even on a pledge they will not trust him.
It is no wonder, then, that the heart aches at such disorders, which the Polish government surely does not condone, but which meanwhile stifle the development of commerce and hold back cultural progress. 'These are perhaps trifles, defects — but with such trifles a country must reckon.' R. Lem.
One Year of Agricultural Work in Zaglembie

[Local/agriculture.] At the beginning of the month the general meeting of the Jewish Society for Agriculture (Yidishe Gezelshaft far Landvirtshaft), Zaglembie branch, was held in Będzin in the hall of the Merchants' Association. The society has existed in Zaglembie only one year. It began its activity in a very small circle of devotees of tourism and agriculture; twenty persons [—] were the participants in its founding meeting. They set themselves the aim of bringing the Jewish public something new [—].
With agriculture, the writer adds, we did not long occupy ourselves, although we Jews have already wandered a great deal [—]. The first Jewish agricultural society in Poland arose three years ago in Warszawa; today it already counts hundreds of members, and from year to year the number of members grows, for whom the society arranges summer and winter colonies and excursions throughout Poland and Europe.
Here in Zaglembie we have far better conditions for agricultural work than in Warszawa: here, where in Upper Silesia (Oybershlezyen) lie the largest factories and mines in the country. [—] they are not accessible to visit, but once we founded the agricultural society we first gained the possibility to become acquainted up close with the industrial works of Zaglembie and Upper Silesia.
Within a few hours by train we can reach a beautiful mountain region, yet it is very rare that Jewish tourists from Zaglembie are met in the Beskidy. This is not about the individual, but about creating a mass movement — as has existed for decades in Western Europe. [—] Berlin alone is left by three million people on a holiday. The cultured person today has a real need to go outside the city to calm his nerves and strengthen his body and spirit with fresh powers [—] in nature, in the mountains [—]. [Signed] W—n.

After Five Years (To the Jewish Population of Będzin), by L. Rubinlicht

[Article — end-of-term accounting.] Five years ago the Jewish population of Będzin entrusted to me the hard office of vice-president, to represent and protect Jewish interests in the Będzin magistrate. At that time a Jewish vice-president was something new, not only among us but in all of Poland; the whole Jewish press in Poland, regardless of its line, then reported the news that in Będzin, in the center of antisemitic Zagłębie, a Jewish vice-president had [been elected]. [...] In my first months in the magistrate, rivals broke their teeth when they had to address a 'Mrs. Vice-President,' but slowly I secured my position and earned [trust] among all the officials, especially the non-Jewish ones, since at that time there was not a single Jewish official in the magistrate. Over the 5 years I had to work with allies of every sort, from Communists to rabid antisemites, yet I always managed to carry through all my demands on behalf of the Jewish population. I must also express my appreciation to the Jewish councilmen (with the exception of 2–3) who gave much time and work and helped realize the economic program, which fundamentally changed the city's outward appearance and its municipal economy. Our program was to create useful public municipal institutions that would give the city treasury revenues, so that within a few years part of the present taxes could be reduced. In a short time we managed to create a municipal electric plant yielding about 300,000 zł a year, which is why the price is cheaper than in all of Poland; the municipal slaughterhouse about 80,000 zł; water pipes were laid in streets that had had no water. We levied certain taxes (e.g. on a [—] bridge) bringing up to 50 thousand zł a year, and other taxes lower than in other towns — 25% from the houses (instead of 50 groszy as in Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Częstochowa, Kielce and others). Especially for the Jewish population: the magistrate today employs 20 Jewish officials, 3 Jewish doctors, 1 Jewish hygienist, 1 Jewish sequestrator, 2 Jewish clerks, 1 Jewish manager at the slaughterhouse, 2 collectors at the electric plant, the deputy director of the plant, 8–10 officials at the Jewish colonies, and up to 30 Jewish workers in public works. In recent years the magistrate paid subsidies to Jewish (cultural, social and other) institutions totaling about 150 thousand zł: the Jewish 'orphanage' 35 thousand, [—] 25 thousand, the Jewish colony 27 thousand, the 'old-age home' 15 thousand, etc. — such a sum for Jewish institutions was not granted in any magistrate's budget. Comparing today's figures with those in the budget 5 years ago, one sees how much the Jewish councilmen and representatives did over the 5 years for the Jewish population of Będzin. How do the streets used only by the Jewish [population] look now — such as Modrzejowska, [—], Czeladzka[?], the Old Market, the Fish Market! — where for 20 years not a stone was moved and nothing was lit? Broad sidewalks, squares, good lighting (Będzin now has 110 electric lamps instead of 52 six years ago). For Jewish children the magistrate built a magnificent school building for 400,000 zł, and a modern outpatient clinic from which the Jewish population greatly benefits (80%); and thanks to the improved sanitary conditions, Jewish mortality in Będzin decreases each year. One must also acknowledge that in the last 6 years Będzin has changed greatly for the better, thanks to the city administration: a modern railway station was built in the city center for 2 million złotys, a magnificent post-office building, and a [—] insurance company is building a 4,000,000 zł structure on the magistrate's sale-plots. We managed [matters] carefully, perhaps even frugally, yet everyone who needed the magistrate's help always received it. The present magistrate was the first to allow taxes (padatkes) to be paid over 3 months without interest or penalties. Every citizen, poor and rich, could always consult me. Throughout our term we had no friction with the supervisory council, and the Będzin population showed great confidence. Now that the supervisory authority has dissolved us on purely political grounds, we are proud that the delegate who inspected our activity in the magistrate over 5 days found nothing with which to reproach us. I step down from the city administration with a clear conscience, having honestly fulfilled the office entrusted to me as a Jewish vice-president in Będzin, and I hope my successors will continue the work that remains to be done for the Jewish population in the Będzin magistrate, and will not let go to waste what has, with great effort, been achieved until now.
Cards

[Satirical feuilleton.] 'Cards.' Among us cards were always a sought-after commodity; people played in the big cities and in the little towns — in the towns even more than in the cities, for what better pleasure could one afford in a shtetl on the long winter evenings? Even yeshiva boys in the yeshivas and study-houses used to 'steal' the 'little Shas' more than the big one. But card-playing as it has gone on among us these last years has never been seen, and the chief [players] are the women — they trail after the card-table more, than, lehavdil, at a Christian funeral... One starts playing in autumn; in summer people go off to the dachas and start there too; in autumn they return to town and start with even more zest, for the head is rested and, thanks to acquaintances made at the dacha, fresh [partners] come along... And once one plunges into the cards one forgets how one stands in the world; for we Jews are made either with measure and limit, or not at all. Today, for example, the 'poker fashion' — the whole Jewish conversation revolves around it: 'there is no house that has no poker'... What is more: people play not only in the evenings but also by day, in the morning and the afternoon; for the balebosteh has no time at all, and, thank God, she lacks for nothing — what is she to do? Run the household? There is a maid. Think about a match? She will not meddle in her husband's affairs, and he in hers — he thanks God she does not pester him, and her head is in the cards and his head is calmer... It even has an advantage for him: at cards she may lose, but she may also win; but if she goes about idle and [bored], the 'vexation' will cost him dearer... [The writer] recalls not only her, her husband and her children, but much else: the whole of Jewish communal life — besides women who now give themselves to poker, did any once occupy themselves with philanthropy and public work? He recalls Jewish [letters], Jewish literature and the whole of Jewish culture. Ask me whether she ever reads a newspaper (apart from the serialized novel she skims with her eyes before she sits down at the card-table), and what she knows about the elections? More than one Jewish woman did not go to the ballot-box because she could not tear herself from the card-table, and more than one Jewish vote was lost for the sake of poker... Interestingly, in America too the Jewish women have lately spread the 'card epidemic,' and the newspapers storm against them. But there, such as it is, at least the sum is apportioned to a sacred purpose — the money won is given to charity, used to maintain Talmud Torahs, or even to write a Torah scroll. [One consoles] oneself that it is a 'law' — good deeds through demoralization; yet by all opinions one feels there that there is something ugly about it, that it is not in order — and among us... Women! Women! After reading these few lines, take a look in the mirror — have you not turned red with shame?... Onkeles.
What Is Heard, What Is Seen (conveyed by Ben Amotz)

[Column of satirical notes.] 'What Is Heard, What Is Seen' (conveyed by Ben Amotz).
'Lehazhir haktanim al hagedolim' (to warn the small about the great). About a year ago the education authority in Zagłębie [gave] an order that in the elementary schools boys and girls should study together; this is against the tradition, the authority declared, and in order to 'save' the [economic?] morality a mechitza (partition) was introduced — 'men apart and women apart': boys study separately and girls separately. We do not come to object and oppose the 'reforms' — there are after all pedagogical rules for that — but one must be consistent. If one fears for the little ones, one must surely also protect the grown ones. As Rashi says, 'to warn the great about the small'; for if it be so established, to keep silent about it is indeed a moral offense. About the eight courses — a member of the school [committee] relates [that they feared]; but toward the 16–17-year-old youths and young ladies who attend the courses the education authority has no fear, 'closes its eyes' and will not know what goes on there...
'A good deed.' A fact — no longer timely, but factual. Perhaps it will have an influence on ours, on the '[—],' who should draw a moral lesson from how a declining Jew is treated. A Jewish immigrant, a 'Polish' Jew in Katowice, stood on the brink of ruin. He had a 'factory' of [—]-water, but the 'skarb' (treasury) wanted to tap wine from that water. And they tapped, drop after drop, until 'the spring' ran dry; then a [clerk] came with a file and said: 'the machines belong to me.' [...] The removal of the machines was set for Simchas Torah. When the Jews of Katowice heard this, they said 'the same thing' as the sequestrators — and 'sang' all the stanzas, 'Atah horeita,' even the grooms[?] too... And it was a brilliant season: the public paid the highest prices — 'Ozer dalim' cost 25 zehuvim, a little 'Atah horeita' — 60 zehuvim. On the table, for the 'goods,' lay a [—] with their [—] etc.; [thus] the desperate Jew was restored to his former standing...
'A word in season.' For several years now, at every election season, our representatives of religion step out onto the 'stage,' preaching in warm words to the holy ones to save Jewishness and vote for this one and that one, [—] who 'wish to guard[?] the honor of the Torah'... For this season too the 'holy' organ of the Agudah came out with the 'Ten Commandments' of the aforementioned, [arguing] that Jewishness is, God forbid, in danger, and also R. Yehuda Mincberg, who, God willing, will become a deputy, so that all Israel may merit [—] and a complete redemption... But not all the rabbonim are drawn into the 'Agudah' politics; there are some who have [something] to say: 'Tzel legim...' [—]... Among the non-political rabbonim is counted also the [—] — the Częstochowa Rebbe, shlita. 'A just complaint.' In [—] [—], in the largest [— torn passage at the foot of the page].

The Arab Problem in Eretz Yisrael — 4. The Ethics of the Iron Wall

[Political essay.] By W. Jabotinsky (Ze'ev Jabotinsky). Part 4 of the series: 'The Ethics of the Iron Wall (eyzerner vant).'
A. [—] if this is clear enough[?], then it is also natural. The political naivety of the Jew is unbelievable! He fails to grasp the simple rule: he who will not meet you with concession — toward him you must by no means be yielding and forthcoming.
In old Russia a typical case occurred: one of the oppressed nations, united as one man, undertook a crusade against the Jews under the slogan of equality and [—]. At the same time that people strove for an autonomy of its own from the [—], making no secret at all that it sought [—] to exploit that autonomy for an even greater oppression of the Jews. Despite this, Jewish politicians and publicists (even national Jews) regarded it as their duty to support in every way the autonomist demands of their enemies, because autonomy as such is a holy thing.
We regard this, as I have already once said, almost as our duty — just as the moment the 'Marseillaise' is played one must at once rise and shout 'hurrah', even when under that same melody, God forbid, [—] Cossacks [trample] Jewish bones. — This we consider political morality. But it is no morality at all; it is savagery/primitiveness[?]. Human nature is built on reciprocity! Limit[?] the reciprocity, and the right turns into a lie. Every person who now passes my window has a right to life only to the extent that he also recognizes my right to life; but if he wishes to [attack][?] my life, then I too can no longer honor his right to life.
B. [—] to the ground [goes] not only the weaker, but also the [—]. The world must be based on a foundation of mutual obligations[?], so that all may live in the same way and all must also perish in the same way. There is no ethic that would grant the wolf and the [—] the right to tear apart, while the modest man must hunger [and] die of starvation. Only one single ethic is possible: the ethic of humanity. And its practical corollary runs roughly thus: [—] (a Talmudic parable from 'two hold a garment': two walking find a piece of cloth (tallit); one says 'I found it and it is mine', the other says 'not true, I found the cloth and it is mine'. The judge, to whom both turned, divides the cloth into two parts, each of the two stubborn ones to receive half.) [—]
This legal case is also viewed another way, namely: one of the two is a stubborn man, while the other resorts to a ruse to deceive the world; for he claims: 'we both found the cloth together, therefore I demand only my half, and the other half belongs to the [—].' [—] and so the stubborn one gets three quarters and the [—] one quarter — and this too is quite correct.
It is very fine[?] to be [an honest man][?], but that by no means means one must be a fool. [Our sages][?] understood this well, but we have [forgotten it][—]. We must engrave it well in memory, especially [—], for [it is written so] with us. As to the acquisition of concessions[?]: the concessions we can offer Arab nationalism [—] are very modest. From the striving to reach a Jewish majority in the land we cannot [retreat].
We also cannot tolerate any Arab [control] over our immigration, we cannot permit any [—] with an Arab majority, and we cannot enter any Arab federation. Moreover, at times we cannot support the Arab movement, because for now it treats us with hostility, and we — all Israel, even the Arab[?] democrats — [recoil] from every manifestation of this movement, not only in neighboring Transjordan [—] in Syria, but also in Morocco[?]. And so it will remain, for otherwise it cannot be, until at a certain moment [—] the wall compels the Arabs, once and for all, to come to terms with Zionism and consent to it.
C. Let us pause for a moment and [look] toward another land for our colonization. Thus for example: Uganda. But on closer examination we would find there too [—] the same trouble. Uganda too has a native population, which would set itself — as all the other examples of history were — instinctively, or consciously, against [—] the colonizers. The fact that the natives[?] there are black does not change the essence of the matter. If it is immoral to colonize a land against the will of the natives, then this morality must apply to blacks exactly as to whites. One may perhaps argue that the blacks are not yet developed enough to send delegations to London — a very weak hope, since [—] white-skinned good friends would be found to teach them[?]. And even if these natives were like helpless children, then the matter is even worse. If colonization is equivalent[?] to a robber's assault, then it would be the greatest crime to rob helpless children. Therefore Uganda too is immoral, and therefore every other territory too, whatever its name, is 'immoral'. Uninhabited[?] islands no longer exist in the world. In every place there has sat from time immemorial a native population, which wants no colonization by any [foreign] majority and not even any influx of strangers. If there exists[?] anywhere at all in the world a landless people, then even a dream of a national home is an immoral dream. The landless must remain landless forever. The whole expanse of ground in the sense of the word is already divided, and therein [consists][?] what the ethic demands.
[D.] Jews number, they say, 17 million souls in all the world, and half of them now live literally like homeless refugees [—]. The number of Arabs amounts together to 38 million; they inhabit Morocco, Algiers (Alushir), Tunis, Tripolis, Egypt, Syria, Arabia and Mesopotamia — a territory occupying a portion [—] the size of half of all Europe. On average there fall on this territory 16 Arabs per English square mile. It is worth mentioning in this connection that in Sicily there fall 352 inhabitants per square mile and in England 699 inhabitants per square mile. It is further worth noting that Palestine makes up about 170 miles of the aforementioned territory. But if homeless Jewry demands Palestine for itself, that is 'immoral' — because the natives do not [permit] it.
Such an ethic may hold among cannibals, not in a civilized world. The soil does not belong to those who possess it in excess, but 'to those who have no soil at all'. It is an act of simple justice, from the peoples counted among the great landowners of the world, to give up a single estate (nachla), in order to provide the wandering people a place of refuge (mekom miklat).
But if such a landowning people will not allow it — one must say, naturally — then one must compel it to. Justice carried out by force does not thereby cease to be holy justice. [Torah.] Regular feature: Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the weekly portion, collected and styled by Y. L. Parshat Toldot.

(a) "Abraham begot Isaac" (25:19). Rashi notes that the verse repeats "Abraham begot Isaac," though "Isaac son of Abraham" was already said, because the scoffers of the generation claimed Isaac was really fathered by Abimelech; so God shaped Isaac's face like Abraham's, to confirm to all: Abraham begot Isaac. [—] Those who spread the slander that Isaac came from Abimelech are not outright jesters; [—] the term "scoffers of the generation" includes the "vertl"-tellers who joked: this is why Sarah was held [captive] by Abimelech [—]. [—] That Isaac was born is what the true Sages meant by "she shall be cleared and bear seed." [—] Not by Abimelech's merit was Sarah preserved. Abraham begot Isaac.

(b) "The children struggled within her" (25:22). Granted, Esau pushed to get out, drawn to idolatry; but Jacob — what had he done, wanting to come out? [—] It is said that in the mother's womb an angel teaches the child Torah; so why "struggle to leave" when the mother passes the study-house of Shem and Ever? Is it not better to learn from an angel? He found the learning pleasant even from an angel, while sitting in his chamber together with Esau... By Rabbi Moshe Sofer.

(c) "Two nations are in your womb" (25:23). The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 11) expounds this of Antoninus and Rabbi, of whom it is said their table never lacked horseradish or radish. And what is the "rum" (greatness)? [—] The ample hospitality at their table. By Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin.

(d) "A wholesome man" (25:27). [—] No one was so "tam." To Laban he said "I sojourned with Laban... [and did not learn] trickery." Jacob was wholesome only when he need not use guile — "a wholesome man"; he mastered his innocence and did not need to exploit it, but when dealing with a trickster he knew how to tuck cunning up his sleeve. By Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin (the "Seer").

(e) "Let me gulp from this red stuff" (25:30). Once the Maggid of Dubno asked a rich man for a donation [—] at a table bearing various coins, and the man handed him a [small one]. The clever Maggid adds: "and the mind of the 'adom' settled once he found his pretext" ... (in his wealth — another small coin, not a ruble) ...

(f) "He sold his birthright to Jacob" (25:33). How could Esau sell the birthright, [being] doubly rich? For the taste [of a stew]? [—] that Isaac was [—] and Esau feared the inheritance would grieve [him], and so [—] "the game of his son." Many verses show Isaac was [right] in this, though he was righteous, since [—] hold that for the righteous wealth is a virtue. Ibn Ezra.

* * * [—] Of those who hold to the Torah the verse says "days are in her right hand," long life; and one asks: [—] length of days, but not wealth and honor? (g) "Perhaps my father will feel me" (27:12). [Rabbi Elimelech] was very strict that [his hasidim] not dress in modern fashion ... In comes a hasid wearing a starched collar, which in those days was deemed a great "progress." [R. Elimelech] clasps him round the neck; the hasid asks a blunt question: how does the Rebbe know the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob wore starched collars? Rabbi David (then still a small boy), son of [—], answered on the spot: Rebecca covered [Jacob's neck] with a kerchief so Isaac would not recognize; and had Isaac's sons worn starched collars, Isaac anyway could not have told whether the neck was hairy or smooth — the collar hid it.

The second time is "a great trembling," for this time the fear is [greater]. [—] the meaning of the old preacher's saying is thus: sad moments befall Jews in exile: once [—] them by force [—], and the second time when Esau comes with "smooth talk" and sweet words — and thus he [leads astray] the [Jews]; the second moment is far more dangerous... What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Satirical feuilleton/polemic.] What was heard, what was seen — compiled by Ben Amotz. 'A shameful document.' At the Senate elections one saw a great deal; for generations the 'mischievous deeds' done in the name of the 'guardians of Torah and faith' will be recorded. Fine bearded Jews were seen shaking hands with the worst dregs of Jewish society, and the vilest libels were read out on the opposing side. The method is nothing new to us: it is well known that the 'Torah-true' hold a monopoly on Jewishness, and a rabbi (even like Rabbi Rubinstein) who is not harnessed to the Agudah's wagon is a 'transgressor of Israel' who eats carrion and treyf; whereas yesterday's sinners, betrayers of Israel, are 'honest Jews, true tzaddikim'... We also saw a document printed in the Agudah organ 'HaMevaser' in the Land of Israel, carrying a 'good tidings' (in Hebrew): 'Since today news has been received that the Zionist and national [enterprise] has been annulled and the National Home — the source of licentiousness, insolence, Sabbath desecration and eating carrion and treyf in our Holy Land — destroyed, therefore all who fear God, take part... This is the day the Lord has made, let us rejoice.' In the Yiddish rendering: since news has come that the English government is annulling and destroying the promised creation of a Jewish national home — the source of licentiousness and insolence, Sabbath desecration and eating carrion and treyf — all the pious and upright should share in the great joy and praise the Almighty...
Then a series of election-day vignettes: (1) A Jew from Piaski who came to vote and stepped in to buy goods from an Agudah merchant; asked which list — '17'; he explains he does not want to live in Poland but in Palestine, and if he does not vote for the Zionists, how will he be able to emigrate. (2) 'He prays every day' — a leftist young man meets an Agudah 'editor': he wanted to vote 17 but read that Rabbi Rubinstein is a 'transgressor of Israel' who eats treyf; the 'editor' answers 'so it is' — and is Reb Rafael a fine Jew? — 'Our Rafael prays every day and lays tefillin.' (3) An old blind Jew is brought in a droshky by two young men, his hand trembling as he votes — what number could the cripple have put in? Who took a blind, sick Jew out of his home? When he left, he was put back in the droshky that rides with 'customers' among the polling stations — that is number 18. (4) '17 and 1' — a modern young woman lost the number her (Hasidic) neighbor gave her, who had explained that list 17 is the symbol of the [—], and that a rabbi figures there as a candidate; as a 'proletarian', a roll-baker, she wants to support the 'candidate of the progressives' — number 18; by the polling building she found a 17 slip and a 1 slip, rolled both together and voted 18. (5) 'The World to Come with a piece of Leviathan' — the wife of a Ger Hasid on Third-of-May Square agitates for 18 and showers pitch and brimstone on 17 and all the Zionists; a supporter of 17 remarks that the well-known rabbi issued a proclamation calling all the pious to vote for 'one', and whoever votes for 'one' is assured of the World to Come and the privilege of enjoying the Leviathan; and a God-fearing woman tries to persuade her friend: 'Yente-Dvoyre, have mercy, vote for one, for man is sinful, and if we vote as the holy rabbi commands it will atone for our sins and we will merit the World to Come and taste the Leviathan a hundred years hence'...
Man and His Wonder-Filled Secrets

[Essay/reflection; by L. Spiegelman; sub-heading: “Such a Conversation.”] In the last two decades circumstances have flung us across a distance of many generations. People could never have imagined that in so short a time such transformations could occur. The wonders happening in our day cannot be grasped by the ordinary mind; they rush past before our eyes with the speed of cinema pictures, as though through a telescope, so that we cannot even pause, observe, and form an opinion about one problem or another. Formerly life was one long, uniform chain: every day, week, month and year resembled one another like two drops of water, everything calculated in advance to the minute and the second, no one hurried and no one was ever late. The leisurely chats between afternoon and evening prayers, sitting before the house on the benches, sitting on the steps of the shop — all took place at the exact time; even nature was obedient and never rebelled. One knew when the frost, the snow or the mild weather would come, and knew by the months and the date how to dress and how to conduct oneself. No one imagined that nature could show wonders, or that new conditions could change the world. But suddenly revolutions broke out that shattered everything from beginning to end: an entirely new world was revealed before our eyes — people are different, the world different, conditions different, the gods different. Gods are burned, ideals annihilated, dreams smashed, and in the place of sacred ideals modern views are exalted, views that shift with the time and the climate. And who knows — perhaps time will show us that problems, views and ideals too can be changed like a fashionable lady’s wardrobe, and perhaps that is even more practical, durable, lively and beautiful; perhaps modern philosophy too must be studied differently. In our day one no longer studies for its own sake to become a scholar or a great mind; learning is perfected more from a practical standpoint, because of the prevailing conditions of existence in which we live. Once there was more time to investigate thoroughly; today we are in another world, among other people. No one is allowed any longer to settle in one place and research and philosophize — not the scholar, not the chemist, [—] nor the idealist. Today’s world cannot permit itself such a luxury; we live in a time when one thing chases another, and the rush is so great that one cannot stop, and whoever tries slips, falls off the magic wheel and breaks his neck and nose. In the modern world people are greatly enamored of inventive medicine. The technicians, chemists and artists cry out: we achieve so much, we invent the new and improve the old, we simply overturn worlds, we show wonder upon wonder, and humanity trembles and marvels at the giant works we have given the world — and we have not yet said the last word. And we doctors, we professors, we who are the mechanics around the mechanism called man — what have we invented for human life? What have we done [—] for the life of man, or at least so as not to shorten it? [—] to prolong human life or to steady it as in former generations? [— the remainder of the text in the left-hand columns is damaged and partly cut off.]
Our Answer

[Poem; by B. Sternberg (Warsaw); sub-heading: “To the English Verdict”[?] — most likely a response to the Passfield White Paper of October 1930.] The blow has fallen, the struggle begins / Hey brother, hold firmer our blue-and-white flag, / With sweat they were hammered, with blood put to use, / We all as one stand ready for the fight! Our breast is like steel, our hands are strong, / We must show the world our power, / And let it feel the blow of the hand, / Together with all those who fight side by side in the ranks. Enough of being trodden by the robber’s hand, / We gathered the crumbs from the robbers’ feet, / The land is ours! We create and build a life in the land / With bloody sweat of generations long past. And what shall become of whoever stands in our way — / We will show with hammers, with scythes, with axes, / We will tear up and destroy the robber’s field, / Together with those who block our life. „The Ghosts” (Gengangere)

[Theatre review; signed Sh. Ratshberg[?]. “The Ghosts” — a drama in three acts by Henrik Ibsen, from the guest performances of the [Lemberg?] theatre in Zagłębie.] Just as in Norway, Ibsen’s homeland, the skies are always clouded over and cold, stormy winds blow, so too it is in his dramas: there too a cold wind blows and one feels in them the harsh chill of [—] Scandinavian nature. In Ibsen’s dramas psychological conflicts find expression against a social background. His worldview is pessimistic, suffused with tragedy and a critical mood. [—] For Ibsen attainment is not the goal but rather the struggle itself, which may be regarded as the true life, in which a person’s character is hardened and defined. In “The Ghosts” it is Mrs. Alving who stands in struggle with the two forces. Soon after her marriage she returns to her husband and stays with him until his death, despite terrible sufferings and humiliations, yet she resolves to suffer and to conceal everything from human eyes, for the sake of her son Oswald, in whom she sees her only consolation in life. She sends her son away from home when he is barely 7 years old, so that he not be poisoned by the spiritual atmosphere prevailing in her house; but the remedy is ineffective, for Oswald is sick in his blood — inherited from his father. Our 'Declassed' Youth

[Social essay.] It has already become a constant[?] phenomenon that the door of our editorial office opens and on the threshold remains standing, embarrassed and not bold, a young man whose mustache is only beginning to sprout, who in a quiet, barely audible voice turns to us: — Perhaps you know of some work for me? When you talk things through with these youths who seek work, you become aware of an abyss of tragic circumstances and neglect. Most are children of specifically middle-class (balebatish) parents, who in normal times would perhaps have settled into their parents' enterprises, or into a private, communal or state post. But in the present conditions in Poland, [while] their parents' businesses [—], they have no entry, and they find themselves as a 'declassed' element, i.e. an element that has no ground under its feet and no place in society. And precisely they are capable[?] young people, with education and abilities, who under other circumstances would surely not have been wasted — graduates (abiturientn)[?] of schools, some even with professions, but.. there is no work. [...] For after all a Jewish editorial office is no labor-exchange and can hardly help them. It has even happened that such a one, after convincing himself that the editorial office could not provide him work, barely uttered: — I have not eaten for two days. This you hear from a young man's mouth not seldom in these times. When we think more deeply about how it stands with our Jewish youth, we reach sad conclusions. One notices such a phenomenon: the declassing of our youth is not a natural one, as happens in certain social processes, but a torn-out[?] one, through the policy of those who lead and [run] the government machine in the country. Our youth is declassed not because of a change in the social milieu, as we see for example in the Soviet Union, but because of the blocked[?] social-economic possibilities of integration, precisely under capitalist conditions, directed straight against that part of the population which does not belong to the ruling nation. The suppression of Jewish commerce and entrepreneurial initiative, the rightlessness of the Jewish schools, the rightlessness regarding work in the monopolies, factories, government offices, administrative and municipal institutions and so on — force our youth, [—] and able-bodied youth, to be seemingly declassed, when in truth they are not; and [democ]racy[?] pushes such youth out beyond the borders of Poland, and we soon receive greetings that so-and-so has settled here or there [—]. But how many such young emigrants can there be? The youngest remain on the spot and must have a livelihood; one cannot let them starve in — [sub-head:] Lumpenproletariat. Do our decisive governing spheres notice[?] the harm of this declassing-policy, which brings the youth of a whole people to beggar's bread merely because it does not belong to the ruling nation[?].
Living Corpses... — Light Chats on Serious Political Themes

[Satirical feuilleton; by 'Felitis'.] [...] that you must push yourself[?] down into the earth, and why exactly [—]? — For, they say, there is already water, and even bitterer water; and however bad a person may feel at heart, he would still want to remain on dry land, on the dry yet blessed[?] dry land with its borders and border-posts, with its states and little-states, with its institutions founded (supposedly) for the good of mankind, and with its parliaments. An institution for which people once gave their lives, brought sacrifices, made revolutions, beheaded kings[?], until it was established. And then, in the democracy, came the ban (cherem). And the ban, as it says in the verse, was traded in power; and power is a sweet tidbit, whose nature it is that one spoils oneself with it if one takes too much. Indeed, they say, many parliaments ruined their stomach and began to ail so long and so wide, that a part of them have now died and others — have become... living corpses. [...] like all other [things], like a human, and is not a human, but some such ugly thing that just drags along like the blind gut (kishke) in the belly? Who needs it, this gut? Can one not live without it? The spiteful[?] Creator planted it in our innards and said: here, whoever bursts with it — bursts; and what, don't people burst? One simply gets torn[?] to pieces. Ask them [—], they'll tell you, they'll lament and sing with tears the old Jewish couplet: 'On a stomach one must not rely, for one can still be left without a pair of pants.' And if I am mistaken, and in the Jewish [—] repertoire there is no such couplet — one must put it in, even if the rhyme limps a bit. And who today isn't limping — the whole world walks about on crutches, and that is because among the 15 million cripples that the World War bequeathed to us, [...] the greatest war-cripple[?]... is the world itself. And it seems it has already remained an eternal cripple, hapless, and even the eternal pillars of the League of Nations will, it seems, no longer be able to sustain it. And perhaps precisely because the world has become such a cripple, our whole life has become so flawed, and there is not one thing in the world that does not limp. [...] in truth — one sees it from how people crawl there so [—] and slowly, as if they had no legs at all. And peace[—] too limps; its legs, they say, were promptly chopped off so it couldn't move in the Sodom-bed of all kinds of [—], peace-accords and confe[rences] [—]. But the greatest cripple is democracy. A lame democratism[?] and a paralyzed people's-will. A paralytic[?] who cannot move from the spot, and if he does lift a foot and by luck makes a step, it is out of a fall — from the party[?], the organization, the program, the leader, the [—], but by no means of his own will. The people's will has long been dead, deceased, and they forgot to bury it; it drags itself around the world like a living corpse (bar-minan), just so, without any intent, without any goal, without body and life. And this living corpse goes round in a dance with the second living corpse — with parliamentarism... Two dead ones dance, and in the middle stands the lame-crooked[?] democracy and whistles. And the one who piped them to their 'luck' in Poland was the P.P.S... — Felitis.
Napoleon's Romance with the Young Widow Joséphine — 4

[Historical-literary essay; by M. Aszerowicz.] 4. The fact that she set no great store[?] by it made no difference to her. It was all the same to her what to put on — such a famous general, marching with an army from victory to victory, taking so many cities, when everything is laid at his feet and all are ready to obey his command — well, it is only fitting that he should not forbid love-affairs here and there[?]; it is after all impossible... He must tell himself the truth! How many women has he already loved? Since he left[?] home? With how many women has he already been intimate?... With this she shut his mouth, and he could no longer speak of what he suspected her of — that she was not faithful to him... In the two days in which [he] was wholly absorbed in Milan with his new beloved Joséphine, the situation on the battlefield became very critical, and the army of the Austrian king nearly[?] smashed the French at the siege of Mantua. Then [Napoleon] could no longer remain alone in Milan with Joséphine, and he went off to the battlefield. The moment was very serious, the danger very great; [—] that the enemy [—] and the French would have to abandon the positions they had taken, after losing many casualties. [...] in order to defeat the enemy — and despite being so occupied, despite having then such heavy duties upon him, he nevertheless found time to write letters to Joséphine, and what letters! Full of love, full of tenderness, full of devotion! One of the letters to Joséphine from that time is very characteristic, and we reproduce it as it is: — Since I left you — he writes to her — I am terribly sad at heart. I can be cheerful only when I am beside you. All the time I do not cease to think of your kisses, of your tears and of your enchanting jealousy. The charm of Joséphine [—] has no equal, and does not cease to fan the flames that burn in my heart and in my senses. If only I were already free for a longer while, free of worries, free of duties, free [—] the whole time for you, free — to do no other thing in life but love you... The more I come to know you, the more respect I have for you, and this proves that what people say — that love comes suddenly — is not true. Nothing in all of nature comes suddenly; everything develops by stages... Be less beautiful, less tender, and above all — less jealous. Your tears ignite my blood... Come back to me, [but] quicker, so that if we go strolling, we may say: 'Yes, we have had many happy days'! A million kisses even for your [—]. Such a letter to a beloved woman [Napoleon] could write from the battlefield at a time when all [—] of the war hung in the balance, and the whole army under his command was in danger of being annihilated. The last remark about Joséphine's [little dog] is very characteristic. The little dog — 'Fortuné' it was called — lay well in the bones[?] and gave him a fair bit of grief in love... Joséphine always kept the little dog with her, and every time Napoleon took her[?], the little dog could not bear it and rose against him: it barked and bit his hands and feet. And perhaps Joséphine kept the little dog with her only then, when Napoleon [was] with her... perhaps it was for her a means [—] the stormy passion he felt for her? Napoleon himself complained more than once about the troubles he had to endure from the little dog. He recounted that even on the wedding night Joséphine kept the little dog with her when she went to sleep... Joséphine cared little that Napoleon pined so strongly for her. Only from time to time did she write him, for form's sake, a short little letter, and from the letter breathed such coldness, 'just as if we had already been [married] fifty[?] years [—]. Napoleon himself expressed [—]. And here, in the army too, the courage of the soldiers and also of the officers began to fall; all were under the impression that they stood on the threshold of a terrible defeat. All looked Napoleon in the eyes and turned to him for help, and Napoleon himself felt that his mind[?] was being deranged, for besides holding in his hand[?] the lives of so many thousands of people, besides having to work out plans how to overcome the enemies all around, he must also think about Joséphine not letting him [—], and about her not being faithful to him. Then he grew angry and sharply [reproached] her in a letter. 'I no longer love you — he wrote to her. — I hate you, you are repulsive to me, you are [—] and impossible, you do not write to me, you no longer love your husband. Tell me just, madam, what do you do all day long? With what important matters are you so occupied that you have no time to write a few words to the husband who loves you?.. And tell me indeed, who is he there, the handsome young man who takes up so much of your time that you cannot even write a letter to your husband? Remember, Joséphine! [—] one fine night the door will suddenly open and I shall come in!.. Yes, yes, in all seriousness, I am very uneasy, my beautiful little wife. Write me a letter at least from [—], full of [—] words, [to] warm[?] my heart [—] happiness. [...] Then I will embrace you tightly and cover your body with a million hot and burning kisses.' In this letter Napoleon's relationship to Joséphine is very accurately reflected: he begins with hate and ends with a million kisses... It is clear that he would want[?] to hate her, but he cannot; he would want to loathe her, but it comes hard[?] to him against her, he cannot help himself at all, his reason[?] indeed suffers from her not being faithful to him, he is indeed burning[?] with jealousy, but he still loves her. A thought [comes] to him, that perhaps he has no [complaint] against her at all for not loving him... He seeks the cause and finds it. [...] 'Yes — he writes to her — it is after all my fault, for nature did not give me the charm that should bind you to me.' And he, the man who [achieved] everything or else nothing at all — brought himself to the point that in his love for Joséphine he would demand of her less — 'just a bit of attention, a bit of respect, because I love her to madness, her and only her.' He was truly faithful to her and devoted with his whole heart; the first while he really took no interest in any other women, but [—] later he did look about him and realize that one must [—] pay faithfulness for faithfulness. Oyneg Shabes

[Torah.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion. Arranged and styled by Y. Y. — Parshas Vayetze.

a) "And Jacob went out from Beer-Sheva and went to Haran" (28:10). Though it could have been written "vayelekh le-Haran," instead of the 'lamed' of the first word the 'he' of the last word can serve — so it is expounded. Seemingly this changes nothing, for what difference does it make whether the letter comes at the start or end of the word? — It teaches: as long as one can hold back and spare a word, one should not bring it out; as long as it can be kept in, keep it. So sparing must a person be with words. — From Rabbi Mendel[?] of Vorki.
*  *  * Rabbi Hershele of Halbersta[dt][?] had a pupil who bore hatred for his rebbe but feared to voice it. On Purim the pupil was chosen 'Purim-rav,' got thoroughly drunk at the feast, and in his drunkenness poured out everything in his heart against his rebbe. An uproar arose among the pupils. When he sobered, R. Hershele told him: the rule 'what is on a sober man's lung is on a drunk's tongue' would seem to apply, and you would deserve a verdict; but that rule does not hold for an animal — for if it did, one would not need to toil to inspect the lung; one would simply get the animal drunk and all the adhesions would show on the tongue. Since the rule does not hold for an animal, I have nothing to hold against you...

b) "And he lay down in that place" (28:11). The Midrash: there he slept, but all the years he studied with Shem and Ever he did not sleep. Another saying: there he slept, but all the years he worked for Lavan he did not sleep. Jacob cannot rest. He went into the study-house and learned; studying only Torah, he was reproached for isolating himself from life and living apart from his neighbors, drawing their hatred. And when he became a worker for Lavan and became productive, he was reproached for taking over everything and exploiting society too much.. Jacob has no rest. Yalkut Marganiyot (RM"H).

c) "And he ran to meet him" (29:13). It is said: why did he run and for what. One who runs — the heart in time senses the deceit; one asks: why did Lavan run? The answer: "he set his eyes on money" — though the running comes from the eyes, it was worth it to him for the money he reckoned to swindle out of him. Siftei Torah (R. Yosef Landau of Jassy[?]).

d) "Is it because you are my brother that you should serve me for nothing?" (29:15). Suddenly Lavan became a man of fairness, unable to bear Jacob working for free — whence fairness in a miser? Hearing Jacob wanted nothing for his labor, Lavan thought: "he is my brother" — Jacob showed me he knows the art of trickery just as I do. "Serve me for nothing"? Would he serve for free? A trickster like me — would he let himself be cheated? Surely, Yankele, you have some speculation in it... Ohel Yaakov.

e) "And Rachel was of beautiful form and fair appearance" (29:17). Solomon says "Grace is false and beauty vain — a God-fearing woman shall be praised," yet here Scripture praises beauty? The answer: grace is false and beauty vain only in the licentious; in a God-fearing woman beauty too becomes her. Derekh Tzvi (the Gaon of Miron/Vilna). *  *  * Another reading: when falsehood wins grace and vain beauty is taken for beauty — "a God-fearing woman shall be praised" — a God-fearing one will be praised; it will be exceptional praise. Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa.

f) "And Lavan gathered all the men of the place and made a feast." Therefore he gathered them and then made the feast. He assembled the men of the place, and when they [—]

g) "And it was in the morning, and behold it was Leah" (29:25). The Midrash: "all that night he called her: Rachel! and she answered him. In the morning — behold it was Leah; he said: deceiver, daughter of a deceiver! Did I not call you Rachel in the night and you answered?!" There is a way to test whether a stranger presenting himself as a certain person is genuine: invite him to sleep and suddenly call his name — if he truly answers, that is his name. Jacob, who knew Lavan's tricks, feared being cheated and used that very device: he waited until Lavan fell asleep and began calling: Rachel! Rachel! She answered — so he was sure it was Rachel. In the morning — it was Leah.. He cried: deceiver, daughter of a deceiver! Even in sleep you deceive.." Sfas Hayeria.

h) "And she said, this time I will thank the Lord . and she ceased bearing." Why, once she thanked God, did she cease to bear? When one already has enough of the good another gives and wants no more — one thanks him, and the thanks means: enough now. When Leah thanked God for the children it meant she had enough, hence "she ceased bearing." Maor VaShemesh.

i) "And Lavan said: I have divined that the Lord blessed me for your sake. And he said: you know how I have served you" (30:27-29). Lavan persuaded Jacob that he grew rich not by Jacob's abilities, loyalty and toil, but by the merit of keeping an idler in the house: "the Lord blessed me for your sake" — God blessed me for keeping a pious good-for-nothing. So the thanks go to God, not to you. Jacob replied: who suddenly gives a righteous man a fur coat? Your wealth came "as I served you" — by my toil; "the Lord blessed you at my feet" — by my feet that ran, God blessed you with riches; so pay me for it... The Maggid of Dubno.

j) "The wrapped ones to Lavan and the bound ones to Jacob" (30:42). A father-in-law buys the groom a tallis, while the groom himself buys tefillin; whence is it derived that it should be so? "Wrapped" — a tallis to wrap in (atifah) belongs to Lavan (ye[—]

The battle over the senate elections could already be seen [?]. After the attack on the List 17 meeting, the "street" got a "tongue" (began talking). One told another that the "Mizrahi" meeting had been disrupted, while at the "Agudah" and "Beys Yakov" meetings they say what the most abominable enemies of Israel once allowed themselves: eyes rolled up to heaven, sidelocks tucked behind the ears, dressed in Sabbath clothes, the most pious souls preached that "the Zionists are not citizens of Israel... and above all, that whoever votes for List 18 is exempt from the commandment of tefillin.."
The general campaign was staged on the Sabbath, from early morning; crowds of cheder-boys, Beys Yakov schoolgirls and young men were dispersed, going house to house and calling to "sanctify the Name" for the righteous R. Rafael...
Their work was wide-ranging, within and without; in the shtiblekh and prayer-houses they campaigned for number 18, and outside, in the streets, posters were pasted up. For the great "rabbis" sanctioned even desecrating the Sabbath, so long as the honor of the Torah be saved — namely, that R. Rafael become a senator...
In all the "shtiblekh" and study-houses, the passionate agitation led to brawls. The fight arose chiefly from the pretexts and means used by the agitators of the Agudah list, who waged the "rescue action" under the sign of the honor of the Torah, yet in fact disgraced the Torah.
Thus we know[?] that in certain "shtiblekh" the rescue-number 18 was pasted on the holy ark, and after reciting Psalms in the study-house it was proclaimed that one should "go the straight path and vote for the holy list number 18."
The true "fire of holiness" first flared up in the course of [the campaign], echoing an agitation the "Agudah" had years earlier in the rabbinic elections, with the phrase "neither mine nor yours shall it be"; and they went out into the Jewish street aiming to bring down the mandate of the hitherto senator, Rabbi Rubinstein.
Young and old were mobilized, from the cheder-boy to grey-haired elders with their pious wives, for the sake of the "holy war"; in the "Yesodei Torah" cheder and in "Beys Yakov" studies were suspended, and the pupils with their teachers, cheder-boys and schoolgirls worked from morning to the last moment with every tool and every means.
For the work the "Agudah" had mobilized nearly all the porters and carriers, with a whole lexicon of bans and curses.

From Danzig Election Day.

[Abroad.]
From our correspondent.
In Danzig the elections to the Danzig Senate were held last Sunday [—]. Two weeks earlier the struggle between the Hitlerites and the Communists had been dangerous. The [—]
[As for the] Jews on the Hitlerite side: every day the swastika-men marched with the great swastika on their armbands, "Down with the Jews" etc. Last Saturday and Sunday the fight was already enormous: the demonstration of the 10,000 Communists on [?] Street, where the Hitlerite morning paper "Danziger Allgemeine Zeitung" is located, was guarded by the "Schupo" (police) and Hitler-militia. They sang "Who betrayed you, the Hitler-democrats" and "the Hitler party, Danzig stays red." Afterward the Communists marched along the main streets to the S.D. party, singing the same; the Socialist demonstrations were held Saturday and Sunday, hurling various slogans. The hundreds of stalls of the various parties — such as the Center, the Nationalists, the German-Nationalists, the [Libera]ls and the Catholics — with their main cries drowned out the passers-by; the Hitlerites marched with their men, singing "Out with the Jews, Danzig stays German, together with the Poles, the Jews take away our bread" etc.
90 percent of the population took part in the elections. In first place were the Social-Democrats — 19 mandates (previously 25), among them 1 Jew, Dr. Bang; the Hitlerites — 12 (previously 1), the Center — 11 (previously 10), the German-Nationalists — 10 (previously 15), the Communists — 7 (previously 5). The total number in the Senate is 72 (previously 120).
The general crisis caused the small number of mandates compared with the previous 20. Abroad, the Hitlerite victory made a shattering impression. The agitation of the left against the Hitlerite victory is enormous.
Among the population various ill opinions arose about the Danzig Jews, that they had supported the Hitlerites to victory.

A Pressing Civic Matter

[Local/economic.] 'S'iz mer keyn sod nisht' (It's no longer a secret).
(What is happening with the express trains [shnel-tsugn]? — Will they stop in Będzin? — What must be done about it?)

In Sosnowiec a conference of the railway directorate (ban-direktsye) was held about the new timetable. [—] Representatives of the Chamber of Commerce (handls-kamer) also took part, [—] the authorities and the press.

Among other things the question was raised that the express trains should stop in Będzin, and we received a reassuring answer that it would be taken into consideration. Of course this does not yet mean the matter is finally settled and that the trains will indeed stop in Będzin; in our view one must still press the case.

It is ridiculous [—] the new timetable is already at the printer, and if Będzin is not included in it, nothing more can be done — it will be a lost cause until next year. [—] What shall we do then? The matter would be put off automatically[?] [—] for further years [—].

[—] Będzin demands that the express trains (kurirn) go on stopping as always, because the station is called Będzin, and because the town's residents and its economic and communal institutions demand it.

We must do everything possible so that the express trains stop with us again. It is enough that a town like Będzin has had to endure a whole year; we are simply amazed that the population has remained so patient — and that only because we have lived in the hope that any day everything would return to how it was.

The new railway station is already being completed and next year it will open to passengers; it is the newest in Poland. [—] Shall the express train really not stop at the very newest station?

The economic and communal institutions, together with the merchants' associations, must intervene at the ministry; and for that one should call on the local authorities to help — the starostwo, the commandant's office[?], the military, the police, and so on.

We have the right to demand that one can reach Będzin by every train, because Będzin is a city and not a village, an old established place and not some small shtetl. The railway administration draws much revenue from Będzin; many goods and products are dispatched (ekspedirt) from here, [—] that we not be treated worse than far smaller towns.

Let us therefore remember that this is a civic matter that must be resolved as quickly as possible.

— Seleks.
