The Grave Housing Question

(The difficulty of the tenants' question — how can the matter be solved?)

Lately there has again been much vigorous talk about introducing reforms in the housing sector, and it is telling that the reforms are calculated precisely on the intention to raise the price of dwellings.

The housing shortage in Poland is dreadful; the population is suffocating in overcrowding. In no cultured country is the housing situation as terrible as it is here in Poland. At a time when elsewhere so much is being done in the field of building modern, hygienic, well-arranged houses, among us nothing has yet been done in this field, and it is therefore no wonder that the situation is terrible and the predicament unbearable.

Here people in our larger towns still live in unheard-of anti-sanitary conditions; whole families live in cramped, tiny little rooms. And when we occasionally come into such families and meet face to face the people of these "holes," we are astonished; we simply cannot grasp how the people live there, how they manage — to raise the children, work, earn a living, run a household and get along with others all at once. At times, when we end up there, we are beside ourselves, contemplating the hard plight of people whose fate it is to bear so heavily the yoke of existence.

There is thus no doubt that our government must seriously begin to think how to ease the hunger for dwellings; and as an expression of that, the plan is to raise the rents and from the increase to create a fund for building new houses. Of course, in that case the increase would have to be large, high — otherwise nothing would be accomplished, otherwise it would amount to illusions and unworkable projects.

And so the question arises: are there possibilities of burdening the population with increases of 50, 75 or 100 percent? One must not forget in what a difficult position the country now finds itself; one must give an accounting of where we stand. One must not close one's eyes to reality. The country is in a terrible crisis that makes it impossible to carry on the already difficult conditions of existence of the present time. The housing question is now, for us, like a dangerously ill patient whom it hurts wherever you touch him.

To leave the question standing unsolved like this is unheard of — it is simply catastrophic, for very many troubles, ruin, illnesses and arrested development arise because of the housing question. Yet to solve the question on the scale that is needed would mean, on the other hand, making the citizens miserable. For one must reckon: is the average population in Poland capable of taking on itself the heavy burden of carrying on its shoulders the building of large networks of houses? Can it be burdened with such high increases? Even now, when dwellings are in fact not dear, one hears that people do not pay the rent because of the serious critical situation; so what would it be then, when a small shopkeeper or an artisan had to raise 75 percent for his little shop or workshop? How heavily would that fall upon the masses and upon the worker, who today lives in modest enough conditions — how could he undertake such a sum to enlarge his budget?

But we would say this: it is indeed bad and bitter and there is no other way out, and if the lower strata of the population will have to and be able to meet it, then it is understandable that in that case conditions of existence would worsen considerably, becoming hard, unheard-of harder than they were, for earnings would then have to be raised significantly, a higher reckoning would have to come into play, so that everything would once again be forced to change for the worse.

It is possible that in time the housing situation would be eased — and that because people would not have had the means to come by dwellings, as we see even now, which was not caused by the rise in rents, since that has not yet come, but merely the crisis has already given a push, so that today, for example, it is easier to obtain dwellings than two years ago.

Yes, one must ponder this problem seriously, one must treat the question from all sides and honestly, one must not after all forget that this is not a matter of a luxury article that whoever wants it should pay for. In short, a roof over the head must be had by every living person, so that no one will doubt that this is a strictly first-class article, without which none of us can get by.

Because of the gravity of this problem and because of the hard situation and the prevailing crisis, it is absolutely necessary that the community not be isolated: everything and everyone — the population and the institutions, the communal activists and the representatives — must occupy themselves intensively with the question. We do have tenants' associations whose task is to stand guard and protect tenants' interests, but that is still not enough, it is far too little. True, as a professional association the tenants' associations ought to take the place of honor; possibly they would have something to say that no other institution would say, but still the question is too generally social and too serious to entrust it to them alone.

We would go even further and say that even the house-owners' associations ought to occupy themselves with the question too, for one must understand that the owners of the houses will gain nothing from the present worsening, and as soon as they gain nothing from it they will, without doubt, be the first "sacrificial chicken." For at the time when the tenant has to enlarge his budget considerably because of his housing expenses and cannot sustain it, there is no doubt that first of all he will have nothing with which to pay the monthly or quarterly rent, so that, willing or not, it will fall also on the shoulders of his landlord; and precisely from this standpoint the house-owners too ought to think seriously about the future of the housing question.

As we have already said above, there is no doubt that the housing question cannot and must not remain standing as it is today, for that would mean non-solution; but just as it must be solved — which we need very, very much — so it can by no means be done at the expense and burden of the average citizens. And therefore it is precisely important that one take it up seriously, with all the sharpness of the situation, so that it is absolutely necessary to carry out consistent [measures][?] with all the economic associations in the country, which should find a modus by which the question may be solved and not so heavily burden the citizens of the land — something that would still many times over make the situation worse.

We are therefore of the opinion that already now, while it is not too late, the question should be taken up by the tenants' associations, the house-owners' associations, the artisans, the small traders and the commercial societies[?], the workers' associations — and all together should form one chain of a single coordinated[?] activity, which, together with the authorities and the Sejm deputies, would find an eased[?] modus to solve the painful housing question in such a way that it will not burden the poor and average strata of the population.

We too, the inhabitants of Zagłębie, ought to take part in this serious question; let Zagłębie too [say][?] its word — it has the right and the responsibility not to remain indifferent to this cardinal matter.

— The question is serious and topical enough, so that it must not be neglected[?] for a single minute.

R. Let.

The Jewish Communities of Olden Times and Their Relationship to Eretz Yisrael

[History.] By Rabbi S. Assaf [Jerusalem]. (Special for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".)
The love and bond between the Jewish people and Eretz Yisrael may be called eternal. In all times the people carried "Zion and Jerusalem" in its heart and never forgot its former splendor and glory. Wherever it was exiled[?], it always carried with it this holy love, and the striving for redemption, for "the comforting of Zion and the rebuilding of Jerusalem," was expressed[?] in the language[?] of the dark[?] exile of Israel itself, which gave hope for the times to come. In every generation there were among the people chosen ones, "yechidei segulah," who could not reconcile themselves to the exile and its troubles[?], and who with self-sacrifice set out on the road to the Holy Land; many[?] were the obstacles, great was the danger on the roads, but the eternal love between people and land prevailed.
These [sole][?] roads became the emissaries of the whole people, who were "upon the Torah and upon the service" and prayed at the holy places on behalf of the whole people scattered among the nations. Should a misfortune, God forbid, occur, the Jews in Eretz Yisrael were at once notified to pray and annul the evil decree. For this reason the exile exerted itself, as far as it could, to support the Yishuv in the Holy Land. Whoever possibly could took part in this mitzvah, and through it felt bound to the land and to the Jewish spirit[?] and hope. And not only individuals took part in it, but also the communities. The masses in exile saw to all communal affairs, and used to elect each year [representatives] such as parnasim, dayanim and various gabaim[?].
In Lithuania the Jewish Council of the Land ordained[?] in the year 5406 (ת"ו) that every community and settlement set aside special sums at the time of the chalukah, so that money be found for the poor of Eretz Yisrael. In the year 5440 (ת"ם) a takkanah was made whereby all communities were obliged to send the "Eretz Yisrael money" each year to the Lublin fair and not to withhold it, so as not to nullify the Eretz Yisrael money through "bal te'acher" (do not delay). And since a single community may[?] lend from this money to communities that were at times hard-pressed for money, the rabbis decided that one should lend only with care, even on the surest promissory note, except on a silver pledge, which must be worth one-and-a-half times the loan.
In most of the Italian communities there were separate special societies under the community's supervision, which dealt with all matters concerning Eretz Yisrael and called themselves "Chevrot Eretz Yisrael." The gabaim and [heads] of these societies occupied themselves chiefly with collecting the donations for the needs of the Eretz Yisrael Yishuv. After the decrees of 5408 (ת"ח, 1648), when the number of communities taking part in the money-collections for Eretz Yisrael greatly diminished, a yearly collection was introduced[?], a takkanah from the year 5383/1623 (שפ"ג), despite the fact that the communities' situation was very difficult. In the year 1655 a special [levy/arrangement] was introduced [—]

The Campaign in Zagłębie for the Yiddish Scientific Institute Begins!

[Culture/YIVO.] Disheartened(?) by the difficult economic situation, harried and worried by the cares of making a living, the Jew has no opportunity all year long — especially lately — to take an interest in higher questions, spiritual questions, cultural questions. That is a fact; but from this sad fact one must not draw the conclusion that one can live by bread alone. It is a long-known rule that a people whose culture does not develop gradually dies out.
Therefore it must be a joy and an encouragement for us Jews that, despite the stormy(?) times, our culture is nonetheless moving(?) forward. Yiddish literature, the Yiddish press, the Yiddish theatre, the Yiddish school are growing stronger. An intensive, many-sided activity is being developed by the highest form of our cultural movement — the Yiddish Scientific Institute [YIVO].
The Institute was founded 6 years ago — only 6 years in all, yet in this time an enormous amount has been accomplished. Even before YIVO there were Jewish scholars who wrote scholarly works, but what was missing was the world centre that would organize scholarship in Yiddish, give scholarly work planning, order and system, encourage scholarly work and help train new scholarly forces. Precisely this is what YIVO had to fulfil(?).
The world must increasingly base itself on scientific foundations. Scholarship therefore ceases to be the affair of individuals only, of a chosen few; on the contrary, ever broader strata must begin to take an interest in scholarly questions.
The sympathy YIVO arouses among the Jewish population all over the world results from the fact that its activity is of great importance for our culture. In various countries, wherever there is a living Jewish community, loyal and devoted friends work for the Institute.
The Institute has 4 scholarly sections and a bibliographic centre that registers the entire printed output in Yiddish, Hebrew and also in other languages, insofar as periodicals and books in foreign languages concern Jews or Jewish problems.
The Institute has an archive holding many very important materials, documents, pinkasim (communal registers), etc.
The Institute has a library holding over 25 thousand books, many of them rarities.
The Institute's work is branching out more and more. From January 1931 the Institute's monthly, 'YIVO Bleter', begins to appear.
YIVO's first world conference, held last year at Sukkot(?) in Vilna [Wilno], resolved to build a building for the Institute where all branches of YIVO would be able to work.
Today the building is already finished on the outside; in the coming half-year the interior work must be completed and the necessary equipment acquired.
In order to acquaint the broad public with YIVO's achievements and to collect larger funds for the Institute, YIVO is now conducting a campaign across the whole country. In a number of places the campaign has already been carried out and has brought satisfactory results. People of various tendencies take part in the work for the Institute. Owing to its purely scholarly, objective work, YIVO arouses great sympathy among persons of differing world-views.
Now the YIVO campaign in Zagłębie begins.
Everyone must take an active part in it!
M. Shur.

Clear, Open Words

[Opinion / local – desecration in the synagogue.] (The desecration of God's name in the synagogue. — What will come of it? — In what way does the rabbinate react?)
And further the town sinks into the deep abyss of loathsome local squabbling; further one finds oneself in the terrible situation of disputes and frictions, of political "inventions" and of tripping one another up(?); further people have put their minds to it and plunged into deep thoughts about how to uproot those who have the audacity to think differently, to reason otherwise than wished by those who, by force and ugly inventions, have shoved their way to the surface and keep demonstrating: here we are, before whom Jewish Będzin must tremble and quiver; here we are, who hold everything in our hands; here we are, to whom everyone must [submit] once he falls into our hands, into our four cubits.
And this conduct, these new inventions, lead to unheard-of lawlessness, to incomprehensible demoralization. Lately we hear of deeds that make us blush with disgrace; it is a shame for us even to touch upon these deeds; we feel defiled merely by having to speak of such things, by having to bring them onto the columns of the printed word.
Week in, week out, it turns out, one must feed readers with quarrelsome news and loathsome intrigues, which as time goes on take on an ever more belligerent character. For a long time we refrained from recording in our paper all the various plans and "brilliant" exploits on the front of our local squabbling. We guarded ourselves against them as one guards against a fearsome fire, and when they came out into public in the full form of their ridiculousness and foolishness, and when the whole town talked about it — one with mockery and laughter, another with shame and pain — we, in order to pass to the general order of the day, looked through our fingers, as though nothing had happened, as though nothing had been done to anyone. Not only did we not want to blow it up and serve it to the readers as if to say: here you are, see what we look like, see what follies can still happen among us — we did not even want to mention it all. And when conscientious readers asked us why we had not reported this or that fact, had not written about this or that intrigue, we answered: a newspaper does not exist in order to get involved, together with the intriguers, in all sorts of follies. Here we held to the standpoint that it was better not to mention all these absurdities and their authors — that when they saw the impression, the bad impression and the anger it had aroused in the public, they would think better of it, would see the follies they commit, and this would teach them a lesson for the future. Of course no one could have imagined that not only would they learn nothing from all this, but on the contrary, the further it went the greater the surprises we had, and the later it got the more the town could observe ever greater disputes, intrigues and strange "for the sake of Heaven" politics.
It has unfortunately come to the stage where the clergy together with our entire community representation have forgotten where they stand in the world. They have grown used to treading the swampy, hard road with rare indifference, and now nobody there knows any longer that it must be otherwise, that it can be otherwise. They have been so drawn into all this that they cannot even imagine that one can live otherwise, manage otherwise. They have learned to trudge along crooked, muddy paths and can no longer climb onto the straight, dry road where one can take light, human steps; and worse still, they do not see on what paths they tread and in what ways they go, and so they feel no need to extricate themselves from these dangerous swamps, from these loathsome intrigues and disputes.
The desecration of God's name in the town synagogue has become an everyday article. At any time and any moment one enters the synagogue one hears insults, and when one has to write about it one blushes with shame, one is ashamed before oneself, one simply does not know where to turn one's eyes. But we are making progress, we are advancing in this field. Now people no longer make do with mere insults: in the synagogue knives already glitter and revolvers flash, and then — then one must already call the police to help, and then... what next, what later, what can come of all this, you can imagine for yourselves.
There are towns where disputes have been carried on for decades, where people are used to nothing else; but here we never knew of such a thing. Będzin, the town of "bachmanes" [toughs], porters and wild youths — an element not seen elsewhere — we have never heard, for all that, that even they would allow themselves to fight in a holy place. On the contrary, even they have respect both for the synagogue and for any representation whatsoever. And now everything has somehow been turned upside down: people have forgotten that there are places where one must stand in reverence and that there are people to whom one must show respect. Those who once knew that their place was by the door later became blind tools in others' hands, with whom everything was carried out, until it came to the point that the blind tools became the opinion-makers and spokesmen.
That is the state to which things have been brought, and that is how a holy place now looks among us.
The synagogue is a holy place; it cannot be otherwise, and actually it must not be otherwise, and no one can say it is not so. Thus, for example, we know that when someone wants to have the synagogue [for a meeting], the community administration answers that it cannot decide this, that it belongs to the rabbinate, from whom permission must be obtained — and this is perhaps understandable, since after all this must be the competence of the rabbinate. We therefore did not regard it as a wrong when they did not always want to hand over the synagogue for purposes that might arouse a suspicion of dispute. In no way whatsoever should such things have any place in a holy place.
Now that it has come to this shameful state, where knives and revolvers already "decide" in a holy place and where the police must be called for help — who reproves the persons who became blind tools, what is being done among us in this case?
We do not know. We have heard nothing up to today; we deliberately waited to see in what way people here would react to these unheard-of shameful events, which grow sharper and worse each time.
What measures has our Jewish community representation adopted so that such a thing — or better said, something worse and more terrible — should not be repeated? And the rabbinate, which is the actual master of the synagogue — in what way did they react to the insolence and disgrace that began to rage there with such force? Who, if not the rabbinate, should have reacted to this with the full power in its possession?
Unfortunately we have so far not heard a word from the rabbinate in this shameful affair; they have not even dared to pass any protest or any resolution, and so one would like to know what secrets and mysteries are going on(?) with them, that they remain indifferent to something that should have moved them most strongly and roused them most sharply? What reasons do they have for remaining indifferent when holiness is defiled in a holy place?
— On the contrary: let Jewish Będzin hear clear and open words.
R. Let.
The Contented Ones

[Satirical feuilleton – the housing tax.] (A short feuilleton)
Heaven and earth and "dire-gelt" [housing tax].
This matter is on everyone's lips. What, after the elections you come to us today with such a clever idea? Where will you get money for the elections?..
Nevertheless there are people, Jews and Christians, landlords and tenants, who are actually satisfied with the project.
One such contented man, a Pole, a former Endek [member of the antisemitic National Democrats] (and today he is what everybody is...), developed for me the "theory" of his contentment.
The "Zhidkes" [Polish slur for Jews] — he says — have been living(?) here lately like God in Odessa, and nevertheless they are still not satisfied; they keep shouting only one thing — taxes, taxes!
And what does the government get out of all the taxes? Altogether one can get a little table and a bench for it — and that has already all been taken away anyway, and the Jew is not impressed: he eats on a board, sits on the floor, as long as there is a roof over his head. But once these taxes are given the name "dire-gelt", one will be able to impose an execution [distraint], and that is something else..
A second contented man, also a Pole, developed a quite different "theory".
We — he says — take after France in everything. One notices(?) at once that we are two sisters. The same culture, almost the same prices for foodstuffs; only housing is expensive with them and cheap with us — so now we want to raise ourselves up to them, and then we'll be evened out..
A third contented man, this time actually a Jew, also rubbed his hands with pleasure.
With him it turns out to be this kind of story:
He is a poor landlord on Modrzejowska(?) Street and the tenants pay him no rent; but they have lived with him a very long time, he is very friendly with them and therefore has no heart to evict them. But if others do it, perhaps he himself will also gain something.
A fourth, also a Jew, who was formerly a small rich man and is today a great pauper, is satisfied for an entirely different reason(?).
I myself — he tells me — owe various kinds of taxes, but I wriggle out of them, since I am afraid that everything has already been taken from me. But the bailiffs give me no rest; every morning they gather in my home — one could almost(?) pray with them as a congregation...
I can't go away, because then they set upon my wife and the children; so I have to sit at home and listen to their sermons...
Now imagine what consolation I will live to see with them, when one fine morning, as I sit like that in their "company", the "dire-gelt" bailiff comes in and [shows?] all of us the way...
Can you picture the spectacle?
———
Thus it turns out once again that every trouble has its consolation — among the tens of thousands of discontented there are also a few contented ones — each in his own way.
Onkelos.
Letters from Home

[Political satire – mock letter.] B"H, for the portion "And Joseph was brought down to Egypt" [Vayeshev], here in Będzin.
My friend R. Shloyme, may his light shine.
After inquiring after your welfare, I inform you that I have great complaints against you, having read your letter in which you permit yourself to make fun at our expense, or rather at the expense of our election campaign, in which we held a brilliant "victory".
You don't like — you write — our tactics in the elections to the Sejm and the Senate. Why so? We danced at 2 weddings at once, at a gentile one and at a rabbinic(?) one? Well, what of it? Did we perhaps make a bad deal? [Te]ll me then, R. Shloyme, had you [—] together with us, would you not [—] have done just as the "[great] in numbers and great in building" did — why not? [—] you must understand that apart from [—] "-tshelekhs" (not "factions" but [—] people who can tell [—]) which we have at every step, we obtained several concessions: to set up eruvin; Jews will be allowed to carry on the Sabbath, and people will shout frankly and freely in all the streets: — fresh bagels, come, little Jews, fresh bagels, fresh — nobody will disturb them. And what about the manifesto of the rabbis? Long may they live — our present-day Agudah rabbis and "good Jews", who are a bit casting off the yoke and are removing the "heavy burden" of Jewishness that has weighed on our everyday life".
The sages of old told us that "one may acquire his world in a single hour" — a man can buy himself the world to come in the course of one hour. But today's "sages" already have greater insights, they understand life better. They have realized that buying oneself a share in the world to come need not take a whole hour, only a minute: as long as it takes to cast a ballot for list 18, one can buy both worlds at once...
If that was not enough, more "reformed rabbis" came along and issued a decree that whoever helps R. Refoel become a senator is exempt from praying and even from reciting the Shema...
Yes, R. Shloyme, what the maskilic fighters of all generations could not achieve is now being realized by today's "spiritual leaders"..
Gone are the old "dark" times, when at every step you were accompanied by the seal of fear of God, holiness, truth and honesty. Gone is the time when a pious Jew had to keep "and you shall meditate on it day and night", and behave decently between man and his fellow, not dance(?) with falsehood, avoid bad company, deal faithfully with communal needs, and so on and so on...
But today, at a time when "democracy" has such power, there are other ways "to serve the Almighty"..
First of all, it is important to subscribe to the holy Agudah organ, so as to be exempt from the "and you shall meditate"..; secondly, to exchange "acquire yourself a friend" for a "strong przyjaciel" [Polish: friend, here: patron] (better a former Legionnaire); and thirdly — and this is really the main thing — to become close to the government. Whoever merits these three principles is assured of this world and can also generously hand out shares of the world to come.
Now, R. Shloyme, I reveal to you a great "secret": I have become a "mshlagenki"(?) in the "Agudah". Why? Quite simply — I want voting rights in the kehillah. You surely know that the "Council of Torah Sages", through its emissary R. Wallach(?), prevailed upon the government that only bearded Jews, i.e. Jews with beards, should have the vote in the kehillah. Well, you understand that around this matter grave contradictions, various complications will arise, for it is not clear whether the decree also applies to "10-millimetre or trimmed(?) beards".., everything depends on what the political commission of the "Agudah" will pronounce about the important beard problem; so I fulfilled [the duty] and became a member of the "Agudah"... To tell the truth, it doesn't suit me, for being an Agudah member, and especially a person like me, I have to greet in the street such "przyjaciels" from whose glance my forefathers would have fled to the ends of the earth; but "bow to the fox in his hour", as they say, "for a livelihood one dances with a cat"..
— What's new with the town-council elections? For now it is still quiet, but we have hope that we will not rest long: the election fair will start again and there will be "light for the Jews"(?) in our darkened little world.
I wanted to give you an exact report of how and by what means a cantor is "engaged"(?) in Będzin, but suddenly I was "invited" to the "[?]-dance", so I must be brief this time, and I wish you a good Sabbath. Your friend
Ben Amotz.
Son of a Stiff-Necked People (On Jabotinsky's Visit to Sosnowiec)

[Banner line at the top of the page:] The upbuilding of Eretz Israel depends on the 17th Zionist Congress — so buy the shekel!
Next Monday Jewish Sosnowiec will welcome the leader of the Zionist-Revisionists, Vladimir Jabotinsky.
He comes to us in our hard, bitter time. On one side great economic worries, on the other — the symptoms that brutally shatter Jewish hopes for the national home.
The Jewish people has had to endure many hard trials in the last few years. A wave of antisemitism in Europe. The severe torments of the Jews of Russia, excesses and persecutions against Jews in a number of countries, restrictions of rights and the pauperization of broad Jewish masses.
The eyes of all Jewry were turned to Eretz Israel. There one saw the only solution of the Jewish question, which cannot be solved[?] in each country separately. Naturally, the present English declaration had to make a shattering impression on all Jews, far more than the decrees and oppressions until now.
In this hard time, when the weaker begin to despair, when the danger of hopelessness threatens especially a part of our youth, which has been struck most terribly[?] in its holiest feelings and dreams — there appears within the walls of Sosnowiec, like a ray of light[?] from the sun on a sad, overcast, rainy autumn day, the wonderful personality of Vladimir Jabotinsky.
He, who in such great measure helped to hold back Jewish youth from despair and assimilation some twenty-odd years ago, when Hebrew literature was ruled by the slogan "be'ein matara" (there is no goal). —
He, who created the Jewish Legion against the will of the entire Jewish public, which only a few years later recognized the rightness of his deed, and against the will of the French and English politicians, even against the will of the then all-powerful Lord Kitchener. —
He, with his national pride as a Jew and as the embodiment of the genuinely Jewish obstinacy of the stiff-necked people. —
He brings us hope for better times and faith that we will overcome all difficulties, because we have the strongest ally in the struggle — the unshakable conviction that truth must prevail, and that in the struggle with the brutality of various power-holders the [?] moral strength of the Jewish people will be crowned with victory.
The Jewish people has produced many geniuses. We have many Jewish geniuses in our generation too. But rarely has one of them remained faithful to the people. Too small does the Jewish people seem to them, too poor the Jewish reality, for them to devote their powers to it. The foreign world is much bigger, richer, outwardly more beautiful. Jabotinsky is one of those who devoted himself wholly to his people — all his powers, his whole soul, all his art and wonderful oratorical talent, which is compared with the world orators Briand and Lloyd George; his whole personality serves day and night one single idea, one single sanctuary, which the world ignores and despises, regardless of the fact that it served[?] the whole world as teacher — that is, the Jewish people.
Vladimir Jabotinsky, the only temperamental fighter for the Jewish people and the Jewish land, the most glorious leader and dreamer, who a few weeks ago quietly and modestly celebrated his fiftieth birthday, is greeted by Jewish Zagłębie with a heartfelt "Welcome!"
M. Grailer.
Open Letter to the District Bureau of "Poale Zion" (Right) in Zagłębie-Silesia

Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Allow me, through the medium of your newspaper, to publish the following open letter:
If until now I have not reacted to the laconic "communiqué" of the District Bureau of "Poale Zion" (Right), which was published in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" no. 48 — I took into account exclusively the prestige and integrity of the party, which surely gains no extra honour from such a kind of public "correspondence". But the babble of the well-known Zagłębie "country sage" Yudl Preger (in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" no. 49) now simply forces me to draw far-reaching consequences from the whole smear campaign that some "patriotic" agitators à la Yudl Preger have raised against me.
For the sake of truth I state first of all that I learned of the decision on my "expulsion" from the press; consequently there can be no talk of the supposed claim that my statement in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" was an answer to the communiqué of the D.B. published in the same issue. For that reason Mr. Preger's claim[?] was also absolutely groundless that by saying we lean toward the "Left" I meant to mislead the average reader, who was led into error. No matter — the Left P.Z. could still have found a better advocate than Yudl Preger. Incidentally, he will answer for his "epithets" in court.
But before I begin to draw the consequences from the vile slander which the D.B. (or part of its members) spread and published about me — I demand — as founder and first chairman of the Zagłębie-Silesian District Bureau of the J.S.D.P.[?] "Poale Zion" (united with Z.S. [Tseirei Zion]):
1) That the D.B. unconditionally publish all facts and documents about party treason that are in its possession.
2) A statement from the D.B. whether Yudl Preger's base insinuation was published with the knowledge and consent of the D.B. or on his own account.
3) Whether the D.B., before sending off and editing[?] the "communiqué", carried out an investigation as to whether I was[?] engaged and appeared with propaganda speeches at all during the recent Sejm and Senate elections.
4) I call upon all party committees affiliated with the D.B. (from Częstochowa to Königshütte) to read my letter aloud at special party meetings and, if they possess any proof — to publish it in the next issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" (this letter is being sent to them by the same post).
5) I call upon the Sosnowiec party committee within 24 hours of the publication of the letter to take from me the party [?].
I take this opportunity to thank all my comrades and supporters who appealed to the C.C. and I declare in answer to their efforts and appeals that I will — regrettably — in any case not return to party work, although I remain in future the same Poale Zionist and of the same ideological conviction in which I led the party for some 8 years.
A. Gancwajch (Abramek[?]).
The 15th of December Is a Day of Judgement for the Jewish Craftsman

All Jewish craftsmen who run independent workshops and who by the 15th of December of this year do not possess master's diplomas will lose, after that deadline, the right to keep apprentices. All Jewish craftsmen who hold craftsman's cards and have not yet concluded agreements with their apprentices still have time to do so until next Monday, and should without delay submit a request to the Chamber of Crafts to admit them to the [?] examination for masters.
Later it will already involve difficulties, and it is not ruled out that complications may arise concerning the right to work with apprentices.
Before the „Harei At“ — Give No Dowry...

Jews, give the bridegrooms no money. As long as he has not gone under the wedding canopy and said the „Harei at“, one must not give any groom a single grosz, because for the most part the little grooms take [the money] off to the „kematkim“[?] and leave the daughters to grow old at their father's in the meantime.
Mr. R. some time ago made a match for a daughter of his. It was not easy for him to make a match for his daughter. Thousands of letters[?] he wrote to his rich relatives in America, asking them to send him a dowry for his daughter. With great effort he received a whole thousand dollars.
Having obtained the „apotika“ [the pledged dowry sum], Mr. R. alerted the resident matchmakers, and one of them brought a young lad, an „et-yungl“[?], all the way from Lemberg.
After the „tnoim“ (engagement contract) the father-in-law counted out 200 dollars and handed them to his future son-in-law, so that he could meanwhile set himself up a livelihood.
The groom began to trade, meanwhile went bankrupt, and in one [—][?] uprooted himself from Lemberg, so that nobody knows where his bones have got to.
The father-in-law has meanwhile been left with the daughter — but without the dowry.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion. Collected and styled by Y. Y.

Parshat Vayeshev.
a) „And Jacob dwelt“ (37:1)
The Midrash says about this: „Jacob sought to dwell in tranquillity — the trouble of Joseph sprang upon him.“ — Was Jacob then punished just because he wanted to sit in peace?
— The whole time Jacob was with Laban in exile he did not want to sit in peace at all. He understood that to establish oneself in life one must work hard. „In the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night“ — and all this was dear to him, „and they seemed unto him but a few days“. The hard toil at Laban the Aramean did not bother him. Only when he came to the Land of Israel did he suddenly get a desire for rest, for repose, and therefore he no longer wanted to work. And had it not come easily to him, had he had to work as hard and bitterly in the Land of Israel as in exile, he would soon have left the land and given as the reason a support[?] for the matter...
That is precisely why he was punished. Imrei Yosher.
b) „And could not speak peaceably unto him“ (37:4)
The saddest thing in quarrels is not talking to each other. If the sides had talked things out, many misunderstandings would have been removed, or one side would have recognised its wrong and apologised. About this the Torah says: „Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart“ — do not carry hatred in your heart against another; if you have something against him — „thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour“ — say it to his face; that prevents many quarrels. The misfortune here too was that „they could not speak peaceably unto him“ — that they did not reproach Joseph himself with his faults, from which peace would surely have come. Tiferet Yehonatan.
c) „Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?“ (37:8)
Melekh means a king whom the people elect, and moshel means a dictator. This is what the brothers said to Joseph: had you at least said that you would be a moshel over us, that you would rule over us by force, with the power of a dictator — that would still have been possible; but a melekh, an elected king — that is surely[?] a lie, and probably everything is a lie. Kol Eliyahu.
d) „Tamar thy daughter-in-law hath played the harlot; and also, behold, she is with child by whoredom“ (38:24)
According to the Aggadah, the Messiah was born through this episode. The question arises: was there really no other way for the Messiah to be born than through such an ugly affair?
— A small-town rabbi of old once wanted to honour a rich man of the town and, according to the old custom, prepared a „harmone“ (— a kind of illuminated address in which the groom is honoured with the title „Morenu“) for his son on the day of his wedding. The harmone was written in a grand florid style; its content was splendid. But being a batlan and a pauper, he wrote it on worn-out, crumpled paper. The magnate, on receiving the harmone, was annoyed at the rabbi's lack of aesthetics and decided to teach him a lesson.
On the following Purim he sent the rabbi magnificent mishloach manot — expensive tortes and fruit — but wrapped them in rags... in ugly, wretched rags...
The moral:
Through Joseph's coming to Egypt the will of Providence, which wished it so, was fulfilled. Judah, the one who advised selling Joseph to the Ishmaelites (see 37:26), carried out the will of Providence. But because it was through an ugly deed, through betraying a brother, he was repaid measure for measure, and the gift that Providence had destined for him — that the Messiah should descend from him — was also given to him through an ugly deed.. Ohel Yaakov.
e) „And sin against God“ (39:9)
Potiphar's wife said to him that, after all, there is a commandment of repentance, and therefore he must sin once in order to fulfil the commandment of repenting...
He answers her: „ve-chatati“ — I have already sinned once.
[?] Rabbi Mendele of Kosów.
f) „He went into the house to do his work“ (39:11)
The Gemara (Sotah 36) expounds: Joseph was already about to sin, but the image of his father's face appeared to him —
Jacob dressed patriarchally, whereas Joseph already dressed in a worldly fashion, because he held that one can be a pious Jew and dress in a worldly manner. So when he nearly stumbled, that was after all because he had adorned and dressed himself up; for had he had a pair of long sidelocks and dressed traditionally, Potiphar's wife would not have seized upon him.
„The image of his father's face appeared to him“ — he had now come to like his father's style of dress..
Rabbi Yitzchak of Warka.
g) „The keeper of the prison looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the Lord was with him“ (39:23)
Joseph concealed his piety; nobody recognised why „the Lord was with him“, why God was with him — no piety at all could be seen in him.
Rabbi Shaul Landau.
The Strike of the Talmud Torah Teachers Continues.

[Local.] As we have already written, 10 days ago a strike broke out in the Talmud Torah. The melamdim (teachers), who are owed tuition pay for several months, have stopped classes, and 450 children, the greater part poor, wretched orphans, are loitering(?) in the streets.
We believed that the news of the Talmud Torah strike would make the greatest impression in town, especially among the religious part of the population — after all, it concerns hundreds of poor Jewish children. But we were mistaken: our religious representatives are busy seeing that the feet of geese(?) get stamped, and conducting "political" negotiations to obtain a concession for the fifth shochet (ritual slaughterer), etc.
As we are informed, the Talmud Torah committee demanded from the kehilla administration a part of the subsidy for 1929 and a guarantee for the 5 thousand zl. that the gmina (municipality) still owes the Talmud Torah from the year 1928.
The administration rejected the claim. Because of this the strike continues to this day, and no one is bothering to settle it.
In connection with this situation, the Talmud Torah committee, which is straining every effort to keep the Talmud Torah in existence, is calling a meeting to take place this motzei Shabbat (Saturday night) in the Talmud Torah premises. Whoever holds it dear that the children of the poor should have somewhere to study should come to the meeting.

[Local.] At the present time, when a severe crisis reigns, the "Beit Lechem" (bread-relief society) relieves(?), according to its means, a large number of respectable families. Every Shabbat challahs, bread and various foodstuffs are given to some 80 families, mostly widows and the sick.
The number of the needy, however, grows every week, and in order to make it possible [to meet] the requests of the hungry, a money collection will be carried out during the days of Hanukkah. Every home will be visited by specially delegated collectors.
It is desirable to support the collection drive and thereby ease the bitter lot of those who beg for food...
Talmud Torah Receives a Concession as a Public School.

[Local.] Several months ago the present committee of the Talmud Torah submitted a request to the school inspector that he grant the Talmud Torah a concession within the framework of a folk (public elementary) school. The matter met with certain difficulties, but at Tuesday's session of the school authority in Sosnowiec it was finally decided to fulfil the wish of the Talmud Torah committee.
The Influenza Epidemic Is Getting Worse.

[Local.] In the course of the week the number of people sick with influenza (grippe) has grown greatly. "There is no house where there is no one sick" — there is hardly a home without sick people, especially schoolchildren. To(?) get a doctor comes only with great difficulty. Moving scenes took place in the course of Monday. In a town such as Będzin only one pharmacy was on duty at the time, that of Ch. Tshekhovski (Czechowski?), where dozens of people came for medicines, so that a "queue" (ogonek) formed, as during the war at a bakery...
The owner of the pharmacy, unable to cope, asked(?) the customers to come tomorrow.. Having no choice, many did so, and the sick "waited" until the next day...
Received his „reward for walking“ in the Beit Midrash

On Saturday morning Mr. Shmuel Yitzchak Hiderszal[?] of Łódź went to pray in the local Beit Midrash (study house). There he unintentionally sat down on the „shtot“ (regular seat) of an „old-timer“. When the „old-timer“ came and saw that a „stranger“ had „occupied“ his place, he „honoured“ him with a slap in the face, from which blood began to run from his nose and the teeth in his mouth began to „tremble“...
After such a „hakafa“ the guest from Łódź quickly went home, where he received the necessary medical help.
Protest against raising the rent

In connection with the plan to raise rents, the board of the local „Tenants' Association“ (Lokatorn Fareyn) decided at its weekly meeting to call the local tenants to a protest meeting.
The protest meeting will take place next Sunday in the premises of the „Tenants' Association“ on Magrushever[?] Street.
Needless to say, the meeting will be attended en masse by tenants who understand what may await them if the new decree against tenants is adopted.
Ida Kamińska and Zygmunt Turkow in Będzin

On Monday the 15th of this month the Jewish theatre-lovers of Będzin will have distinguished guests: the great artists Ida Kamińska with Zygmunt Turkow.
About these great artists and their significance for the Yiddish stage it is superfluous to speak; to this day they are the giants of the European stages in general and of the Yiddish stage in particular.
We still remember Ida Kamińska from her last appearance as the „Jazz Singer“, which surpassed all expectations; and recently, seeing Al Jolson play the jazz singer in the film, we only then became convinced what a great artist our Ida is.
Zygmunt Turkow recently appeared at the Riga State Theatre, where he was a guest performer with our favourites Kadish and Khash[?], and his appearances were received with tremendous success.
On the 15th of this month this pair will give one performance in the „Capitol“ hall; the three-act play „The Cry of Conscience“ (Dos geshrey fun gevisn) by L. Verneuil[?] (spelled װערני[?]) will be staged.

[Local — Będzin; notices of the Merchants' Association.]
The local "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim-Fareyn) has asked us to publish the following notices:
1) The deadline for purchasing patents (trade licences) ends on 31 December. After that date inspections (lustracje) will take place.

Tragic Death of a Young Couple

[Local — Dąbrowa[?]; accident.] They went to sleep and never got up again.
The residents of Konopnicka Street in Dąbrowa[?] were alarmed by the tragic incident that occurred on the street.
Two months ago 19-year-old Anga[?] Gaszycka[?] married her 24-year-old cousin Aleksander.
The couple had taken a flat on Konopnicka Street (in Grzyb's[?] house).
On Wednesday evening the couple went to sleep leaving a burning stove, from which smoke later poured out, and the smoke poisoned the sleeping couple to death.
In the morning, when the neighbours saw that the door of the couple's flat was still shut, they grew uneasy and called the police, who opened the door; only then was the tragedy discovered — both were already stiff.
Dr. Niepielski[?], who was called in, established that death had occurred in the middle of the night.

The Christian association "Macierz" has opened a crafts school for apprentices.

The little son chops off his father's head..
In Czeladź a quarrel arose between a local worker and his son over family disputes; from words the 18-year-old "gem" passed to deeds, and with an axe he murdered his father.

In Będzin too the sale of the shekel began with fervour.
The Będzin shekel committee, in which all Zionist organisations and groupings are represented, has already received 3000 shekels, which were "snapped up"[?] by the parties.

Last Sabbath a members' meeting took place in a packed hall, at which Mr. Hofer[?] spoke on the importance of this year's shekel.

Będzin merchants bought themselves „bargains“...

The Łódź textile (manufaktura) merchant Shmuel Blum, in order to improve his business, sent two agents, Chaim Mazezenetski[?] and Leib Feldman, out to the provinces to sell goods.
A short time passed; the agents returned from the road and brought back a bundle of bills of exchange worth 20 thousand zł.

To the Judgment of the Public (A Letter to the Editors)

We hold that the closed kehilla office does not hold an uncontrolled rule over the Jewish population. We therefore inform the public that in the gmina office, which is "destroyed and destroying", several dozór members together with the "temporary chairman", Mr. Prawer, have adopted a tactic of hiring new officials "on the spot". Thus not long ago a secretary was "pushed through"; now they have taken a fancy to a new shochet, and without regard to the fact that the butchers, partners and the population are against taking on a new shochet at the present moment of crisis, the rabbi and Mr. Prawer installed a shochet "for the time being". The First Works in Poland to Produce Glass Bulbs for Electric Lamps

On Tuesday the ceremonial opening of the Polish "Philips" factories for manufacturing glass bulbs for electric and radio lamps took place in Warsaw; the glassworks is located in Warsaw on Karolkowa Street.
Very many high-ranking guests took part in the ceremonial opening, headed by the President of the State, Prof. Mościcki, Minister of Commerce Kwiatkowski, Minister of Posts Boerner, Minister of Public Works Matakiewicz, Minister of Railways Kühn, representatives of all the ministries and of the press.
The first to speak was the general director of the Philips concern, Dr. A. Philips of Holland, who expressed his admiration for the great work created in Poland during his presence.
Then the director of the Polish "Philips" factories, Mr. Walterscheid, spoke, giving details on the development of the "Philips" factories in Poland since their founding in 1922, when the firm "Philips" released the first bulb in Poland. In his further report Mr. Walterscheid pointed out that the factories now employ 353 workers and 273 clerks. The latest achievement of the "Philips" factories is the newly built glassworks, where the bulbs for electric and radio lamps will be manufactured. On an 8-hour working day the works will produce 8 million lamps a year, i.e. the whole consumption of Poland.
In the name of the government the Minister of Commerce Kwiatkowski gave a greeting, underlining the great importance of the "Philips" factories for the whole economic life.
Afterwards the guests acquainted themselves with the installation[?] of the glassworks and with the whole factory, which consists of bright, large halls where the workers will be in very good hygienic conditions.
It should also be noted that thanks to the "Philips" factories Polish radio has developed very strongly. The permanent radio exhibitions of Philips A.G. "Radio i Światło", which exist in Warsaw, Poznań, Łódź, Lwów, Kraków, Katowice, Bydgoszcz and Wilno, were visited by 80 thousand persons. Besides this the firm "Philips" sent special radio expeditions to almost all small provincial places in a number of voivodeships, in order to acquaint the broadest strata of the population with the latest achievements in the field of radio.

Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Visit to Sosnowiec

[Zionism/Revisionism – Sosnowiec.] On Monday the 15th of this month the Jewish-national public in Zagłębie had something of a holiday. On that day the leader of the Revisionists gave his lecture "Jews, Arabs, England — and Where Is the Way Out". On the same day the Sosnowiec Betar also unveiled its flag. In this honour a memorial service for the martyrs fallen in Palestine was to have been held in the town synagogue. Because of Hanukkah the memorial was not held; only speeches on current affairs were delivered. On the whole Betar saw to it that Jabotinsky's visit should turn out impressive. One thing they forgot entirely — order. No attention was paid to this "trifle", and as a result the impression was not what it should have been; especially at the unveiling of the flag things happened that did the Sosnowiec Betar little credit...
To the "Pałac" cinema hall, where the lecture took place, crowds streamed from the whole surrounding area, trying to get into the hall as early as possible, believing the notice on the posters that "at 8 o'clock sharp the hall will be closed". It turned out otherwise: the hall was only closed at half past nine, and only then did the lecture begin...
On the platform sat representatives of the Zionist organisations. Mr. Klarman greeted (in Hebrew) the distinguished guest, and when Mr. Klarman announced that the floor goes to Ze'ev Jabotinsky, the hall stormed with applause.
Amid tense expectation Jabotinsky began his lecture. Its main points: to blame for everything that has happened is the bad conduct of the Zionist leadership. The English — said the speaker — are neither better nor worse than all other nations; the Arabs too are not wholly bad; Eretz Israel has every quality to be a flourishing land for Jews; the Jewish people gave money and will go on giving, but the Zionist leadership led badly: instead of reacting to the antisemitic tendencies, instead of speaking openly, sounding the alarm — the Jewish people was constantly given soothing promises, and because of that the Jewish people was misled.
The present situation is truly a hard one, but not a hopeless one. Our situation is sick — it must be healed; and if those doctors healed badly, one must take better doctors. We had bad architects — we must take better architects; the leadership must be taken over by others who have new strength and greater intelligence.
What should the Jewish people do in the meantime? The people must not despair, but keep working, believe more firmly in the Zionist ideal, which is a just and a realisable one. Zagłębie Jewry, however, must make a reckoning of conscience so that to the coming Congress such people are elected as will be capable of realising the ideal.
The lecture, which lasted about 2 hours, was delivered in masterly form and style. After the singing of "Hatikvah" the lecture ended, and invited guests, especially the Betarites(?), went to the "Angielski hall", where the unveiling of their flag took place.
The unveiling too took place nearly 2 hours later than the programme. The premises are full of youngsters and there is a commotion as before a bedeken [veiling of the bride]...
At half past midnight it is finally announced that Jabotinsky is arriving; there is a stir, the Betar members form a guard of honour, Jabotinsky walks past and takes(?) the report from the Betar commanders.
The commander, Mr. Glajdman, opens the ceremony, and after greetings by Messrs. Klarman, the kehilla president Wajnryb, L. Jungster(?) and others, the splendid flag is unveiled by Jabotinsky, who gives a short speech to the youth, calling them to the heroism of holiness and not to the heroism of the profane.
Later a "banquet" took place. Jabotinsky left right after the unveiling for his hotel, [—]
Social Narrow-Mindedness

(What is happening with the Sosnowiec old-age home? — The reason why it is not being completed.)
The town of Sosnowiec has been granted the privilege of erecting an old-age home, and it goes without saying that this deed deserves to be welcomed: after all, nowadays it is not so easy to carry out larger undertakings, let alone public ones, for which we still have, to this very day, so little understanding, so little interest and awareness. And precisely because we have so little interest in the community, it must be welcomed all the more[?] whenever something is created, something achieved.
But the truth must nevertheless be told: the town as such gave the institution practically no help. It is just as well that a handful of wealthy Jews were found who devoted themselves body and soul to this institution, and it came into being, and we see the realization of the ideal these people set themselves.
And yet, although the institution stands and we see the splendid building before us, it still cannot be used in daily life. Still the gates cannot be opened to the helpless old people who have no home and so badly need a place of rest where they can live out their old age in peace.
Does anyone here give themselves an account [—][?] of how much Jewish Sosnowiec needs this institution? Does anyone understand the benefit and the consequences and the great thing the town does[?] by realizing this beautiful and useful building?
As far as we can see, as far as we can grasp, nobody stops to think[?] that the institution should be put to use as quickly as possible for the benefit of those waiting for it. We made inquiries and asked in the authoritative circles the reason for the delay, since the building is already finished, and we received an answer — a ridiculous one, truly, a petty one, perhaps not worth talking about, but it characterizes the coldness, the indifference and the apathetic attitude towards the community, however urgent and necessary it may be.
The answer we were given was that "we still need 15 thousand — say, fifteen thousand zł. — and the building will be completely finished." And it is interesting that because of these 15 thousand zł. things are stuck, going neither here nor there. So the question arises: is this sum not a ridiculous one when it has to be obtained from the local Jewish public? Does it not look comical when one has to intervene with a newspaper to agitate for the sum to be collected? Is it really so hard for the Sosnowiec Jews to manage those 15 thousand zł.?
After all, it is an old rule that Sosnowiec is not petty and penny-pinching, not stingy and modest. We know that we have the broad gesture and the open hand, so that for one of ours a smaller or larger sum plays no role.
And that is indeed true, but just as no sum whatever plays a role for us in private life, the exact opposite is the case when it concerns the community. We would never have believed that Jews with large expenditures, both in family life and in their businesses, could be so petty and so narrow when it comes to supporting public institutions. One simply cannot comprehend how penny-pinching and petty their notions then look. Somehow[?] people here become remarkably helpless then, at a loss what to do. People become flustered, they don't know where to turn — so much do they tremble when it comes to giving money for public purposes. And so one asks: what is it with these people, who stint on nothing, who begrudge nothing, yet as soon as a public matter is at stake become incomprehensibly petty? What is it with these people? Where lies the cause of this defect of theirs? Can one assume anything other than that the whole public problem as such is foreign and raw to them, that they simply cannot chew it, that they haven't the slightest understanding of it, that they don't know what use it is in life and why one should bother with such "nonsense"; and so, when they are asked to take part in these problems, it seems superfluous to them, something that need not be created at all, and consequently no money should be thrown away on such matters.
That is why they remain eternally cold to such questions, which in our opinion they ought to approach with full sincerity and seriousness.
And therefore, first of all, the most important thing is to begin with "our citizens" from the ABC: they must simply be given the most elementary lesson in what public problems are, why the people needs them, for what purpose the masses need them. Of course, such a kind of training[?] is not among the easiest things, but what can one do when there is no other way? As the saying goes: if you can't get over, you must go under. We are sure that as soon as they understood the necessity of concerning themselves with the community, they would treat public problems differently; they would approach them[?] as one approaches serious questions, sacred ideals and lovable philanthropic activity.
And when people here understand, in the modern sense, how to help the community, how to concern themselves with it and take an interest in it, then they will demand that its representation consist of conscious, responsible, idealistic and clean people in whom one can have the fullest trust. And now, because it all makes no difference to anyone, because everyone is indifferent to everything and things are done however anyone pleases, that is why it looks this way, why everything is so veiled, and the end of it is that we look around us in the public sphere and see that we have nothing to be proud of and to point to: this we created for such-and-such poor people, with this we surely help such-and-such unfortunate poor, with this such-and-such was adorned and crowned.
If things were as they ought to be, as they really should be, and as they are in all cultured countries and among modern people, people would laugh at the idea of things being held up over a sum of 15 thousand zł.
An old-age home for Sosnowiec! Must one really prove in black and white how necessary a town needs a home for the old, who have nowhere to turn in their old age? Must one give lessons on how necessary it is to create, for old people who have nowhere to lay their heads, a quiet little corner where they can live out their old years in peace and joy?
It seems this is as clear as day; it seems this is as understandable and comprehensible to every average person as two times two is four. And therefore, since all that is missing is such a ridiculous sum as fifteen thousand zł., with which the gates could be opened wide to the helpless old people who need to get in, let this ridiculous sum be raised in a modest way, without drum-beating and advertisements, for that would not befit the Jewish citizens of Sosnowiec.
So make no noise, dear Jews, but collect the few gulden as quickly as possible and in a fine way, so that you will have the possibility of completely finishing the beautiful and useful building.
Dr. Papori.
The Prophet of Yasnaya Polyana

Shimon Rotenberg.
(On Tolstoy's 20th yahrzeit.)
On a frosty dawn, when everything was still covered in dense darkness and a snowstorm[?] stung the body as if with thousands of sharp needles, Tolstoy, 20 years ago, left his house at Yasnaya Polyana in order to wander among the people like a lamed-vovnik, to die there and be forgotten by all.
With the greatest suspense the whole cultured world listened to the last death-throe chords that reached it from the station of Astapovo, where the genius breathed out his wonderful and great soul.
What moved Tolstoy to become a wanderer, at a time when he possessed everything needed to be able to say of himself that he was happy? He was, after all, full of years, rich; he had a beloved and loving family, the name of a spiritual titan which resounded from one end of the world to the other. Was Yasnaya Polyana not the Mecca of[?] millions of people from all over the globe, who sought comfort and healing for their searching souls, sick with despair? Did Tolstoyism not unite the Buddhist with the Brahmin, the Christian with the Mohammedan, and all of them together with the Jew? Was Tolstoyism not the cement that possessed the magic power to bind together the most diverse groups of people? What, then, could have caused life as a whole suddenly to become so indifferent to Tolstoy that he fled even from his own "I"?
Tolstoy had glimpsed death, that elementary, naked and absolute truth which each of us carries — that one day, with mathematical certainty, the thread of our life will be torn. There appeared to him that endless black abyss which freezes the blood and brings the thinking power of the brain down to zero, and which turns the human brain into a labyrinth in which thousands of spirits dance their demons' dance and breathe into a person, with their frosty black breath, the terrible, merciless secret that he alone, death, is the final goal of all our strivings, the last sum total of our existence in the world; and that from the moment of life we pass into the eternal, endless and unknown kingdom from which no one has ever yet returned. And once someone has glimpsed this black and endless abyss, there is no longer any rescue for him. He is no longer able to see in life anything but the great, senseless "nihil", vanity of vanities raised to an infinite power. He finds himself in a situation like that of a spectator at a fakir's tricks to whom the fakir has revealed the secret of the trick, and the spectator suddenly sees the whole foolish senselessness of the sorcery game.
Though descended from generations of counts, Tolstoy had something peasant-like in his whole being, and he was drawn to the peasants, to their primitive, healthy and normal life. He hated pseudo-civilization, which was coated with a thin skin of glossy lacquer, beneath which hid degenerate, internally crumbling Europe with despotic tsardom at its head.
The better Russian intelligentsia, after the unhappy revolutionary attempts, fell into complete apathy. Some emigrated, some were exiled to Siberia, and those who remained in Russia spat on life with the genuinely Russian, broad "naplevat'" ["to hell with it"], making their philosophy of life the motto: — life is so short and there is so much vodka, so one must have a drink — and indeed they drank, and meanwhile let the gigantic colossus, the great Russian mass, sink into want and darkness.
One single man came down to the masses, and with all the strength of his great spirit he called for brotherhood and for the eradication of evil. That was the prophet of Yasnaya Polyana, the count-peasant, Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy.
Tolstoy sees the whole meaning of human life in love of one's neighbour. He is an altruist and holds that egoism cannot bring a person any true happiness; that the light of life must be darkened as soon as the black terror of death appears; that only great love for one's fellow men can save us from that terror and make us forget our own bitter end.
Tolstoy's love of one's neighbour is not Christian love, which has its origin in the Jewish "ve-ahavta" [and thou shalt love], and which over 2 thousand years was shamefully falsified, to the point that in its name millions of innocent human lives were tortured and burned on the pyres. Tolstoy's "ve-ahavta" is no bargain with God, nor a despotic command such as, for example, Kant's "categorical imperative", but a natural striving of the human soul towards the springs of joy. Tolstoy's love knows no conditions whatever; it is the boundless, compassionate love for man, whatever he may have done, however he may have sinned.
Tolstoy, the great artist, does not think much of art and science, for what meaning do they have if they are not able to make man better? Art is perhaps a source of aesthetic pleasures; it can perhaps elevate man, refine his spirit, but it does not have within it the revolutionary power to compel man to become better. Works of art have never yet led to upheavals[?].
Science does not prove it either. It perhaps helps create "homo sapiens"; man perhaps becomes cleverer, but by no means better — on the contrary, man becomes steadily worse, and the Latin saying "homo homini lupus" is not a mere phrase: one to another is truly a wolf. Man exploits science not in order to improve and prolong life, but on the contrary, the various scientific achievements are created a priori for purposes of war, for the eternal, bloodthirsty Cains who are always ready to murder the weaker Abels.
In the last century the world has not known another person who stood up so for humanity, with such religious depth and strength, as Tolstoy did. He therefore belongs without doubt among the ideal, great thinkers who will forever remain the lighthouses in the sea of human baseless hatred; and when someone seeks rescue for his spirit, tormented by despair, he will be able to find it by raising his eyes to the source of light, to the emanation of joy given off by the three magic words: Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy.
