Spreading Diseases

(What are our magistrates doing about it, and what could they have done?)
Influenza — a disease of this kind, a modern, present-day one: wherever you go and wherever you stand there is only influenza and influenza, heaven and earth and influenza; and the disease is in fact such that it torments a person, breaks the bones, makes one shiver with heat and cold — God preserve and protect us. At first people laughed at it, and the gang of humorists got a theme for their feuilletons; later practice showed us that one must treat it a little more seriously and attentively. First of all, every house is being infected, and it has reached the point where we already see shops closed because husband and wife have taken to bed sick.
Besides that, the doctors and the pharmacies cannot cope. As for getting a doctor — if at times it is hard to reach them, nowadays one has to wait for them not hours but days, and at the pharmacies you are told to come the next day for the prescriptions. And perhaps that is no wonder either, since they had not prepared for this panic.
Well, the well-to-do citizen manages somehow, both with a doctor and with getting the prescription filled; but what is the poor man to do, to whom a doctor does not come so quickly because he is not sure whether he will get paid[?] there — how is he to heal himself, and in what way can he get the prescription filled, once he has finally obtained it after great trouble and effort? Who takes an interest in the suffering citizens without means?
We see, after all, that the illness has caused quite serious consequences in Zagłębie, so that it comes to complications and even to cases of death. In such a situation one must reckon with the serious consequences and try to contain the already sufficiently poisoned air and to stop the disease, which penetrates ever deeper into the broad strata of the various popular masses, and in this way the disease becomes ever more serious, more dangerous and more frightening, both for the citizens and for the country.
One should therefore have paused in this matter and reflected on the abnormal phenomenon, which so aggravates the already difficult situation of the masses. The "Opieka Społeczna" [public welfare] occupies quite a broad place among us — so why does it not come to the aid of the suffering poor citizens in this case? Why is it not made easier for them to get doctors and medicines quickly and cheaply? What are those without means to do, who cannot be members of the sick funds? How are they to save themselves from the contagious disease? How are they to save their children, so that the disease does not seize them too?
One sees that the situation and circumstances of the modern disease are taking on quite serious forms, and thanks to the neglect and to not getting doctors and medicines easily and quickly, complications arise which even end in cases of death.
And what about the pharmacies on duty on holidays and Sundays? Why should the number of pharmacies not be increased in a time of epidemic disease? That is a self-evident thing for everyone, so that long queues do not stretch everywhere.
In general, very little attention is paid here to events that bring so much disruption into our economic ranks and make our living conditions abnormal. In other countries such a phenomenon would be treated with far more attention, and they would think first of all how to cure the disease and then how to eliminate and drive it out. We here, unfortunately, pay no heed to all this, as though nothing at all were happening. It seems to be a question for individuals — whoever it catches must save himself. Must one not realize that the question is a public one and must be solved in a public sense? Must such a matter not be rescued like a fire? Is it not so terrible, so frightening? Do diseases not make a ruin of both the citizens and the country? May one remain indifferent and tolerate such an unfortunate phenomenon?
Had the proper precautions been taken from the very beginning, the disease would not have managed to spread so quickly from one town to another and from one district to another.
What more is needed — how many times have we already drawn the attention of the Zagłębie local governments to the necessity of setting up an emergency aid service for the population of Zagłębie. We have dealt with the question several times in the columns of our pages, illuminated it from all sides and came to the conclusion that we must have an emergency service in Zagłębie — and yet nothing went further, and everything remained as it was, as though it were a superfluous thing not worth talking about and not deserving any attention.
Of course, in great and rich Zagłębie one ought not to have remained indifferent to so serious a question, and yet it is not so; no one has even tried to take an interest in it, so that to this very day, when an accident happens in town where quick help is needed, there is no one to give it, and not a few people have already departed this world because of it.
Now, when influenza is raging in such a form that it passes over almost no house, some kind of "pogotowie" [emergency service] would also have been necessary, [whi]ch would come to the aid of the broad strata of the population. At a moment when it is impossible to get a doctor and a remedy. Unfortunately, nothing is being done now either, as though nothing were happening and no one were harmed — and that is why the disease is making progress.
At such a moment, at such a time, one should have thought of something and come to the aid of the population, both with doctors and remedies and by having something done to prevent the diseases in general. One must not remain indifferent to an event that has taken on such a mass character, sparing neither young nor old, rich nor poor.
A duty rests upon our magistrates to see to it, by whatever means, that the diseases do not rage unhindered in every corner — the magistrates are, after all, the masters of the house and the actual leaders of the inhabitants. Thus a sacred obligation lies upon them to concern themselves with everything that harms their inhabitants, let alone when it is a matter of not allowing diseases to spread and of making it possible to help those who need help.
R. Let.
I Sit by the Hanukkah Lamp

By Leonidas.
I sit beside the fifth small candle
and I write my little poem —
(that is, I write by the light of the "shammes",
since it is forbidden to make use [of the Hanukkah lights]).
I sit, as usual, by the "shammes"
and I see, really and truly,
how history is borne before my gaze —
backwards.
Like an arrow flying from the bow,
there race swiftly before my eyes
peoples, lands, times, generations,
ways[?], systems, faiths, teachings.
Like shadows on a white sheet
they fly — on [...][?],
until they bring me home
to the time of "in those days".
There they set me down
and vanish down the mountain,
and I remain behind alone
with a free, clear gaze.
Evolutions, theories,
whole volumes of histories,
all — vanished like smoke.
Lonely I stand on the height.
And I look quietly around:
heroes' graves, still and mute.
But above their places
a spirit hovers and speaks without words:
I am the spirit of Moses' Torah,
I am the light of the Menorah,
I am the fire that burns
when one touches [me] with impure[?] hands.
I am the source of all knowledge,
I am reason and conscience,
I am the spark that kindled
torches in the hours of night.
Since I was lit upon a mountain
I burn strongly.
Both the pious and the freethinker
come to me and borrow fire.
One needs me — to warm himself,
and another — to make a noise[?].
For one I serve as a torch,
and for the other — as a spectacle.
I have friends and I have foes,
I have Maccabees and Greeks.
Eternal, just like me,
is the struggle over my radiance.
And as long as the world has Jews
the war of light will seethe,
for tremendous stubborn ones
are the guardians of my fire.
And the struggle will not cease
until the world grows bright,
before[?] — an eternal night
will come[?] to end the battle.
I sit beside the fifth small candle
and I write my little poem,
and in my head there sway
times, generations — up and down.
Now up, now down —
and the little candles burn merrily.
Now in black, now in red —
yet still the wicks burn on!
I look at the little candles
with their lovely little faces,
how they flash, how they gleam —
how they sway, how they flicker...
I look — but[?] I do not feel heavy[?]:
children's tears! Not dangerous.
God is not so bad at all:
after weeping comes laughter!
Napoleon's Last Years of His Life

By M. Asherovitch.
The wish to have a child would not let Napoleon rest for a long time. Years went by, and he still could not know whether he was really punished by nature with the inability to become the father of a child, or she[?]. From his life with Josephine this could not become clear to him. He had reason to think that he was to blame for it, since she had, after all, had two children before she married him. And he also had reason to think that she was to blame, since it might be that in her frivolity she had gone so far that she had already lost the ability to become a mother of a child again...
In his love for women he sought not only pleasure but also a purpose. He wanted the woman he was close to — be it a wife or a mistress — to bring him an heir into the world — a son. And that is precisely why his joy was so great years later, when he was given the news that a mistress of his had borne him a son.
That was when he was in Poland with his army, a few years after he had already become the crowned Emperor of France; a sizeable part of Europe was already in his hands then, and in his mind, which never rested, new plans had already been sketched for how to recut the map of the world and draw new lines for countries and peoples — and just then, when he sat writing a love letter to Josephine, a special messenger brought him great news:
The beautiful girl whom his sister Caroline had introduced to him, and with whom he had lived for a short time before he left France with his armies, had borne him a son.
This aroused such joy in Napoleon that he entirely forgot the many great plans being woven in his mind, and, giving a leap like a boy, he seized General Duroc by both shoulders and, shaking him with all his might, cried with great enthusiasm:
"Duroc, do you hear? She has had a boy! Had a boy by me!"
In the course of the years he lived with Josephine he had learned to be what one might call a good husband to his wife and an even better lover to other women... As long as she was still young and having a fine time with others, whose heads she turned so skilfully, he burned with jealousy and with love; but later, when she began striding ever closer to her forties, when she could no longer arouse[?] the curiosity of young men, when admirers no longer swarmed around her, his love for her also cooled and he began conducting love affairs right and left.
His sisters helped him a great deal in this. They did not like Josephine at all, and she had no other name among any of them than "the old lady". Caroline hated her most of all. She knew of all the love affairs Josephine had conducted when Napoleon was not at home; this had caused her much unpleasantness, and so she later settled accounts with Josephine: wherever she had a pretty friend, she brought her together with Napoleon, and he made her his mistress...
In love he began to go an entirely different way: he no longer sought only the one woman, but women in general, and since he was a great lover of theatrical art, the actresses played a great part in his life. Each time he carried on an affair with another beautiful actress: with this one he lived for a month, with that one he was bound for a week, and with yet another the love lasted no more than a day and a night, and after that she no longer concerned him...
All sorts of women alternated with him then — younger than he and older than he. With one — Mademoiselle Georgina was her name — he used to play "cat and mouse" from time to time, just as with a child; he liked to hold her on his knees and hear the various stories she told him about her life. Besides love and passion he also had a feeling for her as for a child who must be protected.
At about the same time he also carried on an affair with the beautiful blond Mademoiselle Duchâtel, who was his wife's lady-in-waiting. With her he would sometimes play cards until late at night, and meanwhile quietly[?] whisper in her ear, and she already knew that this meant she should wait for him...
And he always kept his word. On tiptoe, so that Josephine would not hear, he would steal quietly into the blond Mademoiselle Duchâtel's room and stay there an hour or two. But Josephine knew where he disappeared to, and she followed him every time; she was afraid to go inside and make a scene, so she would stand at the door and peep through the keyhole. He knew this, and would angrily fling open the door and shout at her that if she did not go away he would give her a divorce tomorrow...

Hanukkah.

[Hanukkah feuilleton — childhood memories]
"Kindle, kindle, little candles, / and light up my black walls[?], / you alone, you only, / can tell me, can recount, / and we'll speak from the heart..." (M. Bar-Kohen).
Tell me, do you not remember now, as you stand before your Hanukkah lamp, the Hanukkah of long, long ago? Tell me, how often[?] does it happen that a longing[?] kindles in you to live once more a Hanukkah evening of the not-distant past that lives on in memory — when nature was so hard, so wild and yet so beautiful, so genuine?...
You recall a Hanukkah evening during a fiery, breath-taking frost or a great dusty snowstorm...
Hanukkah of old..
It always came on time, always full of mood, always its own self...
Already several weeks before, when the snow began to fall and fall, as though strewn by an invisible hand over the earth, over houses and trees, until it grew into a thick white featherbed; or when snow-mountains piled up[?], sculpted[?] by the wind, sparkling at night in the moonlight with crystal brilliance — then one felt the arrival of Hanukkah...
Then it came.
Everyone's anticipation was wonderful: it seemed as if we were awaiting a quiet, distinguished guest. A great aristocrat whom each wants to receive ever more beautifully, more splendidly and more warmly — everyone awaited him, the children, with all the Jews of the shtetl; each prepared with something different:
Mother — with rendered fat, with "ganzn"[?] latkes; Father — with a pack of cards. Father, an ardent kehilla man, something of an Orthodox, whose life ran so calmly, so orderly, became another man on Hanukkah. All year no card was allowed into the house; he did not hold with it, since it is not a Jewish thing — but Hanukkah, that is something else. It was an old custom of his to play "oke" [twenty-one] on Hanukkah. Then he allowed himself and played with his father-in-law. But he never forgot to take off from every "pot" a share for the "Talmud Torah", which he cared for so much and supported by every means. The "stakes" had to be considerable, and so the game was lively, burning.
And Hanukkah?... Meanwhile it crept up quietly, like a breath, like a song.
Right after Minhah the wind stopped; the frost began to take everything under its power; the further it went, the harder it bit[?] and burned with its cold fire... Wherever you looked, everywhere you saw its power, but that power was already in harmony with the "mood-filled Hanukkah"...
Up onto the window[?] was brought everything needed to light the candles. Soon Father drew us children to him and showed us how to bless the Hanukkah candles. The candles burned and their bright glow poured over the whole room. Later Grandfather came, and we children hung about him:
— Grandpa, give Hanukkah gelt.
— Yes, yes, children, you'll get it; but do you know what Hanukkah is?
— Of course we know.
Then Grandfather stroked us, sat down with us and began telling us all the beautiful stories and miracles and the heroic deeds of the Hasmoneans.
Ah, how warmly everyone's hearts beat then.
Yes, yes — frost reigned in nature. But in the human heart there swayed a sea of light, a sea of gentleness.
The Hanukkah candles burned, smiled[?], flickered and went out again, pouring forth joy, homeliness and memories, lived-through and not lived-through.
Today there are no longer those burning frosts at Hanukkah. Nature has become softer, milder; only the human heart has changed: it has taken over the hardness of the old winter Hanukkah-time.
G. Perlzon.
Who Bears the Kehilla Burden?

[Polemical article — the Będzin kehilla and Agudah]
Several years have passed since the Polish state favored the Jewish population of Poland with a democratic Jewish kehilla. Naturally, as soon as today's kehillot came into being, no one — apart from the Agudah — was satisfied with the form they took, simply because the kehillot were created mainly to deal with religious and klei-kodesh [religious functionaries'] matters. And as soon as anyone once made an attempt[?] to take up a Jewish matter that was not klei-kodesh — such as schools, subsidies for cultural institutions, Eretz-Israel questions — it was promptly struck out, and it became clear that the dissatisfaction with the kehilla "gift" is justified, because the nationally minded Jew wants to see the kehilla as the institution that deals with the whole of Jewish life — creating something positive in the Jewish street — for Jewish culture, and not merely a little kloyz that deals with ritual slaughterers, mikvehs, etc.
Several years have already passed since today's "modern[?] democratic" kehillot were born, and unfortunately we see that the kehilla is the same old "dead shtibl", nothing else; the only difference is that the old dead shtiblekh had just 2–3 balebatim, while today's has in all 31 "opinion-givers".
If we want to convince ourselves of all this, it suffices to take as an example the kehilla in Będzin, and the whole sad picture of kehilla life will stand plainly before our eyes.
Throughout its "life" our kehilla truly has nothing positive to credit to its account. There were several capable and welcome members in the gmina, people whose work could have been useful, but they had no possibility of working because of the obstruction methods of the Agudah people and their hangers-on.
Dr. Weinzieher, Director Fürstenberg or Mr. Winiadzki[?] wanted to work in the gmina — work that would consist not only of klei-kodesh matters but the work Jewish life demands, work embracing all the concerns of the Jewish population; but they realized that the Agudah clique would not allow such work — on the contrary, everything was done to obstruct them — so they slammed the kehilla door and left.
Other people remained who run the work to this day; the term of office has ended, but there is plenty of sitting and standing — "work" goes on. —
And what does the work there look like now? —
Suffice it to point out that when the writer of these lines re-entered[?] the administration 2–3 months ago, the situation there was catastrophic. A large part of the duty-members [dyżury] had long since forgotten that they were on duty and for a long time did not come even to a single meeting. Consequently 1 or 2 persons ran kehilla life in Będzin — and one can say that the kehilla is a sheer ruin: 8–10 months[?] of pensions unpaid, living off the few złotys a collector brought in or when a wealthy man died. The situation today is not much better — only let it be said that as soon as several members showed good will to do something and drag the kehilla out of its plight, the "Torah-loyal" at once appeared and began to be "active": their activity, of course, consists of "dealings", tripping people up, and above all creating new expenses such as slaughterers, secretaries for the rabbinate and the like; and amid this famous activity, under these "fine"[?] working conditions, the Agudah people have got a brand-new joy:
— they have lived to take revenge on the Zionists and the "sinners" (poshim).
The state has given the Agudah people a sweet: "those who can openly [act] against religion may neither vote nor be elected in the kehillot"; and although the matter is still pending[?], the Agudah people are already dancing in the air that they will now settle comfortably in the kehilla shtibl.
But they, the Agudah people, have forgotten that with this "candy" they will, on top of everything, shatter Jewish kehilla life.
Will national Jewry in Poland calmly watch as it is robbed of its Jewish civic rights? Will these "sinners", the beardless citizens, be the money-givers for the privileged "bearded citizens"?
And do the Agudah people not know that the klei-kodesh get their salaries only thanks to the "sinners", who are for the most part the money-givers? Does one not know, for instance here in Będzin, who the big city taxpayers are? Are they perhaps the fine bearded Jews? Has a fine bearded Jew ever given such a large donation for the mikveh as was given precisely by a Zionist, a "sinner"? And the orphanage in Będzin — who has been building it until now? Are not 95 percent of the donors precisely "sinners"?
And who in general the money-givers in Będzin are — in the next article.
A. Liwer.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion: Parshat Miketz

[Column — Torah sayings and anecdotes for Miketz and Hanukkah]
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
a) "Can we find such a man, in whom is the spirit of God?" (Gen. 41:38)
Joseph, as is known, dressed modern and elegant, adorned and decked himself out, "curling his hair and touching up his eyes to look handsome". Pharaoh wondered at this: "can we find such" — is there really such an elegantly dressed man, who knows many languages, in whom "is the spirit of God" — that he should be godly? Pharaoh marveled that one can look elegant and modern, be educated, and still be godly. (Rabbi Bunem of Przysucha)
The Chortkov Rebbe once spoke about dress — that one is compelled[?] to dress in a worldly way — and expressed himself thus: "God tests the Jews each time with something different: once with this kind of dress and once with that kind, but the pintele yid [the Jewish spark] always remains." (Divrei David)
b) "And the famine was over all the face of the earth" (41:56)
"The face of the earth" means the rich, for with them the hunger began. Why are the rich called "the face of the earth"? Because he who is well off shows everyone his smiling face, while the poor man hides his face — he has no face... (Bereshit Rabbah 91:5)
c) "Why do you look at one another" (42:1)
Jacob said to his sons: "Why do you show yourselves?" — do not display yourselves before Esau when you are sated, lest they envy you... (Tractate Ta'anit 10)
d) "When he besought us, and we would not hear" (42:21)
"When he besought us" — where is it mentioned anywhere in the verse that Joseph pleaded with his brothers? Where?
— One who is dragged[?] off to be flogged still has strength and courage to scream; but one condemned to death stays motionless[?], without a sign of life; he is dazed, and if he weeps it is a dazed, confused, incomprehensible weeping.
"When he besought us" — he wept before us so quietly, so incomprehensibly, that "we would not hear" — it could not be heard... (Ohel Yitzhak, R. [?] of Amshinov)
e) "And Benjamin's portion was greater" (43:34)
The sale of Joseph came about through the brothers' envy of Joseph. Now Joseph wanted to test whether they had already corrected the bad trait of foolish envy; so he gave Benjamin more, to see whether they would envy him. (Nifla'ot Hadashot)
Hanukkah.
a) Hanukkah and charity. The "Magen Avraham" (§672) records a custom that on Hanukkah young men go collecting donations. What is the sense of it? — The Hanukkah miracle, as is known, was that only one jug of oil was found and instead of one day it burned eight days. The "Beit Yosef" asks: if so, the miracle was only for seven days, since for one day [oil] had been found. The "Turei Zahav" answers: the Zohar says that a blessing does not rest upon an empty thing. How then did the miracle happen on the first day, when the jug was empty? It must be that although the jug held only enough to burn for one day, a miracle occurred in that something remained for the second day as well, on which the blessing could already rest; thus on the first day too a miracle occurred, in that something remained... There are rich men who, if one comes to them for a donation, give not a penny, but do not stint on blessings: "Trust in God, Reb Jew, He will help you, better than in people"... Therefore one comes to them on Hanukkah, when it is clear that no blessing rests when the pocket is empty, and one tells them: you bless, you give blessings — see to it that there is something in the pocket for the blessing to rest upon... (Yerah la-Mo'adim)
b) The shammashim. The beit-din beadle of Białystok was a very bad man, a thorough villain, and caused much grief to the rabbi R. Velvele (author of "Agudat Ezov"). Once, when R. Velvele was in a good mood, he said to him: you know that Jews have three shammashim: the "shammash" of the Hanukkah lamp, the "shammash" of the tzitzit and the "shammash" of the beit din. The Hanukkah-lamp shammash gets burned up, the tzitzit shammash gets wound around — only the beit-din shammash will neither be burned nor wound, so one can never get rid of him...
c) The "Kedushat Levi" on card-playing. "For our many sins a breach has opened among our brethren the Children of Israel to play cards, and the matter is light in their eyes. But they should know that every card surely has a great kelipah [impure shell] that is not fit to mention. Heaven is my witness that I do not mean merely to preach, only to make people take heed." (Kedushat Levi, Miketz)
d) Hanukkah and the Torah. Antiochus was the worst villain, who wanted to fight the Torah; all the Jews' enemies before him contended only for the Jewish land or wealth, whereas he wanted only to undermine Jewish culture. His methods of struggle against the Jewish spirit [serve] his successors to this day. He, the worst of all, invented a libel that in the Temple a Greek was sacrificed on the altar — and his successors use this libel, saying that Jews need blood for ritual purposes. He spread a lie that in the Holy of Holies there is a "donkey's head", and our opponents decry us as "the people of matter", a people sunk only in materialism, whose soul is nothing but the coin — — — (Derashot RY"N)
Hanukkah Motifs

[Satirical Hanukkah poem opening the humour supplement "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle), "appearing in honour of Hanukkah, by Ben Amotz".]

When the day's takings are no takings
and not a customer is seen,
and the paupers [?] say
"nieszczęście" [? Polish: misfortune] and weep;

and the "urząd" [tax office] assesses [?] him,
one must carry fat sums —
and if one still stays on one's feet,
one may say "Al ha-nissim" ["For the miracles"]...
* * *
When the crisis is almighty,
bills of exchange and taxes must be paid,
and six mouths want to eat —
you can well picture it.

And imagine, surely,
such a picture in your thoughts [?]:
that like little candles
we go out and flicker...
* * *
Today we marvel at the heroic deeds
of the Hasmonean heroes,
how they [beat out?] the Greeks —
wonder of wonders!

But when one gets through a day
without seeing the face of a groszy —
that too, dear Jews,
is surely no small heroic deed..
D. Fletter.
Today's Miracles

[Humorous parody of the "Al ha-nissim" ("For the miracles") prayer.] Miracles and wonders: a blessing came into a jug of oil. Well, well, some miracles!) The real miracles happen today:
When one comes home from the Będzin synagogue with whole bones — for the miracles.
When the Talmud Torah teachers did not [smash] the windowpanes at the gmina [community/municipal office] — for the miracles.
When Shlomo Yitzchak and Avremel Liver [?] sit at one table and both have whole noses — for the miracles.
When one sees the Jewish posters with their "inspired orthography" and can bear such a disgrace — for the miracles.
"Fine Jews" [notables] sit at election meetings with... and see no desecration of God's name — for the miracles.
When one gets out safely from [?] the premises of the Sosnowiec gmina, one really must say — for the miracles.
When the Będzin Revisionists could not manage to get Jabotinsky to come to Będzin — for the miracles.
When one sends for a doctor on Sunday and he comes only on Tuesday — for the miracles.
And when the tenants get out "in peace" from the new housing decree, they will have to say every day — for the miracles.

Between Merchants.
[Joke.] — Tell me, Reb Notl, what is the difference between the Hanukkah miracle and a merchant?
— I'll tell you: at Hanukkah a candle is added every day and it gets brighter, while with a merchant something is taken away every day, and things get darker for him..
Leib Stabinski.
Show Your Shoulders!

[Satire/Hanukkah humour — three short pieces in one column: "Show Your Shoulders!", "Always Hanukkah", "Once and Today".]
(A little scene from the present day)
In one house there are several patients of various "qualities", such as flu, nerves, old-age "weakness", asthma and the like. In comes the feldsher [barber-surgeon/medic], panting, barely gets a word out, and orders:
— "Show me your shoulders, your shoulders!
— What do you mean? We came for an examination.
— No time, — answers the feldsher, — show me your shoulders, yes, yes, flu, flu, flu, compresses, cupping glasses, hand over the couple of gulden, because there's no time.
Going out the door you can still hear the feldsher mutter: flu, flu, compresses, cupping glasses, aspirin...

Always Hanukkah.
For merchants it is Hanukkah all year round:
1) Their heads are "spun" [like a dreidel] all year.
2) Their shoes and clothes are full of latkes (pun: pancakes / patches).
3) When they receive a promissory note (veksl) they say "Al ha-nisim" [for the miracles].
4) After signing a promissory note they light a candle.
5) Over a "nakaz" [?] [court payment order] on a promissory note they say "Shehecheyanu".
Leyb Shtshabinski [?].

Once and Today.
Once you got latkes only at Hanukkah. Today there are latkes [patches] everywhere: in your trousers — patches, in your shoes — patches, on the seats by the eastern wall [of the synagogue] — patches, you walk into any institution whatsoever — patches, and young men who want a three-thousand-dollar dowry — nothing more than patches.

Hanukkah Latkes

[Hanukkah feuilleton in three parts: "Ha-nerot halalu", "The Jewish Dreidel", "Hannah and Her Seven Sons".]
Pini Bal-Loshn [pen name, "Pini the Wordsmith"].
1.
"Ha-nerot halalu" [These lights]...
These lights — these little candles! — Once again the candles, once more the candles! The same thing every time! Nothing new at all!
— No, no, gentlemen, nothing! And we have nothing to be ashamed of in the old candles!
One should be ashamed of darkness, but not of light.
And when we see the darkness in the great world, our own candles ought to become even dearer and more beloved to us.
"Ha-nerot halalu" — these little candles which we do see [?] twinkling here and there, "anu madlikin" — we kindle them for the world.
We are the lighters of the light from eternity until this very day.
Without us there would be even more darkness in the world.
For truly, in what does the great world now stand higher than in the past? What has the world itself ever put right without our help?
Nothing whatsoever.
The world has not yet brought forth any new prophets; the world has not yet created any new luminous ideals.
Apart from the old ones, which we gave it.
The old hatred between nation and nation is now even stronger than before.
Falsehood rules the world now more than ever.
The greatest outcasts still stand at the world's helm today — they are the power-holders and world leaders.
If, for example, Pharaoh were alive today, he would probably be a dictator in Italy.
If Haman were alive he would surely have become premier in Hungary.
If Titus and Antiochus were alive, they would surely have become the chief leaders somewhere in black, yellow and even red parties.
And our candles are still of great use to the world to this day.
The only trouble is that "we have no permission to make use of them" — we are given no right to use them!
The world does not want to use our candles itself, and it doesn't let us either!...
But be ashamed of our old candles — that we certainly need not.
Only what do we gain from our complaints, if we merely stand "by the lamp"?!
2.
The Jewish Dreidel.
Look at the Hanukkah dreidel and see in it the eternal Jew.
A true symbol of the Jewish people. Jews are, as it were, a "dreidel" in all generations and in all countries.
The world spins us and we spin around in the world.
We get dreidel-spun and we spin ourselves.
It has been so from time immemorial: when someone just wants to play a game, they grab us by our little heads and play dreidel with us.
Where is there a people that has not spun us by the head?
And where on the globe is there a country where we have not spun about?
Nowhere, nowhere! We are the only dreidel in the world; everywhere they spin us and everywhere we spin.
They promise us equal rights — at once they spin us.
They even give us a Land of Israel — again they spin us.
And from all this spinning our heads are so dizzy that we keep on spinning without pause.
We spin ourselves into all sorts of foreign interests, we rack our heads for everybody's benefit — and ourselves we forget.
We spin so long until we fall, and every time we fall on another side:
Here — we fall on the socialist side.
There — we fall on the communist side.
Somewhere else — we fall on the capitalist side.
And everywhere it is all only for others, for strangers — and when it comes to ourselves we are left with no side at all!..
Our heads spin only for others — and for ourselves we no longer have a head left!...
And looking at the dreidel every Hanukkah I think:
— When will we finally stop being a dreidel-game for the world?!
3.
"Hannah and Her Seven Sons".
There is a Jewish woman Hannah who has seven sons.
Handsome are the seven sons, no evil eye, like seven suns.
Tall, grown-up, with strong muscles, with plump, rosy cheeks — a delight to behold.
Real Jewish heroes.
Their names are: Józek, Bolek, Stefek, Janek, Adolek, Antek, Salek [?].
All ending in "-ek" — a blessing of a beloved name.
And mother Hannah devotes herself body and soul to her children: she dresses them up early in the morning, gives them the best sweets and sends them off to school.
When they come home she gives them the best dinners and sends them off to learn to play.
One plays the fiddle, the second — the clarinet, the third — the saxophone, the fourth — jazz band, the fifth — the flute, the sixth — the trumpet and the seventh — the drum.
And after this playing they go off to play again: handball, football and just plain ball.
Up comes the old grandfather, plays with the grandchildren, kisses them, strokes them and asks lovingly and faithfully:
— Beniekl [little Ben], are you learning a Yiddish/Jewish word too?
He answers him: "Nie rozumiem" [Polish: I don't understand].
The grandfather sadly lowers his head, tears fall on his grey beard, and he begins telling the children a little story:
"Once upon a time in the Land of Israel there was also a mother Hannah; she too had seven sons; they were all called by Jewish names and good Jewish children they were.
The king called all seven of them to him and ordered them to become gentiles, to forget the God of Israel, to leave the Jewish people.
He made a fire, set up soldiers with swords and told the seven Jewish children that if they did not obey he would kill and burn them all...
Do you know, children, what the seven sons answered? They answered that they would rather die than become gentiles!...
And all seven indeed died for Jewishness"...
His daughter gets angry and shouts at him:
— Why are you frightening the children, father?
— I'm frightening them?! — says the old grandfather — I'm merely telling them how Jewish children must sacrifice themselves for Jewishness, and they don't even want to know a single Yiddish word!
— Oh, don't be such a fanatic! They have so much work already — should I torment them with Yiddish too? It's a pity on them, a real pity!...
The old grandfather sighs:
— Oy-oy-oy, my daughter. That Hannah of the Land of Israel was a "cruel one", and this Hannah of Poland is a "merciful one" — woe and alas for these times!...
Strike of the Talmud Torah Teachers — Ended.

[Local.] On Saturday night a large meeting took place in the Talmud Torah premises, to which representatives of all the "shtiblekh" and minyanim(?) were delegated (except the Agudah and the Ger shtibl). The meeting dealt with the strike of the melamdim, brought about by the improper conduct of the kehilla board regarding the subsidy for the Talmud Torah.
Following the promise of councillor(?) Mr. Rygiski(?) that the subsidy for the Talmud Torah would be paid out, it was resolved to end the strike.
Shop Hours before Hanukkah.

[Local.] This coming Sunday all shops may be open from 1 p.m. until 6 in the evening.
Every day until Hanukkah the shops may stay open until 9 o'clock in the evening.
Protest Meeting against Raising the Rent.

[Local.] In its own premises the Tenants' Association held a protest meeting on Sunday against the bill to raise rents. Messrs. Lewin(?) and Fryde(?) spoke on the question. A protest resolution was adopted and sent to all the Sejm clubs.
On Help for the Poorest Children.

[Local.] At the Starostwo (district office) the organizing meeting took place to found a committee that will concern itself with supporting children of unemployed families. Besides food, the children are also to receive warm clothing.
A board was elected, headed by the Starosta, Mr. Beksa(?).
Large Sums Approved for Building Purposes

[Local news – Będzin.] This week, under the chairmanship of the temporary commissioner, a meeting of the building committee at the Magistrat (town council) took place. The meeting considered the building programme, which is to be carried out over 5 years. According to the programme, a sum of nearly 13 million zł. is needed for building purposes over 5 years. For the coming year 1 million 939 thousand zł. has been allocated for building purposes. This sum includes, on the motion of Mr. Goldsztajn, 50 thousand zł. for the Jewish 'Orphans' Home' (Yesomim-hoyz) and 75 thousand zł. to build a building for teachers.
The Little Watch Saved Him

[Local news – incident.] On Wednesday a sharp quarrel broke out in the local slaughterhouse between Shimon Hersh Szajer and Szwarcberg. It went so far that Szajer struck at Szwarcberg with a knife. The knife hit Szwarcberg's (pocket) watch, which was broken, but thanks to it Sz. was saved from a serious wound.
Policeman Shoots at a Bandit

[Regional news – Strzemieszyce.] At daybreak the policeman on duty in Strzemieszyce noticed a person carrying a hefty load. When the policeman ordered the person to stop, he only began to run faster; the policeman then fired at the suspect, who was wounded.
As it turned out, the wounded man is a well-known bandit who had carried out a theft at Garecki's drugstore warehouse in Strzemieszyce.
On the bandit were found 1,345 zł. and cosmetic goods.
Echoes of an Accident at the Local Hospital. Dr. Jarzębowski Found Not Guilty

[Local news – courts.] Two years ago the following case occurred at the local municipal hospital: the 8-year-old Katalicki, who was in the hospital for treatment, while walking in the garden fell into a sewage pit 4 metres deep.
The boy suffered a serious head wound from the fall and one of his eyes was damaged.
The police drew up a report, and the matter later came before the local court, which sentenced Dr. Jarzębowski, as chief director of the hospital, to 10 days' arrest or a fine of 155 zł.
This week the case was heard by the Sosnowiec District Court, which annulled the verdict of the first instance, on the grounds that the director of the local hospital is not Dr. Jarzębowski but Dr. Kaszybowicz [?], and above all that the accident happened not because the safety measures were not in order, but because the boy himself is temperamental and, being left unsupervised for a while, went off to dangerous places. Sz.
—o—
Tragic Death of an Alcoholic.
On the road to Małobądz a certain Pucek, a worker at the Będzin Magistrat, was found dead. It turned out that Pucek had got drunk on vodka, then threw off his clothes and lay down to sleep in the field...
A Bandit Attack in Strzemieszyce. The Attackers Arrested.

[Local.] On Szosowa(?) Street in Strzemieszyce three bandits attacked several workers who were coming from the "Hiplage"(?) [apparently a workplace; reading doubtful]. Threatening them with knives, the bandits robbed the workers of everything they had on them; even their clothes were taken from them.
The police promptly carried out a round-up (obława) and arrested the attackers.
"Hitachdut" and the Zionist Congress.

[Local.] In connection with the forthcoming 17th Congress, the Zionist labour party "Hitachdut" in Zagłębie has actively joined the shekel campaign, for which all party members have been mobilised.
On Tuesday a consultation about the Congress took place in Będzin with the participation of all the surrounding "Hitachdut" branches. The chairman of the Będzin "Hitachdut", Dr. Rechtman, reported that at the conference of the party council the wish was expressed to go to the Congress independently, without uniting with the Right Poale Zion, because of their conduct during the last Sejm elections.
Today and tomorrow comrade Dr. Rechtman will give reports in Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec on the last session of the "Hitachdut" party council.
An Income of 400 Złoty.

[Local.] This winter the "Malbish Arumim" (Clothing the Naked) society did not confine itself to the clothing campaign, but(?) gave out garments beyond the set quota. Because of this the society, to cover(?) the deficit, arranged a theatre performance, which was a success.
The net income was 400 zł.
From "Tarbut".
For several weeks now the "Tarbut" society has introduced systematic Tanakh (Bible) courses, conducted by comrade Bergsztajn. The courses, held on Friday evenings, are very well attended because they are free of any charge.
Suicide of a Schoolgirl.
The 16-year-old schoolgirl Pierczalk(?) was to have been removed from school; because of this she threw herself under a train, which crushed her.
Again 330 Workers Laid Off.
In the mechanical factories in Poręba another 330 workers have been laid off.
Sosnowiec. Meeting of the Chamber of Commerce.

[Local — Sosnowiec.] On Monday the communications committee of the Chamber of Commerce held a meeting at which the question of improving postal, telegraph and telephone communications was discussed.
After the report by Mr. Gadomski a discussion developed in which Messrs. Rojbiglicht(?), Dr. Patak(?) and Kukarski took part.
The committee resolved to approach the proper authorities so that parcels arriving in Sosnowiec be delivered to the addressees' homes, that the post-office building be built as quickly as possible, that a post-office branch be opened in Pogoń, and that the office hours for registered letters at the Będzin post office be extended.
The proposal to intervene with the Kielce voivode for the improvement of the Olkusz–Sosnowiec highway was also supported.
Intervention by the Artisans' Supreme Council.

[Local — Sosnowiec.] Some time ago many Jewish craftsmen paid for diplomas (craft certificates) at the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce. To this day the Chamber of Crafts has not sent any commission to qualify the craftsmen who run independent workshops.
Because the police fine craftsmen who do not possess diplomas, the Supreme Council of the artisans' associations in Zagłębie submitted a memorandum to the starosta requesting that craftsmen who have paid for diplomas not be fined for the time being.
The starosta promised to settle the matter favourably.
Sensational 'favour' (protection) trial. G., a starostwo official, sentenced to one year in prison.

On Monday and Tuesday the [—] district court heard the trial of Górnicki, a former official (referent) in the Olkusz starostwo, a referent of the P.K.U. [district recruitment command] in Miechów(?), and of the owner and an employee of the firm 'Vesten'(?) in Olkusz, who were accused of helping to free a certain employee, Misel(?), from military service.
The defendants were defended by the well-known advocates Magilicki(?) and Glenbocki(?) of Warsaw and the Sosnowiec advocates Krzemuski(?), König and Pawełek(?).
The court delivered its verdict: Górnicki was sentenced to one year in prison. The others were acquitted.
On extending the deadline for buying trade patents (licences).

As is known, the deadline for buying trade patents is the 31st of this month. On 2 January (styczeń) inspections (lustrations) are already to take place.
In this connection the merchants' associations have turned to the Finance Ministry with a request that, because of the severe crisis, the deadline for buying patents be extended to 15 January, and that no patent inspections take place until then.
Whether the request will be granted is not yet known.
Several schools closed because of the influenza epidemic.

With the participation of the local school authorities, representatives of the Kraków [school] curatorium and doctors, a conference was held because 25 percent of the pupils, boys and girls, are sick with influenza.
It was decided to close the boys' gymnasium named after Staszic ('a. n. Staszic'), the technical railway school, the teachers' seminary and several public (elementary) schools.
Intervention by Sejm deputies concerning the unemployed in Zagłębie.

The [several?] deputies from Zagłębie, headed by the Zawiercie commissioner, presented themselves to the Minister of Labour, to whom they described the grave situation of the unemployed in Zagłębie.
The minister promised to fulfil all the demands (postulates) put forward by the delegation.
Instead of strolling in the mountains, he took up smuggling goods.

The local police arrested Mr Fürst of Cieszyn at the 'Hotel Warszawski'. F. had received from the Tourist Society a permit to walk in the mountains lying on the Czech-Polish border. Mr F., however, used the permit to bring in foreign goods illegally. Together with large quantities of goods, Mr F. was handed over to the customs office.

Took away 'the horse and(?) the whip'.
Piter Radek came here with a cart of coal. Having sold part of the coal, Radek went into a shop on Modrzejowska(?) street to buy goods. Coming out, he found nothing at all — neither the wagon nor the horses. After searching a whole day he finally found his 'outfit' in a side alley, but the cart was empty and instead of his horses he found an old nag (szkapa).
The police began a search and discovered the thief, a resident of Zagórze, who was arrested.

A 'test' of the firemen.
The local town commissioner, Mr Kuszniak(?), organised a fire alarm in order to check the speed of the local firemen. The firemen arrived within 4 minutes.

Terrible accident at the tunnel construction.
During work at the tunnel a board(?) collapsed and 3 workers fell into a pit and were seriously injured.

Short-term loans from the 'Joint'.
The 'Gemilut Hasadim' (free-loan) funds in Sosnowiec and Będzin received loans of up to 4000 zł from the 'Joint'. The funds must repay the sums within 4 months.

Number of doctors increased.
Because of the prevailing illnesses, the sickness fund (Kasa Chorych) has engaged at its disposal almost all the doctors in Zagłębie. In addition, a number of doctors from the nearest towns outside Zagłębie have been engaged.

An old lecher punished.
The 64-year-old Feliks Kuc stood before the district court; he had seduced young girls and [?] them. The lecher was sentenced to one year in prison and loss of all rights.
The trial was held behind closed doors.
